The American Lung Association grades Fulton County poorly for ozone days. Particulate levels are moderate and have improved over the last decade. Winter air is substantially cleaner than mid-summer.

minneapolis.climate: Minneapolis has the most severe winter of any major American city and the score is an honest average of two extremes. January runs -6°C to -15°C with regular stretches below -20°C, and snow cover lasts from December into March. Summers are warm and humid at 27-30°C. Spring and autumn are short. Daily life is organised around the cold for four months.
minneapolis.cost: Minneapolis costs roughly $2,000-2,600 a month, which is moderate for the United States and still high internationally. A one-bedroom in Uptown or the North Loop runs $1,200-1,600, cheaper than comparable coastal cities. Minnesota's state income tax is among the higher ones. Winter heating adds meaningfully to costs from November through March.
minneapolis.wifi: Connectivity is excellent. Fibre from CenturyLink and US Internet reaches much of the city, with US Internet running gigabit and 10-gigabit service across large parts of south Minneapolis. Coworking in the North Loop runs business fibre. 5G coverage is thorough. Cold has no practical effect on service reliability.
minneapolis.nightlife: The scene is better than the city's size suggests, with a live-music history running from Prince onward and venues like First Avenue still central to it. The North Loop and Uptown carry the bar density, and the local brewery scene is one of the strongest per head in the country. Winter suppresses the street-level energy for months at a time.
minneapolis.nature: This is Minneapolis's strongest card and the mid score understates it. The Chain of Lakes sits inside the city with a connected system of trails, the Mississippi runs through the middle with Minnehaha Falls at its edge, and the Grand Rounds is 50 miles of linked parkway. The city consistently ranks first or second in the United States for park systems.
minneapolis.safety: Safety varies by neighbourhood, with Southwest Minneapolis, the North Loop and areas around the lakes comfortable and parts of the North Side carrying higher violent crime rates. Downtown has had well-publicised problems late at night. The winter hazard is more mundane and more likely to affect you: ice, cold exposure and difficult driving conditions.
minneapolis.food: The food scene punches above the metro's size. The Nordic and Scandinavian heritage shows in bakeries and modern restaurants, and the Twin Cities hold the largest Somali and Hmong populations in the United States, which gives the city East African and Southeast Asian food you will not find at this quality elsewhere in the country. Prices are moderate.
minneapolis.community: There is a solid remote-work and startup population around the North Loop, supported by a strong local corporate base. It is not a nomad destination, and very few people pass through on short stays, which the mid score captures. Coworking spaces host regular events and the professional networks are welcoming, but the company you find will be residents.
minneapolis.english: English is the working language everywhere and no daily interaction requires anything else. Somali, Hmong and Spanish are widely spoken in specific communities and visible in signage in some neighbourhoods. Every service, from banking to healthcare to housing, operates in English by default with no barrier for an arriving nomad.
minneapolis.visa: The constraint is the United States immigration system rather than the city. Visa Waiver nationals enter on an ESTA for up to 90 days at $21. Others require a B-1/B-2 visitor visa, with consular waits that can run months. There is no American digital nomad visa, and remote work on a visitor admission falls outside that status.
minneapolis.culture: Minneapolis supports cultural institutions well beyond its size. The Walker Art Center is a major contemporary museum, the Minneapolis Institute of Art is free and substantial, and the Guthrie Theater anchors a theatre scene second only to New York by seats per head. The music history is real and still active. Public funding for the arts here is unusually strong.
minneapolis.cleanliness: The city presents well. Street maintenance is good, the park system is carefully kept, and the compact core means less sprawl-edge neglect than in larger American metros. Winter is the complication: months of road salt, grit and snowbanks leave a grey residue that only clears in April. Spring thaw is the least attractive few weeks.
minneapolis.airquality: Air quality is generally good and among the better records for a large American city. The main degradations are seasonal and increasingly from outside: Canadian wildfire smoke has produced multi-day episodes of unhealthy air each summer since 2021. Winter inversions occasionally trap particulates. Away from those events, readings sit comfortably in the good range.

tampa.climate: Tampa has a humid subtropical climate with a long hot season: highs of 32-34°C from May through September with humidity that rarely lets up, and almost daily afternoon thunderstorms in summer. Winters are the reward, at 15-25°C and dry. Hurricane season runs June to November and Tampa Bay's shallow shelf makes storm surge the real risk rather than wind.
tampa.cost: Tampa costs roughly $2,100-2,700 a month and has risen sharply since 2020, which the low score reflects. A one-bedroom in Hyde Park or the Channel District runs $1,500-2,000. Florida levies no state income tax, a genuine advantage for freelancers, but home and car insurance are among the most expensive in the country because of hurricane exposure.
tampa.wifi: Connectivity is strong. Spectrum and Frontier fibre deliver 300Mbps to 1Gbps across most of the metro, and Tampa's growing financial and tech sector means business-grade service is easy to find. Coworking in Ybor City and downtown runs symmetrical fibre. 5G is comprehensive. Hurricane-related outages are the one real interruption risk each year.
tampa.nightlife: Ybor City is the centre of it, a historic Cuban and Spanish quarter whose brick streets hold the densest run of bars and live venues in the region, and it is genuinely walkable. SoHo along South Howard is the other pole. Downtown and the Riverwalk have improved considerably. The scene is good without being a reason in itself to come.
tampa.nature: Water is the strength here. Tampa Bay, the Hillsborough River and the Gulf beaches at Clearwater and St Pete are all within reach, and the Riverwalk connects much of the waterfront downtown. Manatees gather at Apollo Beach in winter. Inland is flat and heavily developed, so the appeal is coastal rather than in landscape variety.
tampa.safety: Safety is neighbourhood-dependent. Hyde Park, Davis Islands, the Channel District and South Tampa are comfortable. Parts of East Tampa and Sulphur Springs carry considerably higher crime rates. Ybor City is busy and policed but has late-night incidents at closing. The seasonal risk worth planning around is the hurricane evacuation zone rather than crime.
tampa.food: Tampa's food identity is genuinely its own. The Cuban sandwich originated here and the century-old Columbia Restaurant in Ybor City is the oldest in Florida. The Cuban and Spanish heritage runs through the city's cooking, and the Gulf supplies excellent seafood. Newer independent restaurants have raised the ceiling considerably in the last decade. Prices are moderate.
tampa.community: Tampa has attracted a substantial remote-work influx since 2020, drawn by no state income tax and the weather, and the mid score understates the current trajectory. Coworking spaces downtown and in Ybor host regular meetups. The population skews toward relocating professionals rather than short-stay travellers, so the community is stable rather than transient.
tampa.english: English is the working language and Spanish is very widely spoken, reflecting Tampa's long Cuban history and a large Latin American population. Signage and services are frequently bilingual. Nothing in banking, healthcare or administration requires anything other than English. There is no language barrier for an arriving remote worker.
tampa.visa: The low score is about American entry rules rather than Tampa. Visa Waiver nationals use an ESTA for stays up to 90 days at $21. Others need a B-1/B-2 visitor visa, with consular interview waits that run to months in many countries. The United States has no digital nomad visa, and working on a visitor admission is not permitted.
tampa.culture: Ybor City is the cultural anchor, a National Historic Landmark District built by Cuban, Spanish and Italian cigar workers, and it gives Tampa a genuine historic core that most Florida cities lack. The Tampa Museum of Art and the Straz Center cover the institutional side. Beyond that the city's cultural depth is moderate, which the score reflects.
tampa.cleanliness: Presentation is good in the districts a visitor uses. Hyde Park, the Riverwalk, the Channel District and Ybor are well maintained. Older industrial areas east of downtown are noticeably less so. Summer humidity encourages mould and algae staining on buildings, and heavy rain leaves standing water on streets that drain slowly.
tampa.airquality: Air quality is generally good, helped by consistent Gulf breezes that disperse pollutants and the absence of heavy industry. Ozone rises modestly on still, hot summer days. The distinctive local issue is red tide, a coastal algal bloom that can release irritants along Gulf beaches in some years, causing respiratory discomfort near the shore rather than inland.

washingtondc.climate: Washington has a humid subtropical climate with four distinct seasons. Summers are hot and heavy at 30-32°C with humidity that the city's low-lying river setting makes worse. Winters are cold but not severe at 0-8°C, with a few snow events a year that disrupt the city disproportionately. Spring, with the cherry blossoms in late March, and autumn are both excellent.
washingtondc.cost: Washington is one of the most expensive American cities and the low score reflects it. A one-bedroom in Logan Circle or Columbia Heights runs $2,200-2,800, and a realistic monthly total lands at $3,500-4,500. The federal salary base keeps rents high. The compensation is that the Metro works, so you can genuinely live here without a car.
washingtondc.wifi: Connectivity is excellent and unusually well backed up. Verizon Fios and Comcast deliver gigabit fibre across most of the District, and the concentration of federal agencies, contractors and think tanks means business-grade redundancy is standard rather than premium. Coworking is dense downtown and around Dupont Circle. 5G coverage is complete across the city.
washingtondc.nightlife: The scene is good and skews professional. U Street and Shaw carry the live music and bar density, with the Black Cat and the 9:30 Club as long-standing institutions. Adams Morgan is the rowdier option, H Street the newer one. The Metro stops running at midnight on weeknights, which shapes an evening more than anything else does.
washingtondc.nature: Better than most American capitals. Rock Creek Park runs 1,750 acres through the middle of the city, the C&O Canal towpath follows the Potomac for 184 miles, and Great Falls is 20 minutes out. The National Mall gives two miles of open green. Shenandoah National Park is about 90 minutes west for genuine hiking.
washingtondc.safety: Safety varies by ward and the mid score is an average across that range. Northwest DC, Capitol Hill and the areas around the Mall are comfortable. Parts of Southeast carry substantially higher violent crime rates. Car break-ins and phone snatching have risen in nightlife districts. The Metro is safe and well used at commuting hours.
washingtondc.food: Washington's food has improved enormously and the immigrant communities are the reason. The Ethiopian food in Shaw and along Ninth Street is the best outside Addis Ababa, the Salvadoran pupuserías are excellent, and the Vietnamese in nearby Falls Church is serious. Half-smokes at Ben's Chili Bowl are the local institution. Fine dining is strong and priced accordingly.
washingtondc.community: Washington runs on a transient professional population: contractors, diplomats, journalists and graduate students on multi-year stays. That produces an unusually easy city for meeting people who have also just arrived, but it is not a nomad scene. Coworking spaces host policy and tech meetups. Networking is the city's native activity, for better and worse.
washingtondc.english: English is the working language and the city is straightforward to arrive into. Spanish is widely spoken, particularly in Columbia Heights and Mount Pleasant, and Amharic is common in Shaw. The international and diplomatic population means multilingual services are more available than in most American cities. Nothing in daily life requires anything but English.
washingtondc.visa: The low score is about the United States rather than the capital. Visa Waiver nationals enter on an ESTA for 90 days at $21; others need a B-1/B-2, with consular waits running months in many countries. There is no American remote-work visa. The irony of the immigration bureaucracy being headquartered here is not lost on anyone.
washingtondc.culture: This is Washington's strongest suit by some distance. The Smithsonian runs nineteen museums and the National Zoo, and admission to all of them is free, which is close to unique among world capitals. The National Gallery, the Kennedy Center and the Library of Congress are all serious institutions. The monumental core is genuinely impressive on foot.
washingtondc.cleanliness: Presentation is good in the monumental core and the Northwest quadrant, which are maintained to a federal standard. Other parts of the city are ordinary. Summer humidity and the river setting mean mould and staining on older brick. Rats are a persistent and well-documented municipal problem, particularly around restaurant districts in warm months.
washingtondc.airquality: Air quality is moderate and has improved substantially over two decades. The main issue is summer ozone, produced by regional traffic and the humid heat that sits in the Potomac basin, and the American Lung Association records a meaningful number of orange days each summer. Canadian wildfire smoke has added episodes since 2023. Winter air is clean.

honolulu.climate: Honolulu has one of the most stable climates of any city on earth, which is what the score records. Highs sit at 27-31°C year-round and lows rarely fall below 19°C, moderated constantly by trade winds. Rain comes in short showers, heavier from November to March and concentrated on the windward side. There is no cold season and no real seasonal variation.
honolulu.cost: Honolulu is among the most expensive cities in the United States and the low score is straightforward. Almost everything is shipped in, so groceries run 50-70 percent above mainland prices. A one-bedroom costs $2,000-2,600 and a realistic month lands at $3,500-4,500. Hawaii's state income tax is high. The isolation is priced into every line item.
honolulu.wifi: Connectivity is good but not mainland-grade. Spectrum and Hawaiian Telcom deliver cable and fibre at 200Mbps to 1Gbps across urban Honolulu. The constraint is physics: all traffic crosses submarine cable to the mainland, adding roughly 60-80ms of latency to United States west coast servers, which matters for video calls and real-time work but not for most tasks.
honolulu.nightlife: Modest and the score is fair. Waikiki carries the visitor-facing bars and hotel lounges, Chinatown has the small local scene with dive bars and a few live venues, and Kaka'ako has newer breweries. Most things close by midnight or 2am. The island's culture is oriented to early mornings, surf and the outdoors rather than late nights.
honolulu.nature: This is the reason to be here and the mid score badly undersells it. Diamond Head sits at the edge of the city, the Ko'olau range gives ridge hikes with 600-metre drops less than 30 minutes from downtown, and Hanauma Bay, the North Shore and Lanikai are all on one island. Access to ocean and mountain on the same day is routine.
honolulu.safety: Honolulu has one of the lower violent crime rates among American cities and most neighbourhoods are comfortable at night. Property crime, particularly theft from rental cars at trailheads and beach parks, is the common problem and locals leave vehicles empty and unlocked. The real hazards are environmental: strong currents, shore break and flash flooding in valleys.
honolulu.food: The food is genuinely distinctive rather than merely good. Hawaii's mix of Japanese, Chinese, Filipino, Korean, Portuguese and Native Hawaiian influence produced its own cuisine: poke, plate lunch, saimin, malasadas, kalua pork. Local markets and neighbourhood spots are excellent and reasonable; anything aimed at visitors is not. The Japanese food is the best in the United States.
honolulu.community: There is a small but real remote-work community, and the state ran a Movers and Shakers programme specifically to attract remote workers. Coworking exists in Kaka'ako and downtown. The larger dynamic is that Hawaii has a serious and understandable sensitivity about outsiders driving up housing costs, and integrating here asks more of a newcomer than most places.
honolulu.english: English is the working language and Hawaii is fully integrated into United States systems. Hawaiian Pidgin is widely spoken locally and is a genuine creole rather than an accent, though everyone will switch. Hawaiian is an official state language, visible in place names and increasingly in education. Nothing in daily life requires anything but English.
honolulu.visa: The low score reflects United States entry rules. Honolulu is a domestic destination for Americans, but everyone else faces the same system: ESTA for Visa Waiver nationals for 90 days at $21, or a B-1/B-2 with long consular waits. There is no American remote-work visa. Japan's proximity means the airport handles very high visa-waiver volume.
honolulu.culture: Native Hawaiian culture is a living practice here rather than a museum subject, and that is the substance of the score: hula, language revitalisation, and ongoing sovereignty debates are part of public life. The Bishop Museum holds the world's foremost Polynesian collection. Pearl Harbor carries the twentieth-century history. Institutional arts beyond that are limited by the city's size.
honolulu.cleanliness: Urban Honolulu is generally well kept, helped by constant trade winds and a strong tourism incentive. Waikiki and the main corridors are maintained carefully. Beach parks suffer from heavy use, and marine debris washing ashore is a persistent problem on windward coasts. Homelessness is highly visible in parts of the city and has been for years.
honolulu.airquality: Air quality is excellent for most of the year, among the best of any American city, because persistent trade winds carry Pacific air across the island continuously. The exception is vog, volcanic smog from Kīlauea on the Big Island, which reaches O'ahu when winds turn southerly. Those episodes can last days and affect people with respiratory conditions.

saltlakecity.climate: Salt Lake City has a cold semi-arid climate with sharp seasonal swings. Summers are hot and very dry at 33-35°C, which is more tolerable than humid equivalents. Winters run -6°C to 3°C with heavy mountain snowfall that is the region's economic engine. Spring and autumn are short and pleasant. The valley's altitude of 1,300 metres is noticeable on arrival.
saltlakecity.cost: Salt Lake City costs roughly $2,000-2,600 a month, moderate for the United States, though rents rose sharply after 2020 as remote workers arrived. A one-bedroom downtown or in Sugar House runs $1,300-1,700. Utah's flat state income tax is low. Ski passes and outdoor equipment are the local budget line that other cities do not have.
saltlakecity.wifi: Connectivity is excellent and better than the metro's size implies. Google Fiber, CenturyLink and Utah's publicly owned UTOPIA network deliver gigabit and multi-gigabit fibre across much of the valley. The Silicon Slopes tech corridor south toward Provo means business-grade infrastructure is dense. Coworking downtown is well served and 5G coverage is thorough.
saltlakecity.nightlife: Modest, and Utah's alcohol laws are the reason the score is not higher: state-run liquor stores, restrictions on serving, and a culture shaped by the Latter-day Saint majority. Downtown and Sugar House have a growing bar and brewery scene, and it is more normal than outsiders expect. But this is not a late-night city.
saltlakecity.nature: This is among the best in the United States and the mid score substantially undersells it. Seven ski resorts sit within an hour, four of them under 40 minutes, with some of the driest snow anywhere. The Wasatch range rises straight from the valley for hiking and climbing, and Moab and five national parks are within a day's drive.
saltlakecity.safety: Salt Lake City has moderate crime rates, lower than most American cities of its size. Downtown, the Avenues, Sugar House and the university area are comfortable. Property crime, particularly vehicle break-ins at trailheads, is the most common issue. Parts of the west side and the area around the Rio Grande have higher rates and visible homelessness.
saltlakecity.food: The food scene is better than its reputation and improving quickly, which is what the mid score records. Downtown and Ninth and Ninth carry genuine independent restaurants, and the Polynesian and Latin American communities add real range. The state's alcohol rules shape restaurant economics in ways that limit the fine-dining tier. Prices are moderate.
saltlakecity.community: There is a substantial tech population along the Silicon Slopes corridor and a strong outdoor-industry presence, giving the city a specific professional character. Remote-work arrivals since 2020 have been significant. It is not a nomad stopover, and the dominant social structure outside work is often religious, which some newcomers find harder to enter than they expect.
saltlakecity.english: English is the working language throughout and nothing in daily life requires another. Spanish is widely spoken on the west side. Unusually, the returned-missionary population means an exceptional density of fluent second-language speakers across dozens of languages, which makes Salt Lake City one of the more quietly multilingual American cities.
saltlakecity.visa: The low score is the United States immigration system rather than anything local. Visa Waiver nationals use an ESTA for up to 90 days at $21. Others need a B-1/B-2, with consular interview waits running months at many posts. There is no American digital nomad visa and remote work on a visitor admission is not permitted.
saltlakecity.culture: Cultural life is shaped heavily by the Latter-day Saint church, whose headquarters, Temple Square and genealogical archives are here and are substantial in their own right. Beyond that, the Utah Symphony and Ballet West are serious, and the Sundance Film Festival is 45 minutes away in Park City. The mid score reflects a narrower institutional base.
saltlakecity.cleanliness: The city presents well. Streets are unusually wide by design, the dry climate prevents damp staining, and municipal maintenance is good. Newer development dominates much of the valley. The main detractor is the seasonal one: winter inversions leave a visible haze over the valley, and dust from the shrinking Great Salt Lake is an increasing problem.
saltlakecity.airquality: Air quality is the most serious environmental problem here and the score is generous. Winter temperature inversions trap cold air in the valley for days or weeks, producing particulate levels that rank among the worst in the United States. Summer brings ozone and wildfire smoke. The drying Great Salt Lake exposes lakebed dust containing arsenic, an emerging concern.

asheville.climate: Asheville sits at 650 metres in the Blue Ridge Mountains, which gives it a genuinely mild version of the southern climate and explains the high score. Summers reach 27-29°C rather than the 34°C of the Carolina lowlands, and nights cool off. Winters are cool at -2°C to 9°C with occasional snow. Autumn colour here is a regional event.
asheville.cost: Asheville costs roughly $2,000-2,600 a month, which is high for a small southern city because tourism and remote-work arrivals have pushed housing hard. A one-bedroom runs $1,300-1,700. North Carolina's flat income tax is moderate. Wages locally are low relative to costs, which is a persistent source of friction for residents.
asheville.wifi: Connectivity is good for a city of this size. Spectrum cable covers the area at 300Mbps to 1Gbps and AT&T fibre reaches parts of it, and the remote-work influx has pushed providers to expand. Coworking downtown and in the River Arts District is reliable. Mountain terrain means some outlying valleys have noticeably worse service.
asheville.nightlife: Strong for the size, and built on beer. Asheville has among the most breweries per head of any American city and the scene is genuinely central to local social life rather than a marketing claim. Downtown and the South Slope carry the density, with live music most nights. It is a small city, so everything is walkable.
asheville.nature: This is the entire point of Asheville and the score should be higher than it is. The Blue Ridge Parkway runs past the edge of town, Pisgah and Nantahala National Forests surround it, and Great Smoky Mountains National Park is an hour west. Whitewater, climbing, trail running and long-distance hiking on the Appalachian Trail are all immediate.
asheville.safety: Asheville is comfortable overall with moderate crime rates for an American city. Downtown, Montford and West Asheville are fine day and night. Property crime and car break-ins around trailheads are the common issues. The 2024 flooding from Hurricane Helene caused severe damage across the region, and some infrastructure recovery is still ongoing.
asheville.food: The food scene is disproportionate to the city's size and the high score is deserved. Appalachian cooking has been taken seriously here by a generation of chefs, farm-to-table is genuine given the surrounding agriculture rather than a slogan, and the brewery scene supports a strong casual tier. Prices are reasonable by American standards.
asheville.community: There is a real and growing remote-work population, plus a long-established artist community centred on the River Arts District. The city has attracted people leaving larger metros for over a decade. Coworking spaces host regular meetups. What it lacks is international turnover, which is why the score is mid rather than high.
asheville.english: English is the working language and nothing in daily life requires another. Spanish is spoken in parts of the service and agricultural workforce. Asheville is a straightforward place to arrive for any English speaker, with all administration, healthcare and housing operating in English by default and no barrier to plan around.
asheville.visa: The low score is the American immigration system rather than the city. Visa Waiver nationals enter on an ESTA for 90 days at $21; others need a B-1/B-2 and face consular waits measured in months in many countries. There is no United States digital nomad visa, and remote work on a visitor admission falls outside that status.
asheville.culture: The cultural identity is craft and music rather than institutional. Traditional Appalachian old-time and bluegrass are living practice here, buskers downtown are genuinely good, and the River Arts District holds working studios rather than galleries. The Biltmore Estate is the largest private house in the United States. Museums are modest, which the mid score reflects.
asheville.cleanliness: Asheville presents well. The compact downtown is maintained carefully, the mountain setting means clean air and little industrial residue, and the tourism economy provides the incentive to keep it that way. Heavy visitor traffic in autumn strains the centre. Post-flood recovery has left some areas along the French Broad River still visibly damaged.
asheville.airquality: Air quality is good and has improved markedly since regional coal plants were retired and the Great Smoky Mountains haze problem was addressed. Mountain elevation and prevailing winds help disperse pollutants. The main issues are seasonal: summer ozone on hot still days, high pollen in spring, and occasional wildfire smoke from the southern Appalachians.

leeds.climate: Leeds has a temperate maritime climate that is grey more than it is cold, which is what holds the score at 5. Summers are mild at 19-22°C, winters hover around 2-7°C and rarely freeze hard. Rain is frequent rather than heavy, spread across roughly 150 days a year. December daylight runs about seven and a half hours, which is the harder adjustment.
leeds.cost: Leeds costs roughly $1,800-2,400 a month, cheaper than London by a wide margin and still expensive globally, which the mid-low score records. A one-bedroom in the city centre or Headingley runs $950-1,400. Council tax is a separate monthly bill people forget. The city is compact enough that you can live without a car.
leeds.wifi: Connectivity is very good. Openreach and Virgin Media deliver fibre across most of the city at 100-900Mbps, and full-fibre coverage has expanded quickly. Leeds is a major UK financial and legal centre outside London, so business-grade service is easy to arrange. Coworking around the city centre is well provisioned and 5G coverage is comprehensive.
leeds.nightlife: Strong, and the two universities are a large part of why. Call Lane and the Northern Quarter carry the bar density, Belgrave Music Hall and Brudenell Social Club are genuine institutions, and the student population keeps prices low and venues full midweek. Closing is around 2-3am for most places. For a city of this size the scene is disproportionate.
leeds.nature: Leeds itself is urban, but the Yorkshire Dales National Park is an hour away and the Peak District about the same, which is the practical argument. Roundhay Park is 700 acres inside the city, and the Leeds-Liverpool Canal towpath gives a continuous walking and cycling route out of town. Access is good; the immediate surroundings are ordinary.
leeds.safety: Leeds is broadly safe with the usual British urban pattern. The city centre, Headingley and Chapel Allerton are comfortable. Some inner areas have higher rates of burglary and antisocial behaviour. Violent crime involving visitors is uncommon. The main practical risks are late-night incidents around the drinking districts and bicycle theft, which is persistent.
leeds.food: Better than its reputation and improving steadily. The South Asian food is the genuine strength, with Bradford's curry scene ten minutes away by train and strong Pakistani and Kashmiri cooking in Leeds itself. Kirkgate Market is one of the largest covered markets in Europe. An independent restaurant tier has grown considerably around the centre.
leeds.community: There is a solid tech and digital sector, a large student population and a growing freelance scene, which gives the city constant turnover of newcomers. Coworking spaces around the centre host regular meetups. It is not an international nomad destination and few people arrive for a month, which is what keeps the score mid.
leeds.english: English is the first language and Leeds is entirely straightforward for an English speaker. The Yorkshire accent takes a short adjustment and local vocabulary is distinctive, but nothing about daily life, administration, banking or healthcare requires anything else. This is as frictionless a language environment as exists anywhere.
leeds.visa: The mid-low score is the UK immigration system rather than the city. Most Western nationals visit for up to six months without a visa, which is generous, but remote work on a visitor permission sits in a grey area and the UK has no digital nomad visa. Longer stays need a sponsored work route or the Global Talent visa.
leeds.culture: Leeds carries real cultural weight for its size. Opera North is based here, the Leeds International Piano Competition is a significant event, and the Royal Armouries holds the national collection of arms and armour. The Victorian arcades are among the best preserved in Britain. Live music history from goth to grime is genuine.
leeds.cleanliness: Presentation is ordinary for a large British city. The centre and the arcades are maintained well, the student areas around Headingley and Hyde Park noticeably less so, particularly at the end of term. Litter and fly-tipping are persistent complaints in inner suburbs. Rain keeps the air washed and the pavements grey in equal measure.
leeds.airquality: Air quality is reasonable and improving. Leeds dropped its planned clean air zone after emissions fell faster than forecast, and the main remaining problem is nitrogen dioxide along the inner ring road and the M621 corridor. Particulate levels are moderate. The maritime climate means pollutants disperse rather than settle, unlike inland basin cities.

cardiff.climate: Cardiff has a mild maritime climate and is one of the wetter British cities, which is what holds the score at 5. Summers are cool at 19-21°C, winters mild at 3-8°C with little snow. Rainfall is high at around 1,150mm a year, considerably more than London, funnelled in off the Bristol Channel. Genuinely warm days are few.
cardiff.cost: Cardiff costs roughly $1,650-2,300 a month, cheaper than most large English cities and expensive by world standards. A one-bedroom in Cathays or the city centre runs $890-1,270. Wales has the same tax system as England with some devolved rates. The city is small enough to walk or cycle across, which removes most transport cost.
cardiff.wifi: Connectivity is very good. Openreach and Virgin Media fibre reach most of the city at 100-900Mbps, with full-fibre expanding quickly. Cardiff hosts a growing fintech and media cluster, including major BBC production, so business-grade infrastructure is present. Coworking around the centre and Cardiff Bay is well provisioned and 5G coverage is thorough.
cardiff.nightlife: Strong for the size, driven by a large student population and by rugby. St Mary Street and Mill Lane carry the bar density, and international match days at the Principality Stadium transform the whole city centre into something unlike anywhere else in Britain. Closing is around 2-3am. Prices are low compared to English cities.
cardiff.nature: Better placed than most British cities. Bute Park runs 130 acres from the castle through the middle of town, the Brecon Beacons are 45 minutes north with real mountain walking, and the Gower Peninsula's beaches are about an hour west. Cardiff Bay gives waterfront within the city. Access to genuine landscape here is unusually quick.
cardiff.safety: Cardiff is comfortable overall with moderate crime rates. The centre, Pontcanna, Roath and the Bay are fine day and night. Some outer areas have higher rates of burglary and antisocial behaviour. The city centre gets rowdy on match days and weekend nights, which is the main practical consideration rather than any serious risk.
cardiff.food: Decent and improving, which the mid score records honestly. Cardiff Market is a Victorian covered market still in daily use, Pontcanna and Roath carry the independent restaurant scene, and there is a growing modern Welsh cooking movement using local lamb, seafood and cheese. Prices are moderate. The range is narrower than in larger British cities.
cardiff.community: Cardiff University and two others bring a large student population, and the media and creative sector around the BBC studios supports a freelance scene. Coworking spaces in the centre and the Bay host regular meetups. International nomads are uncommon, and the community you join will be Welsh and settled rather than transient.
cardiff.english: English is universal and Cardiff is entirely straightforward for an English speaker. Welsh is an official language and appears on all public signage, and around 11 percent of the city speaks it, but no service requires it. Bilingual presentation is standard across government and transport. There is no practical language barrier at all.
cardiff.visa: The mid-low score is UK policy rather than anything Welsh. Most Western nationals enter without a visa for up to six months. The UK has no digital nomad visa, and working remotely on visitor permission is not clearly provided for in the rules. Longer stays require a sponsored work route or the Global Talent visa.
cardiff.culture: Cardiff carries real cultural weight as a capital. The Wales Millennium Centre hosts Welsh National Opera, St Fagans National Museum of History is one of Europe's best open-air museums and free, and Cardiff Castle sits in the middle of town. The Welsh language revival is visible and active. Rugby is a cultural institution rather than a sport.
cardiff.cleanliness: Presentation is good for a British city. The centre, Cardiff Bay and the Pontcanna area are well maintained, and the city's compact scale keeps standards consistent. Student areas around Cathays are the exception, particularly at term end. Frequent rain keeps streets washed. Match-day litter in the centre clears quickly.
cardiff.airquality: Air quality is good by British urban standards, helped by Bristol Channel wind and the absence of heavy industry since the docks declined. Nitrogen dioxide on Castle Street and a few central corridors has exceeded limits, prompting local measures. Particulates are low. Overall readings compare well with English cities of similar size.

belfast.climate: Belfast has a mild, damp maritime climate. Summers are cool at 18-19°C, winters mild at 2-7°C with very little snow, and rain falls on roughly 200 days a year, usually lightly. Cloud cover is persistent and December daylight runs about seven hours. The score reflects a climate that is rarely severe and rarely bright.
belfast.cost: Belfast is the cheapest capital city in the UK and Ireland, which the mid score understates slightly. A one-bedroom in the city centre or Botanic runs $760-1,150, and a month lands near $1,500-2,150. Rates, the local property tax, are billed separately. The city is compact enough to cross on foot in half an hour.
belfast.wifi: Connectivity is excellent and better than most of the UK. Northern Ireland has among the highest full-fibre coverage rates in Europe, with Openreach and Fibrus delivering gigabit service across most of Belfast. The city's cybersecurity and fintech sector means business-grade infrastructure is dense. Coworking around the centre and the Cathedral Quarter is well served.
belfast.nightlife: Very good for the size. The Cathedral Quarter carries the bar density, with the Duke of York and Kelly's Cellars among the genuine institutions, and traditional music sessions run several nights a week. Queen's University keeps the Botanic area busy. Prices are low and the city is small enough that everything is walkable.
belfast.nature: Well placed. Cave Hill rises directly behind the city with views over the lough, the Mourne Mountains are an hour south, and the Causeway Coast with the Giant's Causeway is about 90 minutes north and genuinely spectacular. Belfast Lough gives immediate water. For a capital, access to serious landscape is unusually fast.
belfast.safety: Belfast is statistically among the safer cities in the UK, with violent crime rates below the British average. The centre, Botanic and south Belfast are comfortable. The legacy of the Troubles persists in interface areas and around some parades in summer, and the peace walls still stand, but none of this affects visitors in practice.
belfast.food: Better than expected and the mid score is fair. St George's Market is a genuine Victorian market with excellent produce, the Northern Irish breakfast is an institution, and a serious independent restaurant scene has developed over the last fifteen years, including Michelin recognition. Local seafood and beef are strong. Prices are low for the quality.
belfast.community: There is a growing tech and cybersecurity cluster and a strong student population from Queen's and Ulster University. Coworking spaces in the Cathedral Quarter host regular events. Belfast is not a nomad destination and international short-stayers are uncommon, which the mid score records rather than any difficulty in meeting people.
belfast.english: English is the first language and everything operates in it. The Belfast accent is distinctive and fast but presents no real difficulty. Irish and Ulster Scots have official recognition and appear in some signage, particularly in west Belfast, but no service requires either. For an English speaker there is no barrier whatsoever.
belfast.visa: The mid-low score reflects UK rules, with a local wrinkle worth knowing: the land border with Ireland is open and unpoliced, but crossing it moves you between the UK and Schengen-adjacent Irish immigration systems. Most Western nationals get six months visa-free in the UK. There is no British digital nomad visa.
belfast.culture: Belfast's cultural offer is substantial and unusually direct. Titanic Belfast sits on the slipway where the ship was built and is a genuinely good museum. The political murals and the Troubles history are a living subject rather than a heritage display, with black taxi tours run by people who lived it. The traditional music scene is real.
belfast.cleanliness: The city presents well. The centre, Titanic Quarter and south Belfast are maintained carefully, and Belfast's compact scale keeps standards even. Regeneration investment over two decades is visible. Some inner areas remain worn. Frequent rain keeps streets washed and buildings damp-stained in roughly equal measure.
belfast.airquality: Air quality is good, among the better records in the UK, helped by constant Atlantic wind and the absence of the heavy industry that once dominated the lough. Nitrogen dioxide on a few central corridors is the main exceedance. Domestic solid-fuel burning raises winter particulates in some residential areas more than traffic does.

halifax.climate: Halifax has a humid continental climate moderated by the Atlantic, which makes it milder than inland Canada and considerably damper. Summers are cool at 20-23°C, winters run -8°C to 0°C with heavy snow and frequent freeze-thaw. Fog is common in spring and early summer. The city sits in the track of nor'easters and occasional hurricane remnants.
halifax.cost: Halifax has become expensive relative to its size, with rents rising sharply since 2020 as remote workers arrived from Toronto and Vancouver. A one-bedroom runs $1,280-1,640 and a month lands near $2,000-2,500. Nova Scotia's income tax is among the higher provincial rates. The mid-low score is an honest reflection.
halifax.wifi: Connectivity is very good. Bell and Eastlink deliver fibre and cable across the peninsula at 150Mbps to 1.5Gbps. Halifax is the largest city in Atlantic Canada with several universities and a growing ocean-technology sector, so business-grade service is straightforward. Coworking downtown is well provisioned. Winter storms are the main outage risk.
halifax.nightlife: Good for the size, sustained by a very large student population across six universities in a city of 450,000. Argyle Street carries the bar density and the live music scene, particularly Celtic and folk, is genuinely active rather than performed for visitors. Last call is 2am. The scene thins noticeably outside the academic year.
halifax.nature: Excellent and close. Point Pleasant Park sits at the end of the peninsula with coastal trails, the Halifax Citadel gives green space in the centre, and Peggy's Cove and the South Shore beaches are within an hour. Kejimkujik National Park is two hours. The Atlantic coastline here is the main draw and it is immediate.
halifax.safety: Halifax is safe with crime rates below the Canadian urban average, and the high score is fair. The peninsula, the North End and the suburbs are all comfortable, including at night. Property crime is the most common issue. Winter conditions, particularly ice on hills and coastal storms, are a more realistic hazard than crime.
halifax.food: Strong for its size and built on the Atlantic. Lobster, scallops and haddock are genuinely local rather than imported, the donair is a Halifax invention and the official food of the city, and the independent restaurant scene downtown is serious. Craft beer here is among the best in Canada. Prices are moderate to high.
halifax.community: The student population brings constant turnover and there is a real remote-work influx since 2020, plus an ocean-technology and startup cluster. Coworking spaces downtown host regular events. International nomads passing through are uncommon, which is what the mid score records; most newcomers are Canadians relocating rather than travellers.
halifax.english: English is the working language and Halifax is entirely straightforward. Canada is officially bilingual so federal services are available in French, and there are Acadian French communities elsewhere in Nova Scotia, but Halifax operates in English throughout. Nothing in daily life, banking or healthcare requires another language.
halifax.visa: Canada admits most Western nationals visa-free for up to six months with an eTA at $5, which is straightforward. The mid score reflects that Canada has no dedicated digital nomad visa, though it has signalled openness to remote workers on visitor status. Longer stays require a work permit or provincial nomination.
halifax.culture: Halifax carries more history than its size suggests. The Citadel is a major fortification, the Maritime Museum of the Atlantic holds the largest Titanic artefact collection in the world, and Pier 21 was Canada's Ellis Island. The Halifax Explosion of 1917 shaped the modern city. Celtic and Acadian musical traditions are living practice.
halifax.cleanliness: The city presents well. The peninsula is maintained carefully, the waterfront boardwalk is a showpiece, and Canadian municipal standards are high. Winter is the complication: months of road salt and grit leave a residue that clears only in spring, and freeze-thaw damages pavements badly. Sea air weathers buildings quickly.
halifax.airquality: Air quality is excellent and among the best of any Canadian city, kept clean by constant Atlantic wind and the absence of heavy industry or a large highway network. Readings sit comfortably in the good range most of the year. The exception is drifting wildfire smoke, which reached Nova Scotia during severe seasons in 2023.

quebeccity.climate: Quebec City has one of the harshest climates of any city in this directory, which is what the low score measures. January runs -13°C to -18°C with regular stretches below -25°C, and annual snowfall averages over three metres. Summers are warm and pleasant at 25-26°C but short. Winter here is not an inconvenience, it is the organising fact of the year.
quebeccity.cost: Quebec City is expensive by global standards and reasonable for Canada. A one-bedroom runs $785-1,070, well below Montreal or Toronto, and a month lands near $1,640-2,070. Quebec has the highest provincial income tax in Canada, offset by the cheapest childcare and university tuition. Winter heating is a substantial line item.
quebeccity.wifi: Connectivity is very good. Bell and Videotron deliver fibre and cable across the city at 100Mbps to 1.5Gbps, and Quebec's provincial programme to bring high-speed service to every household has pushed coverage further than most of North America. Coworking in Saint-Roch is well provisioned. 5G coverage in the urban area is thorough.
quebeccity.nightlife: Decent rather than remarkable. Grande Allée carries the main bar strip, Saint-Roch is the younger and more interesting district, and the Old Town's pubs skew heavily to visitors. Université Laval supports a student scene. Winter drives everything indoors for months, and the city is small, which together hold the score mid.
quebeccity.nature: Very good. Montmorency Falls is higher than Niagara and sits 15 minutes from downtown, the Plains of Abraham give 250 acres in the middle of the city, and Jacques-Cartier National Park is 40 minutes north with genuine wilderness. Île d'Orléans is immediately across the river. Winter turns all of it into ski and snowshoe terrain.
quebeccity.safety: Quebec City is among the safest cities in North America, with a homicide rate close to zero in most years, and the high score is well earned. Every district including the Old Town and Saint-Roch is comfortable at any hour. The genuine hazards are winter ones: ice, falling snow from roofs, and driving conditions.
quebeccity.food: Strong and distinctly Québécois rather than generically Canadian. The French culinary tradition runs deep here, poutine is local rather than adopted, and the sugar shack and maple economy are real. Île d'Orléans supplies the city with produce and cider. The independent scene in Saint-Roch is excellent. Prices are moderate to high.
quebeccity.community: There is a modest tech and video-game sector, and Université Laval brings students, but Quebec City is not a nomad destination and very few pass through. The language requirement filters most international arrivals toward Montreal. Coworking exists in Saint-Roch. Community here is French-speaking, settled and welcoming to those who make the linguistic effort.
quebeccity.english: This is the practical constraint and the mid score is honest about it. Quebec City is overwhelmingly francophone, far more so than Montreal, and French is the sole official language of the province. Tourist-facing staff in the Old Town speak English; away from it, service in shops, clinics and government offices is often French only.
quebeccity.visa: Canada admits most Western nationals visa-free for up to six months with an eTA costing $5, which is straightforward and generous. Canada has no dedicated digital nomad visa, which is what holds the score mid. Quebec runs its own immigration selection for permanent routes, with French proficiency weighted heavily.
quebeccity.culture: Quebec City's cultural depth is high. Old Quebec is the only fortified city north of Mexico and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the French colonial history is continuous rather than reconstructed. The Musée national des beaux-arts is substantial, and the Winter Carnival is among the largest in the world. Francophone identity is a living political subject.
quebeccity.cleanliness: The city is very well kept and the high score is deserved. Old Quebec is maintained to heritage standards because tourism depends on it, and municipal services across the city are good. Snow clearance is efficient and continuous through winter. The spring thaw leaves a few weeks of grit and salt residue before crews clear it.
quebeccity.airquality: Air quality is very good, among the better records in North America. The city is small, industry is limited, and the Saint Lawrence corridor's winds disperse pollutants. Winter wood-burning raises particulates modestly in some residential areas. The main degradations are episodic: Quebec wildfire smoke during severe seasons, notably in 2023.

dunedin.climate: Dunedin sits at 45 degrees south and has a cool temperate maritime climate, which the low score reflects. Summers are mild at 18-19°C rather than warm, winters run 3-10°C with frost but little snow at sea level, and the weather changes several times a day. Wind off the Southern Ocean is constant. Genuinely warm days are rare.
dunedin.cost: Dunedin is the cheapest of New Zealand's main cities and still expensive internationally, which the mid-low score records. A one-bedroom runs $235-325 a week, and a month lands near $1,650-2,120. Imported goods carry a distance premium. Student flats keep the low end of the housing market unusually cheap and unusually cold.
dunedin.wifi: Connectivity is very good. New Zealand's national fibre rollout reached Dunedin comprehensively, with gigabit UFB service available to most of the city at reasonable prices. The University of Otago's research infrastructure adds capacity. The unavoidable constraint is geography: submarine cable to Australia and the United States adds real latency for real-time work.
dunedin.nightlife: Better than the city's size suggests, and the University of Otago is entirely the reason. Around 20,000 students in a city of 130,000 produce a concentrated scene around the Octagon and North Dunedin. The student culture here is famous within New Zealand. Outside term time the city becomes noticeably quieter.
dunedin.nature: This is Dunedin's strongest card and the maximum score is right. The Otago Peninsula holds the world's only mainland royal albatross colony, plus yellow-eyed penguins and sea lions on accessible beaches. Baldwin Street is the steepest residential street on earth. The Catlins, Central Otago and Fiordland are all within a few hours.
dunedin.safety: Dunedin is very safe and the high score is straightforward. Violent crime is rare, the city is small and walkable, and most areas are comfortable at any hour. Student districts get boisterous during term. The real hazards are environmental: cold water, unpredictable coastal weather and steep terrain rather than anything criminal.
dunedin.food: Good for the size without being a destination. The seafood is excellent and genuinely local, Central Otago produces some of the world's best pinot noir 90 minutes away, and the student population supports a cheap and cheerful tier. The independent scene around the Octagon has grown. Range is limited by the city's population.
dunedin.community: The university dominates, bringing constant academic and student turnover, and there is a small tech sector. International nomads are rare, partly because of distance and partly because New Zealand's visa rules do not encourage short working stays. The mid-low score is accurate: you will meet students and academics rather than travellers.
dunedin.english: English is the first language and everything operates in it. Te reo Māori is an official language, increasingly present in signage, place names and everyday greeting, and worth learning a little of out of respect rather than necessity. The New Zealand accent is distinctive but presents no difficulty. There is no barrier at all.
dunedin.visa: New Zealand admits most Western nationals visa-free for three to six months, and since 2025 has explicitly permitted remote work for an overseas employer on a visitor visa, which is a meaningful liberalisation and lifts this score. The NZeTA costs $10 plus a tourism levy. Longer stays still require a work visa.
dunedin.culture: Dunedin's identity is Scottish, and directly so: the name is the Gaelic for Edinburgh and the Victorian and Edwardian architecture is the best preserved in New Zealand. The university, founded 1869, is the country's oldest. The Dunedin Sound produced an internationally significant indie music scene in the 1980s. Otago Museum is substantial.
dunedin.cleanliness: The city is very clean and well maintained, which the high score reflects. New Zealand municipal standards are high, the population is small, and there is no heavy industry. Constant wind and rain keep the air and streets washed. The exception is the student quarter after major events, which has a local reputation.
dunedin.airquality: Air quality is excellent, among the best of any city in this directory. Dunedin sits at the edge of the Southern Ocean with prevailing winds arriving off thousands of kilometres of open water, so background pollution is close to global baseline. The only measurable issue is winter wood and coal burning for home heating in some suburbs.

montegobay.climate: Montego Bay has a tropical climate with very little seasonal variation in temperature: highs of 30-32°C year-round, tempered on the coast by sea breezes. The distinction is rainfall, with a wetter season from May to November peaking in October. Hurricane season runs June to November and is the real climatic risk rather than heat.
montegobay.cost: Montego Bay costs roughly $1,300 a month, which is moderate rather than cheap because the tourism economy prices many things in dollars. Local housing away from the tourist strip runs $500-800; anything in the resort corridor costs several times that. Imported goods and electricity are expensive. Eating and travelling locally is where the value is.
montegobay.wifi: Connectivity is adequate rather than good. Flow and Digicel provide cable and fibre in the urban and resort areas at 50-200Mbps, and the resort corridor is well served because tourism demands it. Outside those zones service degrades quickly. Power interruptions are frequent enough that a battery backup is a sensible purchase.
montegobay.nightlife: Genuinely strong and the high score is earned. The Hip Strip along Gloucester Avenue carries the visitor-facing bars and clubs, but the substance is Jamaica's own: street dances, sound systems and a live reggae and dancehall culture that is exported worldwide and originates here. Reggae Sumfest each July is a major international event.
montegobay.nature: Excellent. Doctor's Cave Beach sits in the middle of town, the Montego Bay Marine Park protects reef immediately offshore, and the Blue Hole and Dunn's River Falls are within reach. The Cockpit Country's limestone karst inland is genuinely wild terrain. Snorkelling, diving and rafting are all immediate rather than day trips.
montegobay.safety: This is the clearest weakness and the low score is honest. Jamaica has one of the higher homicide rates in the Americas, and Montego Bay has been under a state of public emergency more than once. Violence is overwhelmingly concentrated in specific inner-city communities and rarely touches visitors, but the resort corridor is enclosed for a reason.
montegobay.food: Jamaican food is a real draw and the score reflects it. Jerk is a genuine cooking method rather than a sauce, with pimento wood smoking at roadside pits; ackee and saltfish is the national dish; patties, curry goat and escovitch fish are everyday. Local prices are low. The resort restaurants are considerably worse value than the street.
montegobay.community: There is very little established remote-work community, which the low score records. Montego Bay is built around tourism and cruise arrivals rather than long-stay workers, and coworking options are minimal. Jamaica has courted digital nomads with its extended-stay messaging, but the practical infrastructure and the community have not followed.
montegobay.english: English is the official language and all administration, education and business run in it. Jamaican Patois is the everyday spoken language and is a full creole rather than an accent, so conversation between locals can be hard to follow at first. Everyone will switch to standard English readily. There is no practical barrier.
montegobay.visa: Jamaica is unusually easy, which the high score reflects. Most Western nationals enter visa-free for up to 90 days, and extensions are obtainable locally. There is no formal digital nomad visa, but the government has publicly welcomed remote workers on visitor status, and the entry process is quick and inexpensive.
montegobay.culture: Jamaica's cultural output is disproportionate to its size and Montego Bay sits inside that. Reggae and dancehall are global exports with roots here, Rastafari is a living religious and cultural movement, and the Maroon communities in the Cockpit Country descend from people who won their freedom in the eighteenth century. The institutional museum offer is thin.
montegobay.cleanliness: Presentation is mixed. The resort corridor and the Hip Strip are maintained carefully because the economy depends on it. Away from those areas, waste collection is inconsistent, plastic litter is visible along roads and drainage gullies, and there is a persistent problem with informal dumping. Beaches inside the marine park are kept clean.
montegobay.airquality: Air quality is generally good, kept clean by constant trade winds coming off the Caribbean. Vehicle emissions in the town centre and older diesel vehicles are the main local source. The seasonal issue is Saharan dust, which crosses the Atlantic each summer and can raise particulate readings noticeably for several days at a time.

beijing.climate: Beijing has a continental monsoon climate with four sharply separated seasons, which averages out at a 5. Summers are hot and humid at 31-33°C with the July rains, winters are cold and dry from -8°C to 2°C, and spring brings dust and occasional sandstorms off the Gobi. Autumn, roughly late September to early November, is genuinely excellent and short.
beijing.cost: Beijing costs around $1,500 a month, which is expensive for China and moderate globally. A one-bedroom inside the fourth ring runs $620-1,100, and rent is the dominant cost. Local food, metro travel and services are very cheap. Imported goods, Western groceries and international schooling carry heavy premiums.
beijing.wifi: Domestic connectivity is excellent, with fibre at 100-1000Mbps and comprehensive 5G, but the score is held at 6 by the Great Firewall. Google, most Western SaaS and many collaboration tools require a VPN, and VPN reliability degrades around political dates and major meetings. Plan for a paid commercial VPN plus a backup.
beijing.nightlife: Strong and varied. Sanlitun carries the international bar scene, the Gulou and Fangjia Hutong areas the independent one, and Wudaokou the student crowd near the universities. Live music at School Bar and DDC is genuine, and Beijing's craft beer scene, led by Great Leap and Jing-A, is the best in China.
beijing.nature: Mixed. The city itself is flat, dense and short on green, though Jingshan, Beihai and the Fragrant Hills give relief. The compensation is the Great Wall: Mutianyu is 90 minutes away and the unrestored sections at Jiankou and Gubeikou are serious hiking. The Western Hills offer real ridge walking within the municipality.
beijing.safety: Beijing is among the safest large cities anywhere, with very low violent crime and effectively no risk of street robbery at any hour. The high score is accurate. This comes with pervasive surveillance and a heavy police presence, which some find reassuring and others do not. Traffic remains the main practical hazard.
beijing.food: Outstanding. Peking duck is local and the good versions at Dadong or Siji Minfu are extraordinary; jianbing, lamb skewers and hotpot are everyday. Because Beijing is the capital, every regional Chinese cuisine has serious representation here, from Yunnan to Xinjiang to Chaozhou. Prices for local food are very low.
beijing.community: The foreign community contracted sharply after 2020 and has only partly returned, which is what the mid score records. There is a substantial domestic tech sector around Zhongguancun and coworking exists, but Beijing is not a nomad destination and most foreigners here are on employment contracts rather than passing through.
beijing.english: English proficiency is low outside international business and the university districts. Metro signage, station announcements and major museums are bilingual, but shops, clinics, delivery apps and government offices operate in Chinese. Translation apps handle most of it. Living here comfortably for more than a few weeks means learning some Mandarin.
beijing.visa: China has no digital nomad visa, which is what caps this score. Entry has become much easier: many European, Southeast Asian and Latin American nationals now get 30 days visa-free, and the 240-hour transit exemption covers Beijing. Americans, British and Canadians still need a visa. Working legally requires a Z visa.
beijing.culture: Beijing scores a 10 because few cities carry this much. The Forbidden City is the largest surviving palace complex in the world, the Temple of Heaven and Summer Palace are UNESCO sites, and the city has been an imperial capital across the Yuan, Ming and Qing. The 798 Art District covers the contemporary end.
beijing.cleanliness: Streets are swept constantly and the main avenues are immaculate, but the picture is uneven. Older hutong neighbourhoods vary widely, and public toilets remain a common complaint despite a decade of upgrades. Waste sorting rules arrived in 2020 and compliance is patchy. Overall the city presents better than most of its size.
beijing.airquality: This is Beijing's worst category and the low score is earned. PM2.5 has fallen roughly 60 percent since 2013, a real achievement, but the annual average still sits near 30-40 µg/m³, six to eight times the WHO guideline. Winter is worst, when regional coal heating and still air combine. Spring sandstorms add episodic spikes.

chengdu.climate: Chengdu sits in the Sichuan Basin and the climate is humid, mild and famously grey. Summers are hot and sticky at 30-32°C, winters mild at 5-10°C with almost no frost, and the basin traps cloud so effectively that locals joke dogs bark at the sun. Sunshine hours are among the lowest in China.
chengdu.cost: Chengdu costs about $1,200 a month and is noticeably cheaper than the eastern coastal cities. A one-bedroom inside the second ring runs $350-620. Sichuan food is inexpensive even at good restaurants, the metro is extensive and cheap, and teahouse culture means an afternoon out costs almost nothing.
chengdu.wifi: Fibre at 100-1000Mbps and strong 5G coverage across the city, with Chengdu now a major second-tier tech hub hosting large domestic and international offices. The constraint is the same as everywhere in China: a VPN is required for Google and most Western tools, and reliability fluctuates. That is what holds the score at 7.
chengdu.nightlife: Chengdu has a reputation within China as the most relaxed and most social of the big cities, and the nightlife reflects it. Jiuyanqiao along the river carries the club density, Yulin and Kuanzhai Alley the bar scene. The city has a genuine underground and hip-hop scene, and teahouses running until late are a parallel culture.
chengdu.nature: Good and improving. The Panda Base is 30 minutes from the centre, Qingcheng Mountain and the Dujiangyan irrigation system are 90 minutes and both UNESCO listed, and Mount Siguniang's peaks are a few hours west. Chengdu is the practical gateway to eastern Tibet and western Sichuan, which is the real argument here.
chengdu.safety: Very safe. Violent crime is rare, the city is comfortable to walk at any hour, and the strong police presence common to Chinese cities applies here too. Petty theft is uncommon. The most realistic risks are traffic, particularly electric scooters, and the seismic exposure of the Sichuan Basin, which has produced major earthquakes.
chengdu.food: Chengdu scores a 10 and it is not close. This is a UNESCO City of Gastronomy and the home of Sichuan cooking: mapo tofu, twice-cooked pork, dan dan noodles and the mala hotpot that defines the region. Street food at Jinli and neighbourhood stalls is exceptional and cheap. Few cities anywhere eat this well for the money.
chengdu.community: There is a modest foreign community, a large student population and a fast-growing domestic tech and gaming sector, which gives Chengdu more turnover than most Chinese cities outside Shanghai. Coworking exists. International remote workers passing through remain uncommon, and most foreigners here teach or work on contracts, which the mid score records.
chengdu.english: English proficiency is low, lower than in Beijing or Shanghai. Metro signage is bilingual and university areas have pockets of English, but daily life in shops, clinics and offices runs entirely in Mandarin, and the local Sichuanese dialect adds a layer. Translation apps carry the load. Learning basic Mandarin makes a large difference here.
chengdu.visa: China offers no digital nomad visa, which caps this at 4. Entry itself has eased considerably: many European and Southeast Asian nationals now enter visa-free for 30 days, and the 240-hour transit exemption includes Chengdu. Americans, British and Canadians still require a visa in advance. Legal employment needs a Z visa.
chengdu.culture: Chengdu's cultural depth is substantial. It has been continuously inhabited for over 2,000 years, the Jinsha site holds Shu civilisation artefacts predating recorded Chinese history there, and Du Fu's Thatched Cottage commemorates the Tang dynasty poet. Sichuan opera with its face-changing performance is living practice. Teahouse culture is a genuine social institution.
chengdu.cleanliness: Presentation is decent for a Chinese megacity. Central districts and the riverside parks are maintained well and the metro is spotless. Older residential lanes and market areas are noticeably rougher. Waste sorting is enforced unevenly. The persistent damp of the basin leaves buildings stained in a way that regular cleaning does not fix.
chengdu.airquality: Air quality is poor and the low score is honest. The Sichuan Basin is ringed by mountains that trap pollutants, and the same still air that produces the perpetual overcast prevents dispersal. Annual PM2.5 sits around 35-40 µg/m³, with winter inversions producing the worst readings. Conditions have improved since 2015 but remain well above WHO guidance.

guangzhou.climate: Guangzhou is subtropical and humid year-round. Summers are long, hot and wet at 33-34°C with high humidity from May to September and typhoon exposure through autumn. Winters are mild at 10-19°C and there is effectively no cold season. The heat is the real consideration rather than any seasonal extreme.
guangzhou.cost: Guangzhou costs roughly $1,400 a month, cheaper than Shanghai or Shenzhen and expensive by Chinese standards. A one-bedroom in Tianhe or Yuexiu runs $490-830. Cantonese food at neighbourhood level is very cheap, the metro is extensive and inexpensive, and the wholesale markets make goods notably cheaper than elsewhere.
guangzhou.wifi: Very good. Guangzhou has comprehensive fibre at 100-1000Mbps and dense 5G, and as one of China's major trade and manufacturing hubs it has strong business-grade infrastructure. Proximity to Hong Kong helps for some routing. The Great Firewall still requires a VPN for Google and Western tools, which is why this is an 8 rather than higher.
guangzhou.nightlife: Solid. Zhujiang New Town carries the upscale bars and clubs, Party Pier is a purpose-built waterfront nightlife zone, and the Xiaobei and Sanyuanli areas have an African and Middle Eastern trading community with their own restaurants and late venues. The scene is less internationally oriented than Shanghai's but genuinely busy.
guangzhou.nature: Limited, which the mid-low score reflects. Baiyun Mountain gives a real climb inside the city and the Pearl River waterfront is pleasant, but Guangzhou is dense and heavily built. The compensation is regional: Guangdong's coastline, the Danxia Mountain UNESCO site and Guilin's karst are all reachable by high-speed rail within a few hours.
guangzhou.safety: Guangzhou is very safe by international standards, with low violent crime and comfortable streets at night. Petty theft, particularly phone snatching around crowded markets and train stations, is more common here than in Beijing and is the one thing worth guarding against. Traffic and scooters are the main daily hazard.
guangzhou.food: Excellent. Guangzhou is the home of Cantonese cooking and the birthplace of dim sum, and the local saying that Cantonese people eat anything with four legs but the table is not entirely a joke. Morning tea at Guangzhou Restaurant or Lin Heung is an institution. Seafood, roast meats and congee are everyday and cheap.
guangzhou.community: Guangzhou has an unusual international profile for China, with long-established African, Middle Eastern and South Asian trading communities around Xiaobei, plus a business expat population drawn by the Canton Fair. Coworking exists. Remote workers passing through are still rare, which is what keeps this at a 5 rather than higher.
guangzhou.english: English proficiency is low outside the trade and business sector, where it is genuinely functional because import and export depend on it. Metro and airport signage is bilingual. Daily life runs in Mandarin and Cantonese, with Cantonese still dominant among older residents. Translation apps handle most interactions adequately.
guangzhou.visa: No Chinese digital nomad visa exists, which caps the score. Entry has eased: many European and Southeast Asian passport holders now get 30 days visa-free, and the 240-hour transit exemption covers Guangdong. Guangzhou's proximity to Hong Kong and Macau makes visa runs practical. Americans, British and Canadians still need a visa.
guangzhou.culture: Guangzhou carries real history as China's oldest continuously open port, the sole legal channel for Western trade for much of the Qing dynasty. Shamian Island preserves the colonial concession, the Chen Clan Ancestral Hall is exceptional Cantonese craftsmanship, and Cantonese opera is living practice. The modern skyline around Canton Tower is its own statement.
guangzhou.cleanliness: Presentation is ordinary for a Chinese megacity. The central business districts and metro are well kept, the wholesale market areas and older residential lanes considerably less so. Humidity leaves mould stains on buildings that cleaning does not remove. Waste management has improved but street-level litter around markets remains visible.
guangzhou.airquality: Air quality is mediocre but better than northern China, which is what the mid score records. Guangzhou has no coal heating season, and coastal position plus subtropical rain help disperse pollutants. Annual PM2.5 sits around 25-30 µg/m³, still several times the WHO guideline, with vehicle emissions and regional industry across the Pearl River Delta the main sources.

guilin.climate: Guilin is subtropical and wet. Summers are hot and humid at 32-33°C with heavy monsoon rain from April to August, and winters are mild but damp and grey at 6-13°C with no heating in most buildings, which makes them feel colder than the numbers suggest. Annual rainfall approaches 1,900mm.
guilin.cost: Guilin is genuinely cheap at around $900 a month, which the high score reflects. A one-bedroom in the city runs $170-350, considerably below any tier-one Chinese city. Local food costs a few dollars a meal. The tourist zones around Yangshuo price higher, but living locally in Guilin itself is inexpensive.
guilin.wifi: Adequate rather than good. Guilin has fibre and 4G/5G coverage in the city at usable speeds, and the tourist infrastructure means connectivity in Yangshuo is reasonable too. Service is less consistent than in the major cities, and the Great Firewall applies as everywhere, so a VPN is required for Google and Western tools.
guilin.nightlife: Modest in Guilin city itself, which the mid score records. There are bars along the Two Rivers and Four Lakes waterfront and around the pedestrian streets, but the scene is small. Yangshuo's West Street an hour away is the actual nightlife destination, geared heavily to domestic and international tourists.
guilin.nature: This is the whole point of Guilin and the maximum score is right. The karst landscape along the Li River is among the most photographed in the world and appears on the $3 note. Yangshuo offers world-class rock climbing on limestone, the Longji rice terraces are two hours north, and cycling through the karst valleys is exceptional.
guilin.safety: Very safe. Violent crime is rare, the city is comfortable at any hour, and the tourist economy means visible policing. The realistic risks are tourist-facing rather than criminal: overpriced tours, aggressive touts around the river cruises, and genuine outdoor hazards from swimming in the Li River or climbing without proper equipment.
guilin.food: Decent regional cooking rather than a destination. Guilin rice noodles are the local staple and excellent for a dollar, and Guangxi cuisine borrows from both Cantonese and Southeast Asian traditions with sour and fermented flavours. Yangshuo beer fish is the signature dish. The restaurant range is limited compared to a major Chinese city.
guilin.community: Very thin, which the low score records honestly. Guilin has a small rock-climbing community around Yangshuo that includes long-stay foreigners, and there are language students, but there is no meaningful coworking or remote-work scene. Most foreigners here are passing through on a week of tourism.
guilin.english: English proficiency is low. Tourist-facing staff around the Li River cruises and in Yangshuo speak functional English because the trade requires it, but away from those zones daily life runs entirely in Mandarin and local dialect. Translation apps are essential. Guilin is harder linguistically than the tier-one cities.
guilin.visa: China has no digital nomad visa and that caps this at 4. Guangxi does have some regional entry facilitation for visitors from ASEAN countries, and the general easing applies here: many European and Southeast Asian nationals get 30 days visa-free. Americans, British and Canadians still need a visa arranged in advance.
guilin.culture: Guilin's cultural offer is regional rather than national. The Zhuang, Yao and Dong minority cultures of Guangxi are genuinely present, particularly around the Longji terraces where the Yao villages are inhabited rather than staged. The Reed Flute Cave and the Ling Canal, dug in 214 BC, are real heritage. Scholarly rock inscriptions along the river date back centuries.
guilin.cleanliness: Better than most Chinese cities of comparable size, because tourism revenue depends on it. The riverside areas, parks and pedestrian streets are maintained carefully. Residential and market areas away from the tourist route are ordinary. The heavy rainfall keeps streets washed but leaves persistent damp staining on buildings.
guilin.airquality: Air quality is fair to good by Chinese standards and the score reflects that relative position. Guilin has limited heavy industry, no coal heating season and a wet subtropical climate that clears the air regularly. Annual PM2.5 sits near 25-30 µg/m³, above WHO guidance but well below the northern industrial cities. Winter agricultural burning produces episodic haze.

hangzhou.climate: Hangzhou has a humid subtropical climate with genuinely hot summers at 32-34°C and high humidity, and cool damp winters at 2-9°C with little heating in older buildings. The plum rain season in June brings weeks of continuous drizzle. Spring and autumn are pleasant and short. Typhoon remnants reach the city most years.
hangzhou.cost: Hangzhou has become expensive as Alibaba's home city drew tech salaries in, which the mid score reflects. A one-bedroom near West Lake or in Binjiang runs $490-900, and prices approach Shanghai's in the desirable districts. Food, transport and services remain cheap. $1,400 a month is a realistic figure.
hangzhou.wifi: Excellent by Chinese standards. Hangzhou is the headquarters of Alibaba and a genuine national technology centre, with dense fibre at 100-1000Mbps, comprehensive 5G and strong business infrastructure. The city pioneered large-scale digital municipal services. The Great Firewall applies as everywhere, so a VPN is needed for Western tools.
