hangzhou.nightlife: Moderate. The bar scene clusters around West Lake, Hubin and the Wulin district, with student areas near Zhejiang University adding volume. The tech sector supports a decent after-work culture. Hangzhou is quieter than Shanghai by a wide margin and skews toward teahouses, restaurants and lakeside evenings rather than late clubs.
hangzhou.nature: Very good and unusually central. West Lake is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most celebrated landscapes in Chinese culture, and it sits directly in the city. The Longjing tea terraces climb the hills immediately west, Xixi National Wetland Park is inside the municipality, and the Qiantang River tidal bore is a genuine natural spectacle each autumn.
hangzhou.safety: Very safe. Violent crime is rare, the city is comfortable at any hour and public spaces are heavily monitored. Hangzhou has a reputation as one of the more orderly Chinese cities. Petty theft is uncommon. The main practical hazards are traffic and electric scooters, plus typhoon-season flooding in low-lying areas.
hangzhou.food: Strong. Hangzhou cuisine is one of the eight great regional traditions of China, lighter and sweeter than most, with West Lake vinegar fish, Dongpo pork and beggar's chicken as signatures. Longjing tea is grown on the hillsides here and used in cooking. Prices are moderate and the range is broad.
hangzhou.community: Alibaba and the surrounding technology cluster give Hangzhou a substantial domestic professional community and real startup activity, with coworking to match. The foreign population is small and mostly on employment contracts. International nomads are uncommon, which the mid score records rather than any lack of professional density.
hangzhou.english: English proficiency is low outside the tech sector, where it is functional among younger professionals working with international clients. Signage around West Lake and on the metro is bilingual because of tourism. Ordinary transactions, healthcare and administration run in Mandarin. Translation apps handle most of it competently.
hangzhou.visa: There is no Chinese digital nomad visa, which is what caps the score at 4. Entry has become substantially easier, with 30-day visa-free access for many European and Southeast Asian nationals and the 240-hour transit exemption covering Zhejiang. Americans, British and Canadians still need a visa in advance.
hangzhou.culture: Hangzhou's cultural standing in China is high. Marco Polo described it as the finest city in the world, it was the Southern Song capital, and West Lake has shaped Chinese landscape painting and poetry for a thousand years. The Grand Canal terminates here. The China National Tea Museum and Lingyin Temple are both substantial.
hangzhou.cleanliness: Hangzhou presents better than most Chinese cities and the score reflects it. The West Lake area is maintained to a high standard because it is a national showpiece, and the central districts follow. Municipal waste sorting is enforced more consistently here than elsewhere. Older residential lanes are ordinary. Humidity stains buildings regardless.
hangzhou.airquality: Air quality is mediocre and typical of the Yangtze Delta, which the mid score records. Annual PM2.5 sits around 30 µg/m³, several times the WHO guideline, driven by regional industry across Zhejiang and Jiangsu rather than by Hangzhou itself. Winter is worst. Conditions have improved markedly since 2015 under national controls.

xiamen.climate: Xiamen has one of the better climates in China, which the high score reflects. The island position on the Taiwan Strait moderates both ends: summers are hot at 32-33°C but sea breezes help, winters are mild at 12-18°C and frost is unknown. The trade-off is typhoons, which strike the Fujian coast directly most years.
xiamen.cost: Xiamen is expensive for a second-tier Chinese city, driven by property prices that rank among the highest in the country relative to income. A one-bedroom runs $420-760. $1,200 a month is realistic. Food and transport are cheap, which softens the housing burden but does not remove it.
xiamen.wifi: Adequate to good. Xiamen has fibre and 5G across the island at usable speeds, and as a special economic zone and port city it has reasonable business infrastructure. Service is a step below the tier-one cities. The Great Firewall applies, so a VPN is needed for Google and Western tools, which holds this at a 6.
xiamen.nightlife: Moderate. The bar scene clusters around Zhongshan Road, the Shapowei area and near Xiamen University, with a student population keeping things affordable. Gulangyu Island closes early. Xiamen is a relaxed coastal city that skews toward seafood dinners and tea houses rather than late clubs, which the mid score records fairly.
xiamen.nature: Very good. Xiamen is an island city with real beaches along the Huandao Road, Gulangyu Island a short ferry away, and Wanshi Botanical Garden climbing the hills in the middle of town. The Fujian tulou, the circular earthen clan buildings that are a UNESCO site, are two to three hours inland. The coastal cycling route is genuinely good.
xiamen.safety: Very safe. Xiamen consistently ranks among the most liveable and lowest-crime cities in China, and the high score is well founded. Violent crime is rare and the island is comfortable at any hour. Petty theft is uncommon. The realistic hazards are typhoons, which close the city periodically, and traffic.
xiamen.food: Strong. Minnan cuisine is distinctive, with oyster omelettes, satay noodles and peanut soup as local signatures, and the seafood is excellent and immediate. Xiamen also sits at the centre of Chinese tea culture, with Tieguanyin oolong grown nearby and tea houses everywhere. Street food around Zhongshan Road is cheap and good.
xiamen.community: Thin, which the low score records. Xiamen has a small foreign population, mostly teachers and some business people connected to the Taiwan trade, plus students at Xiamen University. There is little coworking and effectively no remote-work scene. Most foreigners here are settled rather than passing through.
xiamen.english: English proficiency is low. Xiamen University has an international programme and some tourist-facing businesses on Gulangyu manage functional English, but daily life runs in Mandarin with the Minnan dialect widely spoken among locals. Signage is largely Chinese only. Translation apps are essential for anything beyond the tourist zones.
xiamen.visa: China has no digital nomad visa, which is what caps this at 4. Fujian has some specific facilitation for Taiwanese visitors given the cross-strait relationship, but that does not extend to others. Many European and Southeast Asian nationals now get 30 days visa-free; Americans, British and Canadians still need a visa arranged in advance.
xiamen.culture: Xiamen's cultural identity is maritime and diasporic. Gulangyu Island is a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its extraordinary collection of colonial-era international architecture, built when thirteen nations held consulates there. The city was a treaty port, and much of the Southeast Asian Chinese diaspora traces back to Fujian. Nanyin music is living tradition.
xiamen.cleanliness: Xiamen is notably clean, one of the better-presented cities in China, and the high score is earned. It has won national civilised city awards repeatedly and the standard is visible: the coastal road, parks and Gulangyu are maintained carefully. Waste sorting is enforced. Sea air and regular rain keep streets washed.
xiamen.airquality: Air quality is good by Chinese standards. The island position on the Taiwan Strait means constant sea wind, there is no coal heating season, and heavy industry is limited relative to the Pearl or Yangtze deltas. Annual PM2.5 sits around 20-25 µg/m³. Xiamen routinely appears near the top of China's national air quality rankings.

xian.climate: Xian has a continental climate with hot humid summers reaching 33-35°C and cold dry winters from -5°C to 5°C. Spring dust and autumn rain bracket the year. The Guanzhong basin position means still air in both winter and summer, which intensifies heat and traps cold. Autumn is the most comfortable stretch.
xian.cost: Xian is inexpensive by Chinese standards at around $1,100 a month. A one-bedroom inside the city walls or near the universities runs $250-490. The street food economy means eating well costs very little, and the metro is extensive and cheap. This is considerably better value than the coastal cities.
xian.wifi: Good. Xian has fibre at 100-500Mbps and comprehensive 5G, plus a substantial university and aerospace research sector that supports business-grade infrastructure. Speeds are reliable for remote work. As everywhere in China, the Great Firewall means a VPN is required for Google and most Western tools, which is what holds this at 7.
xian.nightlife: Moderate. Xian has one of the largest student populations in China, with over a million across dozens of universities, and that supports a cheap and busy bar scene around the South Gate and the university districts. The Muslim Quarter stays open late for food rather than drinking. The scene is domestic rather than international.
xian.nature: Mixed. The city itself is flat and dense, but Mount Huashan, one of China's five sacred mountains and famous for genuinely dangerous plank walks, is 90 minutes east. The Qinling range south of the city separates northern and southern China and offers real hiking. Within Xian, the city wall and Tang paradise parks are the green space.
xian.safety: Very safe. Violent crime is rare, the city is comfortable to walk at any hour, and there is the visible police presence common across China. Petty theft around the railway station and the Muslim Quarter crowds is the most reported problem. Traffic and electric scooters are the main daily hazard.
xian.food: Excellent and distinctive. Xian is the eastern terminus of the Silk Road and the food shows it: roujiamo, the wheat-noodle traditions including biangbiang noodles, cumin lamb and yangrou paomo all come from here. The Muslim Quarter run by the Hui community is one of the best street food districts in China. Prices are very low.
xian.community: Thin, which the low score records. Xian has a large domestic student population and some language learners, but the foreign community is small and mostly teachers. Coworking exists but is limited. Most foreigners here are on a two-day trip to see the Terracotta Army rather than staying to work.
xian.english: English proficiency is low. Major tourist sites and the metro have bilingual signage, and staff at the Terracotta Army and larger hotels manage functional English, but daily life runs entirely in Mandarin with a strong local accent. Translation apps are necessary. This is a harder linguistic environment than the coastal cities.
xian.visa: There is no Chinese digital nomad visa, which is what caps this at 4. Xian is covered by the 240-hour visa-free transit exemption, and many European and Southeast Asian nationals now enter visa-free for 30 days. Americans, British and Canadians still need a visa in advance. Legal employment requires a Z visa.
xian.culture: Xian scores a 10 because it was the capital of thirteen Chinese dynasties over more than a thousand years, including the Han and the Tang. The Terracotta Army is one of the great archaeological discoveries of the twentieth century, the Ming city wall is the most complete in China, and the Big Wild Goose Pagoda dates to 652. The Silk Road began here.
xian.cleanliness: Ordinary. The area inside the city walls and around the major monuments is maintained because tourism demands it, and the metro is clean. Older residential districts and market areas are rougher, and the Muslim Quarter is chaotic by design. Dry dusty air leaves a film on everything that regular sweeping does not fully clear.
xian.airquality: Air quality is poor and the low score is deserved. Xian sits in the Guanzhong basin between the Qinling mountains and the loess plateau, which traps pollutants, and northern China's coal heating season runs November to March. Annual PM2.5 runs near 40-50 µg/m³. Spring dust from the northwest adds episodic spikes on top of the industrial baseline.

ahmedabad.climate: Ahmedabad is hot and dry, and the mid score is generous. April and May regularly reach 41-43°C, with the 2010 heatwave prompting India's first city heat action plan after hundreds of deaths. The monsoon from June to September brings relief and humidity. Winter, December to February at 15-30°C, is the only genuinely comfortable stretch.
ahmedabad.cost: Ahmedabad is one of the cheapest cities in this directory at around $650 a month, and the high score is fully earned. A one-bedroom in a decent area runs $120-235. Street food costs under a dollar a meal, autorickshaws are cheap, and Gujarat's low cost of living is a genuine draw.
ahmedabad.wifi: Good. Fibre from Jio, Airtel and ACT reaches most of the city at 100-300Mbps for very low prices, and India's mobile data is among the cheapest in the world. Ahmedabad has a growing startup and IT presence around SG Highway. Power cuts are less frequent here than in many Indian cities, though a backup is still sensible.
ahmedabad.nightlife: This is the lowest score in the category set and the reason is legal: Gujarat has been a dry state since 1960, with alcohol prohibited outright for residents. Foreign visitors can obtain a permit through hotels, but there are no bars in any conventional sense. Evenings run to cafes, food streets and late-night chai stalls instead.
ahmedabad.nature: Limited. The Sabarmati riverfront redevelopment gave the city a usable promenade, and Kankaria Lake is a decent urban park, but Ahmedabad is flat, dry and heavily built. The compensation is regional: the Rann of Kutch salt desert, Gir Forest with the world's only Asiatic lions, and Velavadar's blackbuck grasslands are all in Gujarat.
ahmedabad.safety: Ahmedabad is regarded as one of India's safer large cities, with lower reported crime rates than Delhi or Mumbai and a comparatively low incidence of crimes against women. Communal tensions have a serious history here, notably in 2002, though the city has been calm for many years. Traffic is by far the biggest daily risk.
ahmedabad.food: Excellent, and specifically vegetarian. Gujarati thali at Agashiye or Vishalla is a genuine institution, with dhokla, khandvi, thepla and undhiyu as everyday items, and the sweetness that distinguishes Gujarati cooking is real. Manek Chowk turns into a street food market after 10pm. Meat and alcohol are both hard to find, which shapes the whole scene.
ahmedabad.community: Thin for remote workers. There is a serious startup and design ecosystem anchored by IIM Ahmedabad and the National Institute of Design, and the textile and pharmaceutical industries are large, but the foreign population is small and coworking is limited. Nomads rarely stop here, which is what the low score records.
ahmedabad.english: English is an official language of India and is widely used in business, higher education and government. In Ahmedabad, Gujarati is the language of daily life and Hindi is broadly understood, with English strongest among the professional and student population. Signage is often trilingual. Getting by is straightforward; conversational depth requires Gujarati.
ahmedabad.visa: India has no digital nomad visa. It does run an efficient e-Visa system covering most Western nationalities, with 30-day, one-year and five-year tourist options that are issued online in a few days. Tourist visas do not permit local employment. The mid score reflects easy entry paired with no remote-work provision.
ahmedabad.culture: Ahmedabad became India's first UNESCO World Heritage City in 2017, for the walled old city with its pols, the tightly organised residential clusters, and its stepwells and mosques. Sabarmati Ashram was Gandhi's base from 1917 and the starting point of the Salt March. The Calico Museum of Textiles holds an extraordinary collection.
ahmedabad.cleanliness: Better than the Indian average, which the mid score reflects. Ahmedabad has performed well in the national Swachh Survekshan cleanliness rankings, and the riverfront and newer western districts are maintained reasonably. The old city and market areas are congested and dusty. Air-borne dust from the dry climate settles on everything.
ahmedabad.airquality: Poor, though better than the Indo-Gangetic plain cities. Annual PM2.5 runs around 45-55 µg/m³, roughly ten times the WHO guideline, driven by traffic, construction dust and industry. Winter is worst when cooler air traps emissions. Ahmedabad avoids the crop-burning smoke that devastates Delhi, which is why this is a 4 rather than a 1.

chennai.climate: Chennai is hot and humid essentially year-round, which holds the score at 6. Temperatures run 28-38°C with May and June reaching 40°C, and humidity rarely drops. The northeast monsoon arrives October to December rather than in summer, and it can be violent: the 2015 floods paralysed the city. Water scarcity in dry years is a recurring problem.
chennai.cost: Chennai is inexpensive at around $750 a month. A one-bedroom in Adyar, Velachery or near the IT corridor runs $140-295. Idli and dosa breakfasts cost under a dollar, the metro and suburban rail are cheap, and only imported goods and international schooling price like a Western city.
chennai.wifi: Good. Chennai is a major IT centre with the Old Mahabalipuram Road corridor hosting large technology campuses, and fibre from ACT, Airtel and Jio delivers 100-500Mbps cheaply across the city. India's mobile data is among the world's cheapest. Chennai is also a landing point for several submarine cables, which helps international routing.
chennai.nightlife: Weak, and the low score is honest. Tamil Nadu's licensing is restrictive, alcohol retail runs through the state-owned TASMAC chain, and most venues close around midnight. There are hotel bars and a small pub scene in Nungambakkam and around the IT corridor. Chennai is a conservative city where evenings run to music, film and food.
chennai.nature: Modest. Marina Beach is one of the longest urban beaches in the world at 13 kilometres, though swimming is unsafe and the water is not clean. Guindy National Park sits inside the city, which is unusual. The real draws are outside: Mahabalipuram's shore temples, the Coromandel coast and the Nilgiri hills a few hours west.
chennai.safety: Chennai is among the safer major Indian cities, with lower violent crime rates than Delhi and a reputation for being comfortable for women relative to the north. Petty theft and scams occur around transport hubs. Traffic is the dominant hazard: Tamil Nadu has some of India's highest road accident numbers. Monsoon flooding is a seasonal risk.
chennai.food: Excellent and distinctly Tamil. The idli, dosa, vada and sambar breakfast tradition is done better here than anywhere, Chettinad cooking brings genuine heat and complexity, and filter coffee is a serious local institution. Saravana Bhavan and Murugan Idli Shop are everyday rather than special. Prices are very low. Seafood along the coast is strong.
chennai.community: Moderate. The IT corridor supports a large professional population including returning diaspora and some foreign staff, and there is a startup scene with coworking around Guindy and OMR. International nomads are uncommon and the community is overwhelmingly Indian professional rather than transient, which is what the mid score records.
chennai.english: English is an official language of India and functions well in Chennai's business, IT and education sectors. Tamil is the language of daily life and Tamil Nadu has historically resisted Hindi imposition, so Hindi is less useful here than elsewhere in India. English is often the practical bridge for outsiders. Signage is usually bilingual.
chennai.visa: India offers no digital nomad visa, which caps this at a 5. The e-Visa system is efficient and covers most Western nationalities, with 30-day, one-year and five-year tourist options issued online within days. Chennai is a major international entry point. Tourist status does not permit working for a local employer.
chennai.culture: Chennai is the centre of Tamil culture, which is one of the oldest continuous literary traditions in the world. The Margazhi music season each December is the largest classical music and dance festival on earth, Bharatanatyam originated in Tamil Nadu, and Kollywood is a major film industry. The Government Museum holds outstanding Chola bronzes.
chennai.cleanliness: Mediocre. Chennai has invested in waste management and the central and IT areas are maintained reasonably, but drainage is inadequate, the Cooum and Adyar rivers are heavily polluted, and monsoon flooding regularly leaves debris. Beach litter along the Marina is a persistent problem despite clean-up drives. The mid-low score is fair.
chennai.airquality: Poor by global standards though better than northern India. Annual PM2.5 sits near 40-50 µg/m³, around ten times the WHO guideline, from traffic, construction and regional industry. Coastal sea breezes provide genuine dispersal that inland Indian cities lack. Chennai avoids the winter crop-burning haze that closes Delhi, which is why this is a 4.

hyderabad.climate: Hyderabad sits on the Deccan plateau at 540 metres, which makes it noticeably more bearable than the Indian plains. Summers still reach 38-40°C in April and May, but the elevation keeps nights cooler and humidity lower. The monsoon runs June to September. October to February at 15-30°C is genuinely pleasant.
hyderabad.cost: Hyderabad costs around $800 a month and is cheaper than Bangalore or Mumbai for comparable quality, which is part of why the IT sector expanded here. A one-bedroom in Gachibowli or Madhapur runs $175-355; older areas are cheaper. Food, transport and services are very inexpensive.
hyderabad.wifi: Excellent by Indian standards. HITEC City and Gachibowli host campuses for Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta, and the infrastructure follows: fibre at 100-1000Mbps from ACT, Airtel and Jio, at prices that would look like errors in Europe. Coworking around Madhapur is well provisioned. Power supply here is more reliable than most of India.
hyderabad.nightlife: Moderate. Telangana permits alcohol more freely than neighbouring states, and Jubilee Hills and Banjara Hills have a genuine pub, brewery and club scene serving the IT professional population. Most venues close by 1am under state rules. The scene is newer and smaller than Bangalore's, which the mid score records fairly.
hyderabad.nature: Limited, which the low score reflects honestly. Hussain Sagar lake sits in the middle of the city but is heavily polluted, and KBR National Park gives a walking loop in Jubilee Hills. The Deccan landscape of granite boulder fields around Hyderabad is genuinely distinctive, and the rock formations at Ananthagiri and Bhongir are within reach.
hyderabad.safety: Hyderabad is regarded as one of the safer large Indian cities, with lower violent crime than Delhi and a substantial police technology programme. The IT districts are comfortable. Old City areas warrant more care at night. Traffic is the main daily hazard by a wide margin, and monsoon waterlogging is a seasonal problem.
hyderabad.food: Outstanding, and Hyderabadi biryani is genuinely worth the reputation: the dum method, cooked sealed with the rice and meat together, originated in the Nizam's kitchens and Paradise or Shah Ghouse still do it properly. Haleem during Ramadan is a citywide event. Irani chai and Osmania biscuits are everyday. Prices are very low.
hyderabad.community: Moderate. The technology sector brings a large professional population including returning diaspora and international staff, and coworking around HITEC City is well developed with active meetups. Genuine international nomads remain uncommon; the community you join will be Indian tech professionals, which is what the mid score reflects.
hyderabad.english: English works well in Hyderabad's IT sector, higher education and business, as it does across urban India. Telugu is the state language and Hyderabadi Urdu is widely spoken, particularly in the Old City, and the local Deccani dialect is distinctive. Signage is usually trilingual. Daily life is manageable in English throughout the newer districts.
hyderabad.visa: India has no digital nomad visa, which is the ceiling on this score. The e-Visa system is efficient, covering most Western nationalities with 30-day, one-year and five-year tourist options issued online in a few days. Hyderabad has a major international airport. Tourist status does not allow work for an Indian employer.
hyderabad.culture: Hyderabad's cultural depth comes from four centuries as a Deccan sultanate and then the Nizam's state, which produced a distinct Indo-Persian synthesis. The Charminar dates to 1591, Golconda Fort is a major hill fortress, and the Salar Jung Museum holds one of the largest single-person art collections in the world. Qawwali and Urdu poetry remain living traditions.
hyderabad.cleanliness: Mediocre and uneven. Gachibowli, Madhapur and the affluent western districts are kept reasonably, and the city has improved in national cleanliness rankings. The Old City and market areas are congested and littered. Hussain Sagar is visibly polluted despite repeated remediation programmes. Construction dust is constant across the expanding western corridor.
hyderabad.airquality: Poor by global measures but better than northern India, which is what the mid score records. Annual PM2.5 runs around 40 µg/m³, roughly eight times the WHO guideline. Plateau elevation and better wind circulation help disperse pollutants, and Hyderabad is far from the crop-burning belt. Construction and vehicle emissions are the dominant local sources.

kolkata.climate: Kolkata is hot and very humid, sitting close to sea level in the Gangetic delta. April to June reaches 36-40°C with oppressive humidity before the monsoon breaks in June, and the rains through September are heavy. Winter, December to February at 14-27°C, is the compensation and is genuinely pleasant. Cyclone exposure from the Bay of Bengal is real.
kolkata.cost: Kolkata is one of the cheapest major cities anywhere at around $700 a month, and the high score is earned. A one-bedroom in a central area runs $95-210. Street food costs cents, the metro is India's oldest and among its cheapest, and hand-pulled rickshaws still operate. Living well here costs very little.
kolkata.wifi: Adequate. Fibre from Alliance, Airtel and Jio reaches most of the city at 50-300Mbps for low prices, and mobile data is very cheap. Kolkata's IT sector at Salt Lake Sector V is real but smaller than Bangalore's or Hyderabad's, and infrastructure outside it is less consistent. Power cuts during monsoon are common enough to plan around.
kolkata.nightlife: Better than expected and improving, which the mid score records. Park Street has been the city's nightlife spine since the 1960s, with Trincas and Someplace Else running live music, and Sector V has newer pubs serving the IT crowd. West Bengal licensing is comparatively liberal. The city has a genuine adda culture of long evening conversation.
kolkata.nature: Weak. Kolkata is dense, flat and short on green, with the Maidan providing the main open space and the Botanical Garden across the river holding the Great Banyan Tree, one of the widest in the world. The real draw is the Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest and a tiger reserve, three hours south.
kolkata.safety: Kolkata is often cited as one of India's safer big cities, with the lowest reported rate of violent crime among the major metros for several consecutive years, and it is generally regarded as more comfortable for women than the north. Petty theft and crowd risk are the everyday concerns. Traffic and monsoon flooding are the real hazards.
kolkata.food: Excellent and distinctly Bengali. The fish and rice tradition is serious, with hilsa and bhetki central, and the sweets, rasgulla, sandesh and mishti doi, are a genuine regional art. The Kathi roll was invented here, the Anglo-Indian and Chinese communities left real culinary legacies, and Bengali sweets shops operate on a scale seen nowhere else.
kolkata.community: Modest. There is an IT sector at Salt Lake, a large student population and a long-standing intellectual culture, but Kolkata attracts few international remote workers and coworking is limited. The city's expat presence is small and mostly institutional. The mid score reflects a warm and social city that simply is not on the nomad map.
kolkata.english: English functions well in Kolkata's professional, academic and business circles, helped by the city's long history as the British Indian capital and a strong tradition of English-medium education. Bengali is overwhelmingly the language of daily life and Hindi is widely understood. Signage is usually bilingual. English carries you further here than in most Indian cities.
kolkata.visa: India offers no digital nomad visa, which is what holds this at a 5. The e-Visa system works well for most Western nationalities, with 30-day, one-year and five-year tourist options issued online within days. Kolkata is a practical gateway to Bangladesh, Bhutan and the northeast. Tourist status does not permit local employment.
kolkata.culture: Kolkata scores a 10 with justification. It was the capital of British India until 1911 and the centre of the Bengal Renaissance, producing Tagore, the first Asian Nobel laureate in literature, and Satyajit Ray. Durga Puja was inscribed on the UNESCO intangible heritage list in 2021. College Street is the largest second-hand book market in the world. The trams still run.
kolkata.cleanliness: Poor, and the low score is honest. Waste collection is inconsistent, drainage is inadequate and monsoon waterlogging is routine, street litter is widespread, and the Hooghly river is heavily polluted. Colonial buildings across the centre are visibly decaying. There are clean and well-kept pockets, particularly Salt Lake and parts of south Kolkata, but they are the exception.
kolkata.airquality: Bad. Annual PM2.5 sits around 55-70 µg/m³, roughly twelve times the WHO guideline, and Kolkata regularly appears among the most polluted cities in the world. Winter is worst, when Gangetic plain inversions trap emissions from traffic, brick kilns and biomass burning. The city has fewer air quality controls than Delhi and considerably less political attention.

newdelhi.climate: Delhi's climate is severe at both ends, which is why this sits at 5. May and June reach 43-47°C, with 2024 setting record highs, and winter drops to 5-8°C with dense fog that closes the airport. The monsoon breaks in late June. October and February to March are the only genuinely comfortable months.
newdelhi.cost: Delhi costs around $900 a month, more than most Indian cities and cheap globally. A one-bedroom in South Delhi neighbourhoods such as Hauz Khas or Saket runs $235-470; Gurgaon and Noida are similar. Street food, autorickshaws and the metro are all very cheap. Rent is what separates Delhi from Kolkata or Chennai.
newdelhi.wifi: Adequate to good. Fibre from Airtel, Jio and ACT reaches most of the National Capital Region at 100-500Mbps cheaply, and Gurgaon and Noida have genuine business-grade infrastructure supporting large corporate campuses. Delhi proper is more variable, with older neighbourhoods less reliably served. Power cuts are less frequent than they were but still occur in summer.
newdelhi.nightlife: Good, and the strongest in northern India. Hauz Khas Village, Connaught Place and the Gurgaon Cyber Hub carry the density, with genuine clubs, breweries and a cocktail scene serving a large professional population. Delhi's licensing is more permissive than most Indian states. Most venues close around 1am, and the scene skews expensive by local standards.
newdelhi.nature: Weak. Delhi is flat, dense and heavily built, with the Lodhi Gardens and the Ridge forest providing the main relief and the Yamuna river badly polluted. The compensation is regional and substantial: the Himalayan foothills at Rishikesh and Mussoorie are five to seven hours, and Rajasthan's desert and Corbett tiger reserve are reachable for a weekend.
newdelhi.safety: This is Delhi's weakest social score and the mid-low rating reflects a real record. The city reports among the highest rates of crimes against women of any major Indian metro, and street harassment is a documented and persistent problem. Petty theft and taxi scams are common around transport hubs. Traffic and air pollution are the largest health risks.
newdelhi.food: Outstanding. Old Delhi's Chandni Chowk area is one of the great street food districts in the world, with Karim's, Paranthe Wali Gali and the kebab tradition of the Mughal kitchens. Punjabi and Mughlai cooking dominate, but every Indian regional cuisine has representation here because the whole country works in the capital. Prices run from cents to expensive.
newdelhi.community: The best in India for meeting people, which the score reflects. Delhi hosts the diplomatic corps, most international NGOs and media bureaux, a large corporate expat population in Gurgaon, and a real startup scene. Coworking is plentiful and meetups are frequent. It remains a city of postings rather than nomads, but the density of foreigners is genuine.
newdelhi.english: The strongest English environment of any Indian city. As the capital, Delhi runs its government, media, corporate and diplomatic life substantially in English, and English-medium education is the norm among the professional class. Hindi is the language of the street and Punjabi is widespread. Signage is bilingual throughout including the metro.
newdelhi.visa: India has no digital nomad visa, which caps this. Entry is straightforward: the e-Visa covers most Western nationalities with 30-day, one-year and five-year tourist options issued online in days, and Delhi is the country's main international gateway with the widest route network. The FRRO office here handles registrations for longer stays.
newdelhi.culture: Delhi scores a 10 on depth. Three UNESCO World Heritage Sites sit inside the city, the Red Fort, Humayun's Tomb and the Qutub Minar, and the layers run from the Delhi Sultanate through the Mughals to Lutyens' imperial capital. The National Museum, Crafts Museum and the Sufi shrine at Nizamuddin with its Thursday qawwali are all serious.
newdelhi.cleanliness: Poor. Waste management is inadequate for the population, the Yamuna is one of the most polluted rivers in India with visible chemical foam, and street litter and construction dust are pervasive. Lutyens' Delhi and parts of South Delhi are the well-kept exceptions. The Ghazipur landfill has become a national symbol of the problem.
newdelhi.airquality: This is the worst score in the entire directory and it is deserved. Delhi is routinely the most polluted major city in the world, with annual PM2.5 near 100 µg/m³, twenty times the WHO guideline. November and December are catastrophic, when Punjab crop burning combines with winter inversion and readings exceed 500. Schools close. This is a genuine health decision, not a nuisance.

dhaka.climate: Dhaka is hot, humid and low-lying. Summers before the monsoon reach 34-36°C with brutal humidity, the monsoon from June to October brings extremely heavy rain and routine street flooding, and winter from December to February at 12-26°C is the only comfortable stretch. Cyclone exposure from the Bay of Bengal is a real seasonal risk.
dhaka.cost: Dhaka is very cheap at around $700 a month and the high score is honest. A one-bedroom in Dhanmondi or Uttara runs $125-250, and areas outside the expat zones cost far less. Street food is a fraction of a dollar, rickshaws cost cents. Gulshan and Baridhara, where most foreigners live, price several times higher.
dhaka.wifi: Weak, which the low score records. Broadband is available in the central and expat districts at 20-100Mbps, and Bangladesh's mobile data is cheap, but reliability is the problem: power interruptions are frequent, load-shedding returned in force during the 2022 energy crisis, and the government has repeatedly shut down mobile internet nationally during political unrest, most severely in July 2024.
dhaka.nightlife: Almost nonexistent by international standards, and the low score is accurate. Bangladesh is a Muslim-majority country where alcohol is restricted, sold legally only to non-Muslims through licensed outlets and a handful of hotel bars and foreign clubs in Gulshan. Social life runs through restaurants, cafes and private gatherings instead.
dhaka.nature: Very limited within the city, which is among the densest urban areas on earth. Ramna Park and the Dhaka University campus provide the main green space. The compensation lies outside: the Sundarbans mangrove forest, Sylhet's tea gardens and the world's longest natural sea beach at Cox's Bazar are all reachable, though travel within Bangladesh is slow.
dhaka.safety: Mixed, which the mid-low score records. Violent crime against foreigners is uncommon and Bangladeshi hospitality is genuine, but political instability is a real factor: the 2024 uprising involved mass protests, curfews and internet blackouts. Petty theft and traffic accidents are everyday risks. Road safety is poor and monsoon flooding causes regular disruption.
dhaka.food: Good and underrated. Bengali cooking here is rice, fish and mustard oil at its base, with hilsa the prized catch, and Old Dhaka's Mughal legacy produced kacchi biryani, bakarkhani and the Chawkbazar iftar market during Ramadan. Prices are extremely low. The restaurant range is narrow compared to a comparable Indian city.
dhaka.community: Very thin. Dhaka has a substantial development and NGO sector plus garment-industry buyers and diplomats, mostly concentrated in Gulshan and Baridhara, but these are postings rather than a nomad community. Coworking is minimal. Almost nobody comes to Dhaka to work remotely, which is what the low score honestly reflects.
dhaka.english: English is widely used in business, higher education and government administration, a legacy of the colonial period and of the country's international development sector. Bengali is the national language and the language of all daily life, and Bangladesh's language movement of 1952 makes it a matter of national identity. Professionals speak good English.
dhaka.visa: Bangladesh offers no digital nomad visa. Visa on arrival is available to nationals of many Western countries for 30 days at Dhaka airport, and e-visas exist, though processing can be inconsistent. Business and work visas require sponsorship. The mid score reflects manageable entry combined with no provision at all for remote work.
dhaka.culture: Bangladesh's cultural identity is strong and specifically Bengali. Pohela Boishakh, the new year celebration, brings hundreds of thousands onto the streets and its Mangal Shobhajatra procession is UNESCO listed. Old Dhaka holds Mughal-era architecture including Lalbagh Fort and Ahsan Manzil. Bengali literature, music and the muslin weaving tradition are all genuine heritage.
dhaka.cleanliness: Poor, and the low score is honest. Dhaka is one of the most densely populated cities in the world and municipal services do not keep pace. Waste collection is inconsistent, the Buriganga river is severely polluted with tannery and industrial discharge, and monsoon flooding regularly leaves streets in a bad state. Gulshan is the maintained exception.
dhaka.airquality: Among the worst in the world. Dhaka regularly tops global pollution rankings alongside Delhi and Lahore, with annual PM2.5 near 80-100 µg/m³ and winter readings that exceed 300. Brick kilns ringing the city, construction dust, and vehicle emissions from an ageing fleet are the main sources. The dry season from November to March is severe.

islamabad.climate: Islamabad sits at the foot of the Margalla Hills at 540 metres, which makes it more comfortable than the Punjab plains. Summers reach 35-40°C in June with the monsoon breaking in July, and winters at 3-18°C are cool and dry with occasional snow on the hills. Spring and autumn are genuinely pleasant. Air quality, not temperature, is the seasonal problem.
islamabad.cost: Islamabad is inexpensive at around $800 a month, though it is the most expensive city in Pakistan. A one-bedroom in the F and E sectors runs $145-320. Food, domestic help and transport are very cheap. Imported goods carry heavy duties. The rupee's decline has made Pakistan cheaper still for foreign-currency earners.
islamabad.wifi: Weak, which the low score records. Fibre is available in the better sectors at 20-100Mbps, and there are decent providers, but reliability is the issue: load-shedding remains part of daily life, and the government has repeatedly throttled or shut down mobile internet and social platforms during political events. A generator or UPS is standard equipment.
islamabad.nightlife: Effectively absent, and the score of 2 is accurate. Alcohol is prohibited for Muslims in Pakistan and available to non-Muslims only by permit through a small number of outlets, so there are no bars. Islamabad is a planned administrative capital that closes early. Social life runs through restaurant dinners, cafes and private homes.
islamabad.nature: Excellent, and the strongest thing about the city. The Margalla Hills National Park begins where the residential sectors end, with the Trail 5 hike to Pir Sohawa a standard weekend activity, and Rawal Lake sits inside the city. Beyond that, the Karakoram Highway, Hunza and the Fairy Meadows below Nanga Parbat are among the great mountain landscapes on earth.
islamabad.safety: Mixed, and the mid score reflects the gap between Islamabad and the rest of the country. The capital is heavily secured, with checkpoints, a diplomatic enclave and a low street crime rate; most residents move freely. Pakistan overall carries genuine security warnings from Western governments, particularly for Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Petty crime in Rawalpindi is more common.
islamabad.food: Very good. Pakistani cooking here is Punjabi at its base: karahi, nihari, seekh kebabs, biryani and the tandoor bread tradition, with Peshawari and Afghan influences from the northwest. Melody and Jinnah Super markets have long-running food streets. Prices are very low. Islamabad has more international restaurants than any other Pakistani city.
islamabad.community: Very thin. Islamabad hosts the diplomatic corps, UN agencies and international NGOs, and there is a small but real technology and freelancing sector, since Pakistan is among the largest suppliers of freelance labour globally. Coworking exists in the Blue Area. Foreign remote workers passing through are almost unheard of, which the low score records.
islamabad.english: English is an official language of Pakistan and is the language of the courts, higher education, government documents and most business. Urdu is the national lingua franca and Punjabi is widely spoken locally. Educated Pakistanis speak good English and signage is often bilingual. This is one of the easier South Asian countries for an English speaker.
islamabad.visa: Pakistan modernised its system with an online e-visa in 2019 and has expanded eligibility considerably, but processing is inconsistent and some nationalities still face long waits or additional checks. There is no digital nomad visa. Certain regions require a No Objection Certificate. The mid-low score reflects genuine improvement from a restrictive baseline.
islamabad.culture: Islamabad itself is a planned city built from 1960 and carries little history, which holds this score at 6. The Faisal Mosque, one of the largest in the world, is the landmark. The depth is next door: Taxila's Gandharan Buddhist ruins are a UNESCO site 40 minutes away, and Rawalpindi's old bazaars predate the capital by centuries.
islamabad.cleanliness: Genuinely good and by far the cleanest major city in Pakistan, which the high score reflects. Islamabad was planned on a grid with wide tree-lined avenues and generous green space, municipal maintenance in the residential sectors is consistent, and there is no heavy industry. Rawalpindi immediately adjacent is a completely different picture.
islamabad.airquality: Moderate by regional standards and poor by global ones, which the mid score records. Annual PM2.5 sits near 35-45 µg/m³. The Margalla Hills and higher elevation give better circulation than Lahore, which is among the worst cities on earth, but winter inversion combined with crop burning in Punjab and brick kilns produces bad episodes from November to February.

belohorizonte.climate: Belo Horizonte sits at 850 metres in the Minas hills, which gives it a milder tropical climate than the Brazilian coast. Highs run 24-28°C most of the year and nights are genuinely cool, unusual for Brazil. The wet season from November to March brings heavy afternoon storms, and the dry winter from May to August is sunny and comfortable.
belohorizonte.cost: Belo Horizonte costs around $1,300 a month, cheaper than Rio or São Paulo and mid-range for Brazil. A one-bedroom in Savassi or Funcionários runs $360-640. Eating at a boteco or a per-kilo lunch buffet is inexpensive, and the city is compact. Imported electronics carry Brazil's notoriously heavy import taxes.
belohorizonte.wifi: Good. Fibre from Vivo, Claro and regional providers reaches most of the city at 200-600Mbps at reasonable prices, and 5G is available across the central districts. Belo Horizonte hosts the San Pedro Valley startup cluster, one of Brazil's more established technology scenes, so coworking and business-grade connections are readily available.
belohorizonte.nightlife: Strong, and BH claims more bars per capita than any other Brazilian city. The boteco is the local institution: informal neighbourhood bars serving cold beer and petiscos, concentrated in Savassi and Santa Tereza. Live music runs to samba, MPB and a real rock tradition. The scene is neighbourhood-based and social rather than club-driven.
belohorizonte.nature: Good. The city is ringed by the Serra do Curral and the Parque das Mangabeiras gives forested trails inside the municipality. Serra do Cipó National Park is 90 minutes away with waterfalls and cerrado landscape, and Ouro Preto's mountains are two hours. Minas Gerais is mining country, which shapes both the scenery and its damage.
belohorizonte.safety: Mid, which is the honest position for a large Brazilian city. Belo Horizonte's homicide rate has fallen substantially over the last decade and is now below the national average, and the central and southern districts are comfortable by day. Street robbery, particularly phone theft, is the everyday concern. Peripheral areas warrant real caution after dark.
belohorizonte.food: Excellent. Mineiro cooking is one of Brazil's great regional traditions, built on pork, beans, couve and corn: feijão tropeiro, frango com quiabo and pão de queijo all come from here. The Mercado Central is a genuine institution with hundreds of stalls. Minas also produces Brazil's best cheeses and most of its cachaça.
belohorizonte.community: Moderate. The San Pedro Valley startup scene gives the city a real technology community with active meetups and coworking, and the federal university brings students, but the foreign population is small. International nomads mostly choose Rio, Florianópolis or São Paulo. The mid score reflects a genuine local scene that few outsiders join.
belohorizonte.english: English proficiency is low, which the score of 3 records. Brazil ranks poorly on global English indices and Belo Horizonte is less internationally exposed than Rio or São Paulo, so outside the startup and academic sectors you will meet very little English. Portuguese is essential for anything beyond the most basic transaction.
belohorizonte.visa: Brazil runs one of the better digital nomad visas, introduced in 2022: one year, renewable, requiring proof of about $1,500 monthly income or $18,000 in savings and remote employment abroad. EU and UK nationals also get 90 days visa-free. Americans, Canadians and Australians now need an e-visa after Brazil reinstated reciprocity in 2025.
belohorizonte.culture: Belo Horizonte was Brazil's first planned modern city, laid out in 1897, and the Pampulha architectural complex by Oscar Niemeyer became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016. Minas Gerais has a distinct cultural identity, from the baroque towns of Ouro Preto to the Clube da Esquina music movement. Inhotim, an hour away, is among the largest open-air contemporary art museums in the world.
belohorizonte.cleanliness: Ordinary for Brazil. The central and southern districts are maintained reasonably, waste collection functions, and the city's hillside layout keeps drainage moving. Peripheral neighbourhoods are less well served. Litter around the market areas and after major events is visible. This is neither Curitiba nor a city with a serious sanitation problem.
belohorizonte.airquality: Moderate. Belo Horizonte's elevation and hill circulation help disperse pollutants, and annual PM2.5 sits around 15-20 µg/m³, which is poor against WHO guidance but reasonable in a global comparison. Vehicle emissions are the main source, with regional mining and steel operations contributing. The dry winter months produce the worst readings.

brasilia.climate: Brasília has a tropical savanna climate at 1,100 metres, which keeps temperatures pleasant at 26-29°C year-round with cool nights. The score of 8 is about temperature rather than comfort throughout: the dry season from May to September is intense, with humidity dropping to 15 percent or lower in August, dry enough that residents run humidifiers and nosebleeds are common.
brasilia.cost: Brasília is expensive for Brazil, with the highest per-capita income in the country driven by federal salaries. A one-bedroom in the Asa Sul or Asa Norte superquadras runs $455-820. $1,100 a month is realistic if you live modestly. The city's car-dependent layout adds transport cost that walkable Brazilian cities do not.
brasilia.wifi: Good. As the federal capital, Brasília has strong telecommunications infrastructure with fibre from Vivo, Claro and Oi reaching the planned sectors at 200-600Mbps, and comprehensive 5G. Government and diplomatic demand keeps business-grade service available. Coworking exists in the commercial sectors, though the scene is smaller than in São Paulo or Belo Horizonte.
brasilia.nightlife: Moderate. Brasília's design works against street life: there are no traditional streets or corner bars, and everything happens in designated commercial sectors reached by car. That said, the city has a legendary rock history, producing Legião Urbana and Capital Inicial, and the bar scene in the 400 blocks and around Lago Sul is genuinely active.
brasilia.nature: Better than the concrete reputation suggests. Brasília National Park is inside the city limits with cerrado savanna and natural swimming pools, and Lake Paranoá is a large artificial lake used for sailing and swimming. Chapada dos Veadeiros, one of Brazil's most spectacular national parks with waterfalls and quartz plateaus, is three hours north.
brasilia.safety: Mid. The Plano Piloto, the planned central area where most foreigners live, is comparatively safe with a heavy federal police presence. The satellite cities that house most of the metropolitan population have considerably higher crime rates. Car dependence means less street exposure than in other Brazilian cities. Vehicle break-ins and robbery at traffic lights are the common problems.
brasilia.food: Decent rather than distinguished. Brasília has no regional cuisine of its own, being a city built from nothing in 1960, but that means every Brazilian region is represented by the migrants who came to build and staff it. Federal salaries support a genuine fine dining scene. Prices are higher than most of Brazil.
brasilia.community: Thin for remote workers, which the low score records. Brasília has a large diplomatic corps, federal civil service and lobbying sector, so foreigners are present, but almost entirely on postings. There is little startup activity relative to other Brazilian capitals and limited coworking. Very few people choose Brasília as a remote-work base.
brasilia.english: Proficiency is low overall, as it is across Brazil, though the diplomatic and federal sectors raise the ceiling: staff at ministries, embassies and international organisations often speak good English. In shops, restaurants and daily services you will need Portuguese. The score of 4 reflects that split between a small fluent minority and everyone else.
brasilia.visa: Brazil's digital nomad visa, introduced in 2022, is genuinely useful: one year, renewable, requiring around $1,500 monthly income or $18,000 in savings from a foreign employer. Brasília is where the Federal Police headquarters handles registration. EU and UK nationals get 90 days visa-free; Americans, Canadians and Australians need an e-visa since 2025.
brasilia.culture: Brasília is itself the cultural artefact. Designed by Lúcio Costa with buildings by Oscar Niemeyer and completed in 1960, it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, the only city built in the twentieth century to receive that status. The Cathedral, National Congress and Itamaraty Palace are landmarks of modernist architecture. Museum and gallery depth is otherwise thin.
brasilia.cleanliness: Good, which the score reflects. The planned sectors are generously spaced with extensive green areas, waste collection is reliable, and Brasília's low density and wide avenues avoid the crowding that strains services elsewhere in Brazil. The satellite cities are a different picture. Dry-season dust settles heavily between May and September.
brasilia.airquality: Good by Brazilian and global standards. Brasília sits at altitude on an open plateau with steady circulation, no heavy industry and relatively low population density, and annual PM2.5 runs near 12-15 µg/m³. The exception is the dry season, when cerrado fires across Goiás and the surrounding region push smoke over the city, sometimes for weeks in August and September.

curitiba.climate: Curitiba sits at 930 metres and has a subtropical highland climate that is genuinely cool for Brazil, which is what holds the score at 6. Summers are mild at 25-27°C, winters at 7-19°C bring frost and occasional freezing nights, and rain is spread evenly through the year. The weather changes several times a day, a local joke with truth in it.
curitiba.cost: Curitiba is mid-range for Brazil at around $1,400 a month. A one-bedroom in Batel or the Centro runs $360-640. The public transport system is efficient and cheap enough to live without a car, which matters. Heating costs during the cool months are a line item most Brazilian cities do not have.
curitiba.wifi: Good. Fibre from Vivo, Claro and regional operators covers the city at 200-600Mbps, and 5G is available centrally. Curitiba has a real technology sector and a well-regarded federal university and engineering school, supporting business-grade infrastructure and a reasonable coworking supply. Service reliability is better than the Brazilian average.
curitiba.nightlife: Moderate. The bar scene concentrates in Batel and around Largo da Ordem, where the historic centre hosts a large Sunday fair. The student population from several universities keeps prices low. Curitiba is a comparatively reserved city by Brazilian standards, and the cool climate pushes social life indoors, which the mid score records.
curitiba.nature: Good. Curitiba is one of the greenest cities in Latin America by park area per resident, with the Botanical Garden's glasshouse as the emblem and Barigui and Tanguá parks genuinely used. Beyond it, the Serra do Mar railway to Morretes is one of the great train journeys in South America, and the Atlantic Forest and Ilha do Mel coast are 90 minutes away.
curitiba.safety: Mid. Curitiba's crime rate is around the middle for Brazilian capitals, better than the northeast and worse than the smaller southern cities. Batel, Água Verde and the central districts are comfortable by day, with the usual caution warranted after dark. Phone theft and street robbery are the common problems rather than violent crime against visitors.
curitiba.food: Decent. Curitiba's food reflects the German, Polish, Italian and Ukrainian immigration that shaped the state, so you will find pierogi, barreado from the coast and a strong bakery culture alongside standard Brazilian fare. The Mercado Municipal is good. Paraná produces excellent coffee. The scene is solid rather than a reason to come.
curitiba.community: Moderate. There is a real technology and startup scene, a large student population and an established coworking supply, and Curitiba's quality of life attracts Brazilians relocating from São Paulo. International remote workers are uncommon, and those in Brazil generally head for the coast. The mid score reflects a good local professional community.
curitiba.english: English proficiency is low, as across Brazil. The technology sector and university population include competent speakers, and the immigrant heritage means some families retain German or Ukrainian, but daily life in shops, clinics and offices runs in Portuguese. The score of 4 is accurate. Learning Portuguese is not optional for a stay of any length.
curitiba.visa: Brazil's digital nomad visa, launched in 2022, offers one year renewable with proof of roughly $1,500 monthly income or $18,000 in savings from foreign sources. EU and UK nationals enter visa-free for 90 days; Americans, Canadians and Australians have needed an e-visa since Brazil restored reciprocity in 2025. The mid score reflects a workable but bureaucratic process.
curitiba.culture: Curitiba's cultural offer is solid and unusually design-conscious. The Oscar Niemeyer Museum, known locally as the Eye, is a major building, and the Ópera de Arame theatre built inside a former quarry is genuinely striking. The city's European immigrant heritage is visible in its neighbourhoods. It lacks the historical depth of Salvador or Ouro Preto.
curitiba.cleanliness: This is Curitiba's calling card and the high score is earned. The city pioneered municipal recycling in Brazil with its 1989 Lixo que não é Lixo programme, achieving separation rates well above the national norm, and street maintenance in the central districts is consistently good. The parks are genuinely well kept. Peripheral areas are less well served.
curitiba.airquality: Good by Brazilian standards, which the high score reflects. Curitiba benefits from elevation, regular rainfall and steady circulation off the Serra do Mar, with annual PM2.5 near 12-16 µg/m³. The city's bus rapid transit system, copied worldwide, genuinely reduced vehicle emissions per capita. Winter wood burning in some residential areas is the main local source.

fortaleza.climate: Fortaleza has one of the most consistently pleasant tropical climates in Brazil, which the high score records. Temperatures hold at 27-31°C year-round with constant trade winds off the Atlantic that make the heat manageable. The rainy season runs February to May and is genuinely wet; the rest of the year is dry and sunny. There is effectively no cold season.
fortaleza.cost: Fortaleza costs around $1,300 a month, moderate for Brazil and cheaper than the southeast. A one-bedroom in Meireles or Aldeota near the beach runs $330-580; inland neighbourhoods are considerably less. Fresh fish, fruit and street food are inexpensive. The tourist strip along Beira Mar prices higher than the rest of the city.
fortaleza.wifi: Good. Fibre from Vivo, Claro and regional providers reaches the coastal and central districts at 200-600Mbps, and Fortaleza is a landing point for several transatlantic submarine cables, which genuinely helps international latency. 5G is available in the central areas. Coworking exists along the beachfront, serving a small but growing remote-work presence.
fortaleza.nightlife: Strong. Fortaleza has a serious reputation for going out, built on forró: the Nordestino music and dance tradition, with the Segunda-Feira forró nights a long-running institution. The Praia de Iracema and Dragão do Mar areas carry the bar and club density. The scene is loud, cheap and runs late. Beach barracas keep going all afternoon.
fortaleza.nature: Excellent. The city has usable urban beaches, but the real argument is the Ceará coastline: Cumbuco with its dunes and lagoons is 30 minutes away, Canoa Quebrada and Jericoacoara are a few hours, and this stretch is among the best kitesurfing coastlines in the world thanks to reliable trade winds from July to January.
fortaleza.safety: This is Fortaleza's clearest weakness and the low score is honest. Ceará has recorded some of Brazil's highest homicide rates, driven by gang conflict in peripheral neighbourhoods, and Fortaleza has appeared repeatedly on global lists of the most violent cities. Visitors are rarely targets and the beachfront is policed, but the underlying rates are serious.
fortaleza.food: Good and strongly regional. Ceará's coast supplies excellent seafood, with caranguejo, peixada and lobster central, and Nordestino staples like tapioca, baião de dois and carne de sol are everywhere. The Mercado dos Pinhões and the beach barracas are where the eating happens. Prices are low. The restaurant range is narrower than in the southeast.
fortaleza.community: Modest. Fortaleza has a growing kitesurf and beach-sport community that includes long-stay foreigners, particularly Europeans in the windy season, plus a small startup scene. Coworking along Beira Mar serves it. This is not an established nomad hub in the way Florianópolis is, which is what the mid score records.
fortaleza.english: Very low, which the score of 3 reflects. Fortaleza is less internationally exposed than Rio or São Paulo and Brazil ranks poorly on English proficiency generally. Some staff in the beachfront hotels and kitesurf schools manage functional English because European clients require it. Everywhere else, Portuguese is necessary.
fortaleza.visa: Brazil's digital nomad visa gives one year renewable on proof of about $1,500 monthly income or $18,000 in savings from a foreign employer, which is a genuine advantage over most of Latin America. EU and UK nationals get 90 days visa-free. Americans, Canadians and Australians have required an e-visa since 2025.
fortaleza.culture: Fortaleza's culture is Nordestino and specifically Cearense: forró music, the cordel literature tradition of printed verse pamphlets, and a strong humour and theatre scene. The Dragão do Mar cultural centre is a serious institution. Ceará also has a distinct handicraft tradition in lacework and coloured sand bottles. Historical architecture is limited compared to Salvador or Recife.
fortaleza.cleanliness: Mediocre. The Beira Mar tourist strip is maintained because the economy depends on it, and the affluent Meireles and Aldeota districts are reasonably kept. Peripheral neighbourhoods have inconsistent waste collection, and urban beaches suffer from sewage contamination that periodically makes them unsuitable for swimming. Litter after weekend beach use is a persistent problem.
fortaleza.airquality: Good. Constant Atlantic trade winds disperse pollutants continuously, there is limited heavy industry, and annual PM2.5 sits near 12-16 µg/m³, better than most large Brazilian cities. Vehicle emissions in the congested central corridors are the main local source. The dry season occasionally brings inland agricultural burning smoke, but it rarely persists.

manaus.climate: Manaus sits in the middle of the Amazon rainforest and the climate is hot and humid without meaningful variation: 30-33°C year-round with humidity around 80 percent. The distinction is rainfall, with the wet season from December to May bringing intense daily downpours and the river rising several metres. The heat here is genuinely draining rather than pleasant.
manaus.cost: Manaus is cheap at around $900 a month, helped by the Free Trade Zone that removes import duties on electronics, making them cheaper here than anywhere else in Brazil. A one-bedroom runs $220-455. The offset is geography: fresh food and most goods arrive by river or air, so groceries cost more than in coastal Brazil.
manaus.wifi: Adequate. Fibre reaches the central and industrial districts at 100-400Mbps, and Manaus has better infrastructure than its isolation suggests because the Free Trade Zone hosts substantial electronics manufacturing. Reliability is the weak point, with the city dependent on long-haul links, and service degrades quickly outside the urban area. Power interruptions occur.
manaus.nightlife: Moderate. Ponta Negra along the river is the main going-out area, with bars and clubs along the waterfront, and there is a local scene built around boi-bumbá and regional forró. The heat pushes everything late. Manaus is an isolated city of two million with a real nightlife of its own, though it is entirely domestic.
manaus.nature: The maximum score, and obviously so. Manaus sits at the confluence of the Rio Negro and the Solimões, where the Meeting of the Waters shows two rivers running side by side without mixing for kilometres. The Amazon rainforest begins at the city edge, with lodges, igapó flooded forest, pink river dolphins and genuine wildlife within a few hours by boat.
manaus.safety: Mid-low, which is honest. Manaus has a homicide rate above the Brazilian average and has been affected by drug trafficking along the river routes. The central areas and Ponta Negra are manageable with normal caution, and the port and outer districts warrant more. Street robbery is the common problem. Jungle excursions carry their own risks entirely separate from crime.
manaus.food: Distinctive and genuinely different from the rest of Brazil. Amazonian cooking uses river fish that exist nowhere else: tambaqui, pirarucu and tucunaré, alongside tucupi, jambu, which numbs the mouth, and fruits like cupuaçu and açaí eaten savoury here rather than as a smoothie. The Mercado Adolpho Lisboa is worth a morning. Prices are low.
manaus.community: Very thin. Manaus has an industrial workforce, some ecotourism operators and researchers at INPA, the national Amazon research institute, but almost no remote-work community and minimal coworking. The isolation is the reason: there is no road connecting Manaus to the rest of Brazil. The low score is accurate.
manaus.english: Very low. Manaus is one of the least internationally exposed large cities in Brazil, and outside ecotourism guides and hotel staff serving foreign visitors you will meet almost no English. Portuguese is essential. Indigenous languages including Nheengatu are spoken in the surrounding region. The score of 3 is if anything generous.
manaus.visa: Brazil's digital nomad visa applies here as everywhere: one year renewable with roughly $1,500 monthly income or $18,000 in savings from a foreign employer. EU and UK nationals get 90 days visa-free; Americans, Canadians and Australians need an e-visa since 2025. Manaus is also a practical entry point for Colombia and Peru by river.
manaus.culture: Manaus carries an extraordinary story. The rubber boom of the late nineteenth century made it briefly one of the wealthiest cities on earth, and it built the Teatro Amazonas, an Italianate opera house with European materials shipped up the river, completed in 1896 and still hosting an annual opera festival. Indigenous Amazonian cultures remain a living presence in the region.
manaus.cleanliness: Mediocre. Waste management struggles with the humidity, the rainfall and the informal settlements built on stilts over the igarapé creeks, which are heavily polluted. The central historic district and Ponta Negra are maintained reasonably. River pollution from the port and the urban creeks is the most visible problem and the hardest to fix.
manaus.airquality: Usually good, with a serious seasonal exception that the mid score reflects. For most of the year the surrounding rainforest keeps air clean and PM2.5 low. During the Amazon dry season from August to October, deforestation and agricultural fires push smoke over the city, and in bad years such as 2023 and 2024 Manaus has recorded some of the worst air quality readings on the planet for weeks at a time.

portoalegre.climate: Porto Alegre has a humid subtropical climate with more seasonal range than most of Brazil. Summers are hot and humid at 30-33°C, and winters at 9-20°C are genuinely cool with occasional frost, which surprises people who expect tropical Brazil. Rain falls year-round. The catastrophic floods of May 2024, the worst in the state's history, are part of the picture now.
portoalegre.cost: Porto Alegre costs around $1,000 a month, which is good value for a southern Brazilian capital. A one-bedroom in Moinhos de Vento or Cidade Baixa runs $270-510. The churrasco culture makes meat cheap and good, and the city is compact. Winter heating is a small cost most Brazilian cities avoid entirely.
portoalegre.wifi: Good. Fibre from Vivo, Claro and regional operators covers the city at 200-600Mbps, and Porto Alegre has a genuine technology sector, having hosted the International Free Software Forum for years and built a startup scene around it. Coworking is well supplied. Flood damage in 2024 disrupted infrastructure temporarily but service has been restored.
portoalegre.nightlife: Good. Cidade Baixa is the nightlife district, dense with bars and live music and busy through the week thanks to the student population from UFRGS and PUCRS. The gaúcho drinking culture is social and outdoor when the weather allows. The scene is affordable and local rather than international, which is what the score records.
portoalegre.nature: Decent. The Guaíba waterfront gives the city its famous sunsets and Parque Redenção is genuinely used, though the urban nature is limited. The state is the real draw: the Serra Gaúcha with Gramado and the Itaimbezinho canyon at Aparados da Serra are two to three hours away, and the coastal lagoons and beaches are within reach.
portoalegre.safety: Mid-low. Porto Alegre's crime rate is around the middle to upper range for Brazilian capitals, with street robbery and phone theft the everyday concerns rather than violence against visitors. The central and northern districts are comfortable by day. Rio Grande do Sul has seen organised crime pressure increase in recent years. Flood recovery has strained services.
portoalegre.food: Good and specifically gaúcho. Churrasco originated in this region as a cattle-country tradition rather than a restaurant format, and the meat quality is genuinely better here than in the rest of Brazil. Chimarrão, the shared yerba mate gourd, is a daily social ritual. Italian and German immigrant cooking is present. The Mercado Público is worth using.
portoalegre.community: Modest. There is a real technology and startup scene with active coworking, a large student population, and the city's free software and open government history left a technically literate culture. Foreign remote workers are uncommon, with most Brazil-bound nomads choosing Florianópolis three hours north. The low score reflects that rather than any unfriendliness.
portoalegre.english: Low, as across Brazil. The technology sector and universities include competent English speakers, and Porto Alegre's international conference history helped, but daily life runs entirely in Portuguese with a distinct gaúcho accent and vocabulary borrowed from Spanish. The score of 4 is accurate. Portuguese is necessary for any stay beyond a few weeks.
portoalegre.visa: Brazil's digital nomad visa gives one year renewable on proof of about $1,500 monthly income or $18,000 in savings from a foreign employer. EU and UK nationals enter visa-free for 90 days; Americans, Canadians and Australians have needed an e-visa since 2025. Porto Alegre's proximity to Uruguay and Argentina makes regional travel straightforward.
portoalegre.culture: Rio Grande do Sul has a strongly distinct identity, closer in some respects to Uruguay and Argentina than to the Brazilian northeast: the gaúcho cattle tradition, chimarrão, and the CTG cultural centres that maintain regional dance and dress. Porto Alegre hosted the first World Social Forum in 2001. The Fundação Iberê Camargo museum by Álvaro Siza is architecturally significant.
portoalegre.cleanliness: Ordinary and currently complicated. The central and affluent northern districts are maintained reasonably and the city has decent waste collection by Brazilian standards. The May 2024 floods inundated large parts of the city including the airport, and the recovery of drainage, sanitation and public space is still ongoing. Guaíba water quality remains a concern.
portoalegre.airquality: Moderate. Porto Alegre has annual PM2.5 near 15-20 µg/m³, poor against WHO guidance and reasonable in a Brazilian comparison. The city sits on a lake with decent circulation, and industry is moderate. Vehicle emissions dominate. Winter inversions and occasional smoke drifting from regional agricultural burning produce the worst readings.

bohol.climate: Bohol has a tropical climate with highs of 30-32°C year-round and warm sea temperatures throughout. The dry season from December to May is the best stretch, with the wet season from June to November bringing heavy but usually short downpours. The Philippines sits in the world's most active typhoon belt, and Bohol has taken direct hits, most severely from Odette in December 2021.
bohol.cost: Bohol costs around $800 a month, cheap by any international measure. A decent apartment on Panglao runs $260-520, and local Filipino food costs a couple of dollars a meal. Diving is the expense that adds up if you take it seriously. Alona Beach prices at tourist rates; living inland or in Tagbilaran costs considerably less.
bohol.wifi: This is Bohol's practical weakness and the low score is honest. Fibre from PLDT and Globe reaches Tagbilaran and parts of Panglao at 50-200Mbps, but coverage is patchy elsewhere on the island and speeds fluctuate. The Philippines has historically had among the slowest average connections in Southeast Asia. Power interruptions are common enough that a backup battery matters.
bohol.nightlife: Limited, which the low score records fairly. Alona Beach on Panglao has a strip of beach bars and a few late venues serving the dive and tourist crowd, and that is essentially the whole scene. Tagbilaran has local karaoke bars. Bohol is a quiet island where most people are up early to dive, not a party destination.
bohol.nature: The maximum score and it is not arguable. The Chocolate Hills, over 1,200 conical limestone mounds, became a UNESCO Global Geopark in 2023, the Philippine tarsier sanctuary protects one of the world's smallest primates, and the diving at Balicasag and Pamilacan is world class with reef walls, turtles and regular whale shark sightings. The Loboc River runs through jungle.
bohol.safety: Bohol is considered one of the safer provinces in the Philippines, with low violent crime and a tourism economy that depends on its reputation. The southern Philippines security advisories that Western governments issue apply to Mindanao rather than here. Petty theft is the main concern. The genuine risks are natural: typhoons, earthquakes and diving accidents.
bohol.food: Decent rather than a highlight. Filipino cooking on Bohol runs to adobo, lechon, kinilaw and very good grilled seafood straight off the boat, and Panglao has an international restaurant scene serving visitors. The range is limited by island logistics and Filipino food generally polarises newcomers. Prices are very low. Fresh fruit is excellent.
bohol.community: Thin. Panglao has a small population of long-stay divers, retirees and a handful of remote workers, and one or two coworking options exist near Alona. There is no established nomad hub in the way Siargao has developed. The low score is accurate: you will meet divers and expat retirees rather than a working community.
bohol.english: Excellent, and this is one of Bohol's genuine advantages. The Philippines is among the largest English-speaking countries in the world, English is an official language used in education, government and business, and proficiency is high even in rural areas. Everything from a tricycle fare to a clinic visit happens in English. Cebuano is the local language.
bohol.visa: The Philippines is unusually generous. Most Western nationals get 30 days visa-free on arrival, extendable in-country repeatedly up to a total of 36 months, which is among the longest tourist stays available anywhere. The country signed off on a dedicated digital nomad visa in 2025. Extensions are handled at the Bureau of Immigration office in Tagbilaran.
bohol.culture: Modest, which the mid score records. Bohol has genuine Spanish colonial heritage in its stone churches, several of which were damaged in the 2013 earthquake and have been rebuilt, and the Blood Compact of 1565 between Sikatuna and Legazpi is commemorated here. The island's culture is rural Visayan rather than a museum or arts destination.
bohol.cleanliness: Mixed. Panglao's tourist beaches are maintained because the economy requires it, and the interior is rural and green. Waste management across the island is inconsistent, plastic litter along roadsides is visible, and rapid tourism development on Panglao has outpaced sewage infrastructure, which is a documented concern for the surrounding reefs.
bohol.airquality: Very good. Bohol is a rural island with no heavy industry, constant sea breezes and minimal traffic outside Tagbilaran, so PM2.5 readings sit low most of the year. The local sources are agricultural burning of crop residue and the older diesel vehicles and tricycles in the towns, neither of which produces sustained poor readings.

haiphong.climate: Haiphong has a humid subtropical climate with four seasons, unusual for Vietnam. Summers from May to September are hot and wet at 32-34°C with heavy monsoon rain, winters from December to February are cool and damp at 15-20°C, and spring brings persistent drizzle. The city is directly exposed to typhoons crossing the Gulf of Tonkin, several most years.
haiphong.cost: Haiphong is very cheap at around $700 a month, and the high score is fully earned. A serviced one-bedroom runs $160-315, well below Hanoi or Ho Chi Minh City. Street food costs a dollar or two, and the local beer economy is famously inexpensive. Haiphong is one of the better value cities in Southeast Asia.
haiphong.wifi: Good. Fibre from Viettel, VNPT and FPT reaches the city at 100-300Mbps for very low prices, and Vietnam's internet infrastructure is generally solid. Haiphong is a major industrial centre hosting LG and VinFast plants, which supports business-grade service. The recurring national weakness is submarine cable faults, which periodically slow international traffic for weeks.
haiphong.nightlife: Modest. Haiphong has a genuine local drinking culture built around bia hoi, the fresh draft beer served on plastic stools for cents, and the area around Lach Tray and the city centre has bars and karaoke. Do Son beach has a small resort scene. This is a working port city rather than a nightlife destination.
haiphong.nature: Good, and the location is the argument. Cat Ba Island, the gateway to Lan Ha Bay and the quieter side of Ha Long Bay, is reachable by ferry or the coastal road, and Cat Ba National Park protects the endangered golden-headed langur.
