Do Son peninsula gives beaches within the city. Ha Long Bay itself is 90 minutes away.
haiphong.safety: Vietnam is one of the safer countries in Southeast Asia and Haiphong follows that pattern, with very low violent crime and comfortable streets at night. Petty theft and bag snatching by motorbike occur in the busier districts. The dominant hazard by a wide margin is traffic: Vietnam's road accident rate is high and motorbike density is extreme.
haiphong.food: Very good. Haiphong's signature dish is banh da cua, a crab and red noodle soup found properly nowhere else, and the port location means excellent and cheap seafood. Nem cua be, the square crab spring rolls, are another local speciality. Northern Vietnamese cooking generally is lighter and less sweet than the south. Prices are extremely low.
haiphong.community: Almost nonexistent for remote workers, which the score of 2 records honestly. Haiphong has a substantial foreign industrial management presence from Korean and Japanese manufacturers, but that is employment rather than a nomad scene, and coworking is minimal. Vietnam-bound remote workers go to Da Nang, Hoi An or Ho Chi Minh City.
haiphong.english: Low. Haiphong is an industrial port city with far less international exposure than Hanoi or Da Nang, and outside the manufacturing management sector and a few tourist-facing businesses you will meet very little English. Vietnamese is a tonal language that is genuinely hard for beginners. Translation apps carry most daily interactions.
haiphong.visa: Vietnam improved substantially in August 2023, extending the e-visa to 90 days with multiple entry for all nationalities, which is a real advantage over the previous 30-day limit. There is no digital nomad visa, and working locally requires a work permit. The mid score reflects easy and cheap entry with no formal remote-work provision.
haiphong.culture: Haiphong's identity is industrial and maritime rather than historical, which is what holds the score at 6. There is French colonial architecture around the opera house and the older central streets, and the city is known within Vietnam for its flame trees and its combative football culture. The Bach Dang River nearby was the site of decisive naval victories in 938 and 1288.
haiphong.cleanliness: Poor. Haiphong is a working port and industrial centre, and it shows: air-borne dust from the port and construction, litter in the canals and drainage channels, and inconsistent waste collection outside the central districts. The colonial core and the newer developments are kept reasonably. Heavy monsoon rain leaves streets in poor condition.
haiphong.airquality: Poor, which the low score records. Northern Vietnam suffers badly, and Haiphong's port traffic, cement and steel industry and coal power generation in the region combine with winter inversions to produce annual PM2.5 near 35-45 µg/m³. The worst readings come between November and March. Summer monsoon rain clears the air substantially.

kohtao.climate: Ko Tao has a tropical climate with warm sea and air year-round at 29-32°C. Its pattern differs from mainland Thailand: the Gulf islands' wettest period is October to December rather than the summer monsoon, and the rest of the year is largely dry and calm. February to April and June to August are the best diving windows. The score reflects genuinely reliable warmth.
kohtao.cost: Ko Tao costs around $1,000 a month, cheap for an island but more than mainland Thailand because everything arrives by boat. A basic bungalow or studio runs $235-590. Thai food remains very cheap, and dive packages are among the least expensive in the world. Imported goods and Western food carry a clear island premium.
kohtao.wifi: Adequate rather than good, and the score of 6 is honest. Fibre reached the island and the main cafes and dive resorts around Sairee offer usable connections at 20-100Mbps, but the whole island depends on a submarine link and speeds drop noticeably at peak times. Power cuts happen. Several cafes cater specifically to remote workers, which helps.
kohtao.nightlife: Moderate and specific. Sairee Beach carries the bar strip, with fire shows, beach parties and a rotating crowd of dive students, and the monthly parties draw people over from Koh Phangan. It is smaller and friendlier than the Full Moon scene next door. Most of the island is up early to dive, which caps how late things run.
kohtao.nature: The maximum score, entirely on account of what is underwater. Ko Tao is one of the highest-volume dive certification destinations in the world, with shallow protected bays, reliable visibility and reef at Chumphon Pinnacle and Southwest Pinnacle. Above water there are viewpoints, granite boulder coves and Koh Nang Yuan's connected sandbars a short boat ride away.
kohtao.safety: Generally safe with real caveats. Petty theft and motorbike rental scams are the common problems, and the island's roads are steep, sandy and genuinely dangerous, producing frequent scooter injuries. Ko Tao attracted international attention over several unexplained tourist deaths in the 2010s. Diving accidents and the limited medical facilities on the island are the more statistically relevant risks.
kohtao.food: Good. Thai food on the island is cheap and reliable, with the local restaurants around Mae Haad and Chalok serving proper southern Thai curries and fresh seafood, and there is a decent international spread of cafes, Italian and burger places serving the long-stay crowd. Range is limited by island size. Prices are low outside the beachfront resorts.
kohtao.community: Better than the island's size suggests, which the mid score records. Ko Tao has a genuine long-stay community of dive instructors, many of whom stay for years, plus a growing remote-worker presence with several dedicated coworking cafes. Turnover is constant, which makes meeting people easy. It is small and can feel claustrophobic over months.
kohtao.english: Good for Thailand. The dive industry runs entirely in English, instructors are overwhelmingly international, and every tourist-facing business on the island operates in English out of necessity. That makes Ko Tao considerably easier than mainland Thailand outside Bangkok. Thai staff away from the dive and hospitality sector speak less. Thai script signage is common.
kohtao.visa: Thailand improved markedly with the Destination Thailand Visa launched in July 2024: five years multiple entry, 180 days per entry extendable once, aimed explicitly at remote workers and costing around $290. Most Western nationals also get 60 days visa-free on arrival. The mid score reflects a genuinely useful new route with income and documentation requirements.
kohtao.culture: The lowest score here and honestly so. Ko Tao was essentially uninhabited until the twentieth century, used as a prison island in the 1930s, and its modern identity is entirely built around diving tourism since the 1980s. There is little Thai cultural infrastructure, few temples of note and no historical depth. Culture here means the dive community, not the island.
kohtao.cleanliness: Mixed and a genuine local concern. The beaches and dive sites are cleaned regularly, often by volunteer groups from the dive schools, but the island's waste and sewage infrastructure has not kept pace with visitor numbers. Freshwater is scarce and desalination-dependent. Runoff and untreated wastewater reaching the reefs is the documented problem.
kohtao.airquality: Very good. Ko Tao is a small island surrounded by open sea with constant breeze, no industry and minimal vehicle traffic beyond scooters, so PM2.5 sits low year-round. The island entirely avoids the agricultural burning haze that afflicts northern Thailand from February to April. Generator exhaust in the built-up areas is the only local source.

vungtau.climate: Vung Tau has a tropical climate moderated by its position on a peninsula, with sea breezes on three sides that make it noticeably more comfortable than Ho Chi Minh City two hours away. Temperatures hold at 28-33°C year-round. The rainy season from May to October brings heavy afternoon downpours; November to April is dry and pleasant.
vungtau.cost: Vung Tau is very cheap at around $800 a month. A one-bedroom near the beach runs $195-395, and inland is less. Street food costs a dollar or two, seafood straight off the boats is inexpensive, and the local beer economy is minimal in price. This is among the better value coastal cities anywhere.
vungtau.wifi: Good. Fibre from Viettel, VNPT and FPT covers the city at 100-300Mbps at very low prices, helped by the offshore oil and gas industry's demand for reliable business connections. 4G and 5G coverage is solid. Vietnam's recurring problem is submarine cable faults, which periodically degrade international traffic for weeks at a time.
vungtau.nightlife: Modest. There are beachfront bars along Thuy Van, a small expat pub scene serving the oil industry crowd, and the Vietnamese bia hoi and karaoke culture throughout. Vung Tau is a weekend resort for Saigon families rather than a party destination, so it is busiest Friday to Sunday and quiet through the week.
vungtau.nature: Very good. Vung Tau sits on a peninsula with beaches on both sides, Back Beach for length and Front Beach for the promenade, and two hills, Nui Lon and Nui Nho, giving genuine views. Ho Tram and Long Hai's quieter coast are close, and Con Dao's islands and national park are a short flight or overnight ferry.
vungtau.safety: Vietnam is among the safer countries in Southeast Asia and Vung Tau reflects that, with low violent crime and streets that are comfortable at night. Petty theft and motorbike bag-snatching occur. Traffic is the dominant risk, as everywhere in Vietnam. Rip currents on the open beaches are a genuine hazard and drownings occur each year.
vungtau.food: Very good. The seafood is the point: banh khot, the small turmeric shrimp pancakes, are a Vung Tau speciality, and the fishing fleet supplies the markets directly. Southern Vietnamese cooking is sweeter and herb-heavy, with banh mi and com tam everywhere. The oil industry left a small legacy of Russian and Western restaurants. Prices are very low.
vungtau.community: Thin, which the low score records. Vung Tau has a long-established foreign community connected to the offshore oil and gas industry, including a notable Russian presence from the Vietsovpetro joint venture, plus some retirees. Coworking is minimal and there is no meaningful nomad scene. Most remote workers in Vietnam choose Da Nang or Ho Chi Minh City.
vungtau.english: Low to moderate. The oil and gas sector operates in English and some tourist-facing businesses manage it, which is better than a typical Vietnamese provincial city, but ordinary daily life runs in Vietnamese. The tonal system makes the language hard for beginners. Translation apps handle most transactions. The score of 5 reflects that mixed picture.
vungtau.visa: Vietnam extended its e-visa to 90 days with multiple entry for all nationalities in August 2023, a genuine improvement on the previous 30-day cap, and the process is online and cheap. There is no digital nomad visa and working for a local employer requires a work permit. The mid score reflects easy entry without a remote-work route.
vungtau.culture: Limited, which the mid-low score records. Vung Tau was a French colonial seaside resort, Cap Saint-Jacques, and some villa architecture survives along with the lighthouse from 1862. The Christ of Vung Tau statue, 32 metres tall on Nui Nho with a staircase inside to the shoulders, is the landmark. Beyond that the city is a working port and resort town.
vungtau.cleanliness: Mixed. The main beach promenades and the tourist-facing areas are maintained because weekend visitors matter to the economy, and the city is generally tidier than Vietnam's industrial centres. Plastic litter accumulates on the less-used stretches of coast, particularly after storms, and waste collection outside the central wards is inconsistent.
vungtau.airquality: Moderate. Vung Tau's peninsula position gives it constant sea breeze and considerably better air than Ho Chi Minh City or the northern Vietnamese cities, with annual PM2.5 near 20-28 µg/m³. The local sources are the port, the offshore support industry and motorbike traffic. The dry season from December to March produces the poorest readings.

yangon.climate: Yangon has a tropical monsoon climate with three distinct seasons. The hot season from March to May reaches 36-38°C with high humidity, the monsoon from May to October is extreme with over 2,500mm of rain, and the cool dry season from November to February at 18-32°C is genuinely pleasant and the only comfortable time to be there.
yangon.cost: Yangon is very cheap at around $800 a month, made cheaper still by the collapse of the kyat since 2021. Local food and transport cost almost nothing. The complication is not price but access: international banking sanctions mean cards frequently do not work, and most transactions require cash brought in physically, usually clean US dollars.
yangon.wifi: This is one of the worst scores in the directory and it is deserved. Since the 2021 coup the military has imposed sustained internet restrictions, blocking social platforms, banning VPNs under a 2025 cybersecurity law with criminal penalties, and cutting service entirely in conflict areas. Electricity shortages mean blackouts of many hours daily. Remote work here is genuinely impractical.
yangon.nightlife: Limited and constrained. Yangon had a developing bar and restaurant scene before 2021, and some of it survives around downtown and Golden Valley, but curfews have been imposed repeatedly, the economy has contracted sharply and much of the international crowd left. The low score reflects a scene that was cut off rather than one that never existed.
yangon.nature: Modest. Yangon is a low-lying delta city with Kandawgyi and Inya lakes providing the main green space and People's Park adjacent to the Shwedagon. Myanmar's genuine landscapes, Bagan's plains, Inle Lake and the Shan hills, are elsewhere in the country, and internal travel is now restricted and in places dangerous due to the ongoing conflict.
yangon.safety: The low score reflects the country rather than street crime. Ordinary crime in Yangon is comparatively low, but Myanmar has been in civil war since 2021, with airstrikes, conscription enforced under a February 2024 law, arbitrary detention and periodic bombings. Western governments advise against all travel. Yangon itself is calmer than the border states, but the risk is systemic.
yangon.food: Good and genuinely distinctive. Burmese cooking sits between Indian, Chinese and Thai without being any of them: mohinga, the fish noodle breakfast soup, is the national dish, laphet thoke is a salad made from fermented tea leaves, and the Indian and Chinese communities in Yangon left substantial legacies. Street food is excellent and costs cents.
yangon.community: Almost entirely gone. Yangon had a growing international business and NGO community during the 2011 to 2020 opening, and most of it departed after the coup. What remains is a reduced humanitarian and diplomatic presence. There is effectively no remote-work community and coworking has largely closed. The score of 2 is accurate.
yangon.english: Moderate. English was the medium of instruction under British rule and older educated Burmese often speak it well, and the reform decade produced a generation of younger professionals with good English. Outside those groups proficiency is limited and Burmese script is impenetrable to newcomers. The score of 5 reflects a real but uneven capability.
yangon.visa: The low score is about conditions rather than paperwork. Myanmar's e-visa system operates and issues tourist visas for 28 days, but banking sanctions complicate payment, flight connections are limited, insurance often excludes the country, and most Western governments advise against all travel, which invalidates many policies outright. There is no remote-work route of any kind.
yangon.culture: Yangon's cultural weight is high and the score reflects it. The Shwedagon Pagoda, gilded and 99 metres tall, is among the most important Buddhist sites in the world and reportedly holds relics of four Buddhas. Yangon also has the largest surviving collection of colonial-era architecture in Southeast Asia, much of it decaying downtown. Burmese Buddhist practice is deeply woven into daily life.
yangon.cleanliness: Poor. Municipal services have deteriorated since 2021 as the economy contracted and administration fragmented. Waste collection is inconsistent, drainage floods badly during the monsoon, and the colonial buildings downtown are visibly decaying without maintenance funds. Some pagoda precincts and wealthier townships are kept well, but they are exceptions.
yangon.airquality: Poor. Annual PM2.5 sits near 35-45 µg/m³, driven by an old and poorly maintained vehicle fleet, widespread diesel generator use because of the electricity crisis, and regional agricultural burning. The dry season from December to April produces the worst readings. The monsoon months clear the air substantially, which is why this is a 4 rather than lower.

male.climate: Malé has an equatorial climate with almost no seasonal variation: 28-31°C air temperature and 28-29°C sea temperature year-round. The southwest monsoon from May to November brings the rain and rougher seas; December to April is dry, calm and the peak season. The high score reflects genuine consistency. Humidity is constant and heat relief comes from sea breeze alone.
male.cost: Malé is the second-worst cost score in this directory and it is deserved. Almost everything is imported by sea or air, and the Maldives has among the highest food and goods prices in Asia. A one-bedroom in Malé or Hulhumalé runs $700-1,200, and $2,200 a month is realistic. Resort prices are a separate universe entirely.
male.wifi: Adequate. Ooredoo and Dhiraagu provide fibre in Malé and Hulhumalé at 50-200Mbps, and mobile coverage across the inhabited atolls is reasonable, but prices are high by regional standards and the country depends on submarine links to Sri Lanka and India. Speeds on outer islands drop sharply. The score of 6 reflects usable but expensive service.
male.nightlife: The lowest possible practical score, and the reason is legal. The Maldives is a Muslim country where alcohol is prohibited outside licensed resort islands and the airport hotel, and Malé itself is entirely dry. There are no bars or clubs. Social life runs through cafes, which are genuinely central to Maldivian culture, and the seafront.
male.nature: The maximum score, on the strength of what surrounds the city rather than what is in it. The Maldives is 1,192 coral islands across 26 atolls with some of the best reef diving in the world, manta and whale shark aggregations at Hanifaru Bay and Ari Atoll, and water clarity that is genuinely exceptional. Malé itself is entirely built over.
male.safety: Safe by international standards. Violent crime against foreigners is rare and the Maldives depends economically on its reputation. Petty theft and gang-related incidents among local youth occur in Malé. The genuine concerns are practical: medical facilities outside Malé are limited so evacuation insurance matters, and the country's low elevation makes it acutely exposed to sea level rise.
male.food: Decent. Maldivian cooking centres on tuna, coconut and rice, with mas huni for breakfast, garudhiya fish soup and the short eats served in local cafes as the everyday staples. Sri Lankan and Indian influence is strong. Malé has a growing cafe scene. The range is limited and prices are high because nearly all ingredients are imported.
male.community: Thin. The Maldives launched itself at remote workers during the pandemic with a long-stay programme, and there is now a small guesthouse-island scene on Maafushi, Thulusdhoo and others where surfers and divers stay for months. Malé itself has almost no coworking and few long-stay foreigners outside the resort and construction workforce.
male.english: Very good. English is the medium of instruction in Maldivian secondary schools and universities and is used throughout government, business and the tourism industry, so proficiency is high across the working population. Dhivehi is the national language and uses the Thaana script. Practically everything a visitor needs can be handled in English.
male.visa: One of the most generous entry policies anywhere: every nationality receives a free 30-day visa on arrival, with no application and no fee, extendable in-country to 90 days. The Maldives also created a long-stay remote-worker programme. The only requirements are an onward ticket and confirmed accommodation. The high score is straightforwardly earned.
male.culture: Mid. The Maldives has genuine heritage in its coral stone mosques, six of which are on the UNESCO tentative list, with the Hukuru Miskiy in Malé dating to 1658 and carved from coral. Bodu beru drumming is living tradition. But the country is small, conservative and heavily oriented toward resort tourism, which limits the cultural infrastructure a visitor can access.
male.cleanliness: Mixed. Malé is dense and functional rather than pretty, and the country's waste problem is genuine: Thilafushi, the artificial island built as a landfill a few kilometres away, has become a widely reported environmental issue. Hulhumalé, the reclaimed island, is planned and better kept. Resort islands are immaculate and not representative.
male.airquality: Very good. The Maldives sits in the middle of the Indian Ocean with constant sea wind, no industry beyond the Thilafushi waste facility, and minimal traffic outside dense little Malé. PM2.5 readings are low year-round. The occasional degradation comes from open burning at Thilafushi and, in some seasons, haze drifting across the ocean from South Asia.

abidjan.climate: Abidjan has a tropical climate on a lagoon, hot and humid year-round at 28-32°C with high moisture. There are two rainy seasons, a heavy one from May to July and a shorter one in October and November, with a dry harmattan-influenced stretch in December and January. The humidity rarely lets up, which is what holds the score at 6.
abidjan.cost: Abidjan is moderate at around $900 a month, expensive by West African standards because it is the region's commercial capital. A one-bedroom in Cocody or Marcory runs $330-830, and the Plateau and Zone 4 expat areas cost considerably more. Local food at a maquis is very cheap; imported goods are not.
abidjan.wifi: Weak to moderate. Fibre from Orange, MTN and Moov reaches Cocody, Plateau and Zone 4 at 20-100Mbps, and Abidjan is a landing point for several West African submarine cables, which helps. Coverage outside the central communes is patchy, prices are high relative to income, and power interruptions are frequent enough that a backup is standard.
abidjan.nightlife: Genuinely excellent and among the best in West Africa, which the high score records. Zone 4 and Marcory carry the club density, and Abidjan is the birthplace of coupé-décalé, the music and dance movement that spread across francophone Africa in the 2000s. Maquis, the open-air grill bars, run into the early hours across every commune.
abidjan.nature: Mixed. Abidjan itself is a lagoon city, dense and built, though Banco National Park sits inside the metropolitan area with genuine rainforest. Assinie and Grand-Bassam's beaches are an hour east, Taï National Park with its chimpanzee population is a UNESCO site in the far west, and the coastline north toward Sassandra is undeveloped.
abidjan.safety: Mid, which is honest. Côte d'Ivoire has been stable since the 2011 crisis and Abidjan functions normally, but street crime is a real concern: phone snatching, robbery around markets and transport hubs, and risk after dark in some communes. Plateau, Cocody and Zone 4 are the areas most foreigners use. Traffic is chaotic and dangerous.
abidjan.food: Good. Ivorian cooking is worth the trip: attiéké, the fermented cassava couscous, with grilled fish is the national dish, alloco is fried plantain, and kedjenou is a slow-cooked chicken stew. The maquis format, open-air grills serving late into the night, is the way most eating happens. French bakeries are a genuine colonial legacy. Prices are low.
abidjan.community: Almost nonexistent for remote workers, and the score of 2 is accurate. Abidjan has a substantial expatriate business community in banking, cocoa trading, oil and development, and it hosts the African Development Bank, but these are postings. Coworking exists in Plateau and Cocody but serves local startups. Very few nomads pass through West Africa at all.
abidjan.english: Low. Côte d'Ivoire is francophone, French is the official language and the language of all administration, education and business, and English is uncommon outside international organisations and the larger hotels. Over 60 indigenous languages are spoken, with Dioula widely used as a trade language. French is genuinely necessary here.
abidjan.visa: Côte d'Ivoire operates an e-visa system that is straightforward by regional standards: apply online, receive pre-approval, and collect the visa on arrival at Abidjan airport, usually for 90 days. There is no digital nomad visa. ECOWAS nationals enter freely. The mid score reflects manageable bureaucracy in a region where visas are often difficult.
abidjan.culture: Abidjan is the cultural engine of francophone West Africa. Coupé-décalé and zouglou both originated here and shape music across the region, the Musée des Civilisations de Côte d'Ivoire holds serious ethnographic collections, and Grand-Bassam, the former colonial capital an hour away, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Baoulé and Senufo mask traditions remain living practice.
abidjan.cleanliness: Poor. Waste collection is inconsistent outside the central communes, the Ébrié lagoon is heavily polluted with untreated sewage and industrial discharge, and drainage floods badly during the heavy rains. Plateau and parts of Cocody are maintained. Abidjan was also the site of the 2006 Probo Koala toxic waste dumping, which remains a live grievance.
abidjan.airquality: Mediocre. Annual PM2.5 sits near 25-35 µg/m³, driven by an ageing vehicle fleet running on high-sulphur fuel, generator use, waste burning and construction dust. The harmattan season from December to February brings Saharan dust that raises readings substantially for weeks. Coastal breezes provide genuine dispersal that inland West African cities do not get.

agadir.climate: Agadir has one of the most reliable climates in this directory and the high score is earned. The Atlantic and the Anti-Atlas mountains combine to give around 300 days of sunshine with mild temperatures: 20-22°C in winter and 25-28°C in summer, far cooler than Marrakech inland. Rain is minimal and concentrated between November and March. Ocean breeze keeps summer comfortable.
agadir.cost: Agadir costs around $900 a month and is cheaper than Marrakech or Casablanca. A one-bedroom near the beach runs $300-610; inland neighbourhoods are less. Fresh fish, produce from the Souss valley and street food are all inexpensive. Alcohol carries heavy tax and imported goods cost more, but the overall picture is good value.
agadir.wifi: Adequate. Fibre from Maroc Telecom, Orange and Inwi reaches the central and tourist districts at 50-200Mbps, and 4G coverage across the city is good with 5G rolling out. Morocco's connectivity is solid rather than outstanding, and Agadir lags Casablanca and Marrakech. Coworking exists but the supply is thinner than in the established Moroccan nomad cities.
agadir.nightlife: Modest. Agadir is more permissive than most Moroccan cities because of its resort economy, so hotel bars, beachfront clubs along the marina and a few late venues operate legally. Alcohol is available but expensive and socially constrained outside tourist zones. The scene serves package holidaymakers rather than locals, which the mid score records.
agadir.nature: Very good. Agadir sits on a 10-kilometre crescent beach, Taghazout 20 minutes north is one of the best surf points in Africa with consistent Atlantic swell, and Paradise Valley's palm gorges are an hour inland. Souss-Massa National Park protects the last wild northern bald ibis population. The Anti-Atlas and the Sahara are reachable for longer trips.
agadir.safety: Morocco is among the safer countries in Africa and Agadir is a resort city with visible tourist police, so the high score is well founded. Violent crime is rare. Petty theft, aggressive touting and taxi overcharging are the usual annoyances. Solo women report street harassment, less than in Marrakech but present. Seismic risk is real: the 1960 earthquake destroyed the city.
agadir.food: Good. Moroccan cooking is a genuine draw, with tagine, couscous on Fridays and pastilla as the standards, and Agadir's Atlantic position means the grilled sardines and fish at the port are excellent and cost very little. The Souss region is the world source of argan oil. International restaurants along the beach serve the tourist market at higher prices.
agadir.community: Modest and growing. Taghazout up the coast has developed a genuine surf and remote-work scene with several coworking and coliving operations, and Agadir itself has a European retiree and long-stay population. It is smaller than the Marrakech or Essaouira scenes. The mid score reflects a real but dispersed community rather than a hub.
agadir.english: Moderate at best. Morocco operates in Arabic and French, with Tamazight now an official language and widely spoken in the Souss region, which is Amazigh heartland. Tourist-facing staff speak English, German and French because package tourism demands it. Away from that, French is far more useful than English. The score of 5 is fair.
agadir.visa: Morocco is easy, which the high score reflects. Most Western nationals enter visa-free for 90 days, no application required, and the country is a long-established base for long-stay foreigners. There is no formal digital nomad visa, and extending beyond 90 days means a border run or a residence application, but in practice the system is permissive.
agadir.culture: Mid, and specifically because Agadir has little old fabric: the 1960 earthquake destroyed the city and killed around a third of its population, so what stands is modernist reconstruction. The Kasbah ruins on the hill survive. The cultural substance is Amazigh rather than architectural, with distinct language, music and the weekly souks of the Souss valley.
agadir.cleanliness: Good by regional standards. Agadir was rebuilt on a planned grid with wide boulevards and generous public space, the beach and promenade are maintained because tourism depends on it, and the city is noticeably tidier than Morocco's older medina cities. Peripheral neighbourhoods are less well served. The dry climate keeps dust rather than mud as the issue.
agadir.airquality: Very good. Constant Atlantic wind, no heavy industry and a dry climate keep Agadir's PM2.5 low, generally around 12-18 µg/m³, which is among the better readings in North Africa. Traffic is the main local source. The exception is occasional Saharan dust carried north on hot chergui winds, which raises particulate readings sharply for a day or two.

algiers.climate: Algiers has a Mediterranean climate and it is genuinely good, which the high score records. Summers are warm and dry at 29-32°C with sea breeze, winters mild and wet at 9-17°C, and the city faces north across the bay so it catches maritime air. Rain falls between November and March. Snow is unknown at sea level.
algiers.cost: Algiers is cheap at around $800 a month, and the parallel exchange rate makes it cheaper still for anyone bringing hard currency. A one-bedroom in Hydra or Bab Ezzouar runs $225-520. Food, transport and services cost very little. The complication is that Algeria's banking system is largely closed, so cash brought in matters.
algiers.wifi: Poor, which the low score records. Algeria has among the slowest average internet speeds in North Africa, with ADSL still widespread and fibre rollout uneven, typically delivering 10-50Mbps. The government has repeatedly cut national internet access during school examination periods to prevent cheating, a practice that continued into recent years. Remote work here requires tolerance.
algiers.nightlife: Very limited, and the score of 3 is honest. Algeria is a conservative Muslim country where alcohol is legal but socially restricted and increasingly hard to buy, with most licensed outlets having closed. There are a handful of hotel bars. Social life runs through cafes, which are ubiquitous and central, and family gatherings.
algiers.nature: Good. Algiers sits on a steep bay with the Mediterranean below and hills behind, and the Atlas ranges are within reach. Tipaza's Roman ruins on the coast are an hour west, the Chréa National Park cedar forests are 90 minutes south, and Algeria contains a vast share of the Sahara, including the Hoggar and Tassili n'Ajjer massifs.
algiers.safety: Mid. Algiers itself is comparatively safe with low violent crime and a heavy security presence, and the civil conflict of the 1990s ended long ago. Western governments still advise against travel to border regions and the deep south. Petty theft occurs. The score reflects a safe capital inside a country with real regional restrictions and heavy state surveillance.
algiers.food: Good. Algerian cooking overlaps with Moroccan and Tunisian but has its own character: couscous, chorba soup, chakhchoukha and the French-influenced bakery tradition. Seafood on the coast is excellent and cheap. Algiers has genuine cafe culture with strong coffee and pastries. The restaurant scene is limited and international options are few.
algiers.community: Effectively zero, and the score of 1 is the lowest in the directory for a reason. Algeria receives very few foreign visitors, has almost no tourism infrastructure aimed at independent travellers, and hosts a small oil and diplomatic expatriate community that lives largely in compounds. There is no coworking scene and no remote-work community of any kind.
algiers.english: Low. Algeria operates in Arabic, with French remaining dominant in business, higher education and daily urban speech despite official Arabisation, and Tamazight is an official language spoken widely in Kabylie. English is taught but rarely used. The score of 3 is accurate: without French or Arabic, daily life here is genuinely difficult.
algiers.visa: One of the harder visas in this directory, which the low score reflects. Most nationalities need a visa arranged in advance at an embassy, requiring an invitation letter or confirmed hotel bookings and a bank statement, and processing is slow and inconsistent. Algeria introduced visa on arrival for the deep south tourism circuit only. There is no remote-work route.
algiers.culture: Substantial. The Casbah of Algiers is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, an Ottoman-era citadel and medina built into the hillside, and the city has some of the finest French colonial architecture anywhere, which is why it was called Alger la Blanche. Algeria holds seven UNESCO sites including Roman Timgad and the prehistoric rock art of Tassili n'Ajjer.
algiers.cleanliness: Mediocre. Central Algiers and the newer districts are maintained reasonably and the seafront boulevards are impressive, but waste collection is inconsistent in the older quarters, the Casbah is visibly deteriorating with buildings collapsing, and litter is common. Coastal pollution is a documented problem. State-owned services function unevenly.
algiers.airquality: Moderate. Algiers benefits from a coastal position and constant Mediterranean wind, giving annual PM2.5 near 25-30 µg/m³. The main sources are an ageing vehicle fleet running on subsidised fuel, and heavy traffic congestion in a city built on steep terrain with limited road capacity. Saharan dust events raise readings episodically.

isfahan.climate: Isfahan sits at 1,570 metres on the Iranian plateau, which gives it a cold desert climate with real seasonal range. Summers are hot and very dry at 35-38°C but with low humidity and cool nights, and winters drop to -3°C to 10°C with occasional snow. Rainfall is minimal at around 120mm a year. Spring and autumn are excellent.
isfahan.cost: Isfahan is the cheapest city in this directory at around $600 a month, and the collapse of the rial is the reason: anyone with foreign currency has enormous purchasing power. A one-bedroom is a small fraction of Western prices, meals cost a dollar or two. The complication is banking: international cards do not work in Iran, so all money must be carried in cash.
isfahan.wifi: One of the lowest scores here and it is deserved. Iran operates one of the most heavily filtered internet regimes in the world, blocking most Western platforms outright, and has imposed complete national shutdowns during protests, most severely in 2022. VPNs are widely used and periodically criminalised. Speeds on domestic connections are modest. Reliable remote work is not realistic.
isfahan.nightlife: Effectively nonexistent in any Western sense, which the score of 2 records. Alcohol is illegal in Iran with serious penalties, there are no bars or clubs, and public mixing of unrelated men and women is restricted. Social life is real but private: family gatherings, tea houses, and the evening promenade along the Zayanderud bridges, which is genuinely lovely.
isfahan.nature: Mixed. The Zayanderud river that defines Isfahan has run dry for much of the last decade because of upstream diversion and drought, which is a visible environmental tragedy locally. The surrounding landscape is high desert. The Zagros mountains offer skiing and hiking within a few hours, and the Dasht-e Kavir desert is accessible for trips.
isfahan.safety: Iran is safer for ordinary crime than most of the region, with low street crime and a genuine tradition of hospitality toward foreign visitors. The risks are political rather than criminal: arbitrary detention of dual nationals is documented, several Western governments advise against all travel, and regional escalation can close airspace at short notice. That is what caps this score.
isfahan.food: Very good. Persian cooking is one of the world's great traditions and Isfahan has its own dishes: beryani, a minced lamb speciality unrelated to Indian biryani, khoresh-e mast, and the gaz nougat the city is famous for. Kebabs, saffron rice and herb stews are everyday. Tea houses under the bridges are an institution. Prices are extremely low.
isfahan.community: Essentially zero, and the score of 1 is accurate. Iran receives few independent Western visitors, there is no remote-work community, no meaningful coworking aimed at foreigners, and the banking and internet situation makes long stays impractical. Iranians themselves are exceptionally welcoming to visitors, which is a different matter from an existing community to join.
isfahan.english: Low. Persian is the language of everything, and English is taught but not widely used outside the tourism sector, where guides and some hotel staff speak it well. Younger urban Iranians increasingly have functional English. The Persian script and the absence of Latin signage outside major sites make independent navigation difficult without help.
isfahan.visa: Difficult, which the low score reflects. Most nationalities need a visa arranged in advance through an authorised agency, and citizens of the United States, United Kingdom and Canada must travel on a guided itinerary with an approved operator. Israeli stamps bar entry. Visa on arrival exists for some nationalities but is unreliable. There is no remote-work provision.
isfahan.culture: Isfahan scores a 10 and earns it. Naqsh-e Jahan Square, built in 1602, is among the largest public squares in the world and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, framed by the Shah Mosque and the Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque, which are peaks of Persian Islamic architecture. The Safavid bridges, the Armenian Vank Cathedral and the covered bazaar are all extraordinary. The old saying is that Isfahan is half the world.
isfahan.cleanliness: Better than expected. Isfahan is a tourism showpiece within Iran and the historic centre, the square and the bridges are maintained carefully. Residential districts are ordinary and the dry desert climate means dust rather than litter is the constant. The dry riverbed running through the middle of the city is the most visible blight.
isfahan.airquality: Poor to moderate. Isfahan is a major industrial centre with a large steel plant and a refinery, and its basin position on the plateau traps emissions during winter inversions, pushing annual PM2.5 to around 30-40 µg/m³. Desert dust storms add episodic spikes. Schools have closed on the worst days. Summer readings are better than winter ones.

mombasa.climate: Mombasa is tropical and coastal, hot and humid year-round at 28-33°C with sea breezes that make it bearable. There are two rainy seasons, the long rains from March to May and the short rains in November, and the monsoon winds shape the year: the kaskazi from December to March and the kusi from June to September. Humidity is constant.
mombasa.cost: Mombasa costs around $800 a month, cheaper than Nairobi. A one-bedroom in Nyali or Bamburi runs $195-465. Local food at a Swahili restaurant costs a couple of dollars, matatus are cheap, and fresh fish and produce are inexpensive. Imported goods, international schools and beachfront housing at Diani price much higher.
mombasa.wifi: Weak to moderate. Fibre from Safaricom and Zuku reaches Nyali, Bamburi and the central island at 20-100Mbps, and Mombasa is the landing point for several East African submarine cables, which genuinely helps regional latency. Coverage drops outside those areas and power interruptions are frequent. Kenya's mobile money and 4G coverage are excellent, which offsets some of it.
mombasa.nightlife: Moderate. Mombasa's scene concentrates on the north coast at Nyali and Bamburi and on the south coast at Diani, with beach bars, clubs and a substantial tourist-driven trade. The old town is quiet and largely Muslim, so nightlife there is minimal. The mid score reflects a real but resort-oriented scene rather than a citywide one.
mombasa.nature: Excellent. Diani Beach on the south coast is repeatedly named among the best beaches in Africa, the Mombasa Marine National Park protects reef immediately offshore, and Watamu and the Kisite-Mpunguti reserve offer serious diving and dolphin watching. Tsavo East and Tsavo West, among Kenya's largest national parks, are two to four hours inland.
mombasa.safety: Mid-low, and the score is honest. Street crime including mugging and bag-snatching is common in Mombasa town, and Western governments advise against travel to counties near the Somali border, though the coastal tourist strip is not included in those warnings. Terrorism risk is a documented concern in Kenya generally. Beach areas are policed; the old town and town centre require care after dark.
mombasa.food: Good and distinctly Swahili. The coastal cooking blends Arab, Indian and African traditions: biryani, pilau, coconut fish curry, viazi karai and mahamri. Street food in the old town is excellent and costs almost nothing. The fresh seafood is the strength. Nyali and Diani have international restaurants at higher prices serving the tourist market.
mombasa.community: Modest. Diani in particular has developed a genuine remote-work presence, with coworking, coliving and an established community of long-stay foreigners drawn by the beach and Kenya's connectivity, and there is a long-standing expatriate and retiree population along the coast. Mombasa city itself has less. The mid score reflects a scene concentrated 30 kilometres south.
mombasa.english: Very good, which is one of Kenya's genuine advantages. English is an official language used throughout government, education, business and media, and proficiency is high across the working population. Swahili is the national language and the coast is its heartland, with Mombasa speaking a particularly rich variety. Everything a visitor needs works in English.
mombasa.visa: Kenya replaced its visa system with a mandatory electronic travel authorisation in January 2024, applied to almost all nationalities and issued online for around $30, valid for 90 days. In 2024 the government also introduced a digital nomad work permit for remote workers meeting an annual income threshold. The high score reflects real and recent liberalisation.
mombasa.culture: Substantial. Mombasa is over a thousand years old and was a major Indian Ocean trading port long before the Portuguese arrived; Fort Jesus, built in 1593, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Old Town's Swahili and Omani architecture is intact, Taarab music is living tradition, and the Swahili coast's blend of African, Arab and Indian culture is genuine rather than curated.
mombasa.cleanliness: Poor. Waste collection in Mombasa town is inconsistent, drainage floods during the rains, and plastic litter is widespread, though Kenya's 2017 plastic bag ban was among the strictest in the world and did make a visible difference. Nyali, Diani and the resort strips are maintained. Beach seaweed and marine litter are seasonal problems.
mombasa.airquality: Moderate. Constant Indian Ocean monsoon winds give real dispersal, and Mombasa's PM2.5 sits near 20-30 µg/m³, better than Nairobi. The local sources are an old diesel vehicle fleet, the port and cement works north of the city, and open waste burning, which is the most visible and the most locally damaging of the three.

monterrey.climate: Monterrey is hot and dry, sitting in a valley ringed by the Sierra Madre Oriental. Summers are severe, reaching 38-40°C from June to August with occasional higher spikes, and winters are mild at 10-22°C with rare cold fronts from the north. Rain is sparse and concentrated in late summer, and the region has faced serious drought and water rationing.
monterrey.cost: Monterrey is expensive by Mexican standards, being the country's industrial and corporate capital with the highest average incomes. A one-bedroom in San Pedro Garza García runs $810-1,620; central Monterrey is considerably less. $1,200 a month is realistic. Food, transport and services remain cheap by North American measures.
monterrey.wifi: Very good. Monterrey is Mexico's business capital with major corporate headquarters and a strong technology sector around Tecnológico de Monterrey, so fibre from Totalplay, Izzi and Telmex delivers 100-1000Mbps widely and business-grade service is easy to arrange. 5G coverage is comprehensive. Coworking supply in San Pedro and the centre is good.
monterrey.nightlife: Good. Barrio Antiguo is the historic nightlife district with bars and live music, and San Pedro Garza García carries the upmarket clubs and cocktail scene serving Mexico's wealthiest municipality. The large student population from Tec and UANL keeps things busy through the week. The scene is affluent and local rather than international.
monterrey.nature: Very good, and unusual for a large industrial city. The Sierra Madre rises directly from the valley: Chipinque and Cumbres de Monterrey National Park offer serious hiking within 30 minutes, the Huasteca canyon is a world-class rock climbing destination, and Cola de Caballo waterfall is nearby. The Cerro de la Silla is the city's defining landmark.
monterrey.safety: Mid. Monterrey went through severe cartel violence around 2010 to 2012 and improved substantially afterwards, with San Pedro Garza García now one of the safest municipalities in Mexico. Violence has risen again in Nuevo León in recent years. Central and southern districts are comfortable; some peripheral areas are not. Most visitors experience no problems.
monterrey.food: Very good and specifically norteño. Cabrito, roast kid goat, is the Monterrey signature, and the region's beef and grilling culture is genuinely different from central and southern Mexican cooking: carne asada is a social institution, machaca is everyday, and wheat flour tortillas rather than corn dominate. The restaurant scene in San Pedro is serious and expensive.
monterrey.community: Moderate. Monterrey has a substantial corporate expatriate population from the manufacturing and industrial sector, a real startup scene, and coworking to match, boosted by nearshoring investment since 2021. International nomads are less common than in Mexico City, Oaxaca or Playa del Carmen, which is what the mid score records.
monterrey.english: Moderate to good by Mexican standards. Monterrey's proximity to Texas, its corporate sector and Tecnológico de Monterrey's international programmes mean English is genuinely functional among the professional class, better than most of Mexico. In shops, taxis and everyday services Spanish is necessary. The score of 6 reflects that professional and everyday split.
monterrey.visa: Mexico is among the easiest destinations in this directory. Most Western nationals enter visa-free for up to 180 days, although immigration officers now exercise discretion and shorter stamps are common. There is no digital nomad visa, but the temporary resident visa, applied for at a consulate abroad on proof of income or savings, gives one to four years and is widely used.
monterrey.culture: Mid. Monterrey is a business city founded in 1596 whose identity is industrial rather than colonial, and it lacks the historic depth of Oaxaca or Puebla. What it has is serious and modern: MARCO, the contemporary art museum, is among Mexico's best, the Museo del Acero occupies a converted blast furnace, and the Macroplaza is one of the largest public squares in the world.
monterrey.cleanliness: Ordinary. San Pedro and the central Macroplaza area are maintained well, and Monterrey's municipal services function better than most Mexican cities. Peripheral areas are less well served. The Santa Catarina riverbed running through the city is usually dry and accumulates debris. Industrial dust from the surrounding plants settles across the valley.
monterrey.airquality: This is Monterrey's worst score and it is deserved. The city consistently records the poorest air quality of any Mexican metropolitan area, worse than Mexico City on particulates, with annual PM2.5 around 30-35 µg/m³ and frequent exceedances. The valley traps emissions from heavy industry, cement and steel plants, and a car-dependent population. Drought and dust make it worse.

tashkent.climate: Tashkent has a cold semi-arid continental climate with real seasonal extremes. Summers are hot and very dry at 35-38°C in July, winters are cold at -3°C to 6°C with snow and occasional deep freezes, and spring and autumn are short and genuinely lovely. Rainfall is low at around 440mm and concentrated in winter and spring.
tashkent.cost: Tashkent is cheap at around $900 a month, and the som's decline since the 2017 currency liberalisation has kept it that way for foreign earners. A one-bedroom in the centre runs $235-470. Plov, samsa and bazaar produce cost very little, the metro is inexpensive, and taxis are cheap. Imported goods carry a landlocked premium.
tashkent.wifi: Adequate. Fibre from Uztelecom and private providers reaches central Tashkent at 30-150Mbps, and the country has invested substantially since 2017, with 4G broadly available and 5G launched in the capital. Uzbekistan is doubly landlocked, which means international bandwidth transits neighbouring countries and adds latency. Service is workable rather than good, which the mid score records.
tashkent.nightlife: Moderate. Tashkent is the most liberal city in Uzbekistan, alcohol is legal and widely available, and there is a real bar, restaurant and club scene in the centre and around Mirabad, helped by a large young population. Soviet-era chaikhanas and modern cafes cover the daytime. The scene is domestic and improving rather than international.
tashkent.nature: Decent. Tashkent itself is flat and green with substantial Soviet-planned parks, and the Chatkal range of the western Tian Shan begins 80 kilometres away, with the Chimgan and Beldersay ski areas and serious summer hiking. The Aral Sea disaster and the Kyzylkum desert are further afield. Regional access is the argument rather than the city itself.
tashkent.safety: Uzbekistan is among the safer countries in Central Asia and Tashkent is comfortable to walk at night, with low violent crime and a visible police presence. Petty theft is uncommon. The country remains authoritarian and surveillance is present, which is a different consideration from personal safety. Traffic and aggressive driving are the main daily hazard.
tashkent.food: Good. Plov is the national dish and Uzbek versions vary by region, with the Tashkent central plov centre cooking it in enormous kazans daily. Samsa, lagman, shashlik and the tandoor bread tradition are everyday. Chorsu Bazaar under its blue dome is genuinely worth using. Prices are very low. Vegetarian options are limited.
tashkent.community: Thin. Tashkent has a diplomatic and development sector, some foreign business presence from the mining and energy industries, and a small but growing startup scene with coworking in the centre. Independent travellers pass through on the Silk Road route. There is no established remote-work community, which is what the low score reflects.
tashkent.english: Low. Uzbek is the state language and Russian remains widely used, particularly among older and urban residents, and both are far more useful than English. Younger Uzbeks increasingly study English and tourism staff manage it, but daily life in shops, offices and clinics runs in Uzbek or Russian. Signage uses both Latin and Cyrillic Uzbek scripts.
tashkent.visa: Uzbekistan liberalised dramatically after 2018 and now admits nationals of over 90 countries visa-free for 30 days, with a straightforward e-visa for most others. The country has also floated an IT-sector residence route. Registration with the authorities within three days of arrival is still required, usually handled by the hotel. The high score reflects genuine and recent opening.
tashkent.culture: Strong. Tashkent itself was largely rebuilt after the 1966 earthquake, so its architecture is Soviet modernist, and the metro stations are ornate enough to be a genuine attraction now that photography is permitted. The deeper heritage is close: Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva are all UNESCO World Heritage Sites on the Silk Road, reachable by fast train.
tashkent.cleanliness: Good. Tashkent is a planned city with wide boulevards, extensive tree planting and irrigation channels, and municipal maintenance is consistent by regional standards. The centre and the parks are well kept and the metro is spotless. Outer districts are more ordinary. The dry climate means dust rather than litter is the persistent issue.
tashkent.airquality: Poor in winter and moderate otherwise, which the mid score averages. Tashkent has recorded some of the worst air quality readings in the world during winter episodes, when temperature inversions trap emissions from coal and gas heating, traffic and regional dust in the valley. Annual PM2.5 runs near 35-45 µg/m³. Summer readings are considerably better.

ulaanbaatar.climate: Ulaanbaatar is the coldest capital city in the world and the score of 2 is not an exaggeration. January averages -20°C to -25°C with regular stretches below -35°C, and the winter runs from October to April. Summers are brief and genuinely warm at 22-25°C. The city sits at 1,350 metres in a river valley, which traps the cold.
ulaanbaatar.cost: Ulaanbaatar is inexpensive at around $900 a month. A one-bedroom in the central districts runs $230-435. Meat, dairy and local food are cheap, and the mining economy has kept some services reasonable. Winter heating is a substantial cost, and imported goods carry a heavy premium because Mongolia is landlocked between two countries.
ulaanbaatar.wifi: Adequate. Fibre in central Ulaanbaatar delivers 30-150Mbps at reasonable prices and 4G coverage in the city is good, with Mongolia having invested seriously in mobile infrastructure. The constraint is international routing through Russia and China, which adds latency, and coverage collapses outside the capital. Power supply is coal-dependent and strained in deep winter.
ulaanbaatar.nightlife: Moderate. Ulaanbaatar has a genuine bar and club scene in the centre around Sukhbaatar Square and Seoul Street, serving a young population in a country where nearly half the people live in the capital. There is a real local rock and hip-hop scene. Winter drives everything indoors for six months, which the mid score records.
ulaanbaatar.nature: The maximum score, and few places earn it more clearly. Gorkhi-Terelj National Park with its granite formations is an hour away, the Gobi Desert and the Orkhon Valley are within reach, and Mongolia has the lowest population density of any sovereign country, so genuine wilderness begins almost immediately. Horse riding across open steppe is ordinary rather than a tourist activity.
ulaanbaatar.safety: Mid. Violent crime against foreigners is uncommon, but pickpocketing and bag theft in the State Department Store area, Sukhbaatar Square and on crowded buses are frequently reported, and alcohol-related street incidents occur at night. Winter conditions are a genuine hazard: exposure, ice and vehicle breakdowns in extreme cold are more dangerous than crime.
ulaanbaatar.food: Limited, which the mid-low score records honestly. Mongolian cooking is built on mutton, beef, dairy and wheat because the climate permits little else: buuz dumplings, khuushuur fried pastries and tsuivan noodles are the staples. Vegetables are scarce and expensive. Ulaanbaatar has Korean, Chinese and Western restaurants that fill the gap for long stays.
ulaanbaatar.community: Thin. Ulaanbaatar has a mining and development expatriate community, a diplomatic presence and some English teachers, plus a small startup scene with a few coworking spaces. Independent travellers pass through in summer for the Trans-Mongolian route and Naadam. There is no established remote-work community, which is what the low score reflects.
ulaanbaatar.english: Low. Mongolian is the language of everything and uses Cyrillic script, which makes signage impenetrable at first. Russian remains common among older Mongolians and English has grown quickly among the young, with some tourism and business staff genuinely fluent. Outside those groups you will need translation apps. The score of 4 is fair.
ulaanbaatar.visa: Mongolia has liberalised substantially, admitting nationals of many countries including the United States, and since 2024 most EU states, visa-free for 30 days, with the policy extended through 2025. E-visas cover most others. There is no digital nomad visa. Registration is required for stays over 30 days. The high score reflects genuinely easy entry.
ulaanbaatar.culture: Strong and distinctive. Mongolian nomadic culture is living practice rather than heritage, with a substantial share of the population still herding, and the Naadam festival each July, featuring wrestling, archery and horse racing, is UNESCO listed. Gandantegchinlen Monastery survived the Stalinist purges that destroyed most Mongolian Buddhism. Throat singing and the morin khuur fiddle are genuine traditions.
ulaanbaatar.cleanliness: Poor. Roughly half of Ulaanbaatar's population lives in the ger districts, informal settlements on the hillsides largely without piped water, sewerage or waste collection, and the environmental consequences are severe. The central districts are maintained reasonably. The Tuul river is polluted. Spring thaw exposes a winter's accumulated waste and coal ash across the city.
ulaanbaatar.airquality: This is the worst air quality in the directory alongside Delhi, and in winter it is arguably worse. Ger district households burn raw coal for heating, the valley traps everything under an inversion, and PM2.5 readings have exceeded 500 and at times 1,000 µg/m³, hundreds of times the WHO guideline. A 2019 raw coal ban helped but did not solve it. Summer air is clean.

kanazawa.climate: Kanazawa sits on the Sea of Japan coast and is among Japan's rainiest cities, receiving around 2,400mm of precipitation annually. Winters are grey, damp, and cold (3-7°C), with frequent snow. Spring (late April to May) and autumn (October to November) offer mild, comfortable conditions. Summer is warm and humid but less brutal than Tokyo or Osaka, with temperatures averaging around 28°C.
kanazawa.cost: Kanazawa is significantly cheaper than Tokyo or Kyoto. Central one-bedroom apartments run $365-500 per month; outer areas drop to $265-365. Eating out is affordable at $5-10 for a sit-down meal. Coworking drop-in rates start at $4 per session. A realistic solo nomad budget lands between $870 and $1,330 per month.
kanazawa.wifi: Japan's broadband and mobile infrastructure is world-class, and Kanazawa is no exception. Dedicated coworking spaces deliver consistent 50-200 Mbps connections. 5G and 4G coverage is reliable across the city center and historic districts. Cafe WiFi at chains like Doutor and Starbucks is adequate for calls and email, though speeds vary. Pocket WiFi rentals and eSIMs are widely available at Komatsu Airport and Kanazawa Station.
kanazawa.nightlife: Katamachi is the main drinking and dining district, with izakayas, cocktail bars, and live music venues concentrated along the Sai River. The area has a local, relaxed feel rather than a tourist-heavy scene. Kiguramachi is a quieter companion area with craft cocktail bars and small restaurants. Kanazawa nightlife is modest by major city standards; bars tend to close by midnight or 1am. The Hirosaka Highball bar has been a neighborhood fixture since 1989.
kanazawa.nature: Kenrokuien is widely considered one of Japan's three most beautiful landscape gardens and sits in the city center. Kanazawa Castle Park adjoins it. The Noto Peninsula, a UNESCO Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System site, is accessible within 90 minutes by bus. The Sea of Japan coastline is reachable in under an hour, and the Hakusan mountain range provides hiking options within a short drive. Green space is integrated into the city fabric in an unusually pleasant way.
kanazawa.safety: Kanazawa is exceptionally safe. Violent crime is virtually nonexistent, and petty theft is rare even in busy market and tourist areas. The city is consistently rated highly for solo female travelers. Streets are safe at all hours, including the Katamachi bar district late at night. Standard Japan precautions apply: natural disaster awareness (earthquakes, the January 2024 Noto earthquake affected the region) and checking emergency alerts via the government app.
kanazawa.food: Kanazawa has one of Japan's most celebrated regional food scenes. Omicho Market supplies the city with fresh Sea of Japan seafood: nodoguro (blackthroat seaperch), snow crab, and shrimp are local staples. Kanazawa oden (simmered in a rich chicken-bonito broth) is a winter specialty. The city has multiple Michelin-starred restaurants alongside affordable conveyor-belt sushi and izakayas. Jibuni, a duck stew thickened with flour, is the signature local dish.
kanazawa.community: The nomad and expat community in Kanazawa is small but growing. LINNAS Kanazawa regularly hosts Urban Retreats bringing 20-30 international and local participants together. The creative and design community around the 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art provides some crossover with internationally minded locals. Expect to build your own social life rather than falling into a ready-made expat network. Locals are welcoming but socializing across the language barrier requires patience.
kanazawa.english: English proficiency in Kanazawa is noticeably lower than in Tokyo, Kyoto, or Osaka. Many restaurant menus are Japanese only, hotel staff may struggle with English, and public signage outside tourist zones is mostly Japanese. Key tourist areas have English signage and some bilingual staff. Translation apps are genuinely useful here. Locals are unfailingly polite and will make every effort to help despite the language gap, but self-sufficiency with basic Japanese phrases is strongly recommended.
kanazawa.visa: Citizens of approximately 70 countries including the US, UK, EU states, Australia, and Canada enter Japan visa-free for 90 days. A Digital Nomad Visa launched in 2024 allows a 6-month stay for remote workers earning at least $67,000 annually with proof of overseas employment and health insurance. The visa is non-renewable without a 6-month gap outside Japan. Remote work on a tourist visa sits in a legal grey area. Always verify current requirements at mofa.go.jp.
kanazawa.culture: Kanazawa was spared wartime bombing and retains intact samurai and geisha districts alongside preserved machiya townhouses. The city has a strong craft identity rooted in Edo-period patronage: Kenzan pottery, Kaga Yuzen silk dyeing, and Wajima lacquerware are all associated with the region. The 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art brings international contemporary work alongside the historical scene. Cultural immersion here feels genuinely layered rather than staged for tourists.
kanazawa.cleanliness: Kanazawa maintains the high cleanliness standards typical across Japan. Streets, public transport, markets, and parks are kept meticulously clean. Omicho Market is busy but orderly. Public restrooms are consistently clean and well-maintained. Kanazawa benefited from significant urban investment ahead of its 2015 Shinkansen opening, which is visible in the quality of public spaces around the station and in the Korinbo district.
kanazawa.airquality: Air quality in Kanazawa is generally good. Japan's industrial zones are not concentrated near the city, and Sea of Japan coastal winds help clear pollution. PM2.5 and AQI readings typically fall in the 'Good' to 'Moderate' range throughout the year. Occasional high-pollen spring days affect allergy sufferers, and dust from continental Asia can spike readings in early spring. No chronic air quality concerns for most remote workers on a medium-term stay.

sapporo.climate: Sapporo has a dramatic four-season climate. Summers (June-August) are mild and low-humidity at 20-26°C, offering relief from the heat that hits the rest of Japan. Winters are genuinely harsh, with temperatures dropping to -12°C and cumulative snowfall near 4-5 meters annually. Autumn from September to October is spectacular and arguably the most comfortable season for remote workers.
sapporo.cost: Sapporo is one of Japan's most affordable major cities. A solo nomad can live comfortably on $1,070-1,470 per month, covering a central one-bedroom apartment at $400-530, food, coworking, and transport. This is roughly 25-30% cheaper than Tokyo for equivalent urban quality and infrastructure.
sapporo.wifi: Public WiFi across Sapporo is inconsistent and not reliable for work. Coworking spaces like BYYARD and Treebase provide stable, fast connections. For any stay beyond a few days, a local SIM card from providers like IIJmio or Mineo is the practical solution. Speeds at dedicated coworking spaces are solid; random cafes are hit or miss.
sapporo.nightlife: Susukino is one of Japan's largest entertainment districts, packed with izakayas, craft beer bars, ramen alleys, and Japanese whisky bars. The Nikka Bar in Susukino specializes in Yoichi and Taketsuru whiskies. Ganso Ramen Yokocho is a 70-year-old alley of miso ramen shops. The scene is lively without being overwhelming, and last trains run until midnight.
sapporo.nature: Sapporo is the gateway to some of Japan's finest outdoor landscapes. Niseko ski resort is roughly 90 minutes away by bus; Furano's lavender fields and ski terrain are under two hours. Daisetsuzan National Park, Lake Toya, and Lake Shikotsu are all within a half-day trip. In summer, Mt. Moiwa and Maruyama Park offer accessible nature within the city itself.
sapporo.safety: Sapporo is extremely safe by any global standard. Violent crime is rare, petty theft is uncommon, and the city functions with Japanese precision even during heavy snow. Women traveling solo consistently report high comfort levels. The subway and bus systems are reliable and well-lit. The only notable hazard is icy sidewalks in winter, which can cause falls without proper footwear.
sapporo.food: Hokkaido's dairy, seafood, and produce make Sapporo one of Japan's best food cities. It is the birthplace of miso ramen: rich, butter-topped bowls for under $8. Hairy crab, sea urchin, and fresh salmon are local staples. Jingisukan grilled lamb is a city specialty. Morihiko Coffee is a beloved local chain for quality brews. Set lunches at neighborhood restaurants run $6-10.
sapporo.community: Sapporo's nomad and expat community is small but growing. Events in English are infrequent. BYYARD coworking hosts some community programming and has English-speaking staff, making it one of the better places to connect with other remote workers. Online groups for Hokkaido expats exist but are modest in size compared to Tokyo or Osaka. Building community here takes more deliberate effort.
sapporo.english: English proficiency in Sapporo is limited outside of tourist areas and some coworking spaces. Station signs and major tourist sites have English translations. However, dealing with landlords, local clinics, utilities, and smaller restaurants often requires Japanese or a translation app. Tourist information centers in Sapporo Station and at the airport offer English support.
sapporo.visa: Japan's tourist visa waiver allows 90 days for citizens of around 68 countries including the US, UK, Australia, and EU nations. Japan launched a Digital Nomad Visa in 2024 valid for 6 months, requiring income of at least $67,000 annually and international health insurance. No extensions are permitted. Working Holiday Visas are available for eligible nationals under age 30-35.
sapporo.culture: Sapporo carries a distinct Hokkaido identity: more spacious, less formal, and less crowded than Honshu cities. The city was founded in 1869 and has a grid layout unusual for Japan. Local pride centers on food, beer (Sapporo Brewery dates to 1876), and outdoor sports. Social norms are quintessentially Japanese: quiet public behavior, punctuality, and respect for shared spaces.
sapporo.cleanliness: Sapporo is immaculate. Streets, public transit, restaurants, and public restrooms are maintained to a high standard typical of Japanese cities. Snow removal in winter is impressively managed, with plowed roads and heated underground walkways keeping the downtown core functional. Recycling rules are strict; learning Sapporo's waste separation system is a practical necessity for longer stays.
sapporo.airquality: Air quality in Sapporo is good year-round. The city is geographically distant from the industrial pollution sources that affect some of Japan's main island cities. Hokkaido's prevailing winds come from the north and northwest, bringing clean air from the Sea of Japan. Pollen season in spring can affect allergy sufferers, but particulate matter and industrial pollution are not significant concerns.

hiroshima.climate: Hiroshima has a temperate humid climate with mild winters rarely dipping below freezing and hot, muggy summers peaking in August. Spring (April to May) and autumn (October) are the most comfortable seasons for nomads. A monsoon rainy season runs through June and July, and typhoons can affect the region from August into early October. Annual rainfall totals around 1,570 mm, making waterproof gear a sensible investment.
hiroshima.cost: Hiroshima is one of Japan's more affordable mid-size cities. A nomad budget of roughly 1,100 to 1,400 USD per month covers a furnished room, meals, transport, and a coworking membership. A one-bedroom apartment in the city centre averages around 330 USD per month. Eating out is cheap, with a solid set lunch at a local restaurant often under 10 USD, and the streetcar network keeps transport costs low.
hiroshima.wifi: Fixed broadband speeds across Japan are excellent, with median downloads often exceeding 200 Mbps in residential buildings. Cafes and coworking spaces typically offer reliable connections, though a handful of older independent cafes can be inconsistent. Mobile data on local SIM cards (IIJmio, Rakuten) is fast and affordable. Coworking spaces like Shake Hands and fabbit Hiroshima Ekimae advertise dedicated high-speed lines.
hiroshima.nightlife: Hiroshima's nightlife centres on the Nagaregawa and Shintenchi districts in Naka Ward, packed with izakayas, cocktail bars, and live music venues. The scene is lively but not overwhelming, suiting nomads who enjoy a social evening without club-level noise. Expat-friendly spots like Molly Malone's Irish pub and KeMBY's Brew Pub near Peace Park draw international crowds and offer English menus.
hiroshima.nature: Hiroshima sits at the confluence of six river deltas flowing into the Seto Inland Sea, offering scenic waterfront walks year-round. Miyajima Island (Itsukushima), a 30-minute ferry ride away, is a UNESCO World Heritage site with forested hiking trails and the iconic floating torii gate. The Chugoku Mountains to the north provide skiing in winter and hiking in summer, all within a short drive or train ride.
hiroshima.safety: Hiroshima ranks among Japan's safest cities with an extremely low crime rate. Violent crime is rare and petty theft is uncommon even in busy tourist zones. Streets feel safe at any hour, including around late-night entertainment areas. Standard city precautions apply: watch belongings in crowded tram stops and tourist spots near Peace Park. Natural hazard awareness is advisable during typhoon season.
hiroshima.food: Hiroshima is famous for its distinct layered-style okonomiyaki, stacked with noodles, cabbage, and egg, distinct from the Osaka version. Fresh Hiroshima oysters are harvested from the Seto Inland Sea and served grilled, raw, or fried at specialist bars across the city. Mazemen ramen and anago (conger eel) rice bowls are other local staples. The Hondori shopping arcade and Nagaregawa area concentrate a wide range of dining options.
hiroshima.community: The expat community in Hiroshima is modest but active, centred around the Hiroshima International Center and informal Facebook groups like Hiroshima Expats. Mazda headquarters draws international engineers and business professionals, creating a small but steady international population. English conversation groups, cultural exchange events, and bachata dance nights offer social entry points for new arrivals.
hiroshima.english: English proficiency in Hiroshima is limited outside tourism-facing businesses. Staff at major hotels, Peace Park attractions, and popular restaurants often speak basic English. Coworking spaces catering to internationals typically have English-capable staff. Navigating daily errands such as banking, clinics, or local izakayas will likely require translation apps or basic Japanese. Signage in tourist zones is bilingual.
hiroshima.visa: Japan launched a Digital Nomad Visa in 2024, valid for up to six months, requiring proof of income above approximately $67,000 annually and health insurance. Many short-stay nomads enter on a 90-day tourist exemption available to over 60 nationalities. Hiroshima's prefectural government has actively promoted startup attraction programs with some relocation support for entrepreneurs willing to register a business locally.
hiroshima.culture: Hiroshima carries a profound historical identity as the first city struck by an atomic bomb in 1945 and has rebuilt itself into a symbol of peace and resilience. The Peace Memorial Museum and Genbaku Dome are deeply moving landmarks that shape the city's civic character. Beyond history, Hiroshima has a strong local identity tied to the Carp baseball team, oyster festivals, and a vibrant arts scene along the Ota River.
hiroshima.cleanliness: Hiroshima maintains the high cleanliness standards typical of Japanese cities. Streets, public transport, and parks are well-kept, public waste bins are scarce but litter is culturally discouraged. Restaurants and cafes observe rigorous hygiene practices. The river network running through the city centre is clean enough for cycling paths and waterfront recreation. Tap water is safe to drink throughout the city.
hiroshima.airquality: Hiroshima's air quality is generally good, with an annual average AQI around 61 (US scale), classified as moderate. The city is less industrially dense than Osaka or Kitakyushu, and sea breezes from the Seto Inland Sea help disperse pollutants on most days. Winter temperature inversions and occasional yellow sand (kosa) blown from China can temporarily degrade conditions. Overall, air quality poses minimal concern for most nomads.

kurashiki.climate: Kurashiki has a humid subtropical climate with four distinct seasons. Spring (March to May) is mild and beautiful, culminating in cherry blossoms along the Bikan canal. Summer (June to August) is hot and humid, with a rainy season in June and temperatures regularly reaching 33 to 35 degrees Celsius through August, uncomfortable for outdoor work. Autumn (October to November) is cool, clear, and pleasant. Winter is mild by Japanese standards, occasionally dipping near freezing but rarely staying there. Overall the climate rewards planning your stay around spring or autumn rather than the punishing summer months.
kurashiki.cost: Kurashiki is not cheap. Japan's cost of living has risen even with a weaker yen, and while the city is more affordable than Tokyo or Osaka, it is pricier than most Southeast Asian nomad hubs. A single remote worker should expect $1,270 to $1,730 a month all-in, covering a modest one-room apartment, utilities, groceries, and some dining out. Tourist-facing restaurants in the Bikan quarter charge a premium; eating where locals eat, a few blocks from the historic streets, saves meaningfully. Budget honestly rather than assuming small-city Japan means small-city prices.
kurashiki.wifi: Wifi infrastructure is excellent and reliable, consistent with the rest of Japan. Home fiber internet is fast and inexpensive to install, typically delivering well over 100 Mbps, and most cafes near Kurashiki Station, including Starbucks, Doutor, and Tully's branches, offer free wifi alongside power outlets. Mobile data coverage is strong citywide with no dead zones worth mentioning. The main limitation is not speed but availability of dedicated workspaces, there is no real coworking space in Kurashiki itself, so most people rely on home internet or a rotation of chain cafes for connectivity.
kurashiki.nightlife: Nightlife in Kurashiki is modest and low-key rather than absent. The Bikan Historical Quarter quiets down considerably after shops close in the early evening, leaving a handful of small bars and izakayas around the station area and Achi neighborhood for a low-key drink. There is no real club scene or late-night district here, this is a smaller city built around history and daytime tourism, not nightlife. Okayama city, 15 minutes away by train, offers noticeably more bars and evening options if you want a bigger night out. For most nomads, evenings in Kurashiki mean a quiet dinner and an early night rather than bar-hopping.
kurashiki.nature: Kurashiki benefits from easy access to the Seto Inland Sea and the gentle hill country of Okayama prefecture, with scenic coastal and island views a short drive or train ride away.
