taichung.cost: Around $1350 a month, which makes Taichung meaningfully cheaper than Taipei for equivalent housing and a comfortable standard of living. Rent is the main saving. Everyday costs, particularly food, are very low given the quality: eating well from street stalls and night markets costs very little. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured cost data, so treat it as a working budget rather than a measurement.
taichung.wifi: Excellent. Taiwan has world-class digital infrastructure with fast, cheap fibre widely available and comprehensive mobile coverage at prices that are among the best value anywhere. Taichung is a major city with a full professional infrastructure and a growing coworking scene. The practical caveat for a foreigner is administrative: getting a local SIM and a home contract requires a residence permit or a passport plus a second identity document.
taichung.nightlife: Good and varied. Taichung has a substantial nightlife around the Yizhong Street and Gongyi Road areas, with clubs, bars and a well-established live music scene, and the city has a reputation within Taiwan for being more relaxed and social than Taipei. The night markets are the real institution: Fengjia is one of the largest in Taiwan and runs late every night, which is a form of nightlife in itself.
taichung.nature: Good. Taichung sits on the western plain with the Central Mountain Range immediately east, which means Dakeng's hiking trails are within the city limits and Hehuanshan, at over 3,400m and one of the most accessible high mountains in Asia, is a few hours away. Sun Moon Lake is an hour south. Gaomei wetlands on the coast are a well-known sunset spot with boardwalks over the mudflats and a large migratory bird population.
taichung.safety: Very safe. Taiwan has low crime by any international standard, Taichung is comfortable at any hour, and violent crime against foreigners is close to unheard of. The realistic hazards are traffic, particularly the enormous number of scooters, and natural: Taiwan sits on a major fault line and earthquakes are frequent, with the 1999 Jiji quake centred near Taichung causing severe damage. Building standards and emergency preparedness are now good.
taichung.food: The joint strongest score here, and Taiwan earns it. Taichung claims the invention of bubble tea, which is contested but taken seriously locally, and the night markets are exceptional: beef noodle soup, oyster omelettes, stinky tofu, sun cakes which are a Taichung specialty, and an enormous variety at trivial prices. Taiwan's food culture generally is one of the best in Asia and the standard of ordinary eating here is remarkable.
taichung.community: Modest but real. Taichung has a long-established foreign population built around English teaching, the universities and a growing technology and manufacturing sector, and it is a friendlier city for newcomers than Taipei by local reputation. There is no large nomad scene, though Taiwan's digital nomad visa has begun to change that. Anyone arriving alone will find English-teaching and university networks accessible and Taiwanese people genuinely welcoming.
taichung.english: Limited outside specific contexts. English is taught intensively but spoken confidence is low, and daily life in shops, markets and offices operates in Mandarin, with Taiwanese Hokkien widely spoken too. Signage on major roads and the metro is bilingual. Taiwan has a government policy goal of becoming bilingual, which is visible in younger people and in Taipei more than here. Translation apps work well. Some Mandarin makes a real difference.
taichung.visa: Taiwan grants most Western nationals 90 days visa-free on arrival, and this is extendable in some cases. Taiwan launched a digital nomad visa in 2025 for remote workers, allowing a six-month stay with an income requirement, alongside the longer-standing Employment Gold Card, which is a combined work permit and residence visa for qualified professionals valid up to three years and one of the more attractive schemes in Asia for those who qualify.
taichung.culture: Good. Taichung has the National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts and the National Museum of Natural Science, both substantial, and the city has invested heavily in architecture, most visibly the Taichung Metropolitan Opera House designed by Toyo Ito, which is genuinely remarkable. Lukang, an hour away, is one of the best-preserved historic towns in Taiwan. Taiwanese temple culture is everywhere and is living rather than preserved.
taichung.cleanliness: Good. Taiwanese cities are well maintained, waste collection operates on the distinctive system of musical trucks that residents bring their sorted rubbish to at fixed times, and recycling rates are high. Streets are clean and public facilities are well kept. The older lanes and the industrial districts are plainer. The standard is clearly above Southeast Asia and slightly below Japan, which is a high bar.
taichung.airquality: The weakest score here and a genuine consideration. Taichung has a large coal-fired power station, one of the biggest in the world, on the coast nearby, and the western plain traps pollution against the mountains during the winter northeast monsoon. From roughly October to March, air quality readings are frequently poor and sometimes bad enough that people stay indoors. Summer is considerably better. Anyone with a respiratory condition should weigh this carefully.

hualien.climate: Hualien sits between the Pacific and the Central Mountain Range, which gives it a warm, extremely wet subtropical climate. July highs reach about 31C and January lows stay around 16C, so winters are mild. Rainfall of 2712mm is the highest in this group, with October the wettest month at 443mm because the northeast monsoon hits this coast directly. Typhoons make landfall here more often than anywhere else in Taiwan, which is a genuine seasonal consideration from July to October.
hualien.cost: Around $1150 a month, cheaper than Taipei or Taichung and reflecting a small city on the less developed east coast. Rent is low and food costs very little. The tourism season around Taroko brings some seasonal pricing. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured cost data, so treat it as a working budget rather than a measured average of what people actually spend living here.
hualien.wifi: Good. Taiwan's infrastructure is strong nationally and Hualien has fast, affordable fibre in the town and reliable mobile coverage along the coastal corridor, which is where almost everyone lives. Coverage weakens quickly in the mountains and the gorge, as you would expect. There is minimal coworking, so most remote work happens from apartments and cafes. For normal work this is entirely sufficient and better than the town's size suggests.
hualien.nightlife: Limited, and the lowest score here. Hualien is a small town where the evening centres on the night market, which is genuinely good, and a handful of bars serving the tourist and student population. The Dongdamen night market is the main gathering place. Anyone wanting nightlife is looking at Taipei, which is two hours away by the fast train along a spectacular coastal line. This is a quiet place by design.
hualien.nature: A perfect score, and Taroko Gorge alone would justify it: a marble canyon that the Liwu river has cut thousands of feet deep, with roads and trails carved into the walls, half an hour from the town. Beyond it, the Central Mountain Range rises to nearly 4,000m, the Pacific coast runs south past Qingshui cliffs and the East Rift Valley, and whale and dolphin watching from Hualien port is reliable. Access to parts of Taroko has been restricted since the 2024 earthquake.
hualien.safety: Very safe from crime, at the Taiwanese standard, and comfortable at any hour. The hazards here are geological and meteorological rather than criminal, and they are real: Hualien sits on the collision zone between two tectonic plates and was hit by a magnitude 7.4 earthquake in April 2024 that caused deaths and major landslides, and typhoons strike this coast directly. Taiwan's emergency preparedness is excellent, and buildings are built for it.
hualien.food: Very good. The night market is the centre of it, with Taiwanese street food at its usual high standard, and Hualien has specialities of its own including mochi, which is a local product, and the seafood landed at the port. The indigenous Amis population, the largest indigenous group in Taiwan, contributes a distinct cuisine using wild greens, river fish and flying fish that is worth seeking out and is not available elsewhere.
hualien.community: Very small. Hualien has a modest foreign population of English teachers, some researchers and a scattering of long-stay travellers drawn by the landscape, and no nomad scene. Taipei has the numbers. The compensation is that Hualien is a relaxed and welcoming small town and the outdoor community around climbing, surfing and hiking is genuinely open. Anyone arriving alone should expect to build through those rather than find an existing group.
hualien.english: Limited. Outside the tourism businesses around Taroko and some younger people, daily life operates in Mandarin, with Taiwanese Hokkien and indigenous languages also spoken locally. Signage on main roads and at the tourist sites is bilingual. Translation apps handle most transactions effectively. This is a smaller and less internationally exposed town than Taichung, and English coverage is correspondingly thinner.
hualien.visa: Taiwan grants most Western nationals 90 days visa-free on arrival. Taiwan launched a digital nomad visa in 2025 allowing a six-month stay for remote workers meeting an income requirement, and the Employment Gold Card remains the stronger option for qualified professionals, combining work permit and residence for up to three years with tax advantages. Both are applied for before or shortly after arrival depending on the route.
hualien.culture: Moderate. Hualien's distinctive cultural content is indigenous: this is the heartland of the Amis people and several other groups, whose harvest festivals, music and crafts are living traditions rather than museum pieces, and the Amis Folk Center and the local cultural parks present them. Japanese colonial architecture survives in the old town, including the Pine Garden. The marble industry that Taroko's geology supports is a genuine local trade.
hualien.cleanliness: Very good. Taiwanese standards of maintenance and waste management apply, the town is small and tidy, the national park is properly managed, and the coastline and rivers are largely clean. The musical rubbish truck system operates here as everywhere in Taiwan. Earthquake damage and reconstruction are visible in places since 2024. The overall standard is high and comfortably above most of the region.
hualien.airquality: Very good, and much better than western Taiwan. The east coast faces the open Pacific with prevailing onshore winds, the Central Mountain Range blocks the pollution that accumulates over the western plain, and there is no heavy industry here beyond the marble and cement works, which are a local source. Readings are consistently good and the contrast with Taichung or Kaohsiung is dramatic, which is one of the real arguments for this side of the island.

cameronhighlands.climate: At 1453m the Cameron Highlands are the only part of Malaysia where you need a jumper, which is the entire point of the place. March highs reach only about 23C and January lows drop to 15C, so it is cool and spring-like year-round while the lowlands are hot and humid. Rainfall of 2622mm is heavy with a November to December peak, and mist and afternoon rain are normal rather than exceptional. There is no dry season.
cameronhighlands.cost: Around $900 a month, moderate for Malaysia and higher than the lowland cities because this is a domestic tourist destination with limited accommodation. Long-term rentals in Tanah Rata and Brinchang are reasonable outside the school holidays, when Malaysian and Singaporean families fill the place and prices jump. Food and transport are cheap. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured cost data, so treat it as a planning figure.
cameronhighlands.wifi: The weakest score here and the main practical obstacle. Connectivity in Tanah Rata and Brinchang is usable but not fast, the mountain terrain limits both fixed and mobile coverage, and reliability during heavy rain and mist is inconsistent. There is no coworking infrastructure. Mobile data is the more dependable option and coverage is patchy in the valleys and on the estates. Anyone dependent on stable video calls should test carefully before committing.
cameronhighlands.nightlife: Essentially none, and the lowest score in this set. The Cameron Highlands is a family holiday and hiking destination where things close early, alcohol is available but not central, and the evening consists of dinner and a night market. Malaysia's licensing and the largely Muslim domestic visitor base shape this. Anyone coming here expecting an evening scene has misunderstood the destination, which is genuinely about the daytime.
cameronhighlands.nature: Excellent, and the reason to come. The tea plantations that cover the hillsides are working estates and are genuinely beautiful, with several open to visitors. Beyond them, the mossy forest at the top of Gunung Brinchang is a rare and strange cloud forest ecosystem reachable by road, and the jungle trails through the Titiwangsa range offer real walking, including the routes to Gunung Irau. Rafflesia, the world's largest flower, grows in the surrounding forest.
cameronhighlands.safety: Safe. Malaysia has low violent crime and the Cameron Highlands is a quiet, family-oriented area where the main risks are not criminal. The genuine hazards are the trails, which are poorly marked in places and where people have become seriously lost, the mountain roads, which are narrow and busy with tour buses, and leeches in the wet forest. Medical facilities are basic, with serious cases going to Ipoh two hours away.
cameronhighlands.food: Good. The highlands grow much of Malaysia's vegetables, strawberries and tea, and the produce is genuinely fresh in a way that is unusual in the tropics. Steamboat is the local institution, eaten because it is cool enough to want hot soup. The Indian and Chinese restaurants in Tanah Rata are solid, the tea houses on the estates are a real experience, and prices are low. The range is limited by the small population.
cameronhighlands.community: Very small. The Cameron Highlands has essentially no foreign resident community and no nomad presence, and its visitors are Malaysian and Singaporean families and backpackers passing through for a few days. The permanent population includes a large Nepali and Bangladeshi workforce on the farms and estates. Anyone staying long should expect complete isolation from other foreigners, and to organise life around the landscape rather than people.
cameronhighlands.english: Good, which is normal for Malaysia. English is widely spoken across the country as a legacy of the colonial period and remains a working language in business, education and tourism, and coverage in the Cameron Highlands guesthouses, restaurants and shops is comfortable. Malay is the national language and Tamil and Chinese are widely spoken. A visitor can conduct essentially all of daily life in English without difficulty.
cameronhighlands.visa: Malaysia grants most Western nationals 90 days visa-free on arrival, which is more generous than most of Southeast Asia. The DE Rantau Nomad Pass is Malaysia's dedicated digital nomad visa, valid for up to twelve months and renewable once, open to remote workers and freelancers in digital fields with an income requirement, and it is one of the more straightforward schemes in the region. The Malaysia My Second Home programme covers longer commitments.
cameronhighlands.culture: Limited, and the score is honest. The Cameron Highlands was developed by the British as a hill station in the 1920s, and the legacy is mock-Tudor architecture, tea estates founded by Scottish planters, and a strawberry-and-scones tourism aesthetic that Malaysians enjoy unironically. The Orang Asli, Malaysia's indigenous peoples, live in the surrounding forest and some villages receive visitors. The disappearance of Jim Thompson here in 1967 remains the area's most famous story.
cameronhighlands.cleanliness: Middling. The main towns of Tanah Rata and Brinchang are ordinary Malaysian small towns, and the area has a visible problem with the environmental cost of its own success: intensive farming has cleared hillsides, plastic sheeting covers large areas, and landslides have followed. Litter along the roads and trails is noticeable. The tea estates themselves are well kept. This is a beautiful area under real development pressure.
cameronhighlands.airquality: Good most of the year, helped by the altitude, the forest and the constant rain. The regional exception is the haze from agricultural and peatland burning in Indonesia and sometimes in Malaysia itself, which in bad years blankets the whole peninsula for weeks between roughly June and October and reaches even here, though the altitude helps. Outside haze episodes the air is clean and noticeably fresher than the lowlands.

quetzaltenango.climate: Xela sits at 2341m, the highest place in this dataset, and the altitude defines everything. February highs reach only about 18C and January lows drop to 7C, so it is cool by day and genuinely cold at night, and heating is rare in Guatemalan buildings, which visitors consistently underestimate. Rainfall of 2605mm falls almost entirely in the May to October wet season, with September the peak, while the dry season from November to April is bright and clear.
quetzaltenango.cost: Around $700 a month, which makes Xela one of the cheapest cities in this dataset. Guatemalan prices are low, the city has no significant tourist premium, and the large population of Spanish students has produced an inexpensive homestay and rental market. Food from the markets costs very little. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured cost data, so treat it as a working budget rather than a measurement.
quetzaltenango.wifi: Adequate but not a strength. Xela has fibre available in the centre and the newer neighbourhoods at usable speeds, and mobile data coverage is reasonable, but reliability is inconsistent, power interruptions are not rare, and speeds are well behind what a European or East Asian city offers. Some coworking exists serving the language-school population. Anyone dependent on stable high-bandwidth work should test a specific connection before committing.
quetzaltenango.nightlife: Modest but real. Xela has a university population and a long-standing student and Spanish-school crowd, and the bars around Parque Centro America and the zona uno have a decent circuit with live music, salsa nights and cheap drinks. It is local and unpolished rather than a scene. The city has more going on after dark than Antigua's tourist bars would suggest, and the crowd is more Guatemalan.
quetzaltenango.nature: Excellent. Xela sits in a bowl surrounded by volcanoes: Santa Maria rises directly above the city and can be climbed in a long morning, with the active Santiaguito vent below it erupting regularly and visibly. Tajumulco, the highest peak in Central America, is a few hours away, and the Fuentes Georginas hot springs are close. The highland trek to Lake Atitlan is a well-established three-day route through Maya villages.
quetzaltenango.safety: The weakest score in this group and it needs a direct answer. Guatemala has high rates of violent crime nationally, and while Xela is considerably safer than Guatemala City and the tourist-facing parts feel comfortable, this is a country where caution is genuinely required: no walking alone at night, no isolated areas, taxis or arranged transport after dark, and awareness that armed robbery on intercity buses and on some volcano trails has occurred. Use guides for the mountains.
quetzaltenango.food: Adequate. Guatemalan highland cooking is based on maize, beans and the market vegetables of the altiplano, with pepian and kak ik among the genuinely good regional dishes, and the markets are excellent and very cheap. Xela has a reasonable range of restaurants serving the student population, including some international options. What is limited is the depth and ambition of the restaurant scene compared with Antigua, which is an hour and a half away and much more developed.
quetzaltenango.community: Better than most cities in this set, and specifically because of the Spanish schools. Xela is one of the main language-learning destinations in Latin America, with dozens of schools and a constant flow of foreign students, many staying weeks or months, plus a well-established NGO and volunteer sector. That produces a genuine, if transient, international community with meeting points and a social rhythm. It is not a nomad scene but it functions like one.
quetzaltenango.english: Limited, and that is largely the point of coming here. Xela is not a tourist city and English is spoken mainly at the language schools, some hostels and by younger educated Guatemalans. Everything else operates in Spanish, and in the surrounding villages in K'iche' Maya, which many people speak as a first language. This makes Xela an excellent place to learn Spanish and a demanding one to visit without any.
quetzaltenango.visa: Guatemala is part of the CA-4 agreement with El Salvador, Honduras and Nicaragua, which functions as a single zone: most Western nationals get 90 days across all four countries combined, so crossing between them does not reset the clock, which surprises people. Extensions of a further 90 days can be applied for in Guatemala City. Mexico or Belize are the practical exits. Guatemala has no digital nomad visa.
quetzaltenango.culture: Strong. Xela is the second city of Guatemala and the centre of K'iche' Maya culture, with a large indigenous population, living traditional dress in daily use, and the surrounding highland villages holding markets and festivals that are genuinely local rather than staged. The city's neoclassical centre reflects a period of nineteenth century prosperity from coffee. The Maya spiritual practices in the surrounding hills are active. Nearby San Francisco El Alto has one of the largest indigenous markets in Central America.
quetzaltenango.cleanliness: Middling to poor. Xela has the waste management and drainage problems common to Guatemalan cities, with litter visible on the streets and in the ravines, air pollution from old vehicles, and a general standard of public maintenance that is well below what visitors from Europe or North America expect. The historic centre around the main park is better kept. This is a working highland city rather than a presented one.
quetzaltenango.airquality: Moderate. The altitude helps but Xela sits in a bowl that traps air, and the main sources are heavy diesel emissions from the old buses and trucks that dominate Guatemalan transport, plus wood smoke from cooking and heating in the surrounding communities. Agricultural burning in the dry season adds to it. The volcano Santiaguito emits ash and gas regularly, which affects the area downwind. Readings vary considerably by day and location.

puertoviejo.climate: Puerto Viejo is tropical rainforest and very wet, taking around 3463mm a year with no dry season: even the driest month brings 159mm and December peaks at 523mm. Temperatures barely move, with highs around 29C and lows around 22C year-round, and the humidity is constant. The Caribbean coast runs on a different rhythm from the Pacific side of Costa Rica, with short drier windows in September and October and again around February, which is when the surf and the visitors peak.
puertoviejo.cost: Around $1700 a month, and the cost score of 4 is honest: Costa Rica is expensive by Central American standards and has become more so, with imported goods, restaurant prices and rentals in the tourist corridor all well above what Guatemala or Nicaragua ask. Puerto Viejo's popularity has pushed housing up further. Living locally and shopping at the markets helps considerably. This is our own estimate rather than measured cost data.
puertoviejo.wifi: Adequate but the weakest infrastructure aspect. Puerto Viejo has fibre in the town and the main coastal strip at usable speeds, driven by the number of remote workers who have settled here, but reliability is inconsistent, power cuts happen, and the heavy rain affects service. Coverage weakens quickly outside the main road. Several cafes and a couple of coworking spaces cater to remote workers. Test the connection before committing to a longer stay.
puertoviejo.nightlife: Good for a town this size and genuinely distinctive. Puerto Viejo has a reggae and Afro-Caribbean music culture that is real rather than performed, with beach bars along the strip, live music several nights a week and a crowd that mixes locals, long-stay foreigners and travellers. It is relaxed rather than intense, and it runs year-round rather than seasonally. This is one of the more sociable small towns in the region.
puertoviejo.nature: Excellent. The Gandoca-Manzanillo wildlife refuge runs south along the coast with rainforest meeting the beach, coral reef offshore and sloths, howler monkeys and toucans genuinely common rather than a promise. Cahuita National Park is just north with a good coastal trail. The Talamanca mountains rise inland into indigenous territory and some of the least disturbed forest in Costa Rica. Leatherback and green turtles nest along this coast between March and July.
puertoviejo.safety: Mixed, and worth a plain answer. Costa Rica is one of the safer countries in Central America but the Caribbean coast has a higher crime rate than the Pacific side, and Puerto Viejo has a real and persistent problem with theft from accommodation, beaches and parked vehicles. Violent crime against visitors is uncommon but drug-related activity is present. The practical advice is the standard one: nothing valuable on the beach, secure accommodation, no isolated night walks.
puertoviejo.food: Good and genuinely different from the rest of Costa Rica. This is Afro-Caribbean cooking, brought by Jamaican workers who built the railway: rice and beans cooked in coconut milk, rondon stew, patacones, jerk-style chicken and plenty of fresh fish. The Caribbean influence extends to the spicing, which is bolder than the mild Central Valley cooking. Prices in the tourist restaurants are high; the sodas and the roadside stands are much better value.
puertoviejo.community: Strong for a town this size. Puerto Viejo has a long-established international population, originally travellers and surfers who never left, now including a steady number of remote workers, yoga and wellness people and small business owners. There are cafes that function as meeting points and an easy social entry for anyone arriving alone. The mix of Afro-Caribbean, indigenous Bribri, Costa Rican and foreign residents gives it a genuinely unusual character.
puertoviejo.english: Widely spoken, which is unusual for Costa Rica. The Caribbean coast has an English-based creole spoken by the Afro-Caribbean population as a heritage language, and the tourism economy plus the large foreign resident community mean English works for almost everything in daily life. Spanish is the national language and is needed for administration and outside the tourist strip. This is one of the easiest places in Latin America for an English speaker.
puertoviejo.visa: Costa Rica grants most Western nationals 180 days on arrival, which is one of the most generous tourist entries anywhere and a major part of why so many foreigners base here. Costa Rica also has a digital nomad visa, introduced in 2022, valid for a year and extendable, with an income requirement and exemption from local tax on foreign income. Panama and Nicaragua are the practical land borders if a reset is needed.
puertoviejo.culture: Distinctive rather than monumental. The Caribbean coast's Afro-Caribbean culture, brought from Jamaica in the nineteenth century, gives the area its language, food, music and calypso tradition, and it remains culturally separate from the Spanish-speaking Central Valley. The Bribri and Cabecar indigenous territories inland are the largest in Costa Rica and some communities receive visitors on their own terms. There are no monuments here; the culture is what people do.
puertoviejo.cleanliness: Middling. The beaches and the town centre are reasonably kept and the national parks are properly managed, and Costa Rica takes its environmental reputation seriously. Against that, the main road through town is dusty and busy, waste collection is ordinary, and plastic on the beaches after heavy rain and river discharge is a recurring problem. This is a small tropical town rather than a manicured one, and it looks it.
puertoviejo.airquality: Very good. There is no industry, the population is small, the constant rain washes the air, and the surrounding rainforest and sea breeze do the rest. The only local sources are vehicle traffic on the coast road and occasional agricultural burning inland. Costa Rica's air quality generally is among the best in the Americas, and this coast is at the better end of that. Nothing here should concern anyone with a respiratory condition.

lafortuna.climate: La Fortuna has the highest rainfall in this entire dataset at around 5253mm a year, and there is genuinely no dry season: the driest month still brings 255mm and December peaks at 623mm. Sitting at 251m on the windward side of the continental divide beneath Arenal, the town catches everything the Caribbean trade winds carry. Temperatures are stable at around 28C by day and 20C at night. Mornings are often clear and afternoons often are not.
lafortuna.cost: Around $1750 a month, the highest in this group, and the cost score of 4 reflects it. La Fortuna is one of Costa Rica's most visited destinations and prices are set accordingly, with accommodation, tours and restaurants all at tourist levels. Living locally, away from the main strip, and shopping at the feria costs far less. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured cost data.
lafortuna.wifi: Adequate. La Fortuna's tourism industry has driven decent connectivity into the town, with fibre available and usable speeds in the centre and the main accommodation, and reliable mobile coverage in the valley. Reliability suffers in heavy weather and power cuts occur. Coverage falls away quickly on the roads out towards the lake and into the forest. There is minimal coworking. For normal remote work the town centre is workable.
lafortuna.nightlife: Limited. La Fortuna is a tour town where people go to bed early because the activities start early, and the evening consists of restaurants along the main street and a handful of bars, plus the hot springs, which many people treat as the evening itself. There is no scene to speak of. The crowd is families, couples and adventure tourists rather than a drinking one, which shapes everything.
lafortuna.nature: A perfect score, and Arenal alone would earn much of it: a near-perfect volcanic cone that was in continuous eruption from 1968 to 2010 and remains the town's backdrop. Around it sit Arenal Volcano National Park, the enormous lake, the La Fortuna waterfall, hanging bridges through primary rainforest, and the Rio Celeste with its improbably blue water at Tenorio. Monteverde's cloud forest is a few hours away. Wildlife is abundant and easy to see.
lafortuna.safety: Safe. La Fortuna is a small, prosperous tourism town with low crime and a comfortable feel, noticeably safer than the Caribbean coast or the larger Costa Rican cities. Petty theft from vehicles and accommodation is the realistic concern. The genuine hazards are the activities: river and canyoning accidents, and the volcano itself, whose slopes are restricted for good reason. Medical facilities are limited, with serious cases going to San Jose.
lafortuna.food: Adequate. Costa Rican cooking is mild and comforting rather than exciting, based on the casado plate of rice, beans, plantain and a protein, with gallo pinto for breakfast, and the sodas that serve it are cheap and good. La Fortuna's tourist restaurants offer international food at high prices and variable quality. The local produce is excellent and the coffee is a genuine national product. Range is limited outside the tourist offering.
lafortuna.community: Modest. La Fortuna has a small foreign resident population working in tourism and a constant flow of visitors who stay days rather than months, so there is no settled international community and no nomad scene. The town is Costa Rican and works for a living. Anyone basing here should expect a quiet, practical town and a social life built through work or activities rather than an existing group.
lafortuna.english: Widely spoken in the tourism industry, which is essentially the entire town economy, and the level is good because so many people work with international visitors daily. Away from the tourist businesses, in the shops, the clinic and any official dealing, Spanish is the working language. Costa Rica generally has better English than most of Latin America. A visitor manages entirely in English; a resident will want Spanish.
lafortuna.visa: Costa Rica grants most Western nationals 180 days on arrival, among the most generous tourist entries anywhere. The Costa Rican digital nomad visa, introduced in 2022, allows a year with a one-year extension for remote workers meeting an income threshold, and exempts foreign income from local tax. Nicaragua and Panama are the practical land borders. Note that Costa Rica requires proof of onward travel at entry and enforces it.
lafortuna.culture: Limited, and the score is honest. La Fortuna was a farming village called El Borio until the 1968 eruption changed everything, and its identity now is entirely built around the volcano and the tourism it generates. Costa Rican culture here is the pura vida version presented to visitors alongside a genuine rural Tico life running underneath it. For history and museums the answer is San Jose, three hours away.
lafortuna.cleanliness: Good. La Fortuna is well kept because its economy depends on it, with a tidy centre, maintained parks and trails, and Costa Rica's strong environmental regulation applying properly here. Waste collection functions and the national park is well managed. The main road and the areas around the bus terminal are ordinary. Overall this is one of the cleaner small towns in Central America and noticeably better than most of the region.
lafortuna.airquality: Excellent. There is no industry, the population is small, the rainfall is extraordinary and constantly washing the air, and the town is surrounded by rainforest. Arenal is currently in a resting phase and emits little. Vehicle traffic in the centre is the only local source of note. Costa Rica's air quality is among the best in the Americas and La Fortuna sits at the good end of that.

durban.climate: Durban is subtropical and warm year-round, which is its main draw within South Africa. January highs reach about 28C with heavy humidity and June lows sit around 12C, so winter is mild and dry rather than cold. Rainfall of 1010mm falls mostly between October and March as afternoon storms, with July almost dry. The Indian Ocean here is warm enough to swim in every month of the year, which is not true anywhere else in the country.
durban.cost: Around $1050 a month, which makes Durban cheaper than Cape Town or Johannesburg and good value at prevailing exchange rates for anyone earning in dollars or euros. Rent, food and services are all inexpensive by international standards. The practical caveat is that the cheapest areas are not the ones a foreigner should live in, and safety considerations narrow the housing choice considerably. This is our own estimate rather than measured cost data.
durban.wifi: Adequate. South African fibre has reached the main Durban suburbs and offers reasonable speeds at prices that are high relative to income, and mobile data is workable but expensive. The larger practical problem is electricity: load shedding, the scheduled rolling blackouts, has been a persistent feature of South African life and takes connectivity down with it unless the building has battery backup or a generator. Asking about that is essential rather than optional.
durban.nightlife: Decent and spread out. Durban's nightlife concentrates in Florida Road and Morningside, with bars, restaurants and a genuine social scene, and in the Umhlanga area north of the city. The surf and beach culture supports a relaxed daytime-into-evening pattern. Safety considerations shape how people move around at night, and driving rather than walking between venues is the norm. The city has a strong live music and jazz tradition.
durban.nature: Good. The beaches run for miles along the Golden Mile and north to Umhlanga, with warm water and reliable surf. Inland, the Valley of a Thousand Hills is close, the Drakensberg with its escarpment and hiking is three hours west, and the iSimangaliso Wetland Park, a UNESCO site with hippos, turtles and coastal lakes, is a few hours north. Hluhluwe-iMfolozi, one of Africa's oldest game reserves, is within reach for a weekend.
durban.safety: The lowest score in this group and it requires directness. Durban has high rates of violent crime, including armed robbery and carjacking, and South Africa's crime statistics are among the worst in the world for a country not at war. The city centre and beachfront require real caution, walking at night is not advisable, and the July 2021 unrest that hit this region badly is a reminder of how quickly conditions can change. Residents live with security systems as standard.
durban.food: Very good and specifically Indian. Durban has the largest population of Indian descent of any city outside India, and the food is the result: bunny chow, a hollowed loaf filled with curry that was invented here, along with a distinctive Durban curry tradition that is hotter than most Indian regional cooking. Add excellent seafood, the Zulu food traditions and South African braai culture. Prices at prevailing exchange rates are remarkable value.
durban.community: Modest. Durban has a smaller foreign population than Cape Town and no nomad scene to speak of, with the international presence largely tied to the port, the universities and business. Cape Town has South Africa's remote-work community. Durban's own social world is diverse and layered along the city's communities, and entering it takes time. Anyone arriving alone should expect to build through work or interest groups.
durban.english: The strongest score in this group. English is an official language and the working language of business, government and daily life in Durban, spoken to a high standard by most people the visitor will encounter. Zulu is the most widely spoken first language in the province and Afrikaans and several Indian languages are also present. There is no situation requiring anything other than English, which makes daily life straightforward.
durban.visa: South Africa grants most Western nationals 90 days visa-free on arrival, extendable once by a further 90 days through an application process that is slow and should be started early. The remote work visa introduced in 2024 covers people employed by foreign companies but sets a high income threshold well above local averages, and the tax and regulatory details took time to settle. Eswatini, Lesotho and Mozambique are the nearest borders.
durban.culture: Good and genuinely layered. Durban's identity is built on the meeting of Zulu, Indian and colonial histories: the Victoria Street Market and the Juma Masjid, one of the largest mosques in the southern hemisphere, sit near the Zulu heritage of the surrounding province. Gandhi developed satyagraha here during his twenty-one years in South Africa, and the Phoenix Settlement north of the city records it. The city has a strong music, poetry and film festival culture.
durban.cleanliness: One of the weaker aspects. The beachfront promenade and the affluent northern suburbs are maintained reasonably, but municipal service delivery across Durban has deteriorated markedly in recent years, with well-documented problems in waste collection, water infrastructure and sewage that have affected beach water quality and forced closures. The 2022 floods worsened it. This is a genuine and much-discussed local issue rather than a visitor's impression.
durban.airquality: Moderate. The South Durban industrial basin, with its refineries, paper mills and the largest port in Africa, sits alongside dense residential areas and has been a long-standing environmental justice issue with documented health effects for the communities there. The northern suburbs and beachfront are considerably better, helped by the sea breeze. Readings vary sharply by area, which makes where you live in Durban matter for air as well as for safety.

knysna.climate: Knysna has a mild oceanic climate with a remarkably even year, sitting on the stretch of the Garden Route where the Cape's winter rainfall pattern meets the eastern summer one, so rain falls in every month and totals only 768mm. January highs reach about 24C and July lows sit around 10C, so nothing is extreme. The forest and the lagoon keep humidity up, and the sea here is cooler than the Indian Ocean coast further east.
knysna.cost: Around $1200 a month, moderate for South Africa and reflecting Knysna's position as an established holiday and retirement town rather than a cheap one. Rent rises sharply over the December and January South African holiday season and is much better value from February to April. Groceries, eating out and services are excellent value at prevailing exchange rates. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured cost data.
knysna.wifi: Adequate. Fibre has reached the main Knysna suburbs and offers reasonable speeds, and mobile data is workable though expensive relative to what it costs in Europe or Asia. The dominant practical issue is South Africa's load shedding, the scheduled power cuts, which take internet down along with everything else unless the property has an inverter, battery or generator. Confirming that before booking a long stay is essential rather than optional.
knysna.nightlife: Very limited. Knysna is a small town of retirees, families and holidaymakers, with restaurants, a few pubs and the waterfront development rather than any nightlife. It comes alive briefly over the South African summer holidays and during the Oyster Festival in July. Otherwise the evening ends early. Anyone wanting a night out is looking at George or accepting that this is not the sort of place that offers one.
knysna.nature: Excellent, and the reason the Garden Route exists as a destination. Knysna sits on a large tidal lagoon that opens to the sea between two sandstone cliffs called the Heads, with the Knysna forest, the largest remaining indigenous forest in South Africa, immediately inland. The Outeniqua mountains rise behind it, the Tsitsikamma section of the Garden Route National Park is east with its suspension bridge and coastal trail, and whales pass offshore in season.
knysna.safety: Mixed. Knysna is safer than South Africa's cities and the tourist and residential areas are comfortable in daylight, but the country's general crime situation applies, property crime is a constant background concern, home security is universal, and the townships on the edge of town have serious problems. Walking alone at night is unwise. Driving the Garden Route is safe. The other real hazard is wildfire: Knysna burned catastrophically in 2017.
knysna.food: Good. The lagoon produces oysters that are a genuine local product and the focus of an annual festival, and the seafood generally is excellent. The surrounding region has a growing food and wine culture, with the Plettenberg Bay area and the small wine farms of the southern Cape close by. South African braai culture is everywhere. Prices at prevailing exchange rates make eating out here extremely good value.
knysna.community: Small. Knysna's foreign population is largely retirees and holiday-home owners, both South African and international, and there is no remote-working community. Cape Town, five hours west, has that. The social world here is settled, comfortable and older, organised around clubs, churches and the boating community. Anyone arriving alone should expect a quiet life and to travel for professional contact, which for some people is precisely the appeal.
knysna.english: The strongest score in this group. English is an official language and the working language of everything in the Western Cape, spoken to a high standard throughout Knysna, and Afrikaans is the first language of much of the local population with Xhosa also widely spoken. No situation a visitor encounters requires anything other than English, including banking, healthcare and administration, which makes daily life notably straightforward.
knysna.visa: South Africa grants most Western nationals 90 days visa-free on arrival, extendable once by a further 90 days through a slow application that should be started well in advance. The remote work visa introduced in 2024 is available to people employed by foreign companies but sets a high income threshold relative to local wages, and the practical process took time to settle. Namibia and Botswana are the nearest overland resets.
knysna.culture: Limited. Knysna's history is timber and gold: the indigenous forest was logged from the nineteenth century and a brief gold rush at Millwood left a ghost town in the hills, both of which small museums record. George Rex, reputedly an illegitimate son of George III, founded the settlement and the story is enthusiastically maintained. The forest elephants, now reduced to perhaps a single animal, are the area's most persistent local legend.
knysna.cleanliness: Good. Knysna is a prosperous town that maintains its waterfront, lagoon frontage and public spaces properly, and the national park areas around it are well managed. The lagoon's water quality is monitored and generally good. The contrast with the informal settlements on the edge of town is stark, as it is across South Africa. The tourist and residential areas themselves are tidy and in good repair.
knysna.airquality: Excellent. The sea air, the surrounding indigenous forest and the absence of any industry keep the air consistently clean, and readings along the Garden Route are among the best in South Africa. The one significant qualification is wildfire smoke: the 2017 fires destroyed a large part of the town and burned for days, and fire risk in the fynbos and plantation areas remains a real seasonal factor in dry, windy conditions.

puertovaras.climate: Puerto Varas has a cool oceanic climate with a great deal of rain: around 1833mm a year, concentrated in the winter months with June bringing 283mm, though no month is genuinely dry. February highs reach only about 19C and June lows sit around 5C, so summers are mild and short and winters are cold, wet and grey. The weather changes fast off the Pacific. January and February are the reliable window and the town is busy then.
puertovaras.cost: Around $1400 a month, and Chile is the most expensive country in South America, which the cost score of 5 reflects. Puerto Varas is also a domestic tourist and second-home town, which pushes accommodation up further, particularly over the Chilean summer. Puerto Montt nearby is cheaper and plainer. Food and transport are moderate. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured cost data, so treat it as a planning figure.
puertovaras.wifi: Adequate to good. Chile has the best digital infrastructure in South America with widespread fibre and reliable mobile coverage, and Puerto Varas is well served in the town itself at reasonable speeds. Coverage weakens in the countryside and around the lake. There is minimal coworking, so most remote work happens from apartments and cafes. For normal work this is entirely sufficient and better than most of the region.
puertovaras.nightlife: Limited. Puerto Varas is a small lakeside town of restaurants, cafes and a casino rather than a nightlife destination, and the evening ends early outside the summer weeks when Chilean holidaymakers fill the place. There are a few bars and a growing craft beer scene reflecting the German brewing heritage. Puerto Montt, twenty minutes away, has more and is a working port city with the character that implies.
puertovaras.nature: A perfect score. Puerto Varas sits on Lake Llanquihue, the second largest in Chile, framed by the near-perfect cone of Osorno volcano and the jagged Calbuco, which erupted spectacularly in 2015. Vicente Perez Rosales National Park, the oldest in Chile, is close with the Petrohue falls and Todos los Santos lake. The Patagonian fjords begin south of here, Chiloe island is a short ferry away, and the whole Lakes District is walking and paddling country.
puertovaras.safety: Safe. Chile has the lowest crime rates in South America and Puerto Varas is a small, prosperous town where walking at night is unremarkable. Petty theft in the summer season is the realistic concern, and it is worth noting that opportunistic theft has risen across Chile in recent years. The genuine hazards are natural: this is a seismically and volcanically active region with a major earthquake history, and the weather in the mountains changes quickly.
puertovaras.food: Good and distinctive. The German settler heritage shows in the kuchen, the smoked meats and the beer, and it sits alongside Chilean cooking and the seafood from the Reloncavi sound: salmon, mussels, the curanto pit-cooked feast of Chiloe, and merken, the smoked chilli of the Mapuche. Chilean wine is excellent and cheap. The produce from the surrounding farmland is good and the markets in Puerto Montt are worth the trip.
puertovaras.community: Small. Puerto Varas has a foreign resident population of retirees, adventure-tourism operators and a scattering of remote workers, plus the long-established German-descended Chilean community which is a different thing entirely. There is no nomad scene; Santiago and Valparaiso have what Chile offers. Anyone arriving alone should expect a quiet town, a Spanish-speaking social world and the outdoor community as the realistic route in.
puertovaras.english: Limited. Chilean English proficiency is moderate and Puerto Varas has more than the national average because of the adventure tourism, so tour operators, hotels and some restaurants manage. Everyday life, shops and all administration operate in Spanish, and Chilean Spanish is notoriously fast and full of local idiom, which makes it harder than the textbook version even for competent speakers. Functional Spanish is close to necessary here.
puertovaras.visa: Chile grants most Western nationals 90 days visa-free on arrival, extendable once. Chile does not have a dedicated digital nomad visa, though a temporary residence permit for people with independent income exists and the country has generally been open to longer stays. Argentina is across the Andes at Bariloche, a few hours away by bus, which makes a border reset straightforward. Chile enforces strict agricultural import rules at every border.
puertovaras.culture: Moderate and specifically German. Puerto Varas was founded by German settlers in the 1850s under a state colonisation programme, and the wooden houses, the churches modelled on those in the Black Forest and the surnames all record it, along with a genuine cultural persistence in food and festivals. The Mapuche and Huilliche presence in the region is older and larger. Chiloe island nearby has UNESCO-listed wooden churches and a distinct mythology.
puertovaras.cleanliness: Very good. Puerto Varas is a well-off town that maintains its lakefront, gardens and public spaces properly, and Chile generally has better municipal services than most of South America. The national parks are well managed. The salmon farming industry in the surrounding fjords is a genuine environmental controversy with documented pollution effects on the water, which is worth knowing though it does not affect the town's appearance.
puertovaras.airquality: Very good in Puerto Varas itself, helped by the lake, the wind and the absence of industry. The regional caveat is real: southern Chilean cities have a serious winter air pollution problem from wood-burning stoves, and nearby Osorno and Temuco have among the worst readings in the Americas as a result. Puerto Varas is smaller and better ventilated, so it escapes the worst, but still winter evenings do bring woodsmoke.

vinadelmar.climate: Vina del Mar has a mild Mediterranean climate cooled substantially by the Humboldt current, which makes the sea genuinely cold year-round despite the latitude. January highs reach about 24C and July lows sit around 9C, so the range is narrow. Rainfall of only 339mm falls entirely in the winter months and February is completely dry. Coastal fog, the camanchaca, is a regular morning feature, and the ocean keeps summer temperatures well below inland Santiago.
vinadelmar.cost: Around $1450 a month, which reflects Chile being the most expensive country in South America and Vina being a desirable coastal city within it. Rent in the central and seafront areas is the main cost, with better value inland and in Valparaiso next door. Food and transport are moderate by international standards. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured cost data, so treat it as a working budget.
vinadelmar.wifi: Good. Chile leads South America on digital infrastructure, with widespread fibre, fast speeds and reliable 4G and 5G coverage, and Vina del Mar as part of the country's second largest urban area is fully served. There is a coworking presence, and the universities in the Valparaiso conurbation support a professional infrastructure. Connectivity is a genuine strength here and unlikely to factor into a decision either way.
vinadelmar.nightlife: Good. Vina has the beach clubs, casino and summer season crowd, while Valparaiso ten minutes away has the bohemian bar and music scene on its hills, and the two function as one nightlife between them. The student population across the conurbation is large and keeps things going through the year. The Vina del Mar International Song Festival each February is the biggest music event in Latin America and takes over the city.
vinadelmar.nature: Good. The beaches run north from the city through Renaca and Concon with dunes and surf, though the Humboldt current makes the water cold enough that swimming is a brief business. La Campana National Park inland holds Chilean palm forest and the peak Darwin climbed. The Casablanca valley wine region is between here and Santiago. Further north the coast runs to Zapallar and eventually the Atacama, and the Andes are two hours east.
vinadelmar.safety: Mixed, and Chile's situation has changed. The country was long the safest in South America and remains comparatively safe, but street crime and robbery have risen markedly in recent years, particularly in the Valparaiso conurbation, and phone snatching and opportunistic theft are now common concerns. Vina is safer than Valparaiso's hills but the ordinary precautions matter: no phones out in public, care after dark, awareness on public transport.
vinadelmar.food: Good. Chilean coastal cooking is built on the extraordinary seafood of the Humboldt current: congrio, machas, erizos, the fish market at Caleta Portales in Valparaiso is worth an early morning. Add empanadas, the completo hot dog tradition, and Chilean wine from the Casablanca valley next door, which produces the country's best whites. Prices are moderate and the produce is excellent. Range beyond Chilean food is decent in the conurbation.
vinadelmar.community: Modest. Vina and Valparaiso have a foreign population of students, some remote workers drawn by Chile's stability and infrastructure, and a scattering of long-term residents, but no established nomad scene. Santiago has more. The universities are the most accessible entry point. Chilean social life is warm but takes time and Spanish. Anyone arriving alone should expect to build rather than join, with Valparaiso's arts scene a realistic route.
vinadelmar.english: Limited. Chilean English proficiency is moderate and concentrated among younger and more educated people, and the tourism sector manages. Everyday life and all administration operate in Spanish. Chilean Spanish is particularly challenging: fast, heavily elided and full of local slang, to the point that fluent Spanish speakers from elsewhere find it difficult at first. Functional Spanish is close to necessary for a stay of any length.
vinadelmar.visa: Chile grants most Western nationals 90 days visa-free on arrival, extendable once for a further 90 days. There is no dedicated Chilean digital nomad visa, though temporary residence for people with independent income or a Chilean contract is available and the country has generally been open. Argentina is across the Andes and Peru is far to the north, so a land reset means a long journey. Chile's agricultural import controls are strictly enforced.
vinadelmar.culture: Moderate here and strong next door. Vina itself is a twentieth century garden and resort city with the Quinta Vergara park, the Fonck museum holding a genuine Easter Island moai, and the flower clock, which is the city's postcard. The real cultural weight is Valparaiso ten minutes away: a UNESCO-listed port of funicular railways, painted hills and Neruda's house, with a street art and music culture that is among the best in Latin America.
vinadelmar.cleanliness: Middling. Vina's seafront, parks and central avenues are maintained reasonably and the city has a garden reputation it works at. Standards drop in the outer neighbourhoods and along the boundary with Valparaiso, and the beaches suffer from ocean litter and periodic water quality issues after rain. Valparaiso next door is visibly rougher. Chile's municipal services are better than most of the region without being exceptional.
vinadelmar.airquality: Reasonable. The constant onshore wind off the Pacific keeps the coastal air moving and Vina avoids the severe winter smog that traps Santiago in its basin two hours inland. The local sources are traffic through the conurbation and the port and industrial activity around Valparaiso and Quintero, the latter a notorious pollution hotspot further north that has caused documented health emergencies. Vina's own readings are generally acceptable.

arugambay.climate: Arugam Bay runs on the opposite monsoon to the rest of Sri Lanka, which is the whole logic of the place. The dry season here is roughly May to September, when the west of the island is wet, and the northeast monsoon brings the rain from October to January with November peaking at 346mm. June highs reach about 34C and January lows sit around 23C. The surf season aligns with the dry months, and the town largely closes outside them.
arugambay.cost: Around $700 a month, low even by Sri Lankan standards outside the season. During the surf months from May to September, accommodation on the main strip is priced for the international crowd and costs considerably more; from November the town empties and long stays become very cheap. Food is inexpensive throughout. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured cost data, so treat it as a working budget.
arugambay.wifi: The weakest score here. Arugam Bay is a small town on Sri Lanka's least developed coast, and connectivity is usable rather than good: fibre has reached parts of the strip, speeds are modest, and outages during weather and power cuts are common. Mobile data is cheap and often the more reliable option. There is minimal coworking. Anyone dependent on stable video calls should verify carefully and plan for redundancy.
arugambay.nightlife: Seasonal and lively within its season. From May to September the strip has beach bars, reggae nights and a young international surf crowd, and the town has a genuine party reputation for a place this small. Sri Lanka's alcohol licensing and periodic poya day restrictions shape it. From October the bars close and the town reverts to a quiet fishing settlement. This is a seasonal town in every respect.
arugambay.nature: Excellent. The point break at Arugam Bay is the main draw and is among the most reliable in Asia, with Whiskey Point, Peanut Farm and Elephant Rock nearby offering variety. Kumana National Park is close and holds elephants, leopards and enormous birdlife with a fraction of Yala's visitors, and Lahugala park is closer still. The lagoons and the coast are largely undeveloped, and elephants genuinely do cross the roads here.
arugambay.safety: Generally safe. Sri Lanka is a safe country for visitors and Arugam Bay is a small community where crime against foreigners is uncommon, though petty theft from accommodation and beaches happens. The genuine hazards are the ocean, with strong currents and a reef break that catches out inexperienced surfers, road traffic including tuk-tuks and buses, and wildlife: elephants on the roads at night are a real and serious risk. Medical facilities are basic.
arugambay.food: Good. Sri Lankan cooking is one of the great cuisines of Asia and underrated internationally: rice and curry with many small dishes, hoppers, kottu roti, seafood from the bay, and a chilli and coconut palate that is distinct from Indian cooking. The east coast has a Muslim population with its own biryani and pastry traditions. The strip has the usual international surf-town food, and the local places off it are far better value.
arugambay.community: Strong for the season and non-existent outside it. During the surf months Arugam Bay has a genuine international community of surfers, seasonal workers and a growing number of remote workers who combine the two, with an easy social structure built around the breaks and the bars. From October it empties almost completely. Anyone considering a long stay should understand the town has two entirely different personalities.
arugambay.english: Reasonably good. English is widely used in Sri Lanka as a link language and is taught in schools, and Arugam Bay's tourism economy means guesthouse owners, surf schools and restaurants all operate in it comfortably. Tamil is the first language of much of the east coast and Sinhala is the national one. Away from the tourism strip English thins. For a visitor the coverage is comfortable throughout the season.
arugambay.visa: Sri Lanka requires an Electronic Travel Authorisation in advance for most nationalities, granting 30 days on arrival, extendable to 90 days and in some cases longer through the immigration department in Colombo. Sri Lanka introduced a digital nomad visa in 2024 allowing longer stays for remote workers, though the details have shifted since announcement and should be checked directly. Fee structures for the ETA have changed repeatedly, so verify close to travel.
arugambay.culture: Limited in the town itself, which is a surf settlement rather than a historic one. The genuine cultural interest is nearby: Pottuvil and the surrounding villages have a distinct east coast Muslim and Tamil character quite different from the Sinhalese south, and the ancient Buddhist site of Muhudu Maha Viharaya sits in the dunes just north. Further inland, the ruins at Lahugala and the long history of the eastern kingdoms are largely unvisited.
arugambay.cleanliness: Middling. The main strip and the beaches are cleaned reasonably during the season because the businesses depend on it, but waste management in the town is basic, plastic on the beach and in the lagoons after rain is a persistent problem, and the infrastructure has not kept pace with the tourism growth. Out of season the beaches accumulate. This is a normal small Sri Lankan coastal town in this respect.
arugambay.airquality: Very good. There is no industry, the population is small, and the sea breeze is constant along this exposed coast. The surrounding area is scrub, lagoon and national park rather than agriculture, so burning is limited. The only local sources are vehicle traffic on the strip during the season and cooking fires. Air quality here is among the better readings in Sri Lanka and considerably cleaner than Colombo.

dianibeach.climate: Diani is tropical and warm year-round, with February highs around 31C and July lows around 22C, which is the coolest and most comfortable stretch. Rainfall of 1390mm arrives in two distinct seasons: the long rains from April to June, with May the wettest at 277mm, and shorter rains in November. The Indian Ocean monsoon governs everything, with the kaskazi wind from the northeast in the hot months and the kusi from the southeast bringing the cooler, breezier weather.
dianibeach.cost: Around $950 a month, moderate for East Africa and reflecting Diani being an established coastal destination rather than a cheap one. Rent varies widely between the beachfront villas and apartments aimed at foreigners and ordinary local housing further back from the sand. Food from the markets is very cheap, imported goods are not. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured cost data, so treat it as a working budget.
dianibeach.wifi: Adequate, and better than most of the Kenyan coast because the remote-work community demanded it. Fibre has reached the main Diani strip and there are coworking spaces and cafes set up specifically for people working online, which is unusual in the region. Reliability is inconsistent and power cuts occur, so a backup mobile connection is standard practice. Kenyan mobile data is cheap and widely used. Test the specific connection before a long stay.
dianibeach.nightlife: Modest and spread along the strip. There are beach bars, a few clubs and the restaurants that serve the resort and residential population, busy in the December to March high season and much quieter otherwise. The scene is relaxed rather than intense, mixing tourists, expatriates and the local Kenyan crowd. Ukunda town behind the beach has its own ordinary Kenyan nightlife. Nothing here approaches Nairobi or Mombasa in scale.
dianibeach.nature: Excellent. Diani's beach is genuinely one of the best in Africa, white sand with a reef offshore that makes the water calm and clear for swimming and snorkelling. The Kaya Kinondo sacred forest is a rare surviving coastal forest fragment protected by local tradition. Shimba Hills National Reserve is half an hour inland with elephants and sable antelope, Wasini island and Kisite marine park are south for dolphins, and colobus monkeys live in the coastal canopy.
dianibeach.safety: Mixed, and it needs a plain answer. Diani itself is comparatively safe and the beach strip is well policed because tourism matters to the local economy, but Kenya has significant crime and the coast has had periods of security concern, with several governments having issued travel advisories for parts of the coast at various times. Petty theft on the beach, care after dark, and using arranged transport rather than walking at night are the practical baseline.
dianibeach.food: Good. Swahili coastal cooking is the local tradition and it is distinct from inland Kenyan food: coconut rice, fish and seafood curries, biryani, samosas and the Indian Ocean spice trade influences. The seafood from the reef and the deeper water is excellent and cheap. Nyama choma, grilled meat, is the national institution. The resort strip has international restaurants at higher prices, and the local places behind it are much better value.
dianibeach.community: Strong for the region. Diani has a small but genuine remote-working community, one of the few in East Africa, alongside a long-established expatriate population of retirees, dive operators and business owners, and there are coworking spaces and social structures that make it easy for someone arriving alone. Kenya's improving connectivity has drawn more people in recent years. This is a real if small scene rather than a claimed one.
dianibeach.english: The strongest score in this group. English is an official language of Kenya, used in education, government, business and signage, and spoken to a good standard by most people a visitor will encounter. Swahili is the national language and is widely used alongside it, and the coastal dialect is the classical form. Learning basic Swahili is appreciated and useful. Daily life, banking and healthcare all operate in English without difficulty.
dianibeach.visa: Kenya replaced its visa system with an Electronic Travel Authorisation that all visitors must obtain in advance, granting stays of up to 90 days, extendable once. Kenya introduced a digital nomad work permit in 2024 for remote workers employed outside the country, with an income requirement, valid initially for a year. East African Community arrangements allow some regional movement. Check the current ETA fee and process close to travel, as it has changed repeatedly.
dianibeach.culture: Moderate. The Swahili coast has a thousand years of trading history linking East Africa to Arabia, Persia and India, and it survives in the language, the architecture and the sacred kaya forests of the Mijikenda people, which are UNESCO-listed. Diani itself is a modern beach development rather than a historic town. Mombasa an hour north has Fort Jesus and a genuine Swahili old town, and Lamu further up the coast is the real thing.
dianibeach.cleanliness: Middling. The beach itself is cleaned by the hotels and is generally in good condition, though seaweed accumulates seasonally, and the resort areas are maintained. Ukunda town behind the strip and the roads through it are ordinary Kenyan infrastructure with the waste management problems that implies, and plastic is visible away from the swept sand. This is a normal coastal Kenyan standard rather than a poor one.
dianibeach.airquality: Very good. Constant ocean breeze, no industry, a small population and coastal forest keep the air clean along the beach. The local sources are vehicle traffic on the main road and, more noticeably, the burning of household waste, which is still common in Kenya and produces localised smoke. Away from the road and on the beach itself the air is excellent, and readings here are far better than Nairobi's.

hurghada.climate: Hurghada is desert on the Red Sea and effectively rainless: around 10mm falls in an entire year, which is the lowest total in this dataset by a wide margin. July highs reach about 35C and January lows sit around 13C, so the summer is genuinely hot and the winter is warm and clear, which is the entire tourism proposition. The sea moderates the extremes and the constant north wind cools the coast and drives the kitesurfing that the area is known for.
hurghada.cost: Around $700 a month, which makes Hurghada one of the cheapest places anywhere to live by the sea. Egyptian currency devaluation has made the country remarkably inexpensive for anyone earning in hard currency, and rent for a sea-view apartment costs a fraction of what a comparable place in Europe or Turkey would. Food and transport are very cheap. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured cost data.
hurghada.wifi: Adequate. Hurghada has fibre in the newer developments and the tourist districts at usable speeds, and mobile data across the city is reliable and cheap. Reliability is inconsistent by building and power interruptions occur. Egypt periodically restricts certain services and VoIP calling has historically been limited on some networks, so a VPN is standard equipment. Some coworking exists serving the growing foreign resident population. Test a specific connection before committing.
hurghada.nightlife: Substantial and specific. Hurghada has a large and long-established resort nightlife along the Sheraton Road and in the marina, serving a mainly Russian, eastern European and German visitor base, with clubs, bars and a scene that runs year-round rather than seasonally because the weather does. Alcohol is available in the tourist zones. Away from those areas, this is an ordinary Egyptian city where the pattern is cafes and shisha.
hurghada.nature: Good, and almost entirely underwater. The Red Sea reef system off Hurghada is world-class, with the Giftun islands, the wrecks including the Thistlegorm, and coral and marine life that make this one of the great diving and snorkelling destinations anywhere. On land, the Eastern Desert runs inland to the Red Sea mountains with wadis and Bedouin routes. The coast itself is heavily developed. This is a place you go into the water rather than walk around.
hurghada.safety: Mixed. Ordinary crime is low and Hurghada is generally comfortable, but Egypt has had security concerns and several governments advise against travel to parts of the country, though the Red Sea resorts are usually excluded from those warnings. The practical daily issues are persistent hassle and overcharging in the tourist areas, and traffic, which is genuinely dangerous. Diving accidents and shark incidents, though rare, have occurred on this coast. Check current advice before travelling.
hurghada.food: Adequate. Egyptian cooking is good and very cheap: koshari, ful, taameya, grilled meats and fresh bread, and the seafood from the Red Sea is a local strength. The resort restaurants serve international food of variable quality at high prices, and the local places away from the strip are far better and cost almost nothing. The range of international options has grown with the foreign resident population. Fresh produce is inexpensive.
hurghada.community: Modest and growing. Hurghada has a substantial permanent foreign population, mainly Russian, Ukrainian and German, that has expanded considerably since 2022, along with a smaller number of remote workers drawn by the cost and the diving. There are social structures, associations and cafes serving them. This is an expat resort community rather than a nomad hub, and the composition is specific, but anyone arriving alone will find people.
hurghada.english: Moderate. English is widely spoken in the tourism industry, which is most of the visitor-facing economy, though Russian and German are often more useful given who comes here. Away from the tourist zones, in the markets and in any official dealing, Arabic is the working language. Signage is bilingual in the resort areas. Coverage is adequate for a visitor and thin for a resident handling administration.
hurghada.visa: Egypt issues a 30-day tourist visa on arrival to most Western nationals for a fee, or in advance as an e-visa, and it is extendable at a passport office. There is no Egyptian digital nomad visa. Longer stays are typically managed through repeated tourist visas or a residence permit tied to property ownership or study, both of which involve bureaucracy. The Red Sea resorts also have a restricted entry permit option for visitors staying only in the area.
hurghada.culture: The weakest score here and honestly so. Hurghada was a small fishing village until the 1980s and is now a purpose-built resort city with essentially no historic content of its own. Egypt's extraordinary heritage is elsewhere: Luxor is four hours west by road and holds the Valley of the Kings and Karnak, the Coptic monasteries of St Anthony and St Paul are in the Eastern Desert, and Cairo is a long journey north.
hurghada.cleanliness: Middling. The resort compounds and the marina are maintained to a good standard because they are sold on it, and the beaches within them are kept clean. The public areas of the city, the older districts and the roadsides are ordinary, with visible litter and construction dust from continuous development. Reef damage from tourism pressure is a documented environmental concern. The contrast between the compounds and the city is sharp.
hurghada.airquality: Good. The desert location, the constant sea wind and the absence of heavy industry keep the air clear, and Hurghada avoids the severe pollution that affects Cairo. The local sources are construction dust, which is constant given the pace of building, vehicle traffic, and occasional sandstorms that reduce visibility and raise particulates for a day or two. Compared with Egypt's major cities the difference is substantial.

mindo.climate: Mindo sits at 1253m on the western slope of the Andes in genuine cloud forest, and the rainfall reflects it: around 5280mm a year with April bringing 757mm and even the driest month delivering 202mm. Temperatures are stable and mild, with highs around 22C and lows around 17C, so it is neither hot nor cold but almost always damp. Mist through the forest is the normal state rather than an event, and afternoons are usually wet.
mindo.cost: Around $650 a month, which is low even by Ecuadorian standards. Ecuador uses the US dollar, which removes exchange rate uncertainty, and Mindo is a small village where rent, food and transport are all inexpensive. The tourism aimed at birdwatchers supports some higher-priced lodges, but ordinary living costs very little. This is our own estimate rather than a reconciliation against measured cost data, so treat it as a working budget.
mindo.wifi: The weakest infrastructure in this group. Mindo is a village of a few thousand people in a mountain valley, and connectivity is basic: usable for email and light work in the centre, unreliable in heavy rain, and prone to outages. Mobile coverage is limited and patchy on the surrounding slopes. There is no coworking. Anyone considering remote work from here should treat the connection as the primary constraint and verify it thoroughly first.
mindo.nightlife: Essentially none, and the lowest score alongside Siwa in this set. Mindo is a birdwatching and nature village where people are up before dawn and asleep early, and the evening consists of a handful of restaurants and a bar or two on the main street. There is no scene of any kind. Anyone coming here for anything other than the forest has chosen the wrong destination entirely.
mindo.nature: A perfect score, and the case is easy to make. Mindo sits in the Choco-Andean corridor, one of the most biodiverse places on earth, with over 500 recorded bird species in the immediate area including dozens of hummingbirds, the Andean cock-of-the-rock, and toucans. Add butterfly farms, waterfall routes, tubing on the river, canopy zip lines and orchid gardens. Serious birders travel from around the world specifically for this valley, which is the whole point.
mindo.safety: Reasonably safe. Mindo is a small rural community with low crime and a comfortable feel, and it is considerably safer than Ecuador's cities, which have deteriorated markedly with organised crime in recent years, particularly on the coast. The realistic hazards here are natural: the river runs fast after rain, the trails are steep and slippery, and the road from Quito is mountainous. Medical facilities are minimal, with serious cases going to Quito.
mindo.food: Limited, and the score is honest.
