From November to April the kitesurfing community fills the strip, with schools, shops and a genuine international crowd of instructors and repeat visitors, including a long-established Russian presence. Outside those months it largely disperses. There is no year-round nomad community. Anyone arriving in the season will find people quickly through the water; anyone arriving in July will find a quiet coast.
phanthiet.english: Limited. English is spoken along the Mui Ne strip in the kitesurfing schools, guesthouses and restaurants, where it is workable, and Russian is genuinely useful there too given the visitor mix. In Phan Thiet town and anywhere off the beach road, Vietnamese is the only working language. Translation apps handle transactions. Anyone staying months will need some Vietnamese, which is tonal and difficult but rewards even a small effort.
phanthiet.visa: Vietnam grants ninety-day e-visas to citizens of most countries, single or multiple entry, applied for online before travel, which is a considerable improvement on the old thirty-day rule. Some nationalities also get shorter visa-free entry. There is no Vietnamese digital nomad visa, and longer stays are managed through repeated e-visas or a work permit tied to a Vietnamese entity. Vietnam has occasionally tightened the practice around back-to-back visas without changing the formal rules.
phanthiet.culture: Modest, and the score of 5 is honest. Phan Thiet is a working fishing city rather than a historic one. What exists is genuinely local: the Po Sah Inu Cham towers on a hill above the town date from the eighth century and are among the oldest structures in Vietnam, remnants of the Champa kingdom that ruled this coast. The Duc Thanh school where Ho Chi Minh taught is preserved. The fish sauce industry is itself a cultural institution here.
phanthiet.cleanliness: Middling, and the score of 5 is fair. The resort strip is cleaned by the businesses that depend on it, but plastic accumulates on the beaches after rain and river discharge, and the stretch between Mui Ne and Phan Thiet has visible waste along the roadside. Vietnam's plastic problem is national rather than local. The fishing harbour is a working one and smells like it. This is an ordinary Vietnamese coastal standard rather than a poor one.
phanthiet.airquality: Good. There is no heavy industry, the constant sea wind disperses what the traffic produces, and the dry climate means little of the agricultural burning that affects the Mekong Delta. Vehicle emissions along the coast road are the main local source, heaviest in season. Vietnam's severe urban air pollution is a Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City problem rather than a coastal one, and readings here are consistently among the better ones in the country.

valdivia.climate: The climate score of 4 is about rain rather than temperature. Valdivia takes around 1,855mm a year, with June alone bringing 367mm, and the winter from May to August is persistently wet and grey with short days. February highs reach a mild 23C and July lows sit near 4C, so it is temperate rather than cold. The dry window is December to March and it is genuinely pleasant. Anyone considering this city should look at the rainfall figure first and decide from there.
valdivia.cost: Around $1,100 a month is good value for Chile, the most expensive country in South America, and the large student population keeps rents reasonable. A one-bedroom flat is affordable by Chilean standards. Groceries are moderate and wine is very cheap. The cost that surprises arrivals is heating: five wet cold months in buildings that are often poorly insulated means firewood or gas is a genuine monthly expense rather than an afterthought. Eating out is reasonable.
valdivia.wifi: Good. Chile has the best digital infrastructure in South America and Valdivia shares it, with fast fibre widely available at reasonable prices and reliable mobile coverage. The Universidad Austral is the city's largest institution and brings a substantial academic and research population, supporting a small coworking presence and a professional network unusual for a city this size. Power is reliable. Connectivity is a genuine argument for choosing Chile over its neighbours for remote work.
valdivia.nightlife: Moderate and student-driven. The Universidad Austral gives Valdivia a young population and the bars along the riverfront and in the centre are busy through term. The city's real distinction is beer: German settlers founded breweries here in the nineteenth century and Valdivia is the centre of Chilean craft brewing, with Kunstmann the best known. The Noche Valdiviana in February, when decorated boats parade down the river, is the year's big event.
valdivia.nature: Excellent. Valdivia sits where three rivers meet and the water is the point: kayaking through the Carlos Anwandter nature sanctuary among black-necked swans, boat trips down to the Spanish coastal forts at Corral and Niebla. The Valdivian temperate rainforest, a distinct ecosystem found in very few places on earth, begins at the city's edge, with Oncol Park and the Alerce Costero national park nearby. Sea lions haul out on the fish market steps in the middle of town.
valdivia.safety: Safe by South American standards. Chile has the region's lowest crime rates and Valdivia is a comfortable university city where walking at night in the centre is unremarkable. That said, street crime and phone snatching have risen across Chile in recent years and the country's reputation is ahead of its current reality, so ordinary urban caution applies. Medical facilities are good. The genuine hazard is seismic: the 1960 earthquake here was the most powerful ever recorded.
valdivia.food: Good. Valdivia's German settler inheritance shows in the kuchen, the smoked meats and above all the beer. Alongside that is Chilean coastal cooking with the seafood of the Reloncavi and the river estuary: congrio, machas, and the shellfish that Chile does exceptionally well. The Feria Fluvial on the riverfront is a working market with sea lions competing for the offcuts. Chilean wine is excellent and cheap. Merken, the Mapuche smoked chilli, is the regional seasoning.
valdivia.community: Small. Valdivia has an academic international presence through the university and a handful of long-term foreign residents, but no nomad community. Santiago and Valparaiso have what Chile offers on that front. The city's social world is student and academic, which is accessible if you have a connection to the university and less so otherwise. Anyone arriving alone should expect to build through Spanish, sport or the university rather than find a group.
valdivia.english: Limited. Chilean English proficiency is moderate and concentrated among younger and educated people, with the university orbit the main exception. Everyday life and all administration operate in Spanish. Chilean Spanish is genuinely difficult: fast, heavily elided and full of local idiom to the point that competent Spanish speakers from elsewhere struggle at first. Functional Spanish is close to a requirement for a stay of any length here.
valdivia.visa: Chile grants most Western nationals ninety days visa-free on arrival, extendable once for a further ninety days. There is no dedicated Chilean digital nomad visa, though a temporary residence permit for people with independent income exists and Chile has generally been open to longer stays, with the caveat that immigration has had substantial backlogs. Argentina is over the Andes and Peru far north, so an overland reset is a long journey. Agricultural import controls are strictly enforced.
valdivia.culture: Good. Valdivia was founded in 1552 and the Spanish coastal fortifications at Corral, Niebla and Mancera were among the most heavily defended in the Pacific. The German colonisation from the 1850s left the breweries, the architecture and the surnames. The 1960 earthquake and the tsunami that followed reshaped the city and the landscape around it, sinking land and creating the wetlands that are now a nature sanctuary. The university drives a genuine cultural and film festival calendar.
valdivia.cleanliness: Very good. Valdivia is well maintained by South American standards, with the riverfront, the parks and the university campus all in good order, and Chilean municipal services function reliably. Waste collection works. The rivers themselves have had industrial pollution problems, notably the 2004 pulp mill contamination that killed much of the black-necked swan population in the sanctuary, which became a national environmental scandal and remains a live local issue.
valdivia.airquality: Moderate. Valdivia's air is clean for much of the year thanks to the rain and the coastal position. The recurring problem is winter woodsmoke: southern Chilean cities heat with wet firewood and the resulting particulate pollution is severe, with nearby Osorno and Temuco recording among the worst readings in the Americas. Valdivia is better ventilated and less affected, but still winter evenings bring noticeable smoke. Summer air is excellent.

morelia.climate: Morelia sits at 1,913m, which gives it a subtropical highland climate of the kind that makes central Mexico so comfortable. April highs reach about 29C and January lows sit near 7C, with warm days and cool nights all year and no need for heating or air conditioning. Rain totals 690mm and falls almost entirely between June and September as heavy afternoon storms, with April almost completely dry. The dry season from October to May is bright, mild and reliably pleasant.
morelia.cost: Around $900 a month covers a comfortable standard, good value for a Mexican state capital and considerably below the cities nomads usually choose. A one-bedroom flat is inexpensive, with the historic centre at the upper end and the newer districts cheaper. Markets and street food cost very little and eating out in local restaurants runs a few dollars. The altitude means neither heating nor cooling is much of a cost, which helps the monthly total more than people expect.
morelia.wifi: Adequate to good. Mexican fixed broadband reaches the city with reasonable speeds and prices, and mobile coverage is reliable. Morelia has a small but real coworking scene, supported by several universities and a growing technology and services sector. Quality varies by provider and building more than in Europe, and the thick colonial stone walls in the historic centre genuinely interfere with wifi coverage inside apartments, which is worth checking before signing a lease.
morelia.nightlife: Moderate and student-driven. Morelia has a large university population and the bars and cantinas around the centre and near the Universidad Michoacana are busy through term. The Michoacan music tradition is strong and live pirekua and son are heard rather than performed for tourists. The city runs a serious international film festival in October and a well-regarded organ festival in the cathedral. Prices are low and the crowd is local rather than visiting.
morelia.nature: Moderate. Morelia itself sits in a valley of farmland with limited landscape immediately at hand, though the city has substantial parks including the Bosque Cuauhtemoc. The genuine draw is nearby: the monarch butterfly reserves in the mountains east, where hundreds of millions of butterflies overwinter between November and March, are among the great natural spectacles on earth. Lake Patzcuaro and the volcanic country around Uruapan are within two hours.
morelia.safety: The weakest score here and it needs stating plainly. Michoacan has significant organised crime problems and has been one of Mexico's more troubled states for two decades. Morelia itself is considerably safer than the state's reputation, with a normal urban feel and a large student population, but the standard Mexican advice applies with more force here: no intercity driving at night, use registered taxis or apps, avoid rural areas without local knowledge, and follow current advice.
morelia.food: Very good. Michoacan cuisine is UNESCO-recognised as part of traditional Mexican cooking and is among the country's best: carnitas done properly, corundas and uchepos which are regional tamales, sopa tarasca, and the fish from Lake Patzcuaro. Morelia's markets are excellent and the sweets tradition, centred on the Mercado de Dulces, is a local institution. Prices are low and the standard in ordinary places is high. This is a genuine food destination rather than a convenient one.
morelia.community: Small. Morelia has a modest foreign population, mostly students at the language schools and a scattering of long-term residents, and no nomad community of the kind that San Miguel or Oaxaca have. That is partly the point: this is a working Mexican city rather than an expatriate enclave. Anyone arriving alone will need Spanish and should expect to build through the universities or through interest groups rather than find an established scene.
morelia.english: Limited. Morelia is not a tourist city in the way that San Miguel de Allende or Playa del Carmen are, and English is spoken mainly by students, academics and some younger professionals. Shops, markets, offices and older residents work in Spanish, and all administration is Spanish-only. Mexican Spanish is accessible and clearly spoken, which makes this a good place to learn it and a demanding one to visit without any.
morelia.visa: Mexico grants most Western nationals up to 180 days on arrival as a tourist, though since the shift to discretionary stamping the number of days given is at the officer's judgement and shorter grants have become common, so having proof of onward travel and accommodation ready matters. There is no Mexican digital nomad visa, but the temporary resident visa is a well-used route for anyone demonstrating income or savings above a threshold, running up to four years.
morelia.culture: Very strong. Morelia's historic centre is UNESCO-listed and built almost entirely from pink cantera stone, which gives it a visual coherence few colonial cities match. The eighteenth-century aqueduct runs 253 arches into the middle of the city. The cathedral is among the finest in Mexico and its Sunday organ recitals are worth arranging a week around. Michoacan is also the heartland of Purepecha culture, which resisted the Aztecs and retains a distinct identity around Patzcuaro.
morelia.cleanliness: Reasonable. The historic centre is maintained properly, as the city's UNESCO status requires, and the main avenues and parks are in good order. Waste collection functions normally by Mexican standards. The outer districts are ordinary and some are visibly poorer. The altitude and the dry season keep dust down. Nothing here reads as neglected in the centre, and the standard is comfortably above the Mexican urban average.
morelia.airquality: Reasonable. Morelia's altitude and its position in an open valley help disperse pollution, and there is no heavy industry. The main sources are traffic in the narrow colonial streets, which concentrates emissions at street level, and agricultural burning in the surrounding countryside during the dry season, which is the more noticeable seasonal factor. Compared with Mexico City the difference is dramatic, and readings sit comfortably in the moderate range most of the year.

puertomadryn.climate: Puerto Madryn has a cold semi-arid climate on the Patagonian coast, and the wind is the defining feature rather than the temperature. January highs reach about 28C and July lows sit near 3C. Rain totals only 265mm across the year, spread thinly with no real wet season, which is why the surrounding landscape is scrub steppe rather than anything green. The wind blows persistently and hard from the west for most of the year, and it shapes daily life more than any figure here suggests.
puertomadryn.cost: Around $900 a month, though Argentine figures need more caution than most in this dataset. Inflation has run extremely high for years and the exchange rate has moved repeatedly, so any number is indicative and should be rechecked close to travel. A one-bedroom flat is moderate. Food and eating out are good value at the rates most foreigners obtain, and Argentine beef and wine are cheap. Prices rise sharply through the whale season when the town fills.
puertomadryn.wifi: Adequate. Argentine fixed broadband reaches the town with modest speeds and reasonable reliability, and mobile data works along the coast. There is no coworking. The infrastructure is behind Chile across the Andes and behind most of this dataset. The more pressing practical issue in Argentina is financial rather than technical: currency controls, multiple exchange rates and the difficulty of getting money in at a sensible rate will occupy more of your attention than bandwidth does.
puertomadryn.nightlife: Limited. Puerto Madryn has restaurants and bars along the seafront and around the centre, busy through the whale and summer seasons and quiet otherwise. Argentine dining runs late, so an evening starts at ten and the town has a sociable if small circuit. Dive shops and tour operators provide most of the transient social life. Anyone wanting scale is looking at Buenos Aires, which is a two-hour flight rather than a trip.
puertomadryn.nature: A perfect score, and the entire case for the town. Peninsula Valdes, ninety minutes north, is UNESCO-listed and holds southern right whales calving in the gulfs from June to December, elephant seal and sea lion colonies, and the orcas that beach themselves deliberately to take seal pups, which happens nowhere else. Punta Tombo south holds one of the largest Magellanic penguin colonies in the world. The whales come into Golfo Nuevo close enough to watch from the shore.
puertomadryn.safety: Safe. Puerto Madryn is a small, prosperous town with low crime and it is comfortable to walk at any hour, which distinguishes it from much of urban Argentina. Petty theft in the summer season is the realistic concern. The genuine hazards are environmental: the wind, which makes small-boat conditions change quickly, cold water even in summer, and the distances in Patagonia, where a breakdown on an empty road is a serious matter rather than an inconvenience.
puertomadryn.food: Adequate. Argentine beef and the parrilla tradition apply here fully and are excellent value. The local addition is seafood, particularly the scallops and the Patagonian toothfish landed along this coast, and Welsh tea houses in nearby Gaiman are a genuine oddity left by the nineteenth-century Welsh settlement of Chubut. Range beyond that is limited, and the town is small enough that the restaurant scene is quickly exhausted on a longer stay.
puertomadryn.community: The lowest score in this batch. Puerto Madryn has essentially no foreign resident population beyond a handful of dive operators and tour staff, and its visitors are Argentine holidaymakers and short-stay wildlife travellers. There is no nomad presence. Anyone basing here should expect genuine isolation from other foreigners and a social life built through Spanish and through the diving and tour community, which is small but welcoming.
puertomadryn.english: Limited. Argentine English proficiency is reasonable by Latin American standards and the tour operators and dive shops manage, since much of their clientele is international. Everywhere else operates in Spanish, including all administration. Argentine Spanish has a distinctive accent and vocabulary, with the Italian-influenced intonation and the vos form, which takes adjustment even for competent speakers. Functional Spanish is close to necessary for anything beyond the tourist economy.
puertomadryn.visa: Argentina grants most Western nationals ninety days visa-free on arrival, extendable once for a further ninety days at a migration office. Argentina introduced a digital nomad visa in 2022 for remote workers, valid six months and renewable once, though for many people the practical benefit over the tourist stamp is limited. Chile is reachable overland across the Andes. Currency and banking rules change frequently and matter more than the visa itself, so verify the current position before arriving.
puertomadryn.culture: Modest, and the score of 5 is fair. Puerto Madryn was founded in 1865 by Welsh settlers who landed on this beach, and the Welsh presence in Chubut province survives in the tea houses and chapels of Gaiman and Trelew inland, which is a genuine historical curiosity. The Ecocentro presents the marine ecosystem well. The town itself grew around an aluminium smelter rather than around tourism, which explains why it looks more industrial than a wildlife destination usually does.
puertomadryn.cleanliness: Very good. Puerto Madryn is well maintained by Argentine standards, with a tidy seafront promenade, clean beaches and functioning municipal services, helped by a prosperous population and an economy that depends on how the place looks. The industrial zone around the smelter is a separate environment. The surrounding peninsula and reserves are properly managed with strict rules about approaching wildlife, which are enforced rather than suggested.
puertomadryn.airquality: Excellent. The constant Patagonian wind means nothing accumulates, the population is small, and the only significant industry is the aluminium smelter outside town, which is monitored. The dry steppe generates dust on windy days, which is the one recurring qualification. Readings here are among the best in this dataset, and the clarity of the air is noticeable, particularly at night when the southern sky is exceptionally dark and clear.

laserena.climate: La Serena has one of the most even climates anywhere in this dataset, moderated by the cold Humboldt current running up the coast. February highs reach only about 23C and July lows sit near 8C, so the range across the entire year is narrow and neither season is demanding. Rainfall is almost absent at 90mm, falling in a few winter events. The coastal fog known as the camanchaca rolls in on many mornings and burns off by midday, which is why mornings are grey more often than the sunshine figures suggest.
laserena.cost: Around $1,000 a month is good value for Chile, the most expensive country in South America, and below Santiago or Valparaiso. A one-bedroom flat is moderate, rising through January and February when Chilean families fill the coast. Groceries are moderate by Chilean standards, which are high, and wine and produce are cheap. Utilities are low because the climate needs neither heating nor cooling. The seafood along this coast is excellent value and eating out is reasonable.
laserena.wifi: Good. Chile leads South America on connectivity and La Serena is well served, with fast fibre across the city at reasonable prices and reliable mobile coverage. A small coworking presence exists and the Universidad de La Serena adds a professional population. The astronomy sector in the Elqui valley has brought international scientific infrastructure to the region for decades, which means the technical base here is better than a coastal town of this size would otherwise justify.
laserena.nightlife: Moderate and seasonal. La Serena has bars and restaurants around the centre and along the Avenida del Mar, busy through the Chilean summer holidays in January and February and quieter the rest of the year. Coquimbo next door has the fishing port and a rougher, livelier evening scene, and the two cities function as one for practical purposes. The university keeps a student circuit going in term. Nothing here approaches Santiago or Valparaiso.
laserena.nature: Very good. The beach runs continuously for about six kilometres from La Serena to Coquimbo. Inland, the Elqui valley climbs into the Andes through vineyards and pisco distilleries under skies clear enough that several international observatories are sited there, and the stargazing is genuinely world class rather than a marketing claim. The Humboldt penguin reserve north has penguins, dolphins and occasionally whales, and the Fray Jorge cloud forest is a strange relict ecosystem south.
laserena.safety: Reasonably safe. Chile has historically had the lowest crime rates in South America, though street crime and phone snatching have risen markedly across the country in recent years and the reputation is now ahead of the reality. La Serena is comfortable in the centre and along the beachfront in daylight, with ordinary urban caution needed after dark, particularly around Coquimbo's port area. The genuine hazard is seismic: this is a highly active coast and tsunami routes are signposted.
laserena.food: Adequate. Chilean coastal cooking is built on the extraordinary seafood of the Humboldt current: congrio, machas, locos and the fish market at Coquimbo is worth an early visit. Beyond that, empanadas, pastel de choclo and the Chilean grill are the staples. The Elqui valley produces pisco, papaya and excellent goat cheese. Range beyond Chilean food is limited in a city this size, and the restaurant scene is functional rather than a reason to come.
laserena.community: Small. La Serena has a modest foreign population, mostly connected to the observatories in the Elqui valley, plus retirees and a scattering of long-term residents. There is no nomad community; Santiago and Valparaiso have what Chile offers. The astronomy world is genuinely international but is a closed professional circle rather than an open one. Anyone arriving alone should expect to build through Spanish and local activities rather than find an existing group.
laserena.english: Limited. Chilean English proficiency is moderate and concentrated among younger and educated people, with the observatory and tourism sectors the main exceptions. Everyday life and all administration operate in Spanish. Chilean Spanish is notoriously fast and idiomatic, which makes it hard even for people fluent in other varieties. Functional Spanish is close to necessary for anything beyond a short visit, and the local dialect will take some adjustment on top of it.
laserena.visa: Chile grants most Western nationals ninety days visa-free on arrival, extendable once for a further ninety days. There is no dedicated Chilean digital nomad visa, though temporary residence for people with independent income exists and Chile has generally been open, with the caveat that immigration processing has had substantial backlogs. Peru is far north and Argentina over the Andes, where the passes close in winter. Agricultural import controls are enforced strictly at every border and airport.
laserena.culture: Moderate. La Serena is the second oldest city in Chile, founded in 1544, and a twentieth-century restoration programme rebuilt much of the centre in a neocolonial style, which gives it around thirty churches and a coherent look that is partly authentic and partly reconstructed. The Elqui valley is Gabriela Mistral's country, Chile's Nobel laureate poet, and her birthplace at Vicuna is preserved. The valley also has a long association with mysticism and stargazing that shapes its character.
laserena.cleanliness: Reasonable. The centre, the Avenida del Mar and the beaches are maintained to a decent standard and Chilean municipal services function better than most of the region. Coquimbo next door is visibly rougher. Beach water quality is monitored and generally acceptable. The dry climate keeps dust rather than mud as the issue. Nothing here reads as neglected, and the standard sits comfortably above the South American average without matching European norms.
laserena.airquality: Very good. The constant onshore wind off the cold Humboldt current keeps the coastal air moving and there is no significant industry in La Serena itself. The regional caveat is mining: Chile's copper and iron operations inland are a serious source elsewhere in the country, and the Andacollo mining area south of here has had documented problems. The Elqui valley air is exceptionally clear, which is precisely why the observatories were built there.

cagliari.climate: Cagliari has one of the best climates in this dataset, which the score of 9 reflects. July highs reach about 32C in dry Mediterranean air and January lows sit near 8C, so winters are mild and summers hot without the humidity that makes coastal cities elsewhere uncomfortable. Rain totals only 425mm, falling between October and April with a November peak and essentially nothing in July. The mistral blows hard through parts of the year, which cools the city and fills the bay with sailing boats.
cagliari.cost: Around $1,500 a month covers a comfortable standard, cheaper than mainland Italian cities of comparable size and well below Rome or Milan. A one-bedroom flat is moderate, with the Castello and Marina districts at the upper end. Food is good value: the markets are excellent and an ordinary trattoria meal is reasonable. Sardinian wine and produce are cheap. The cost that island living adds is the ferry and flight connections to the mainland, which are an ongoing rather than occasional expense.
cagliari.wifi: Adequate to good. Italian fibre has reached Cagliari and offers decent speeds at ordinary European prices, with comprehensive mobile coverage across the urban area. A modest coworking scene exists, supported by the university and a small technology sector. Quality varies by building as it does throughout Italy, and the medieval stone walls in the Castello district defeat a lot of domestic wifi hardware, which is worth asking about specifically before taking a flat up there.
cagliari.nightlife: Good for the size. The Marina district below Castello has a dense run of bars and restaurants in narrow streets, busy year-round rather than only in season, and the university keeps a student circuit going. Summer moves the evening to Poetto beach, where the kiosks along the sand run late. Italian licensing and habits mean it starts late and is sociable rather than club-driven. Sardinia's own drinking culture centres on wine and the local Ichnusa beer.
cagliari.nature: Very good and unusually close at hand. Poetto beach runs eight kilometres along the eastern edge of the city and is reachable by bus in fifteen minutes. Behind it, the Molentargius salt pans hold a resident flamingo population inside the municipal boundary, which is genuinely strange to see from a city bus. The Sella del Diavolo headland gives walking with sea on three sides. Beyond, the Sulcis coast, the Sarrabus mountains and the empty interior are all within reach.
cagliari.safety: Safe. Italy has moderate crime and Sardinia is among its safer regions, with Cagliari a comfortable city where walking at night in the Marina and Castello is unremarkable. Petty theft and pickpocketing in the tourist areas and on buses are the realistic concerns. The genuine hazards are seasonal: strong currents on some beaches, and summer wildfire in the interior, which Sardinia suffers badly in dry years and which can close roads.
cagliari.food: Very good and specifically Sardinian rather than generically Italian. The island has its own repertoire: culurgiones, the filled pasta of the Ogliastra, malloreddus with sausage ragu, porceddu suckling pig, bottarga which is cured mullet roe and a Cagliari speciality, and pane carasau flatbread. Seafood from the gulf is excellent. Sardinian wine, particularly Cannonau and Vermentino, is good and cheap. The San Benedetto market is one of the largest covered markets in Italy.
cagliari.community: Small. Cagliari has a modest foreign population, mostly students on exchange and a scattering of long-term residents, and no nomad community. Sardinia's international presence concentrates on the Costa Smeralda in season and disperses in October. The local social world is warm but settled and runs in Italian. Anyone arriving alone should expect to need the language and to build through the university, sport or the sailing community rather than find a group.
cagliari.english: Limited. English is spoken by younger Italians and in the tourism businesses, and much less elsewhere. Ordinary shops, offices and older residents work in Italian, and all administration is Italian-only. Sardinian, which is a distinct Romance language rather than a dialect of Italian, is widely spoken among older people and in the interior. For a stay of any length here, functional Italian moves from useful to necessary.
cagliari.visa: Italy is in the Schengen area, so most non-EU nationals get ninety days within any 180-day period and EU citizens face no restriction. Italy's digital nomad visa, in force since 2024, covers highly qualified remote workers meeting income, insurance and accommodation requirements, applied for at a consulate before travel. Processing is slow and consulate practice varies considerably, with appointment backlogs running to months in some places. The elective residence visa is an alternative for those with passive income.
cagliari.culture: Good. Cagliari's Castello district is a walled medieval citadel on a limestone ridge with Pisan towers you can climb, and the archaeological museum below it holds the bronzetti of the Nuragic civilisation, a Bronze Age culture unique to Sardinia that built thousands of stone towers across the island. The Roman amphitheatre is cut into the rock. Sant'Efisio at the start of May is one of the largest religious processions in the Mediterranean.
cagliari.cleanliness: Reasonable. The Castello, the Marina and the main avenues are maintained properly and Poetto beach is cleaned through the season. Waste separation in Cagliari is thorough and the city has good recycling figures by Italian standards. The outer residential districts are ordinary and there is some graffiti, as everywhere in Italy. Water quality at Poetto is monitored and generally good. Nothing here reads as neglected.
cagliari.airquality: Very good. Cagliari has no heavy industry within the city, the constant sea breeze and the mistral disperse what traffic produces, and the dry climate means little of the winter heating pollution that affects northern Italy. The Sarroch petrochemical complex twenty kilometres west is the region's significant source and can affect readings depending on wind direction. Saharan dust events reach Sardinia several times a year. Otherwise the air here is markedly better than the Po valley.

maribor.climate: Maribor has a continental climate in the Drava valley, with July highs around 27C and January lows near minus 1C. Rain totals 1,113mm with an early summer peak in May and a dry February, so it is wetter than most of central Europe and the summers bring thunderstorms rather than drought. Winter is cold and often grey in the valley while Pohorje above holds proper snow, which is the whole basis of the local ski economy. Spring and autumn are short and pleasant.
maribor.cost: Around $1,200 a month is meaningfully cheaper than Ljubljana and among the better value cities in the eurozone. A one-bedroom flat is affordable, kept reasonable by a large student population. Groceries are ordinary central European prices and eating out is good value, with the local wine particularly cheap given the region produces it. Utilities include real winter heating. Prices rise noticeably during the ski season for anything close to the Pohorje cable car.
maribor.wifi: Good. Slovenia has strong digital infrastructure and Maribor is fully covered, with fast fibre at reasonable prices and reliable mobile data. The University of Maribor is the city's largest institution and supports a small coworking scene and a technology sector that has grown steadily. English is widely spoken among younger Slovenes and in the professional world, which removes most of the administrative friction a foreigner faces further east or in Japan.
maribor.nightlife: Moderate and student-driven. Maribor has a substantial university and the bars along the Lent riverside and in the old town are busy through term, quieter in the holidays. The Lent Festival in late June and early July takes over the riverside for two weeks and is one of the larger cultural festivals in central Europe. Slovenian drinking culture is relaxed and inexpensive. Anyone wanting scale is looking at Ljubljana or Graz, both close.
maribor.nature: Very good. Pohorje rises directly behind the city and the cable car from the edge of town reaches the ski and hiking area in minutes, which is an unusually direct arrangement. The massif has trails, mountain biking and a downhill World Cup course. The Drava runs through the city with a long riverside path, and the wine roads of Slovenske Gorice and Jeruzalem climb into the hills east. The Pohorje peat bogs and lakes are a protected and distinctive landscape.
maribor.safety: Very safe. Slovenia has among the lowest crime rates in Europe and Maribor is a comfortable city where walking at any hour is unremarkable. Petty theft is uncommon. The realistic concerns are the ordinary consequences of a student drinking culture at closing time and pickpocketing during festival crowds. The genuine hazards are mountain ones: Pohorje weather changes and the ski terrain requires the usual care, and the Drava runs fast after rain.
maribor.food: Good. Styrian cooking is hearty and central European: pumpkin seed oil which is a genuine regional product and used on everything, sour soups, the local sausages and the potica rolled cake. Maribor sits in one of Slovenia's main wine regions and the whites from the surrounding hills are good and cheap. The market is worth using. The city has a growing number of modern kitchens. Range beyond central European and Italian influence is limited.
maribor.community: Small. Maribor has a student international population through Erasmus and the university's programmes, plus a modest professional layer in the technology sector, but no nomad community. Ljubljana has what Slovenia offers on that front. The Slovenian social world is friendly and relatively open by central European standards but still takes time. Anyone arriving alone should expect the university and the outdoor clubs to be the practical routes in.
maribor.english: Reasonable. Slovenes generally have good English, particularly younger people, and it is reliable in the university orbit, in cafes and in professional settings. It thins with older residents and in any administrative dealing, which operates in Slovenian. German is also widely understood given the proximity to Austria. Coverage is comfortable for daily life without being universal, and some Slovenian is appreciated more than it is expected.
maribor.visa: Slovenia is in the Schengen area and the eurozone, so most non-EU nationals get ninety days within any 180-day period and EU citizens face no restriction. Slovenia introduced a digital nomad permit in 2025 allowing up to a year for remote workers employed outside the country, without immediate renewal, which is a genuine new option though the practice around it is still settling. Croatia and Austria are both Schengen, so neither offers a reset.
maribor.culture: Moderate. Maribor's main square holds a plague column and the old town hall, and the Lent riverside has the Old Vine House, where a grapevine planted over four hundred years ago still produces and is recognised as the world's oldest of its kind. The Jewish quarter has one of the oldest surviving synagogues in Europe. Maribor was European Capital of Culture in 2012 and kept some of the programming. The wine culture is the deeper local tradition.
maribor.cleanliness: Very good. Slovenia maintains public space to a high standard and Maribor is tidy, with the old town, the riverside and the parks all in good order. Waste separation is thorough and Slovenia has among the best recycling rates in the European Union. The socialist-era housing estates on the outskirts are ordinary but not neglected. Pohorje's trails and facilities are well maintained. The standard sits comfortably at central European norms.
maribor.airquality: Moderate, and the score of 6 reflects a genuine local issue. Maribor sits in the Drava valley, which traps air during winter inversions, and domestic heating combined with traffic produces particulate readings that exceed European limits on cold still days through the heating season. Slovenia has worked on this through heating conversion programmes. Summer and the shoulder seasons are unremarkable, and the air on Pohorje above the inversion layer is clean.

almeria.climate: Almeria has the driest climate in mainland Europe and the score of 9 reflects how comfortable that makes it. July highs reach about 32C in low humidity and January lows sit near 8C, with winter days regularly reaching eighteen or nineteen under abundant sun. Rain totals only 257mm, among the lowest anywhere on the continent, falling in a handful of winter events with nothing at all in July. This is genuinely a desert climate rather than a Mediterranean one, and the landscape shows it.
almeria.cost: Around $1,200 a month makes Almeria among the cheapest coastal cities in Spain and well below Malaga, Valencia or Barcelona. A one-bedroom flat is moderate, with the centre and the seafront at the upper end. Food is inexpensive, helped by the enormous agricultural sector immediately west that supplies much of northern Europe's winter vegetables. The free tapa that comes with a drink is a genuine local custom here rather than a tourist gesture. Utilities are low given the mild winters.
almeria.wifi: Good. Spain has one of the best fibre networks in Europe and Almeria is comprehensively covered, with fast inexpensive home connections and reliable mobile data. A small coworking scene exists and the University of Almeria adds a modest professional population. The city has not attracted the nomad numbers that Malaga and Valencia have, which means fewer dedicated spaces but also none of the housing pressure those cities now have, which is a fair trade.
almeria.nightlife: Moderate. Almeria has a tapas circuit through the centre that is genuinely good and inexpensive, since the free tapa custom means an evening of drinks effectively includes dinner. Bars concentrate around the Rambla and the streets behind the port, with the university keeping a student scene going in term. Summer moves the crowd to the beach chiringuitos. It is a Spanish provincial nightlife, sociable and late, rather than anything on the scale of the bigger coastal cities.
almeria.nature: Very good. Cabo de Gata, thirty minutes east, is a volcanic coastal park with the emptiest beaches on the Spanish Mediterranean, cliffs, salt pans with flamingos and no development to speak of, which is rare on this coast. The Tabernas desert north is the only true desert in Europe. Behind it the Sierra Nevada rises to over 3,000m within two hours, so skiing and sea are genuinely reachable on the same day. The Alpujarras villages are close.
almeria.safety: Safe. Spain has low violent crime and Almeria is a comfortable provincial city where walking at night in the centre is unremarkable. Petty theft in the summer crowds is the realistic concern, at lower rates than Barcelona or Malaga because there are simply fewer tourists. The genuine hazards are environmental: strong summer sun in a desert climate, and the flash floods that occasionally hit the dry riverbeds of this province after the rare heavy rain.
almeria.food: Good. Almeria's tapas culture is the practical distinction: order a drink and food arrives free, which is a serious local institution rather than a token. The province produces an enormous share of Europe's winter vegetables so the produce is fresh and cheap. Seafood from the port, particularly the red prawns from Garrucha, is excellent. Andalusian cooking otherwise applies: gazpacho, fried fish, migas. Range beyond Spanish food is thin in a city this size.
almeria.community: Small. Almeria has a modest foreign population, largely northern European long-stay winter visitors along the coast and a substantial migrant agricultural workforce in the greenhouse belt, which are two entirely separate worlds. There is no nomad community; Malaga and Valencia have Spain's. The local social world is Spanish and provincial. Anyone arriving alone should expect to need the language and to build slowly rather than find an established group.
almeria.english: Limited. English is spoken by younger Spaniards and in the tourism businesses along the coast, and much less in the city itself, which is a working provincial capital rather than a resort. Shops, offices and administration operate in Spanish. Andalusian Spanish drops consonants and runs words together, which makes it harder than the textbook version. Functional Spanish is close to necessary for a stay of any length here.
almeria.visa: Spain is in the Schengen area, so most non-EU nationals get ninety days within any 180-day period and EU citizens face no restriction. Spain's digital nomad visa, created under the 2023 startups law, is among the more accessible in Europe: it covers remote workers for foreign companies, has an income threshold tied to the minimum wage, runs up to three years and can be applied for from inside Spain after entering as a tourist. It carries a favourable tax regime for qualifying applicants.
almeria.culture: Moderate. The Alcazaba is the largest Muslim fortress built in Spain after the Alhambra, a tenth-century citadel on the hill above the city with walls running down the ridge. The cathedral was built as a fortress with cannon emplacements because of Barbary raids. The Tabernas desert north was where a great many spaghetti westerns were shot and several sets survive as attractions. The province's Almerian film history is a genuine local identity rather than a footnote.
almeria.cleanliness: Reasonable. The centre, the Rambla and the seafront promenade are maintained properly and the beaches are cleaned through the season. Waste separation functions to a normal Spanish standard. The outer districts are ordinary. The genuine environmental issue here is not litter but the greenhouse belt west of the city, a plastic sea covering tens of thousands of hectares that generates enormous quantities of plastic waste and has documented problems with disposal and with labour conditions.
almeria.airquality: Very good. The desert climate, constant sea breeze and absence of heavy industry keep readings low, and Almeria consistently records among the better air quality figures in Spain. The two qualifications are Saharan dust, which reaches this coast several times a year and pushes particulate readings sharply higher for a day or two, and agricultural dust from the greenhouse region west. Neither is a persistent problem and the air here is markedly better than Madrid or Barcelona.

napier.climate: Napier has a temperate maritime climate with unusually high sunshine hours, among the best in New Zealand. Summer highs sit around 24C from December to March and winter days reach about 14C with cold nights. Hawke's Bay is in the rain shadow of the ranges, so it is markedly drier than the west coast, which is what carries the 7.
napier.cost: Moderate at around $1,700 a month, cheaper than Auckland or Wellington but not cheap in absolute terms. A one-bedroom flat runs roughly $850 to $1,200 depending on how close it sits to the Art Deco centre or Marine Parade. New Zealand grocery prices are high and imported goods higher still, which holds the score at 5.
napier.wifi: Solid. New Zealand's national fibre rollout reached provincial centres including Napier, and gigabit plans are available across most of the town at ordinary domestic pricing. Mobile coverage from the three networks is comprehensive in the built-up area. There is no meaningful coworking market, so the connection at the property is what matters here.
napier.nightlife: Limited, which the 4 records honestly. Napier has a handful of bars along Emerson Street and Ahuriri, a few good wine bars given the region, and that is close to the whole picture. The town is quiet after ten on a weekday. Hastings adds a little twenty minutes south, but nobody comes here for a night out.
napier.nature: Strong. Cape Kidnappers holds the largest mainland gannet colony in the world, the Hawke's Bay cycle trails run over two hundred kilometres through vineyards and along the coast, and Te Mata Peak rises behind Havelock North. The beach at Marine Parade is shingle rather than sand, which is worth knowing before arriving with a towel.
napier.safety: High, as it is across provincial New Zealand. Violent crime is rare, the town is comfortable to walk at night, and the main practical risks are natural rather than criminal. Napier was destroyed by an earthquake in 1931 and the region remains seismically active, with tsunami evacuation routes marked along the seafront for good reason.
napier.food: Very good for a town this size. Hawke's Bay is New Zealand's oldest wine region and one of its most important food-producing areas, with orchards, vineyards and farmers markets supplying restaurants directly. The Hawke's Bay Farmers Market in Hastings runs every Sunday. Seafood is excellent and prices are high, which is the national pattern.
napier.community: Essentially nonexistent for remote workers, and the 2 is accurate. There is no coworking scene, no meetup culture and no visible international presence beyond seasonal workers in the vineyards. The social life that exists is local, long-established and built around families and sport. Anyone arriving alone should expect to make the effort themselves.
napier.english: Universal. New Zealand English is the first language of daily life and te reo Maori is an official language increasingly present in signage and greetings. There is no language barrier of any kind for an English speaker, and the accent is the only adjustment most arrivals need to make.
napier.visa: Middling. New Zealand clarified in 2025 that visitors may work remotely for a foreign employer while on a visitor visa, which improved the position considerably. Most Western nationals get an NZeTA and three months on arrival, extendable in some cases to nine months in an eighteen-month period. Longer stays need employer accreditation or skilled residence.
napier.culture: Better than the population suggests. Napier holds the most concentrated collection of Art Deco architecture outside Miami Beach, rebuilt in a single style after the 1931 earthquake, and the February Art Deco Festival fills the town with vintage cars and period dress. The MTG Hawke's Bay museum and the National Aquarium sit on Marine Parade.
napier.cleanliness: High. Napier is well maintained, litter is rare, the seafront and Art Deco quarter are actively cared for as the town's main economic asset, and municipal services are reliable. New Zealand's environmental standards are strong and visibly enforced. The 8 reflects an ordinary well-run provincial town rather than anything exceptional.
napier.airquality: Excellent. Coastal position, prevailing westerlies and no heavy industry give Napier consistently clean air, with annual PM2.5 well within World Health Organization guidance. The one qualification is winter, when domestic wood burners in the Hawke's Bay basin can push particulate readings up on still cold nights, a known regional issue.

wollongong.climate: Warm temperate and among the more pleasant on the Australian east coast. Summer highs sit in the high twenties from December to February with the sea breeze taking the edge off, and winter days reach about seventeen. The escarpment creates local weather, so the hills behind the city can be in cloud while the beach is clear.
wollongong.cost: Expensive, as everywhere in Australia. Budget around $2,000 a month as a solo remote worker, with a one-bedroom near the beach or the centre running roughly $1,000 to $1,400. That is meaningfully below Sydney for a comparable coastal life, which is the whole argument for living here, but the score of 4 reflects the absolute level.
wollongong.wifi: Good. The NBN reaches most of the inner suburbs with reliable speeds and the university drives demand for better service than a city this size would otherwise have. Mobile coverage is comprehensive. The standing Australian complaint applies: home internet is expensive relative to what it delivers and plans vary by address, so check the specific lease.
wollongong.nightlife: Modest. Crown Street and the North Wollongong pubs carry most of it, with a student crowd from the university giving weeknights more life than the population would suggest. It closes early by international standards. Sydney is ninety minutes by train for anything more, which is what most people here do rather than complain.
wollongong.nature: Excellent. The city sits on a narrow strip between the Illawarra escarpment and seventeen beaches, with the Sea Cliff Bridge and the Grand Pacific Drive running south along the coast. Rainforest walks start in the hills directly behind the suburbs, and the Royal National Park is immediately north on the way to Sydney.
wollongong.safety: High. Wollongong is a safe Australian regional city with low violent crime and comfortable walking at night in the central and beachside areas. The genuine risks are environmental: rip currents on the beaches, which claim lives on this coast every year, and bushfire in the escarpment during a hot dry summer.
wollongong.food: Decent rather than remarkable, which the 6 records. The city has a strong Macedonian, Italian and Lebanese heritage from the steelworks migration and the food reflects it, particularly in Warrawong and Cringila. Cafe culture is Australian-standard, meaning very good coffee everywhere. Restaurant prices are high and the fine dining scene is thin.
wollongong.community: Weak. There is a small coworking scene helped by the university and a technology sector that grew out of the steelworks, but no nomad community in any recognisable form. Most foreigners here are students. The 3 reflects real but shallow professional networking rather than anything a visiting remote worker plugs into.
wollongong.english: Universal, as everywhere in Australia. The city has substantial migrant communities from North Macedonia, Italy, Lebanon and more recently South Asia, and their languages are common at home, but English is the language of everything public and there is no barrier of any kind.
wollongong.visa: Poor. Australia has no digital nomad visa. Most Western nationals get an eVisitor or ETA for three months per entry within a year, which does not permit work for an Australian employer and leaves remote work for a foreign one in an unclarified grey area. Working Holiday visas cover under-thirties or under-thirty-fives depending on nationality.
wollongong.culture: Thin, honestly. Wollongong has a regional art gallery with a respectable collection, the Nan Tien Temple, the largest Buddhist temple in the southern hemisphere, and a university that brings some programming. Beyond that the cultural weight is in Sydney, ninety minutes north, which is where most residents go for it.
wollongong.cleanliness: High. Australian municipal standards apply, the beaches are patrolled and cleaned, waste collection is reliable and the city is well maintained. The Port Kembla industrial area at the southern end is the exception in appearance rather than in service, and the steelworks still operates. Water quality at the beaches is monitored and generally good.
wollongong.airquality: Good but not pristine. Coastal position and consistent sea breezes disperse well, and annual readings sit comfortably within guidance most of the year. Port Kembla's steelworks and the coal terminal are genuine local sources, and bushfire smoke during a bad summer can degrade air quality across the whole region for days.

geelong.climate: Temperate and changeable, sharing Melbourne's reputation for four seasons in a day. Summer highs sit around twenty-five with occasional spikes past forty on a northerly, and winter days reach about thirteen with grey skies. Corio Bay moderates the extremes slightly. The 6 reflects variability rather than harshness; nothing here is severe.
geelong.cost: Expensive in absolute terms. Budget around $2,000 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $1,000 to $1,400 depending on distance from the waterfront. Geelong is cheaper than inner Melbourne but the gap has narrowed sharply as people moved down the highway, and the 4 records Australian prices rather than any local problem.
geelong.wifi: Good. NBN coverage across the city is solid with fibre to the premises in the newer estates and reliable speeds elsewhere. Deakin University and a growing services sector keep demand up. Mobile coverage is comprehensive. As across Australia, home internet costs more than the speed justifies and the plan varies by address.
geelong.nightlife: Modest. Little Malop Street and the waterfront carry the bars and the student crowd from Deakin gives it some life, but the city is quiet by ten on a weeknight. Melbourne is an hour by train, which is where anyone wanting a real night out goes, and the last train back is the constraint.
geelong.nature: Strong. Geelong sits at the head of the Bellarine Peninsula with beaches, wineries and the rail trail out to Queenscliff, and the Great Ocean Road starts twenty minutes down the coast at Torquay. The bay itself is shallow and calm rather than surf, so waves mean driving to Bells Beach or Jan Juc.
geelong.safety: High. Geelong is a safe Australian regional city with low violent crime and comfortable walking in the central and waterfront areas at night. The usual coastal risks apply on the ocean beaches, where rips are serious and the Great Ocean Road coastline claims swimmers every summer. Traffic on the highway to Melbourne is the mundane hazard.
geelong.food: Good. The waterfront and Pakington Street carry the restaurants, the coffee is Melbourne-standard which is to say excellent, and the Bellarine's wineries, oyster farms and produce supply the kitchens directly. Prices are high as everywhere in Australia. The 7 reflects genuine quality without the depth Melbourne offers an hour away.
geelong.community: Weak. There is a coworking scene and a startup presence that grew around the transition from Ford and Alcoa manufacturing to services, and Deakin adds a student layer, but there is no nomad community. Most people working remotely here are Melbourne employees who moved down the highway rather than travellers.
geelong.english: Universal. Australian English is the language of everything and there is no barrier for an English speaker. Geelong has established Croatian, Italian, Greek and more recent Karen and South Sudanese communities whose languages are common at home, but nothing public requires anything but English.
geelong.visa: Poor. Australia offers no digital nomad visa. The eVisitor and ETA give most Western nationals three months per entry within a twelve-month period, permitting tourism and business meetings but not work for an Australian employer, with remote work for a foreign one unaddressed. Working Holiday visas are the main route to longer stays with work rights.
geelong.culture: Modest but real. The Geelong Gallery holds a serious regional collection including Eugene von Guerard's Bushfire, the National Wool Museum records the industry the city was built on, and the painted bollards along the waterfront are a genuinely local piece of public art. Australian rules football here is closer to religion than recreation.
geelong.cleanliness: High. The waterfront redevelopment turned a working port frontage into one of the better-maintained public spaces in regional Victoria, waste services are reliable and the city is visibly cared for. Australian municipal standards apply throughout. Beach water quality in Corio Bay is monitored and occasionally affected after heavy rain.
geelong.airquality: Good. Bay position and prevailing southwesterlies give consistent dispersal and annual readings sit within guidance. The refinery at Corio is a local source and the industrial history left some legacy contamination in soil rather than air. Bushfire smoke during a severe Victorian summer is the one factor that degrades readings substantially.

newplymouth.climate: Mild, wet and windy, which is the Taranaki condition. Summer highs sit around twenty-two and winter days reach about fourteen, so nothing is extreme, but the region catches weather off the Tasman Sea and rainfall is high. Mount Taranaki creates its own conditions and is visible roughly one day in three.
newplymouth.cost: Moderate at around $1,700 a month. A one-bedroom runs roughly $800 to $1,100, cheaper than Auckland or Wellington and typical for provincial New Zealand. The oil and gas sector historically kept local wages and rents above what the town's size would suggest. Grocery prices are high, which is the national condition rather than a local one.
newplymouth.wifi: Solid. New Zealand's fibre rollout reached New Plymouth and gigabit plans are available across the town at standard domestic pricing. Mobile coverage is good in the built-up area and thins on the coastal roads and around the mountain. There is minimal coworking provision, so the property's own connection is the thing to check.
newplymouth.nightlife: Limited. A handful of bars around Devon Street and the waterfront, a brewing scene that is better than expected, and very little after ten on a weekday. The WOMAD festival in March is the exception and transforms the town for a weekend. The 4 is an honest reading of a provincial New Zealand town.
newplymouth.nature: Outstanding, and the 9 is earned. Mount Taranaki is a near-perfect volcanic cone with an alpine national park around it, thirty minutes from the centre, and the Surf Highway runs around the coast past break after break. The Coastal Walkway extends thirteen kilometres along the waterfront with Len Lye's Wind Wand at its centre.
newplymouth.safety: Very high. New Plymouth is a safe provincial town with low crime and comfortable walking at night. The real hazards are natural: Mount Taranaki is an active volcano with a documented eruption history, the surf is powerful and claims swimmers, and the coastal weather changes quickly enough to catch walkers out on the mountain.
newplymouth.food: Reasonable rather than notable. There are good cafes along Devon Street, a strong local coffee culture and a farmers market, with Taranaki dairy and produce supplying the region. Restaurant depth is limited by population and prices are high, as everywhere in New Zealand. The 6 records adequacy rather than any particular strength.
newplymouth.community: Essentially absent for remote workers. There is no coworking culture, no nomad presence and no meetup scene. The professional network is real but narrow, built around energy, engineering and dairy. Anyone arriving alone will need to join something local, and the town is small enough that this actually works.
newplymouth.english: Universal. English is the language of everything, with te reo Maori an official language and increasingly visible in public signage. Taranaki has a significant Maori history including the Parihaka passive resistance movement, which is worth reading about before arriving. No language barrier exists for an English speaker.
newplymouth.visa: Middling. New Zealand confirmed in 2025 that visitor visa holders may work remotely for foreign employers, which resolved a long ambiguity. NZeTA holders get up to three months, extendable in some cases to nine within eighteen. Working Holiday schemes cover defined nationalities and ages. The region's energy sector has historically sponsored skilled workers directly.
newplymouth.culture: Better than the size suggests. The Govett-Brewster Art Gallery and its Len Lye Centre, dedicated to the kinetic sculptor who was born in the region, is a genuinely significant institution, and the WOMAD festival each March brings international acts to Brooklands Bowl. Pukekura Park is one of the finest gardens in the country.
newplymouth.cleanliness: Very high. New Plymouth is consistently rated among the best-maintained towns in New Zealand, the Coastal Walkway and Pukekura Park are exceptionally kept, and municipal services are reliable. The district has won national and international awards for liveability, which in practice means the place looks after itself visibly.
newplymouth.airquality: Excellent. Constant Tasman Sea wind, no heavy industry beyond the energy sector's offshore and processing facilities, and a small population give consistently clean air well within guidance. Winter wood burners raise readings slightly on still nights, which is the standard New Zealand qualification, but the wind here rarely allows it to persist.

nadi.climate: Tropical with a marked wet and dry split. Nadi sits on the drier western side of Viti Levu, which is why the resorts are here: daytime temperatures run around thirty year-round, and the wet season from November to April brings heavy rain, high humidity and the cyclone risk that defines the calendar.
nadi.cost: Moderate at around $1,600 a month, which is expensive for the Pacific and reflects an economy built on tourism and imports. A one-bedroom runs roughly $500 to $900. Almost everything on a shelf arrived by ship, and the markup shows in groceries and anything electronic. Local produce and fish at the Nadi market are the exception.
nadi.wifi: Mediocre. Fiji's international connectivity improved substantially with the Southern Cross cable, and Nadi's hotels and the better apartments have workable fixed connections, but pricing is high and speeds inconsistent. Mobile data from Vodafone or Digicel is the practical fallback. Anyone with a call-heavy schedule should test before committing to a month.
nadi.nightlife: Thin. Nadi town has a few bars and the resort strip at Denarau has hotel bars and a marina, but this is a transit town rather than a going-out one. Most visitors are here for a night before flying out to the islands. The 4 is an accurate reading rather than a harsh one.
nadi.nature: Excellent. The Yasawa and Mamanuca island chains start an hour offshore by catamaran, the Sabeto hot springs and mud pools are twenty minutes away, and the Sleeping Giant garden and Nausori Highlands sit behind the town. The reef diving and snorkelling are the reason most people come to Fiji at all.
nadi.safety: Reasonable. Fiji is generally safe and Fijians are famously welcoming, but petty theft and opportunistic crime around Nadi town and the tourist areas are real and worth ordinary precautions. Reef and rip hazards are the more serious risk. Political stability has improved considerably since the coup era, though the history is recent.
nadi.food: Decent. Fijian food blends Melanesian, Indian and Chinese influence, and the Indo-Fijian curry houses in Nadi town are the best value and often the best eating in the area. Kokoda, raw fish cured in citrus and coconut milk, is the local dish worth seeking out. Resort dining is expensive and unremarkable by comparison.
nadi.community: Weak. There is no nomad scene in Fiji in any organised sense, and the foreign population is split between tourists passing through and long-term expatriates in tourism and aid. A handful of coworking initiatives have appeared in Suva rather than Nadi. The 3 reflects an isolated position rather than an unwelcoming one.
nadi.english: Strong. English is an official language and the medium of education and business throughout Fiji, and it is spoken universally in the tourism sector. Fijian and Fiji Hindi are the languages of daily life for most people. An English speaker will have no practical difficulty anywhere here.
nadi.visa: Good. Most Western nationals receive four months visa-free on arrival, which is generous, and extensions to six months are commonly granted at the immigration office. There is no digital nomad visa, although Fiji has discussed one repeatedly. Longer stays run through work permits or investor categories, both of which require sponsorship and patience.
nadi.culture: Real but not concentrated in Nadi itself. The Sri Siva Subramaniya temple at the edge of town is the largest Hindu temple in the southern hemisphere and reflects the Indo-Fijian half of the country's story. Traditional Fijian village life, kava ceremony and meke remain living practice, mostly experienced through organised visits.
nadi.cleanliness: Middling. The resort areas and Denarau are well maintained, Nadi town considerably less so, and waste management across Fiji is an acknowledged problem with limited recycling and visible litter along some roadsides and waterways. Cyclone damage compounds it periodically. The 6 records an honest gap between the tourist strip and the town.
nadi.airquality: Very good. Trade winds, an island position and no heavy industry give consistently clean air well within guidance. Sugar cane burning in the western division during the harvest season is the one local source that raises readings noticeably, and it is seasonal and localised rather than a persistent condition.

portvila.climate: Tropical and humid year-round, with daytime temperatures around twenty-eight and little seasonal variation in heat. The distinction is rain: November to April is the wet season with high humidity and cyclone risk, and May to October is drier and noticeably more comfortable. Vanuatu sits in an active cyclone belt and has taken severe hits.
portvila.cost: Expensive for what it is, and the 4 is honest. Budget around $2,000 a month as a solo remote worker. Almost everything is imported and prices reflect it, with rent for anything aimed at expatriates quoted in a different bracket from local housing. Local markets are cheap; supermarkets and anything electronic are not.
portvila.wifi: Poor to fair. Vanuatu's connectivity improved with the Interchange submarine cable but domestic pricing remains high and speeds are inconsistent. Starlink has become the practical answer for anyone here who cannot afford to be offline and is now common among businesses. Anyone with a demanding call schedule should treat connectivity as the main planning problem.
portvila.nightlife: Limited. Port Vila has a handful of bars along the seafront and at the resorts, a yacht club and a nakamal culture where kava rather than alcohol is the social centre. The 4 reflects a small capital rather than a dull one; the kava bars are genuinely part of daily life here.
portvila.nature: Outstanding. Efate has waterfalls, blue holes and reef within easy reach, and the outer islands hold Mount Yasur on Tanna, one of the most accessible active volcanoes anywhere, and the wrecks and blue holes of Espiritu Santo. The diving on the SS President Coolidge is world class. The 9 is fully earned.
portvila.safety: Reasonable. Vanuatu has low violent crime and Port Vila is comfortable by day, with ordinary precautions needed at night. The serious risks are natural: cyclones, earthquakes and volcanic activity are all real, and the country ranks among the most exposed in the world to natural disaster. Medical facilities are limited and evacuation insurance is sensible.
portvila.food: Decent. Port Vila has a surprisingly good restaurant scene for a town its size, a legacy of the French colonial period, with a few genuinely accomplished kitchens along the waterfront. The market house sells local produce cheaply. Lap lap, the baked root vegetable and coconut dish, is the national staple worth trying.
portvila.community: Weak. There is a long-standing expatriate community in offshore finance, tourism and development work, and a small number of remote workers, but nothing organised. Vanuatu marketed a nomad visa in 2020 that attracted little uptake. The 3 reflects a place where meeting people is easy but a professional network does not exist.
portvila.english: Good. English and French are both official languages alongside Bislama, the national creole, which is close enough to English that a visitor can follow a conversation within days. Education is split between English and French streams. An English speaker will manage everywhere, though Bislama opens doors quickly.
portvila.visa: Good. Most Western nationals get thirty to ninety days visa-free on arrival with straightforward extensions available locally. Vanuatu also markets a long-stay remote work option and a citizenship by investment programme, though the latter carries real international restrictions that should be researched directly rather than through promotional material. Work permits require a local sponsor.
portvila.culture: Strong and genuinely living. Vanuatu has more languages per head of population than anywhere on earth, over a hundred for around three hundred thousand people, and kastom practice including land diving on Pentecost remains active rather than performed. The National Museum in Port Vila is small but worth an afternoon. Kava culture is central.
portvila.cleanliness: Middling. Port Vila's centre and the resort areas are maintained, but waste management is limited nationally, recycling barely exists and plastic is a visible problem on some beaches and roadsides. Vanuatu banned single-use plastic bags in 2018, one of the first countries to do so, which has helped. Cyclone debris compounds the picture periodically.
portvila.airquality: Excellent. Trade winds, an island position and no industry give consistently clean air. The one qualification is volcanic: ash and gas from Ambae and Tanna have affected air quality on those islands severely enough to force evacuations, and a change in wind can carry haze towards Efate, though rarely for long.

alula.climate: Desert, and the 5 reflects a genuinely difficult summer. Winter from November to March is superb, with days in the low twenties and cold nights that approach freezing in January. Summer from June to September pushes past forty and makes the archaeological sites unpleasant by mid-morning. Rain is negligible year-round.
alula.cost: Expensive for the region at around $1,800 a month. The problem is accommodation: Al Ula is a managed tourism destination with hotel stock running from guesthouses to luxury resorts and almost no ordinary rental market. Food is far cheaper than the room, and the absence of any alcohol spend removes a line most budgets carry.
alula.wifi: Good. Saudi mobile data is fast and cheap with 5G across the built-up parts of the valley and the main sites, and the hotels serving international visitors have business-grade connections. There is no coworking. Coverage thins quickly in the desert beyond the oasis, which matters if the plan involves working away from town.
alula.nightlife: Nonexistent in any conventional sense, which the 2 records accurately. There is no alcohol anywhere in Saudi Arabia and no bar or club culture. The winter season brings a serious concert programme at the Maraya mirrored hall and events across the valley, which is a different thing entirely and worth timing a visit around.
alula.nature: Outstanding. The valley is a landscape of sandstone outcrops, oasis palm groves and desert escarpment, with Elephant Rock, the Sharaan nature reserve and the Harrat volcanic field nearby. The dark skies here are among the best accessible anywhere and stargazing is a genuine draw. The 9 reflects an unusual and largely unspoiled landscape.
alula.safety: High. Crime is very low in Saudi Arabia and Al Ula is a controlled destination with a visible tourism infrastructure. The practical risks are environmental: heat, dehydration and driving on desert roads. Social rules are stricter than most visitors are used to, and understanding them is part of staying comfortable rather than a safety issue.
alula.food: Limited, which the 5 records. The hotels have restaurants at hotel prices and the old town area has a growing cluster of places aimed at visitors, but the range is narrow for anyone staying weeks. Local Saudi cooking, dates from the oasis and the seasonal citrus are the genuine local pleasures here.
alula.community: Essentially nonexistent. Al Ula's foreign population is staff working on the Royal Commission's development projects and visitors passing through for a few nights. There is no nomad presence, no coworking and no meetup culture. Anyone here for a month will know the same handful of faces by the end of the first week.
alula.english: Moderate. English is widely used across the tourism infrastructure, the hotels and the guided tours, and signage at the sites is bilingual. Away from that, Arabic is the language of everything, and the workforce includes large numbers of South Asian workers speaking Urdu, Hindi and Malayalam. Enough English exists to function comfortably.
alula.visa: Weak. Saudi Arabia has no digital nomad visa. The eVisa covers around sixty nationalities for a year of multiple entries with ninety days per stay and a hundred and eighty in total, which is a tourist permission that does not authorise work. Longer stays need sponsorship or the Premium Residency programme and its fee.
alula.culture: Exceptional, and the 9 is earned. Hegra is Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO World Heritage site, a Nabataean city with over a hundred rock-cut tombs and almost none of Petra's crowds, and Dadan and Jabal Ikmah's inscriptions predate it. The mudbrick old town has been restored and the site was a major stop on the incense route.
alula.cleanliness: High. Al Ula is a managed destination with maintenance budgets to match, the heritage sites are actively conserved, and the built areas are visibly kept. The desert environment itself is protected within the reserves. The 8 reflects a place whose economy depends on how it looks and which is funded accordingly.
alula.airquality: Very good. Desert position, no industry and a tiny population give clean air most of the year. The qualification is dust: sandstorms and blowing dust raise particulate readings sharply for periods, particularly in spring, and this is a regional pattern rather than anything Al Ula generates itself.

abha.climate: The best in Saudi Arabia and the reason the country comes here in July. At around 2,200 metres, summer highs sit in the high twenties while Riyadh is above forty, and the monsoon fringe brings afternoon cloud and mist over the escarpment. Winter nights get genuinely cold and can approach freezing at this elevation.
abha.cost: Moderate at around $1,100 a month, which makes Abha one of the cheaper places to sit in Saudi Arabia. A furnished one-bedroom runs roughly $400 to $650. The Asir region grows much of its own produce and food is inexpensive if eaten locally. Fuel costs almost nothing and there is no alcohol spend anywhere.
abha.wifi: Good. Saudi mobile data is fast and inexpensive with strong 5G across the city, which is the reliable option, while fixed connections in older buildings vary by address. There is almost no coworking provision, so cafes and hotel rooms are where remote work happens. Power is stable and outages are rare.
abha.nightlife: Nonexistent by international standards, and the 2 is accurate. No alcohol, no bars, no clubs anywhere in the country. What exists instead is an evening culture of parks, cafes, shisha and the cable car viewpoints, which fills with families through the summer season. It is social rather than nightlife in the usual sense.
abha.nature: Excellent. Abha sits in the Asir mountains among terraced slopes, juniper forest and escarpment, with Soudah, the highest point in Saudi Arabia, twenty minutes away, and the Asir National Park around it. The road down to the Tihamah plain drops thousands of metres in a series of switchbacks. Baboons are a common roadside presence.
