abha.safety: High. Crime is very low, the city is comfortable to move around, and the main practical risks are the mountain roads and the weather that comes with altitude. Asir province borders Yemen and the wider region has seen cross-border incidents in recent years, so current travel advice should be read directly rather than assumed.
abha.food: Decent. Asiri cooking differs from the rest of the kingdom, with more use of local grains, honey and the region's coffee, and the markets sell produce grown on the terraces. Restaurant range is limited compared with Jeddah or Riyadh and aimed at domestic visitors. The 6 records adequacy without any particular depth.
abha.community: Essentially nonexistent for remote workers. Abha's foreign population is largely workers in construction, healthcare and services rather than anyone here by choice, and there is no nomad presence, coworking culture or meetup scene of any kind. The 2 reflects a city that has not organised itself around outsiders at all.
abha.english: Weak. English is limited to the university, parts of the healthcare sector and some of the tourism infrastructure, and Arabic is the language of daily life and all administration. Translation apps do a lot of work here. Anyone staying more than a few weeks will find some Arabic changes the experience considerably.
abha.visa: Weak. There is no digital nomad visa. The eVisa gives around sixty nationalities a year of multiple entries with ninety days per stay and a hundred and eighty in total, permitting tourism rather than employment. Longer stays require employer sponsorship or Premium Residency. Policy has changed repeatedly since the country opened to tourism in 2019.
abha.culture: Strong regionally. Rijal Almaa, the stone tower village on the escarpment below the city, is a UNESCO-listed heritage site and one of the most distinctive settlements in Arabia, and the Asiri tradition of painted interiors, known as al-qatt al-asiri, is on the UNESCO intangible heritage list. Abha itself hosts a growing arts programme.
abha.cleanliness: Good. Abha is reasonably well maintained and the tourism investment of recent years is visible in the parks and viewpoints. Waste management outside the built-up area is less consistent and litter along the mountain roads is a visible issue during the busy summer season. The 7 reflects a city that is improving rather than immaculate.
abha.airquality: Very good. Altitude, mountain wind and the absence of heavy industry keep readings low most of the year. Regional dust events can raise particulates, and the summer influx of domestic tourists brings traffic that is noticeable in the city centre, but neither is persistent. Air here is markedly cleaner than the Saudi lowlands.

fujairah.climate: Difficult in summer, which the 5 records. November to March is excellent, with days in the mid twenties and warm sea. June to September pushes past forty with heavy coastal humidity, and outdoor life stops between mid-morning and evening. The east coast is marginally cooler and less humid than Dubai across the mountains.
fujairah.cost: Moderate at around $1,600 a month, well below Dubai and Abu Dhabi while still being the UAE. A one-bedroom runs roughly $600 to $950 depending on distance from the corniche. Imported groceries carry the usual Gulf premium and alcohol is expensive and licensed. The saving against Dubai is the main argument for the emirate.
fujairah.wifi: Good. UAE internet infrastructure is strong nationally, with fibre widely available and comprehensive 5G, though prices are high. The persistent annoyance is the country's blocking of most voice-over-internet services, which makes a VPN standard practice among remote workers. Coworking exists in a small way around the free zone rather than as a market.
fujairah.nightlife: Thin. Alcohol is served in hotels and a small number of licensed venues and there is no bar district in any meaningful sense. Dubai is ninety minutes away and is where anyone wanting a night out goes. The 3 is an accurate reading of a quiet emirate rather than a criticism of it.
fujairah.nature: Strong. Fujairah is the only emirate entirely on the Gulf of Oman, with the Hajar mountains rising directly behind the beaches and the best diving in the country around Snoopy Island and Dibba. Wadi Wurayah is a protected mountain area with waterfalls and pools. The 7 balances real coastline and mountains against limited access.
fujairah.safety: Very high. The UAE has among the lowest crime rates anywhere and Fujairah is safe at any hour. The genuine hazards are environmental: heat, flash flooding in the wadis after rain, and driving standards on the mountain roads. Laws around alcohol, public behaviour and social media are stricter than most visitors expect.
fujairah.food: Decent. The corniche has fish restaurants working from the local catch, and the usual Emirati mix of Indian, Pakistani, Filipino and Lebanese places serves the workforce well and cheaply. Fine dining is thin compared with Dubai. The 6 reflects good everyday eating with limited range at the top end.
fujairah.community: Essentially nonexistent. Fujairah's foreign population works in the port, shipping and services, and almost nobody is here as a remote worker by choice. There is no nomad scene, no meetup culture and very little coworking. Anyone wanting a professional network drives to Dubai, which is what the 2 reflects.
fujairah.english: Strong. English is the working language of business, retail and most daily transactions across the UAE, and the majority-expatriate workforce means Arabic is often not the common tongue. Signage is bilingual everywhere. An English speaker will have no difficulty at any point in the emirate.
fujairah.visa: Reasonable. The UAE has a genuine one-year remote work visa for people employed outside the country, requiring around $3,500 a month in income, an employment contract and valid health insurance, and it can be applied for from abroad. Short visits run on visa on arrival for most Western nationalities. The Golden Visa covers longer horizons.
fujairah.culture: Limited. Al Bidyah Mosque, the oldest in the UAE at around 1446, and Fujairah Fort are the significant heritage sites, and the emirate maintains bull-butting contests on Friday afternoons, a local tradition unlike anything else in the country. Beyond that the cultural weight of the UAE sits in Sharjah, Abu Dhabi and Dubai.
fujairah.cleanliness: High. UAE municipal standards are strong and consistently applied, streets and beaches are maintained, and waste collection is reliable. The port and industrial zone at the southern end are functional rather than attractive. Beach water quality is generally good, though the bunkering traffic offshore is a permanent feature of this coast.
fujairah.airquality: Mediocre. The Gulf region has some of the highest particulate readings in the world, driven by desert dust rather than industry, and Fujairah shares that baseline. The port's bunkering operations and the cement industry in the northern emirates add local sources. Sea breezes help, but the 6 reflects a genuine regional problem.

amasra.climate: Oceanic and wet, which is the Black Sea condition rather than the Mediterranean one most people expect of Turkey. Summer highs sit around twenty-five with high humidity, winter days around eight, and rainfall is substantial year-round with the heaviest months in autumn and winter. The 5 records grey wet winters more than anything else.
amasra.cost: Very cheap. Budget around $700 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $200 to $350. Fish is the local staple and inexpensive in season, and the region's produce keeps grocery costs low. Turkish inflation makes any figure a moving target, so the number is a working budget rather than a fixed one.
amasra.wifi: Adequate. Turkish fibre reaches the town and mobile data is cheap and fast by European standards with good coverage. The weakness is the building stock: older properties on the peninsula have the worst connections and quality varies considerably by address. There is no coworking, so testing before signing a month is essential.
amasra.nightlife: Minimal. A few harbourside restaurants and tea houses, busy through the summer season with domestic tourists and close to empty from October. Alcohol is available but the town is not a drinking one. The 3 accurately reflects a small Black Sea town rather than any Turkish coastal resort further south.
amasra.nature: Strong. Amasra sits on a peninsula between two bays with a beach on each side, and the Black Sea coast road east towards Sinop runs through forested hills that see almost no foreign visitors. Kure Mountains National Park with its canyons and caves is inland. The 8 reflects genuinely unspoiled coastline.
amasra.safety: High. Turkey's small coastal towns are safe and Amasra is comfortable to walk at any hour, with petty theft the only common concern and even that rare. Swimming safety is the real issue: the Black Sea has strong currents and drownings occur every summer on this coast, often where there is no lifeguard.
amasra.food: Very good. Amasra is known nationally for its fish, particularly the fried hamsi and the local salad that carries the town's name, and the harbourside restaurants serve the day's catch simply and cheaply. The Black Sea region's corn bread, anchovies and hazelnuts define the wider cuisine. Prices are a fraction of Istanbul's.
amasra.community: Nonexistent for foreigners. Amasra is a domestic Turkish holiday town and almost no international visitors come here, let alone remote workers. There is no coworking, no meetup culture and no English-speaking social scene. The 2 records a place where anyone arriving alone will be genuinely alone, which some people want.
amasra.english: Weak. English is barely spoken outside a few younger people in the tourism trade, and Turkish is the language of everything. Translation apps carry most of the load for a visitor. Anyone staying beyond a few weeks will need some Turkish for anything administrative, and the effort is repaid quickly in a town this size.
amasra.visa: Reasonable. Most Western nationals get ninety days in any hundred and eighty visa-free or via a quick e-visa. Turkey introduced a Digital Nomad Identification Card in 2024 for citizens of a defined list of countries with a degree and a minimum income, which eases the residence permit process. Residence permits themselves have become notably harder.
amasra.culture: Real and underappreciated. Amasra was the Greek colony of Sesamos and later a Genoese trading post, and its castle walls, Byzantine church and Roman Bird's Rock monument are all still standing. The small museum holds a good local collection. Wooden craft work is a living local trade rather than a tourist product.
amasra.cleanliness: Middling. The harbour front and the main streets are maintained for the season, but waste management outside the centre is inconsistent and litter is visible along parts of the coast, particularly after the summer crowds. Black Sea marine pollution is a broader regional problem. The 6 is an honest reading rather than a harsh one.
amasra.airquality: Good. Coastal wind, forest cover and a tiny population keep readings low most of the year. The qualification is regional: the Bartin province coalfield and the heavy industry at nearby Zonguldak and Eregli are significant sources, and a wind from the wrong direction can carry that towards the coast. Winter heating adds locally.

sanliurfa.climate: Harsh, and the 4 is earned. Sanliurfa sits on the edge of the Mesopotamian plain and summer is severe, regularly above forty degrees through July and August with nights that stay warm. Winter is cool and wet with daytime temperatures around ten. Spring and autumn are brief and genuinely pleasant, which is when to come.
sanliurfa.cost: Extremely cheap. Budget around $600 a month, one of the lowest figures on this site. A one-bedroom runs roughly $150 to $300 depending on district, with the newer developments away from the old centre offering the better value. Food costs almost nothing and is excellent. Turkish inflation moves these figures, so treat them as approximate.
sanliurfa.wifi: Adequate. Fibre reaches most of the modern districts and Turkish mobile data is fast and cheap with strong coverage, which is the practical answer for most people. There is no coworking aimed at foreigners, though the city is large enough to have business centres serving its own economy. Power and water are reliable.
sanliurfa.nightlife: Nonexistent in the usual sense. Sanliurfa is one of the most conservative cities in Turkey, alcohol is scarce and there is no bar culture. What exists is an evening life of tea gardens, the parks around Balikligol and long meals, which fills up after dark in summer for obvious reasons. The 2 records this accurately.
sanliurfa.nature: Weak. The surrounding landscape is dry plain and low hills, hot and largely treeless, and the region's water comes from the Ataturk Dam project rather than from any local abundance. Halfeti, partly submerged by the dam, and the Euphrates itself are the nearest scenery worth a trip. The appeal here is archaeological rather than natural.
sanliurfa.safety: Mid. The city itself is safe by ordinary measures, with low violent crime and normal urban precautions sufficient. The score reflects context: the Syrian border is around fifty kilometres away, the city hosts a large refugee population, and government travel advice for the southeastern provinces varies and should be read directly rather than assumed.
sanliurfa.food: Excellent. Sanliurfa is one of Turkey's serious food cities, home to the Urfa kebab, the isot pepper that defines the regional cooking, and a raw kofte tradition made without meat that is genuinely local. Liver kebab for breakfast is normal here. Prices are trivially low and the quality is high across the board.
sanliurfa.community: Nonexistent for remote workers. Foreign presence in the city is archaeologists, aid organisations working on the refugee response and occasional tourists heading to Gobekli Tepe. There is no nomad scene, no coworking culture and no English-speaking social infrastructure. The 2 reflects a city that has never had reason to build any of it.
sanliurfa.english: Weak. English is very limited outside the archaeological tourism around Gobekli Tepe, and Turkish is the language of everything. Arabic is widely spoken given the Syrian population and Kurdish is common across the southeast. Anyone working here should expect to do daily business in Turkish or through a translation app.
sanliurfa.visa: Reasonable. Most Western nationals get ninety days in any hundred and eighty, visa-free or through a quick e-visa. The 2024 Digital Nomad Identification Card is open to citizens of a defined list of countries with a degree and a minimum monthly income and smooths the residence permit process. Residence permits themselves have become considerably harder.
sanliurfa.culture: Exceptional. Gobekli Tepe, twenty minutes outside the city, is around eleven thousand years old and rewrote the timeline of monumental building; Karahan Tepe and a dozen related sites sit on the same plain. Balikligol, the Pool of Abraham with its sacred carp, is a pilgrimage site, and the old bazaar quarter is among Turkey's most atmospheric.
sanliurfa.cleanliness: Below average. The old city and the pilgrimage areas are maintained, but waste management across the wider city is inconsistent, the summer dust is constant and the rapid population growth from the refugee influx has outpaced services in some districts. The 5 is an honest reading of a city under real strain.
sanliurfa.airquality: Mediocre. Annual particulate readings sit above guidance, driven by dust from the surrounding plain, traffic and winter heating, with the dry climate keeping dust suspended for long periods. There is limited heavy industry, so the problem is geographic and seasonal rather than industrial. Spring dust events raise readings substantially for days at a time.

oudtshoorn.climate: Semi-arid Karoo, hot and dry in summer with January and February pushing into the mid thirties, and cold winter nights that drop close to freezing at this inland elevation. The dryness makes the heat considerably more bearable than the number suggests. Rainfall is low and unreliable, and the region has been through serious drought.
oudtshoorn.cost: Cheap. Budget around $900 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $300 to $500 and houses with land within reach at figures impossible on the coast. Groceries are inexpensive and local produce is excellent. The two lines to add are a vehicle, which is not optional here, and power backup, which effectively is not either.
oudtshoorn.wifi: Adequate. Fibre has reached much of the town at reasonable prices and mobile data on the main networks is workable, though South African data costs remain high relative to local income. The real constraint is electricity rather than connectivity: load shedding has eased but not ended, and an inverter is standard in any serious working setup.
oudtshoorn.nightlife: Minimal. A few pubs and restaurants on the main street and very little after ten. The KKNK Afrikaans arts festival each autumn transforms the town for a week and is the exception. The 3 reflects a small Karoo town where social life happens at braais and around farms rather than in venues.
oudtshoorn.nature: Excellent. The Cango Caves are one of the largest cave systems in Africa, the Swartberg Pass over the mountains is a national monument and one of the great drives on the continent, and Route 62 runs through the Klein Karoo past wine and olive farms. The Garden Route coast is an hour over the Outeniqua Pass.
oudtshoorn.safety: Mid. Oudtshoorn is calmer than South Africa's cities and violent crime is lower, but property crime is real and the country's baseline requires ordinary situational awareness everywhere. Farm security is a live local concern. Driving at night on rural roads carries its own risks from livestock and pedestrians. The 6 is an honest national reading.
oudtshoorn.food: Good. Karoo lamb is among the best meat in the country, ostrich appears on every menu given the local industry, and the Klein Karoo's wine, olives and port-style fortified wines are produced within a short drive. Prices are very low by international standards. The 7 reflects real quality with limited range.
oudtshoorn.community: Nonexistent for remote workers. There is an established local community and a scattering of retirees and small-holders, but no coworking, no meetup culture and no foreign nomad presence. The 2 reflects a working South African country town rather than anywhere organised around visitors. Anyone arriving alone will need to join something local.
oudtshoorn.english: Strong. English is an official language and universally understood, though Afrikaans is the mother tongue of most people in the Klein Karoo and the language of daily life here more than in most of the country. The KKNK festival is specifically an Afrikaans arts event. No English speaker will have any difficulty.
oudtshoorn.visa: Reasonable. South Africa introduced a remote work visa in 2024 for people employed by a foreign company earning above roughly $36,000 a year, initially for up to three years, with tax registration rules since clarified. Before that most visitors used the ninety-day visitor visa granted on arrival to many nationalities, extendable once. Processing times vary considerably by mission.
oudtshoorn.culture: Modest but distinctive. The ostrich feather boom of the late nineteenth century built the town's sandstone feather palaces, which still stand, and the CP Nel Museum records the industry. The KKNK is one of the largest Afrikaans arts festivals in the country. The Cango Caves have been a visitor attraction since the 1800s.
oudtshoorn.cleanliness: Good. The town centre and the tourist infrastructure are maintained, municipal services function adequately by South African standards, and the dry climate limits some of the problems wetter towns face. Service delivery in the townships is weaker than in the centre, which is the national pattern. The 7 records a reasonably well-run small town.
oudtshoorn.airquality: Excellent. Semi-arid inland position, no industry and a small population give consistently clean air well within guidance, and the dryness keeps humidity-driven haze away. Winter wood and coal fires raise readings on still cold evenings, and dust from the surrounding farmland is seasonal. Neither is enough to trouble the 9.

ifrane.climate: Continental and unusual for Morocco, which the 5 reflects rather than criticises. At around 1,665 metres Ifrane has warm dry summers rarely above twenty-eight and genuinely cold snowy winters, and it holds the record for the lowest temperature ever recorded in Africa. Heating is a real consideration in a country where most buildings lack it.
ifrane.cost: Cheap internationally but not by Moroccan standards, which the 7 records. Budget around $800 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $250 to $400. The university and the summer visitors keep local prices above what a town this size would otherwise charge. Food is inexpensive and the Middle Atlas produce is good.
ifrane.wifi: Adequate. Moroccan fibre reaches the built-up area and mobile data on the main networks is fast and cheap. Al Akhawayn University raises the general standard of infrastructure in the town well above comparable Moroccan settlements. There is no dedicated coworking, though the cafes around the campus are used to people working.
ifrane.nightlife: Nonexistent. Ifrane is a quiet university town in a country where alcohol is restricted, and the evening amounts to cafes and the occasional restaurant. Term time brings student life but not a bar scene. The 2 records this accurately; anyone wanting a night out is looking at Fes, ninety minutes away.
ifrane.nature: Outstanding. The cedar forest starts at the edge of town and holds one of the last populations of Barbary macaques, the Michlifen ski area is twenty minutes up the road, and the lakes and gorges of the Middle Atlas spread out in every direction. Air, forest and altitude together make this unlike anywhere else in Morocco.
ifrane.safety: High. Ifrane is among the safest towns in Morocco, with very low crime, a visible university presence and comfortable walking at any hour. The practical risks are winter driving on mountain passes and the macaques, which are habituated to people and will take food aggressively. Feeding them is both common and a bad idea.
ifrane.food: Limited. There are decent tagine places and cafes serving the student population, but the range is narrow and Ifrane is not a food destination in a country full of them. Local honey, trout from the mountain streams and the Middle Atlas produce are the genuine strengths. Fes, ninety minutes away, is the answer for anything more.
ifrane.community: Weak for remote workers. Al Akhawayn University brings an international student and faculty population that gives the town more English-speaking company than anywhere comparable in Morocco, but there is no nomad scene, no coworking and nothing organised. Much of the town's life follows the academic calendar and empties in the holidays.
ifrane.english: Moderate, and unusually good for Morocco because of the university, which teaches an American curriculum in English. Outside the campus, French is the second language of administration and business and Moroccan Arabic and Tamazight are the languages of daily life. English will get further here than in most Moroccan towns.
ifrane.visa: Good. Morocco gives most Western nationals ninety days visa-free on arrival, which is generous and simple. There is no digital nomad visa despite periodic announcements, so longer stays run through the carte de sejour residence card, requiring a local sponsor, a lease and proof of means through the local prefecture. Border runs are tolerated rather than guaranteed.
ifrane.culture: Thin locally. Ifrane was built by the French in the 1930s as an alpine resort and its pitched-roof architecture is a colonial import rather than a Moroccan tradition, which is precisely what makes it strange and interesting. The Lion Stone is the town's landmark. Fes, one of the great Islamic cities, is ninety minutes away.
ifrane.cleanliness: Exceptional by Moroccan standards. Ifrane is known nationally as the cleanest town in the country, with active municipal maintenance, well-kept parks and none of the litter that troubles most Moroccan urban areas. The town's identity and its tourism both depend on this. The 9 is genuinely earned rather than generous.
ifrane.airquality: Excellent. Altitude, cedar forest and the absence of industry or heavy traffic give consistently clean air, among the best readings in Morocco. Winter heating with wood raises particulates on still cold evenings, which is the only meaningful local source. Regional dust events from the south occasionally reach the Middle Atlas but rarely persist.

djerba.climate: Excellent. Djerba has a mild semi-arid Mediterranean climate with hot dry summers above thirty in July and August, and winters around seventeen with very little rain. The island position moderates the extremes that the Tunisian interior suffers. Sunshine hours are among the highest in the Mediterranean, which is why the charter flights come.
djerba.cost: Cheap. Budget around $750 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $200 to $400 and Houmt Souk and the beach strip at the top of that. Food bought locally costs very little and the island produces its own olives, dates and fish. The dinar is a closed currency, which complicates how money moves in and out.
djerba.wifi: Mediocre. Tunisian fibre reaches the main towns and mobile data is inexpensive with reasonable island coverage, but speeds are modest by European standards and evening congestion is noticeable in the resort areas. There is almost no coworking provision. Power cuts are occasional rather than routine. Testing a specific property before a monthly commitment is sensible.
djerba.nightlife: Limited and largely confined to the resorts. The hotel bars along the Sidi Mahrez strip serve the package tourism market, Houmt Souk has a few cafes and restaurants, and outside the season much of it closes. Tunisia is relatively relaxed about alcohol by regional standards. The 4 reflects a seasonal resort rather than a town with its own scene.
djerba.nature: Fair. Djerba is flat, low and largely cultivated, with long sandy beaches on the eastern shore, palm groves inland and a lagoon that attracts flamingos in winter. It is pleasant rather than dramatic, and anyone wanting landscape will be looking at the mainland: Matmata, the Sahara and Tataouine are all within a few hours.
djerba.safety: Mid. Djerba is calm and ordinary crime is low, and the island has long depended on tourism to function. The score reflects national context rather than local conditions: Tunisia has seen serious incidents including an attack near the El Ghriba synagogue in 2023, and government travel advice should be read directly before booking.
djerba.food: Good. Tunisian cooking is the most distinctive in North Africa, built on harissa, olive oil and preserved lemon, and Djerba's fish is excellent and cheap at the Houmt Souk market. The island has its own dishes and a Jewish culinary tradition that survives with the community at Erriadh. Resort dining is the weak part.
djerba.community: Weak. The island's foreign presence is package tourists on one and two week stays, with a small number of longer-term European residents and second-home owners. There is no nomad community, no coworking and nothing organised. The 3 reflects a place where meeting people is easy socially and impossible professionally.
djerba.english: Weak. Arabic is the language of daily life, French is the language of administration and business and is widely spoken, and English is limited to the tourism trade and younger people. Anyone here for a stretch will get considerably further with some French than without it. German and Italian are also common in the resorts.
djerba.visa: Reasonable. Tunisia gives most Western nationals ninety days visa-free on arrival, which is straightforward and rarely questioned. There is no digital nomad visa. Longer stays mean either leaving and returning, generally tolerated, or a residence permit requiring local sponsorship and patience. Overstays incur a fine calculated by duration and levied at departure.
djerba.culture: Strong and unusual. El Ghriba is among the oldest synagogues in the world and the annual Lag BaOmer pilgrimage still draws visitors, the island's settlement pattern of dispersed fortified farmsteads was UNESCO listed in 2023, and the Djerbahood project brought street artists from thirty countries to paint the village of Erriadh.
djerba.cleanliness: Middling. The resort strip and Houmt Souk's centre are maintained, but waste management across the island is inconsistent and litter is visible along roadsides and some beaches, particularly at the end of the season. Tunisia's recycling infrastructure is limited. The 6 is an honest reading of a gap between the tourist areas and the rest.
djerba.airquality: Very good. Island position, constant sea breeze and no industry give clean air well within guidance most of the year. Saharan dust events raise particulate readings sharply for periods, particularly in spring and early summer, which is a regional pattern rather than a local one. Traffic is light outside the summer season.

nanyuki.climate: Excellent, and not what the equator suggests. At around 1,950 metres Nanyuki has daytime temperatures in the low twenties year-round and nights that get genuinely cold. The rains come in two seasons, the long rains from late March into May and the short rains in November, both bringing afternoon storms rather than continuous wet.
nanyuki.cost: Cheap. Budget around $800 a month, which buys considerably more here than in Nairobi. A one-bedroom runs roughly $250 to $450 and houses with gardens are within reach, which is why the town has a long-standing settler and expatriate farming community. Add a vehicle and a power backup arrangement to any realistic budget.
nanyuki.wifi: Adequate and improving. Fibre has reached parts of the town and Safaricom mobile data is the reliable fallback almost everywhere with good 4G across the built-up area. There is a small coworking presence, unusual for a Kenyan town this size, driven by the conservation and tourism organisations. Power cuts happen and an inverter is standard.
nanyuki.nightlife: Thin. A handful of bars and hotel terraces, a couple of places catering to the British Army training presence, and very little beyond that. The town is quiet after dark. The 3 reflects a small upcountry town rather than any deficiency, and social life here happens at homes and clubs rather than in venues.
nanyuki.nature: Outstanding. Mount Kenya rises directly behind the town with trailheads within reach, Ol Pejeta and Lewa conservancies are on the doorstep with rhino, elephant and big cats, and the Laikipia plateau holds one of the highest concentrations of wildlife outside the formal parks. The equator runs through the town itself.
nanyuki.safety: Reasonable. Nanyuki itself is calm and the resident community is long established, with petty theft the main ordinary concern. The wider region varies considerably: parts of northern Laikipia and the counties beyond have seen banditry and land conflict, and government travel advice for areas north of the town should be checked directly.
nanyuki.food: Decent. There is a good market, excellent local produce from the Mount Kenya slopes, and a scattering of restaurants serving the conservation and tourism crowd at prices above the Kenyan norm. Kenyan coffee and the highland vegetables are the genuine strengths. The 6 reflects adequacy with a few genuinely good places.
nanyuki.community: Modest but real, which the 4 records. Nanyuki has an unusual resident population of conservationists, ranchers, pilots, aid workers and long-term expatriates, and a small coworking presence to match. It is not a nomad scene, but it is far more of a network than most towns this size anywhere in Africa can offer.
nanyuki.english: Strong. English is an official language of Kenya and the medium of education, business and administration, and it is spoken universally in the town. Swahili is the other national language and the common tongue between communities. An English speaker will have no practical difficulty at any point here.
nanyuki.visa: Reasonable. Kenya replaced its visa system with an Electronic Travel Authorisation in January 2024, required of almost all arrivals and granting up to ninety days. A digital nomad work permit for remote workers was announced in late 2024 with a reported income threshold around $55,000 a year, and implementation details have shifted since.
nanyuki.culture: Modest. Nanyuki is a colonial-era settler town rather than a historic centre, and its interest is in the working landscape around it: Maasai and Samburu communities on the plateau, the conservancy model that has reshaped Kenyan wildlife management, and the Mount Kenya massif itself, which is sacred in Kikuyu tradition. The equator marker is a tourist stop.
nanyuki.cleanliness: Middling. The town centre is reasonably maintained and the conservancies and lodges keep their areas immaculate, but municipal waste management is limited and litter is visible on the outskirts and along the roads. Kenya's national plastic bag ban has made a real difference since 2017. The 6 records honest inconsistency.
nanyuki.airquality: Excellent. Altitude, constant wind off the mountain and no industry give clean air well within guidance for most of the year. Dry season dust from the plateau and roadside burning are the local sources that raise readings occasionally. Compared with Nairobi, four hours south, the difference is immediately noticeable.

lome.climate: Tropical savanna on the Gulf of Guinea, hot and humid year-round with daytime temperatures around thirty. Two rainy seasons, a long one from April to July and a shorter one in September and October, split the year. The harmattan brings Saharan dust in December and January. Coastal humidity is the constant most arrivals underestimate.
lome.cost: Cheap. Budget around $700 a month, low for a West African capital and reflecting a country that never had the oil or mining money of its neighbours. A one-bedroom runs roughly $200 to $400, with the beachfront and diplomatic quarter well above and the inland neighbourhoods well below. Street food and markets cost very little.
lome.wifi: Mediocre. Fibre reaches parts of the city and mobile data on the main networks is workable, but West African internet pricing remains high relative to speed and evening congestion is real. Power cuts happen and any serious workplace has a generator. There is a small coworking and startup scene, more developed than the country's size suggests.
lome.nightlife: Better than expected, which the 5 records. Lome has a genuine bar and live music culture, maquis-style open-air places along the coast road and in the neighbourhoods, and a nightlife that runs late. Togolese and wider West African music is played everywhere. It is not Abidjan or Accra, but it is not quiet either.
lome.nature: Limited within the city. Lome is a coastal capital with a long beach running through it, though swimming is dangerous on much of that coast because of the currents. The Kpalime region with its hills, waterfalls and forest is around two hours north and is where anyone here for the landscape actually goes.
lome.safety: Mid. Togo is politically calmer than its recent history suggests but street crime in Lome is a real concern, with phone snatching, robbery around the markets and risk after dark in some areas. The beach at night is specifically avoided. Ordinary precautions and local advice go a long way. Traffic and motorcycle taxis are the daily hazard.
lome.food: Decent. Togolese cooking runs on maize, cassava and yam with peanut and tomato sauces, and the fufu and grilled fish along the coast are the everyday pleasures. The French colonial legacy left genuinely good bread and pastry. Street food is cheap and plentiful. The 6 reflects solid everyday eating without much range at the top.
lome.community: Weak. Lome's foreign population is diplomats, development workers and traders, most of them on postings rather than by choice, plus a Lebanese and Indian business community of long standing. There is a small startup and coworking scene serving locals. For a visiting remote worker there is effectively nothing organised, which the 3 records.
lome.english: Weak. Togo is francophone and French is the language of all administration, education and business. Ewe and Kabye are the main national languages. English is uncommon outside international organisations and the border trade with Ghana, which is close enough to matter. Operating here without French is genuinely difficult.
lome.visa: Reasonable. Togo offers an eVisa and visa on arrival at Lome airport for most nationalities, typically seven to thirty days and extendable at the immigration office in the city, which is the normal route rather than an exception. There is no digital nomad visa. Yellow fever vaccination is required on entry. ECOWAS nationals enter freely.
lome.culture: Strong. The Akodessewa fetish market is the largest of its kind in the world and reflects a living Vodun tradition rather than a display for visitors, the Grand Marche and its Nana Benz textile traders shaped West African commerce for decades, and the National Museum holds a good ethnographic collection. Togolese music and dance are widely exported.
lome.cleanliness: Poor. Waste collection is inconsistent outside the central areas, drainage floods badly in the rainy seasons, and plastic waste on the beaches and in the lagoons is a visible and persistent problem. The port and the informal settlements around it are the worst of it. The 4 is an honest reading rather than a harsh one.
lome.airquality: Mediocre. An ageing vehicle fleet on high-sulphur fuel, generator use, waste burning and the port's traffic are the main sources, and readings sit above guidance for much of the year. The harmattan season from December to February brings Saharan dust that raises particulates substantially for weeks. Sea breezes provide genuine dispersal that inland cities lack.

tofo.climate: Tropical and warm year-round, with daytime temperatures around thirty in summer and the mid twenties in the dry winter months. April to September is the drier, cooler and clearer half. The wet season from October to March brings heat, humidity and the cyclone risk, which has been serious in the Mozambique Channel in recent years.
tofo.cost: Moderate at around $800 a month, low for the diving it buys but higher than the surrounding country because everything on this beach is priced for visitors. A room or simple one-bedroom runs roughly $250 to $450. Food from the Inhambane market is cheap; the beach restaurants are not. Diving is the real budget line.
tofo.wifi: Poor, and the 4 is honest rather than harsh. Mobile data on Vodacom or Tmcel is the primary connection for most people and speeds vary by hour and by weather. Fixed lines exist in a few of the better lodges. Power cuts are routine and most established places run an inverter or a generator.
tofo.nightlife: Small but genuine. Tofo has a handful of beach bars that fill with divers and travellers, live music some nights, and a scene that is entirely about who happens to be in the village that week. It is social rather than large. The 4 reflects a beach village where everyone ends up in the same two places.
tofo.nature: Outstanding. Tofo is one of very few places on earth where whale sharks and giant manta rays are present year-round rather than seasonally, with humpback whales passing between roughly June and October. The reef diving is world class, the beach runs for kilometres, and the dunes and bays around Barra and Tofinho are largely undeveloped.
tofo.safety: Mid. Tofo itself is calm and the village community is used to visitors, with opportunistic theft the main ordinary concern, particularly on the beach and in unsecured accommodation. The more serious considerations are medical, since facilities are limited and the nearest real hospital is far, and marine, since the currents here are strong.
tofo.food: Good. Fresh seafood is the point: prawns, crab, calamari and the day's fish, cooked simply and cheaply, with the Portuguese colonial legacy visible in the bread, the piri piri and the coffee. The Inhambane market supplies everything else. Range is narrow but quality is high, which is what the 7 records.
tofo.community: Moderate by the standards of this list, and the 5 is generous but fair. Tofo has a long-established diving community, marine researchers studying the whale sharks and mantas, and a rotating population of travellers who stay longer than they planned. It is not a nomad scene, but it is a real community that outsiders join easily.
tofo.english: Moderate. Portuguese is the official language and the language of administration, but Tofo's diving and tourism economy runs substantially in English and most people working with visitors speak it well. Away from the beach, Portuguese and local languages including Xitswa take over. Some Portuguese makes daily life considerably easier.
tofo.visa: Reasonable. Mozambique removed visa requirements in 2023 for citizens of a long list of countries including most of Europe, the United States, Canada and Australia, allowing visits of up to thirty days, which transformed access. Others get a visa on arrival at main entry points. Extensions are handled in the provincial capitals rather than at the beach.
tofo.culture: Modest. Tofo is a small fishing village that became a diving destination, so the cultural interest is in Inhambane twenty-five minutes away, one of the oldest settlements on the coast with a Portuguese cathedral, a mosque and a dhow-building tradition. Timbila marimba music from this province is on the UNESCO intangible heritage list.
tofo.cleanliness: Middling. The beach itself is generally clean and the community and dive operators run regular clean-ups, but waste management infrastructure is minimal, plastic accumulates in the village and along the road, and there is no recycling. The 6 records a place that is cared for locally without any system behind it.
tofo.airquality: Excellent. Constant sea breeze, no industry and a tiny population give consistently clean air. Cooking fires and occasional bush burning inland are the only local sources and neither persists. The 9 is straightforward: this is about as clean as coastal air gets, and it is one of the genuine pleasures of being here.

burlington.climate: Cold, and the 4 records a genuinely long winter. January averages sit below freezing with heavy lake-effect snow and the cold runs from December into March. Summers are warm and humid and the lake is swimmable. September and October bring the foliage the region is known for. April is mud season and best skipped entirely.
burlington.cost: Expensive, and the 3 is earned. Budget around $2,200 a month for a city of forty-five thousand people. A one-bedroom runs roughly $1,300 to $1,700 and finding one at all is harder than affording one, with the housing market squeezed by the university and very limited new construction. Vermont grocery prices run above the national average.
burlington.wifi: Good. Fibre is available across most of the city and Burlington has a coworking scene disproportionate to its size, built on a startup community, the University of Vermont and a culture of small independent business. Burlington Electric has run the city on entirely renewable sources since 2014 and the grid is reliable.
burlington.nightlife: Moderate. Church Street and the surrounding blocks carry the bars and music venues, and the student population from UVM and Champlain College gives the city more life than its size suggests. Higher Ground is a genuinely good venue. It is small and closes early, which is what holds the score at 5.
burlington.nature: Excellent. Lake Champlain runs along the whole waterfront with the Adirondacks visible across it, the Island Line Trail heads north on an old rail causeway with a seasonal bike ferry, and Stowe, Sugarbush and Mad River Glen are all under an hour. The Green Mountains and the Long Trail are immediately east.
burlington.safety: Very high. Vermont consistently records among the lowest violent crime rates in the United States and Burlington is comfortable at any hour. The practical hazards are weather rather than crime: winter driving, ice and the cold itself. Opioid-related issues exist here as across northern New England but rarely affect visitors directly.
burlington.food: Very good for the size. Vermont's farm-to-table culture is genuine rather than marketing, with dairy, cheese, maple and produce from working farms in the surrounding counties supplying the restaurants directly. The brewing scene is nationally significant, and Ben and Jerry's was founded here in a converted petrol station in 1978. Prices are high.
burlington.community: Modest. There is a real startup and coworking culture, a strong student population and an unusually engaged civic community, but no international nomad presence to speak of. The 4 reflects a genuine local network that a visitor can enter more easily than in most American cities of this size, without any organised scene for outsiders.
burlington.english: Universal. English is the language of everything. Vermont has a long connection with Quebec and French is more present here than in most of the United States, and Burlington has resettled substantial refugee communities from Bosnia, Somalia, Bhutan and Congo whose languages are common at home. Nothing public requires anything but English.
burlington.visa: Poor. The United States has no digital nomad visa. Visa Waiver nationals get ninety days with an ESTA, permitting tourism and business meetings but not productive work, with remote employment for a foreign company in an unresolved grey area. Longer stays need sponsorship, investment or family. The Canadian border is forty-five minutes away but resets nothing.
burlington.culture: Decent. The Flynn Center anchors the performing arts, the Shelburne Museum a few minutes south holds a genuinely significant American folk art collection, and the city's political culture, which produced Bernie Sanders as mayor in 1981, is part of its identity. The Discover Jazz Festival each June is the largest annual event.
burlington.cleanliness: Very high. Burlington is well maintained, the waterfront and Church Street are actively cared for, recycling and composting are mandated statewide under Vermont's universal recycling law, and the city has a visible environmental ethic. The 9 reflects both good municipal service and a genuinely different regulatory baseline from most of the country.
burlington.airquality: Excellent. Vermont records some of the cleanest air in the United States, helped by low population density, no heavy industry and prevailing winds off the lake. Winter wood heating raises particulates in the valleys on still cold nights and Canadian wildfire smoke has reached the northeast in recent summers, but neither troubles the annual picture much.

boise.climate: Semi-arid with four distinct seasons. Summer is hot and dry, regularly above thirty-five in July and August, and winter sits around freezing with modest snow in the valley and considerably more in the mountains. Spring and autumn are the good months. Late-summer wildfire smoke has become a recurring feature that affects air quality for days.
boise.cost: Expensive now, which the 4 records. Budget around $2,100 a month; a one-bedroom runs roughly $1,100 to $1,500. Boise was a genuine bargain before 2020, and a wave of arrivals from the west coast reset the housing market permanently. Health insurance sits outside this figure and dominates any American budget.
boise.wifi: Good. Fibre reaches most of the city at competitive American prices and mobile coverage is comprehensive. Boise has a real coworking market for its size, built on a technology sector anchored by Micron and a startup scene that grew through the last decade, with desks from roughly $200 a month. Remote work needs no explanation here.
boise.nightlife: Moderate. Downtown Boise has a decent bar and brewery scene, a few music venues and a student presence from Boise State, and it is livelier than most western cities of this size. It closes earlier than a coastal city would. The 5 reflects a real but modest scene rather than anything a visitor travels for.
boise.nature: Outstanding. The Boise River Greenbelt runs about forty kilometres through the city, the Ridge to Rivers trail network starts at the edge of downtown, Bogus Basin ski area is thirty minutes up the mountain, and the Sawtooths and Sun Valley are a couple of hours away. Whitewater and desert are both within reach.
boise.safety: High. Boise consistently ranks among the safer mid-sized American cities, with low violent crime and comfortable walking downtown at night. The practical risks are environmental: summer heat, wildfire and the mountain driving. Idaho's gun laws are among the most permissive in the country, which is context rather than a day-to-day concern here.
boise.food: Good. Boise's restaurant scene has grown substantially with the population, and the Basque Block reflects the largest Basque community in the United States outside Spain, with genuinely distinctive food and a festival every five years. Idaho produce and the local wine industry supply the kitchens. Prices are moderate by American standards.
boise.community: Modest. There is a real technology and startup network and a coworking culture that supports it, and remote workers are numerous enough to be unremarkable, but there is no international community and almost no nomad presence. The 4 reflects a domestic professional network rather than anything a visiting foreigner plugs into.
boise.english: Universal. English is the language of everything here and no visitor will encounter a barrier of any kind. Boise has a significant Spanish-speaking population, a long-established Basque community with its own cultural centre, and more recent refugee communities including Iraqi, Congolese and Bhutanese families whose languages are common at home but not in public life.
boise.visa: Poor. The United States has no digital nomad visa and no plans for one. Visa Waiver nationals enter with an ESTA for ninety days, permitting tourism and business meetings but not productive work, with remote work for a foreign employer in an unresolved grey area judged individually at the border. Longer routes require sponsorship or investment.
boise.culture: Modest. The Basque Block with its museum and cultural centre is genuinely distinctive, the Idaho State Capitol and the Boise Art Museum cover the civic bases, and the Idaho Shakespeare Festival plays outdoors through the summer. Beyond that the cultural weight is limited and most residents look to the landscape rather than the institutions.
boise.cleanliness: High. Boise is well maintained, the greenbelt and parks are actively cared for, waste and recycling services are reliable, and the city has a visible civic pride about its river corridor. American municipal standards apply throughout. The 8 records an ordinary well-run city rather than anything exceptional.
boise.airquality: Mediocre, which surprises people. Boise sits in a valley that traps winter inversions, holding particulates and vehicle emissions close to the ground for days, and late-summer wildfire smoke from across the interior west has become an annual event that pushes readings into unhealthy ranges. Spring and autumn air is genuinely clean.

spokane.climate: Four real seasons with a semi-arid baseline. Summer is hot and dry, often above thirty-two in July and August, and winter is cold and grey with genuine snow and daytime temperatures around freezing. Spring arrives late and wet. Wildfire smoke in late summer has become a recurring feature rather than an occasional event.
spokane.cost: Moderate by American standards, which the 5 records. Budget around $1,800 a month; a one-bedroom runs roughly $900 to $1,300. Spokane is one of the cheaper mid-sized cities in the American west and roughly half what the same life costs in Seattle. Washington has no state income tax, which matters for anyone earning locally.
spokane.wifi: Good. Fibre is widely available at ordinary American prices and mobile coverage is comprehensive across the valley. There is a modest coworking market serving a healthcare, education and aerospace economy, with desks from roughly $150 a month. Gonzaga University and the medical school give the city more professional depth than its size suggests.
spokane.nightlife: Moderate. Downtown and the Garland district carry the bars, breweries and music venues, with a student crowd from Gonzaga giving weeknights some life. It closes earlier than a coastal city and the range is limited, but for a city this size it is respectable. The 5 is an accurate middle reading.
spokane.nature: Excellent. The Spokane River runs through downtown over a genuine waterfall, the Centennial Trail follows it sixty kilometres towards Idaho, and three ski areas including Mount Spokane and Schweitzer sit within ninety minutes. Coeur d'Alene and the northern Idaho lakes are forty minutes east. Access to serious outdoors is the city's strongest card.
spokane.safety: Mid, which is honest for an American city of this size. Violent crime rates sit above the national average and property crime is a real and frequently discussed local issue, concentrated in specific areas rather than citywide. Downtown and the residential districts are comfortable with ordinary awareness. Homelessness is visible and a live political question.
spokane.food: Decent. Spokane's restaurant scene has improved substantially over the last decade, with good options downtown and in Kendall Yards, and the surrounding Palouse and Washington wine country supply the kitchens. It is not a food destination and the range is limited compared with Seattle. The 6 records real competence without depth.
spokane.community: Weak. There is a coworking scene and a professional network built on healthcare, education and aerospace, and remote workers are common enough to be unremarkable, but there is no international community and no nomad presence of any kind. The 3 reflects a domestic city that visiting foreigners have essentially no route into.
spokane.english: Universal. English is the language of everything here and no visitor will meet a barrier of any kind. Spokane has a significant Spanish-speaking population and long-established Russian and Ukrainian communities from decades of resettlement across the Inland Northwest, whose languages are common at home and in some churches but not in public life.
spokane.visa: Poor. The United States offers no digital nomad visa. Visa Waiver nationals enter with an ESTA for ninety days, permitting tourism and business meetings but not productive work, and remote work for a foreign employer sits in an unresolved grey area judged individually at the border. Longer stays require employer sponsorship, investment or family.
spokane.culture: Modest. Riverfront Park is the legacy of Expo 74, the smallest city ever to host a world's fair, and the pavilion and clock tower remain. The Northwest Museum of Arts and Culture covers the region's history including its Native American communities. Hoopfest and Bloomsday are the largest events of their kind anywhere and genuinely define the calendar.
spokane.cleanliness: Good. Riverfront Park and the downtown core are well maintained and municipal services are reliable, though the city has visible problems with encampments and litter in specific corridors that residents discuss constantly. American standards apply generally. The 7 records a city that is mostly well kept with real exceptions.
spokane.airquality: Mediocre. Spokane sits in a valley that traps winter inversions and holds particulates close to the ground, and the late-summer wildfire smoke that reaches the Inland Northwest has produced some of the worst readings in the United States during bad years. Spring and early summer air is clean, which the annual average hides.

nanaimo.climate: Mild oceanic, which the 7 records fairly. Summers are warm and dry, rarely above twenty-five, with long light evenings. Winters are wet rather than cold, sitting around five to eight degrees with frost occasional and snow rare. The east coast of Vancouver Island is considerably drier than the west, which matters more than the averages suggest.
nanaimo.cost: Expensive, as everywhere in coastal British Columbia. Budget around $1,900 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $1,100 to $1,500. That is meaningfully cheaper than Victoria and dramatically cheaper than Vancouver, which is why the city has grown, but the gap has been narrowing steadily. Grocery and fuel prices are high provincially.
nanaimo.wifi: Good. Fibre is widely available at Canadian prices, which are high by international comparison, and mobile coverage is solid in the built-up area and patchy on the island roads inland. There is a small coworking presence serving healthcare, education and the population that left the mainland. Power is reliable outside winter storm outages.
nanaimo.nightlife: Limited. Downtown Nanaimo has a handful of pubs and a small live music scene, and the harbour area has improved considerably, but the city is quiet by ten most nights. The 4 reflects a working island city rather than a destination. Victoria and Vancouver are both accessible for anything more.
nanaimo.nature: Outstanding. Vancouver Island wraps the city in forest, coast and mountain, with Saysutshun island a ten-minute foot ferry from downtown, the Wild Pacific and Tofino side about three hours west, and Strathcona Provincial Park north. Kayaking, diving and hiking all start within minutes. The 9 is straightforwardly earned.
nanaimo.safety: Reasonable. Nanaimo is safe by international standards with low violent crime, but property crime rates sit above the Canadian average and the city has visible issues with homelessness and the opioid crisis that affects British Columbia broadly. Downtown at night requires ordinary awareness. The genuine hazards otherwise are marine and wilderness rather than criminal.
nanaimo.food: Decent. There is good seafood, a strong local farm and cidery scene on the island, and Canadian-standard cafes, but the range is limited and the fine dining is thin compared with Victoria. The Nanaimo bar, the no-bake dessert named for the city, is genuinely from here. Prices are high, as everywhere in coastal Canada.
nanaimo.community: Weak. The city's incomers are mostly Canadians who left Vancouver's housing market rather than international remote workers, and there is no nomad scene, minimal coworking culture and nothing organised for visitors. Vancouver Island University keeps a student layer. The 3 reflects a functional local network with no route in for outsiders.
nanaimo.english: Universal. English is the language of everything in British Columbia. Nanaimo sits on Snuneymuxw territory and Indigenous languages are the subject of active revitalisation work, and the city has established Punjabi and Filipino communities, but nothing public requires anything but English.
nanaimo.visa: Reasonable. Canada has no digital nomad visa, but its 2023 tech talent strategy confirmed that visitors may work remotely for a foreign employer during a normal visitor stay of up to six months, which is the practical route and needs only an eTA for visa-exempt nationalities. International Experience Canada covers working holidays for defined countries and ages.
nanaimo.culture: Thin. The Nanaimo Museum and the Bastion, a Hudson's Bay Company fort from 1853, cover the settler history, and Snuneymuxw cultural work is increasingly visible. The World Championship Bathtub Race each July, in which people race modified bathtubs across the Strait of Georgia, is the city's genuine and slightly absurd claim to fame.
nanaimo.cleanliness: High. Canadian municipal standards apply, waste and recycling services are comprehensive, and the harbour front and parks are well maintained. British Columbia's environmental regulation is strong. Some downtown blocks show the strain of the housing and drug crisis, which is the qualification behind an otherwise straightforward 8.
nanaimo.airquality: Good. Coastal position, prevailing westerlies and no heavy industry give clean air most of the year, well within guidance. The exception is increasingly serious: British Columbia's wildfire seasons have pushed smoke across Vancouver Island in recent summers, degrading air quality for days or weeks. Winter wood heating adds locally on still days.

stjohns.climate: Hard, and the 3 is honest. St John's is among the foggiest, windiest and cloudiest cities in Canada. Summers are short and cool, rarely above twenty, and winters are long, wet and windy rather than deeply cold, with heavy snow and storms that close the city for a day at a time.
stjohns.cost: Moderate. Budget around $1,700 a month, which makes this the cheapest provincial capital in Canada. A one-bedroom runs roughly $900 to $1,300 and the painted row houses downtown are within reach rather than aspirational. Groceries cost more than the national average because everything arrives by ship or plane. Heating is a serious winter line.
stjohns.wifi: Good. Fibre reaches most of the city at Canadian prices and mobile coverage is solid in the built-up area. There is a small but real coworking and startup scene built on ocean technology, Memorial University and the offshore energy industry. The time zone is the useful quirk: closer to European hours than anywhere else in North America.
stjohns.nightlife: Genuinely good, and the 7 is earned. George Street claims more bars and pubs per square foot than any other street in North America, and the traditional music scene in them is living practice rather than performance for tourists. It is small, loud and unpretentious, and it runs late every night of the week.
stjohns.nature: Outstanding. The East Coast Trail runs over three hundred kilometres along the cliffs north and south of the city, icebergs drift down Iceberg Alley between roughly April and June, whales feed offshore in summer, and Cape Spear, the easternmost point of North America, is twenty minutes away. Signal Hill sits above the harbour entrance.
stjohns.safety: Very high. Newfoundland and Labrador has among the lowest violent crime rates in Canada and St John's is comfortable at any hour, including George Street at closing time. The real hazards are environmental: winter storms, ice, wind strong enough to knock people over, and cliff edges on the coastal trail in fog.
stjohns.food: Good and improving. St John's has developed a serious restaurant scene over the last fifteen years built on the province's fish, game and foraged ingredients, and Raymonds put the city on the national map. Traditional Newfoundland cooking, from fish and brewis to toutons, is still served everywhere. Prices reflect the island freight cost.
stjohns.community: Modest. Memorial University, the ocean technology sector and the offshore industry give the city a professional network, and Newfoundlanders are famously welcoming to newcomers in a way that is genuinely unusual. There is no nomad scene, but the 4 reflects a place where an outsider can actually meet people, which most cities on this list cannot claim.
stjohns.english: Universal, with the most distinctive English in North America. Newfoundland English has its own dictionary, vocabulary and accents that vary between communities a few kilometres apart, and visitors occasionally struggle in the outports. In St John's itself nothing requires any adjustment beyond an ear for the rhythm.
stjohns.visa: Reasonable. Canada has no digital nomad visa, though the 2023 tech talent strategy confirmed that visitors may work remotely for a foreign employer during a visitor stay of up to six months. Newfoundland and Labrador runs its own provincial nominee stream and has actively recruited remote workers and skilled migrants, which makes permanent routes more realistic here.
stjohns.culture: Strong. St John's has a music, theatre and comedy culture out of all proportion to its size, producing a steady stream of national performers, and the traditional Irish-influenced repertoire is played nightly rather than annually. Signal Hill is where Marconi received the first transatlantic wireless signal in 1901. The Rooms holds the provincial collections.
stjohns.cleanliness: High. The city is well maintained, Canadian municipal standards apply, and the downtown heritage streetscape is actively protected as the city's main visual asset. Wind means litter travels, which is a visible small-scale nuisance. Harbour water quality has improved substantially since sewage treatment was introduced in the 2000s.
stjohns.airquality: Excellent. Constant Atlantic wind, no heavy industry and a small population give consistently clean air, among the best readings in Canada. There is effectively nothing to trap pollutants here: the wind that makes the weather difficult is the same wind that keeps the air clear. Winter wood heating is a marginal local source.

manta.climate: Warm and stable year-round, which the 8 records. December to May is hot and wetter with short heavy afternoon showers, and June to November is drier and cooler with grey overcast mornings locals call garua and highs around twenty-five. The Humboldt current keeps the coast milder than the latitude would suggest. Nothing here is extreme.
manta.cost: Cheap, and usefully denominated: Ecuador has used the United States dollar as its currency since 2000, so a budget of around $800 a month needs no conversion. A one-bedroom runs roughly $250 to $450, with the Murcielago beachfront and Barbasquillo at the top. Fish is exceptional and cheap in a city built on the tuna fleet.
manta.wifi: Adequate. Fibre has reached the better neighbourhoods and mobile data is inexpensive with reasonable coverage, though speeds and reliability sit below what the larger Latin American cities offer. There is a small coworking presence serving the port and the university rather than visitors. Ecuador has had scheduled outages during drought years when hydroelectric output falls.
manta.nightlife: Moderate. The Malecon and the area around Murcielago beach carry the bars and clubs, busier at weekends and during the domestic holiday season, and the university keeps some weeknight life. It is a working port city rather than a resort, so the scene is local. The 5 is an accurate middle reading.
manta.nature: Fair. Manta has a long city beach and the coastline north towards Canoa and south to Puerto Lopez holds better ones, with Machalilla National Park and Isla de la Plata, sometimes called the poor man's Galapagos, a couple of hours away. Humpback whales pass between June and September and are visible on day trips.
manta.safety: Weak, and the 5 is a warning rather than a technicality. Ecuador's security situation has deteriorated sharply in recent years, with the coastal provinces including Manabi among the worst affected by organised crime linked to the drug trade. Ordinary tourists are not the target, but current government travel advice should be read directly before booking.
manta.food: Good. This is a tuna port and the seafood is the point, with ceviche, encebollado and the local encocado in coconut sauce all done well and cheaply. Manabi cuisine is among the most distinctive in Ecuador, built on peanut, plantain and green banana. Market eating is excellent value. The 7 reflects real regional strength.
manta.community: Modest. There is a small foreign residential population along this coast, mostly North American retirees drawn by the dollar economy and the climate, concentrated more in the smaller beach towns than in Manta itself. No nomad scene exists. The 5 is generous but records a genuine if unglamorous foreign presence.
manta.english: Weak. Spanish is the language of everything and English is limited to the university, a few businesses and the retiree community. Ecuadorian Spanish on the coast is spoken quickly and clipped, which catches out learners trained on highland Spanish. Anyone here for a stretch needs functional Spanish rather than an app.
manta.visa: Good. Ecuador gives most nationalities ninety days visa-free on arrival, extendable to a hundred and eighty within a twelve-month period. The country also introduced a remote work visa in 2022 for people employed or contracted abroad, requiring proof of a monthly income around three times the national basic salary and granting two years with renewal available.
manta.culture: Thin locally, which the 4 records. Manta is a working port rather than a colonial town, and the cultural interest sits nearby: Montecristi, twenty minutes inland, is where the hats the world calls Panamas are actually woven, a UNESCO-recognised craft, and the region's pre-Columbian Manteno culture is documented in the city's small museum.
manta.cleanliness: Below average. The beachfront and the tourist-facing areas are maintained, but waste management across the city is inconsistent, the port and fishing industry generate their own problems, and litter is visible in the outer neighbourhoods. The 2016 earthquake's damage is still evident in places. The 5 is an honest reading.
manta.airquality: Fair. Sea breezes give constant dispersal and the readings are better than most Ecuadorian cities, but the fishing fleet, the canning industry and an ageing vehicle fleet are genuine local sources. Dust in the dry season adds to it. The 7 reflects coastal advantages partly offset by a working industrial port.

belem.climate: Equatorial and demanding, which the 5 records. Daytime temperatures sit around thirty-two year-round with humidity that never really drops. The practical split is between the wetter months from December to May and the drier ones from June to November, though drier here means the afternoon downpour is less certain rather than absent.
belem.cost: Cheap for a state capital of two million. Budget around $850 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $250 to $450 and Nazare and Umarizal at the upper end. Food is the real bargain: the market at Ver-o-Peso supplies produce from across the Amazon basin at prices that make eating well trivially cheap.
belem.wifi: Adequate. Fibre reaches the central neighbourhoods and Brazilian mobile data is cheap and fast with good coverage. The coworking scene grew considerably in the run-up to the thirtieth United Nations climate conference the city hosted in November 2025, which brought infrastructure investment the region had waited decades for. Power cuts happen in the heavy rain season.
belem.nightlife: Good. Belem has a real music culture, with carimbo, brega and tecnobrega all rooted in this region, and the bars around the Estacao das Docas and the Cidade Velha fill late. The 6 reflects a scene that is genuinely local rather than aimed at visitors, and one most foreigners never find out about.
belem.nature: Excellent. Belem sits where the Amazon meets the Atlantic, with boats leaving the docks for Ilha do Marajo, a river island larger than Switzerland, and for communities upriver. The Mangal das Garcas and the Bosque Rodrigues Alves put rainforest inside the city. The 8 reflects proximity to the largest forest on earth.
belem.safety: Weak, and the 4 is a genuine warning. Belem's violent crime rates are among the higher ones in Brazil and robbery is a real risk in the centre after dark and around the port areas. Ride-hailing rather than walking at night is the standard local practice. Ordinary precautions matter more here than in southern Brazilian cities.
belem.food: Exceptional, and the 9 is earned. Para's cuisine is the most distinctive in Brazil, built on ingredients found nowhere else: tucupi, the fermented cassava broth, jambu, the herb that numbs the mouth, tacaca, pato no tucupi and acai eaten savoury with fish rather than as a dessert. Ver-o-Peso is the largest open-air market in Latin America.
belem.community: Nonexistent for remote workers. Belem's foreign presence is researchers, NGO staff and the occasional traveller heading upriver, and the 2025 climate conference brought a temporary wave that has largely gone. There is no nomad scene, no English-speaking social infrastructure and nothing organised. The 2 accurately reflects a city no remote worker has considered.
belem.english: Weak. Portuguese is the language of everything and English is rare outside the federal university and the hotel trade. Northern Brazilian Portuguese has its own accent and vocabulary. Anyone working here needs functional Portuguese; Spanish helps less than people expect and is often received poorly.
belem.visa: Good. Brazil launched a digital nomad visa in January 2022 for remote workers employed or contracted abroad, requiring around $1,500 a month in income or $18,000 in savings, valid a year and renewable. Note that Brazil reinstated visitor visa requirements for United States, Canadian and Australian citizens in April 2025 through an eVisa system.
belem.culture: Strong. The Belle Epoque centre was built on the rubber boom and the Theatro da Paz from 1878 is one of the great opera houses of the Americas. The Cirio de Nazare procession each October draws around two million people and is among the largest religious gatherings on earth. Emilio Goeldi Museum holds serious Amazonian collections.
belem.cleanliness: Below average. The restored waterfront and the central heritage area are maintained, but waste management across the wider city is inconsistent, drainage floods in the rainy season and the canals carry visible pollution. Ver-o-Peso itself is chaotic by design. The 5 records honest urban strain rather than neglect.
belem.airquality: Fair. The city benefits from Atlantic humidity and constant rain washing the air, and there is limited heavy industry. The regional problem is fire: dry-season burning across the Amazon basin sends smoke over the region in bad years, and the 2024 fire season produced serious haze. Traffic is the persistent local source.

bucaramanga.climate: Excellent and remarkably steady, which the 8 records. At around a thousand metres Bucaramanga sits near twenty-three degrees most of the year with little seasonal variation. The distinction that matters is rain: April to May and October to November bring heavy afternoon storms, while December to March and July to August are drier.
bucaramanga.cost: Cheap. Budget around $800 a month, less than Medellin and considerably less than Bogota for much the same climate. A one-bedroom runs roughly $250 to $450, with Cabecera and the newer Floridablanca developments at the top and the areas north of the centre well below. Santander's cooking is distinctive and inexpensive.
bucaramanga.wifi: Good. Fibre is widely available in the newer neighbourhoods at low prices and Colombian mobile data is cheap with strong 4G coverage. There is a small coworking market with desks from roughly $80 a month, serving health services, engineering and the department's oil sector. The Universidad Industrial de Santander gives the workforce a technical base.
bucaramanga.nightlife: Good. Cabecera and the Zona Rosa carry the bars and clubs, the student population from several universities keeps weeknights alive, and Colombian nightlife culture means it runs late. It is entirely local rather than aimed at foreigners, which is either the appeal or the problem depending on Spanish. The 6 is fair.
bucaramanga.nature: Excellent. The Chicamocha canyon is half an hour away, one of the largest in the world, with a cable car crossing it, and the Ruitoque mesa above the city is among the best paragliding sites in South America. San Gil, the country's adventure sports capital, and the colonial town of Barichara are two hours south.
bucaramanga.safety: Weak to mid. Bucaramanga is calmer than Colombia's reputation suggests and better than several larger cities, but street robbery is a real concern, particularly around transport hubs and in the centre after dark. The standard Colombian advice about not displaying phones or valuables applies fully. The 5 reflects genuine urban risk rather than danger.
bucaramanga.food: Good. Santander's cooking is among the most distinctive in Colombia, built on cabro, the local goat, mute santandereano soup, and hormigas culonas, the seasonal fried ants that are a genuine regional delicacy rather than a novelty. Arepas here are made with maize and yuca. Prices are very low and quality is high.
bucaramanga.community: Weak. There is essentially no foreign remote-worker presence, which is precisely what distinguishes Bucaramanga from Medellin, and no organised nomad scene, English-speaking meetups or coworking aimed at outsiders. The professional network is local and real. The 3 reflects a Colombian city that has not been reshaped by foreign demand.
bucaramanga.english: Weak. Spanish is essential and English is limited to the universities and a handful of businesses. Colombian Spanish from Santander is clear and relatively slow, which makes it a good place to learn, but nothing here accommodates a non-speaker. This is the main practical difference from Medellin.
bucaramanga.visa: Good. Colombia gives most Western nationals ninety days visa-free on arrival, extendable once to a hundred and eighty within a calendar year. The country also has a dedicated digital nomad visa introduced in late 2022 for remote workers earning around three times the local minimum wage, valid up to two years and applied for online.
bucaramanga.culture: Modest. Bucaramanga is a commercial city rather than a historic one, though Giron, a preserved colonial town fifteen minutes away, carries the architectural interest, and Barichara two hours south is widely called the prettiest village in Colombia. The city itself is known for its parks, which is how it earned the name Ciudad Bonita.
bucaramanga.cleanliness: Good. Bucaramanga is better maintained than most Colombian cities of its size, the park network is genuinely cared for and municipal services are reliable in the central and newer districts. The outer neighbourhoods and the ravines that cut through the city are less consistent. The 7 reflects a city that works reasonably well.
bucaramanga.airquality: Mediocre. The city sits on a plateau where the surrounding topography limits dispersal, and traffic in a metro area spread across four municipalities is the main source, with readings sitting above guidance for much of the year. There is limited heavy industry. Regional biomass burning in the dry season adds to it periodically.

campogrande.climate: Hot with a clear seasonal split. April to September is the dry half, warm by day and genuinely cool at night by Brazilian standards, with July occasionally cold. October to March is the wet season, hot and humid with heavy afternoon storms. The Pantanal to the west floods in the wet and drains in the dry.
campogrande.cost: Cheap for a Brazilian state capital. Budget around $850 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $250 to $450 and the areas around Afonso Pena and the Parque dos Poderes at the upper end.
