Beef is exceptional and cheap, following from the cattle economy the whole state runs on. Fuel and internal flights cost more.
campogrande.wifi: Good. Fibre reaches most of the central neighbourhoods and Brazilian mobile data is cheap and fast, with solid 4G and expanding 5G. There is a modest coworking market serving agribusiness, logistics and services, with desks at low prices by any international measure. The federal university and the state government keep professional depth in the city.
campogrande.nightlife: Moderate. There are bars and clubs around the centre and in the university areas, and Brazilian social life means things run late, but Campo Grande is a working inland capital rather than a destination. The central market's food stalls are where a lot of the evening actually happens. The 5 is accurate.
campogrande.nature: Outstanding, mostly because of what is nearby. The Pantanal, the largest tropical wetland on earth, begins a few hours west, Bonito's crystal-clear rivers and caves are around three hundred kilometres southwest, and the Serra da Bodoquena is beyond that. Inside the city, the Parque das Nacoes Indigenas is among the largest urban parks anywhere.
campogrande.safety: Weak to mid. Campo Grande's crime rates sit around the Brazilian average, which means real risk of robbery in the centre after dark and around transport hubs, with the residential and newer districts considerably calmer. The state's position on the Bolivian and Paraguayan borders makes it a trafficking corridor. Ordinary precautions and ride-hailing at night apply.
campogrande.food: Good and genuinely unusual. Campo Grande has a large Okinawan Japanese community dating from post-war migration, and their soba, served at the central market, is a local dish found nowhere else in Brazil. Pantanal river fish and the state's beef are the other pillars, and tereré, cold mate, is drunk constantly.
campogrande.community: Nonexistent for remote workers. The city's foreign presence is limited to agricultural business, some Paraguayan and Bolivian migration and the descendants of the Japanese community. There is no nomad scene, no English-speaking social infrastructure and nothing organised for visitors. The 2 records a place no remote worker has thought about.
campogrande.english: Weak. Portuguese is essential and English is rare outside the university. Spanish is more useful here than in most of Brazil given the borders, and Guarani is spoken in the region. Anyone working here without Portuguese will find daily life genuinely difficult rather than merely inconvenient.
campogrande.visa: Good. Brazil's digital nomad visa, introduced in January 2022, is open to remote workers employed or contracted abroad showing around $1,500 a month in income or $18,000 in savings, valid a year and renewable. Travellers from the United States, Canada and Australia should note that Brazil reinstated visitor visa requirements for them in April 2025.
campogrande.culture: Modest. Campo Grande is a young city by Brazilian standards, founded in the 1870s, and its cultural interest is in the mix rather than the monuments: Okinawan, Paraguayan, Bolivian and Indigenous Terena influences all visible in the market. The Bioparque Pantanal, opened in 2022, is the largest freshwater aquarium in the world.
campogrande.cleanliness: Good. The city is laid out on a wide grid with tree-lined avenues and is better maintained than most Brazilian cities of comparable size, with reliable municipal services in the central and residential districts. The red laterite dust that gives the city its Cidade Morena nickname gets into everything. The 7 is fair.
campogrande.airquality: Fair. There is little heavy industry and the wide, low-density layout helps dispersal, but the dry season brings agricultural burning across Mato Grosso do Sul and smoke from Pantanal and Amazon fires, which in bad years including 2020 and 2024 pushed readings well above guidance for weeks. Traffic is the persistent local source.

hakodate.climate: Cold, and the 4 reflects a Hokkaido winter rather than anything unusual. Summers are mild and pleasant, rarely above twenty-six, which makes the city a refuge when the rest of Japan is unbearable. Winter runs from December to March with the city under snow, and spring arrives about a month later than in Tokyo.
hakodate.cost: Low for Japan. Budget around $1,300 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $400 to $650, a fraction of Tokyo for considerably more space. This is a regional city that has been losing population for decades, which is what keeps rents down. Food is a bargain given the fishing port. Heating is a serious winter cost.
hakodate.wifi: Excellent. Japanese fibre is fast, widely available and cheap relative to speed, and mobile coverage is comprehensive. The obstacle is administrative rather than technical: fixed contracts generally require residency and a Japanese bank account, so short stays run on rented pocket wifi or a data SIM. There is very little coworking provision here.
hakodate.nightlife: Limited. Daimon Yokocho, the alley of small bars and yatai-style stalls near the station, is the best of it, and there are izakaya scattered through the centre. The city is quiet by Japanese standards and considerably quieter in winter. The 4 reflects a shrinking regional city rather than any lack of character.
hakodate.nature: Excellent. Mount Hakodate rises directly behind the city with the night view that draws most visitors, Onuma Quasi-National Park with its lakes and the volcano behind them is half an hour by train, and the Tsugaru Strait and its seafood define the local economy. Southern Hokkaido's forest and coast start immediately outside town.
hakodate.safety: Exceptional. Japan has among the lowest crime rates in the world and Hakodate is safe at any hour in any district, with lost property routinely returned and violent crime essentially absent. The real hazards are natural: this is a seismically active region, tsunami risk on the coast is real, and winter snow and ice cause most injuries.
hakodate.food: Exceptional. Hakodate's morning market sells squid pulled live from the tank, the city is known nationally for its uni, crab and scallops, and the local shio ramen is one of Japan's three great ramen styles. Hokkaido dairy and produce supply everything else. Prices are a fraction of what the same quality costs in Tokyo.
hakodate.community: Nonexistent for remote workers. Hakodate's foreign population is a small number of teachers, students and workers, and there is no nomad scene, no coworking culture and no English-speaking social infrastructure. Tourism is largely domestic and East Asian. The 2 records a city with no route in for a visiting professional.
hakodate.english: Weak. English is limited to parts of the tourism trade and signage at the main sites, and Japanese is the language of everything else. Anything administrative, from a rental contract to a phone plan, assumes Japanese and rewards patience. Translation apps carry a lot of the load for a visitor.
hakodate.visa: Middling. Japan launched a digital nomad visa in 2024 granting six months to citizens of countries with the relevant agreements who can show an annual income around ten million yen, which is a high bar and not renewable in place. Most visitors use the visa waiver instead: ninety days for roughly seventy nationalities, extendable for some.
hakodate.culture: Strong. Hakodate was one of the first Japanese ports opened to foreign trade in 1854, and the Motomachi slope district still carries the Russian Orthodox church, the British consulate and the Western-style buildings that followed. Goryokaku, the star-shaped fort, was the site of the last battle of the Boshin War in 1869.
hakodate.cleanliness: Exceptional. Japanese standards apply throughout: streets are immaculate, waste sorting is meticulous and public spaces are maintained to a level that surprises most visitors. Snow clearance in winter is systematic. The 9 is straightforward and reflects a national norm rather than anything specific to Hakodate.
hakodate.airquality: Excellent. Coastal position, constant wind off the Tsugaru Strait, no heavy industry and a small population give consistently clean air well within guidance. Winter heating raises particulates marginally on still days. Hokkaido generally records the best air quality in Japan, and the southern coast is among the cleanest of it.

kagoshima.climate: Warm and humid subtropical, which the 7 records. Winters are mild and rarely near freezing, making this one of Japan's more comfortable cold seasons. Summers are hot and humid through July and August with the rainy season in June before them. Typhoons reach this coast between roughly August and October and are a genuine planning factor.
kagoshima.cost: Low for Japan. Budget around $1,350 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $400 to $700 depending on district and distance from the tram line. Food is very good value, built on Kurobuta pork, Satsuma sweet potato and the shochu the prefecture produces more of than anywhere else. Onsen bathing is genuinely cheap here.
kagoshima.wifi: Excellent. Japanese internet is fast, widely available and inexpensive relative to speed, with comprehensive mobile coverage. There is a small coworking presence serving the prefectural economy and the university. As across Japan, fixed contracts assume residency and a bank account, so short stays generally run on pocket wifi or a data SIM.
kagoshima.nightlife: Moderate. Tenmonkan, the covered arcade district in the centre, holds the izakaya, bars and shochu specialists, and it is livelier than most Japanese regional cities of this size. Kagoshima drinks shochu rather than sake, and the local bars take it seriously. The 5 reflects a real scene without much scale.
kagoshima.nature: Outstanding. Sakurajima, an active volcano four kilometres across the bay, erupts hundreds of times a year and is reachable by a fifteen-minute ferry. Kirishima's volcanic range and onsen are inland, the Ibusuki sand baths are down the peninsula, and ferries leave for Yakushima's ancient cedar forest, a UNESCO site, and the Amami islands.
kagoshima.safety: Exceptional. Japan's crime rates are among the lowest in the world and Kagoshima is safe at any hour anywhere in the city. The genuine hazards are geological and meteorological: an active volcano that drops ash on the city regularly, earthquakes, and typhoons that reach this coast most years. The city is well prepared for all three.
kagoshima.food: Excellent. Kagoshima is a serious food prefecture: Kurobuta black pork, Satsuma-age fish cakes, kibinago sardines, the sweet potato that gives the region its shochu, and some of the best beef in Japan. Tenmonkan's restaurants and the shochu bars are where it happens. Prices are far below Tokyo for equivalent quality.
kagoshima.community: Nonexistent for remote workers. There is a small international student population at Kagoshima University and a handful of teachers, but no nomad scene, no coworking aimed at foreigners and no English-speaking social infrastructure. Tourism is overwhelmingly domestic. The 2 accurately records a city with no route in for a visiting professional.
kagoshima.english: Weak. English is limited outside the university and some tourism infrastructure, and Japanese is the language of everything. The Kagoshima dialect is difficult enough that other Japanese speakers struggle with it, which is a genuine local quirk. Anything administrative assumes Japanese and takes time.
kagoshima.visa: Middling. Japan's 2024 digital nomad visa gives six months to citizens of countries with the relevant agreements who can show an annual income around ten million yen, a high threshold that is not renewable without a break. Most visitors use the visa waiver: ninety days for around seventy nationalities, extendable to a hundred and eighty for some.
kagoshima.culture: Strong. Kagoshima was the seat of the Satsuma domain, which drove the Meiji Restoration, and Saigo Takamori, the samurai who led and then rebelled against it, is the city's defining figure. Sengan-en garden and the Shoko Shuseikan are UNESCO-listed as part of Japan's industrial revolution sites. The pottery and textile traditions remain active.
kagoshima.cleanliness: High. Japanese standards apply, streets are well kept and waste sorting is meticulous. The specific local factor is volcanic ash, which falls on the city regularly and requires constant clearing; the city distributes yellow collection bags for it and residents sweep as a matter of routine. The 8 accounts for a genuinely unusual condition.
kagoshima.airquality: Mediocre, and the 6 has a specific cause. Sakurajima's near-continuous activity puts volcanic ash and sulphur dioxide into the air over the city whenever the wind blows from the east, which is often, and readings spike accordingly. Between eruptions the coastal air is clean. It is a natural source rather than an industrial one.

vizag.climate: Tropical coastal with a hard summer. November to February is the good season, with days in the high twenties and low humidity by Indian coastal standards. March to May is hot and increasingly humid into the mid thirties. The southwest monsoon runs June to September, and cyclones form in the Bay of Bengal, peaking in October and November.
vizag.cost: Very cheap. Budget around $600 a month, one of the lowest figures for any city with this level of infrastructure. A one-bedroom runs roughly $150 to $300, with the beach road and MVP Colony at the top and the inland areas well below. Andhra food costs almost nothing. Rents in the newer IT areas have risen.
vizag.wifi: Good. Fibre from the main providers reaches the developed neighbourhoods at low prices, and Indian mobile data remains among the cheapest in the world with solid coverage. There is a real and growing coworking market alongside the Rushikonda IT park. Power cuts are occasional rather than routine. The technology sector here is expanding fast.
vizag.nightlife: Limited. Andhra Pradesh has restrictive alcohol policies and Visakhapatnam is not a going-out city, with a handful of hotel bars and restaurants along the beach road carrying most of it. Beach walking in the evening is the actual social ritual here. The 4 reflects policy and culture rather than any shortage of people.
vizag.nature: Good. The city sits between the Bay of Bengal and the Eastern Ghats, with Kailasagiri hill park above it, beaches along the coast road, and the Araku Valley coffee country a scenic narrow-gauge train ride inland through tunnels and hills. The Borra Caves are on the same route. The 7 balances real access against urban density.
vizag.safety: Reasonable. Visakhapatnam is calmer than most large Indian cities, with low violent crime and comfortable movement for foreigners in the main areas. Ordinary precautions against petty theft and scams apply. Traffic is the genuine daily hazard, as everywhere in India. The Eastern Naval Command is headquartered here and restricts photography near some port areas.
vizag.food: Excellent. Andhra cooking is among the spiciest and best regarded in India, built on chilli, tamarind and gongura, and the coastal seafood adds another layer, with the local prawn and fish curries genuinely distinctive. Meals are absurdly cheap. Anyone unused to Andhra heat should build up to it rather than dive in.
vizag.community: Weak. There is an Indian professional network around the IT park and the port, and English works well in it, but no foreign nomad community exists here at all. Visakhapatnam has never appeared on any remote-work circuit. The 2 records absence of foreigners rather than any unfriendliness, which is not a problem here.
vizag.english: Good for the price point, which is the city's underrated advantage. English is widely used in professional and business settings, signage is bilingual and educated urban Indians switch into it readily. Telugu is the language of daily life and the streets. Anyone working here in a technology context will find English entirely sufficient.
vizag.visa: Middling. India has no digital nomad visa. Most visitors use the e-Visa, issued online in thirty-day, one-year and five-year tourist variants depending on nationality, with individual stays generally capped at ninety days and less for some passports. It does not permit employment in India, and extensions inside the country are genuinely difficult.
vizag.culture: Moderate. Visakhapatnam is a port and industrial city rather than a heritage one, though the submarine museum on the beach, the Simhachalam temple above the city and the Buddhist sites at Thotlakonda and Bavikonda give it depth. The Araku Valley's tribal communities and coffee culture inland are the more distinctive regional draw.
vizag.cleanliness: Middling. The beach road and the newer IT districts are maintained and the city has performed reasonably in national cleanliness rankings, but waste management in the older and industrial areas is inconsistent and the port and steel plant have their own footprint. The 6 records genuine improvement from a low base.
vizag.airquality: Weak. The steel plant, the port, the refinery belt and an ageing vehicle fleet put annual particulate readings above guidance, and the industrial corridor north of the city is the main source. Sea breezes give real dispersal that inland Indian cities lack, which is why the reading is not worse. Winter months are the worst.

shymkent.climate: Continental with a hot dry summer, which the 5 records. July and August regularly pass thirty-five degrees, though the low humidity makes that more bearable than the number suggests. Winter is mild by Kazakh standards, sitting around freezing rather than the deep cold of the north, with snow that rarely settles for long.
shymkent.cost: Very cheap. Budget around $700 a month, among the lowest figures for any city of a million people on this site. A one-bedroom runs roughly $200 to $350, with the newer developments and the centre at the top. The bazaars supply produce from the Turkestan region and the Uzbek border trade keeps prices down.
shymkent.wifi: Good. Kazakh internet is fast and remarkably cheap, with fibre widely available in the city and strong mobile coverage, and it is one of the country's genuine practical advantages. There is a small coworking market, well behind Almaty's but real, serving trade, agriculture and light industry. Power is reliable throughout.
shymkent.nightlife: Limited. There are bars, restaurants and a few clubs in the centre, and the city is more conservative than Almaty, with a stronger religious character in the south of the country. Tea houses and long meals are the social default. The 4 reflects a provincial Central Asian city rather than any shortage of life.
shymkent.nature: Fair. The city itself is flat and dry, but the Aksu-Zhabagly reserve, the oldest protected area in Central Asia, is within reach to the east, and the Tian Shan foothills and the Sayram-Ugam park offer real mountain country. The steppe around the city is bleak in a way some people find compelling.
shymkent.safety: Reasonable. Kazakhstan is safe by regional standards and Shymkent is comfortable to move around, with petty theft and taxi overcharging the main ordinary concerns. Corruption in routine policing has improved but is not absent. The country saw serious unrest in January 2022, which is context rather than a current condition. Traffic standards require attention.
shymkent.food: Good. Southern Kazakh and Uzbek cooking meet here: plov, samsa, laghman and shashlik are everywhere, the bazaars sell dried fruit and nuts from the whole region, and the bread from the tandyr ovens is genuinely worth the trip. Prices are trivially low. Vegetarians will find the meat-heavy default a real constraint.
shymkent.community: Nonexistent for remote workers. Shymkent's foreign presence is limited to business travellers, a small number of Turkish and Chinese traders and the occasional overland traveller passing between Uzbekistan and Almaty. There is no nomad scene, no coworking for foreigners and no English-speaking social infrastructure of any kind. The 2 is accurate.
shymkent.english: Weak. Russian is the working language of business and daily life alongside Kazakh, with Uzbek widely spoken given the border and the population, and English is rare outside a few younger professionals. Some Russian makes an enormous difference here and is close to necessary for anything administrative or medical.
shymkent.visa: Reasonable. Kazakhstan gives citizens of around eighty countries thirty days visa-free on arrival, which is simple but short. A Neo Nomad Visa for remote workers launched in 2024 offering up to a year for people employed abroad above an income threshold, and the scheme is new enough that requirements have shifted since announcement.
shymkent.culture: Moderate. Shymkent is an old Silk Road settlement and the region around it carries the weight: Sayram, on the city's edge, is one of the oldest inhabited places in Kazakhstan and the birthplace of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi, whose mausoleum at Turkistan two hours north is the country's most important Islamic monument and a UNESCO site.
shymkent.cleanliness: Middling. The centre and the newer districts built since the city gained republic status in 2018 are maintained, but waste management in the older neighbourhoods and around the bazaars is inconsistent and litter is visible. Dust from the surrounding steppe is a constant. The 6 is an honest reading of uneven service.
shymkent.airquality: Weak. Winter is the problem: coal heating across southern Kazakhstan, combined with an ageing vehicle fleet and dust from the steppe, pushes particulate readings well above guidance from November to March. Summer air is considerably better despite the dust. The 5 reflects a seasonal problem shared across Central Asian cities.

bridgetown.climate: Tropical and steadier than most of the Caribbean, sitting around thirty degrees year-round with constant trade winds off the Atlantic. December to May is the dry half. Barbados lies on the eastern edge of the hurricane belt and is struck far less often than the islands to its west, though Hurricane Elsa in 2021 ended a long run.
bridgetown.cost: Expensive, and the 3 is honest. Budget around $2,400 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $900 to $1,500. The grocery bill is what catches people: Barbados imports nearly all its food and the markup is heavy enough that the supermarket can cost more than the rent. Local rum shops and the Oistins fish fry are the cheap end.
bridgetown.wifi: Good. Fibre from Flow and Digicel covers the developed parts of the island at speeds that hold up for video calls, and mobile coverage is comprehensive. Several coworking spaces around Bridgetown and the west coast were set up specifically for Welcome Stamp holders, with desks from roughly $200 a month. Outages happen in storm season.
bridgetown.nightlife: Reasonable. St Lawrence Gap is the concentrated strip of bars and clubs, Oistins on a Friday night is the island's real institution, and Crop Over from June to August turns the whole place into a season. It is not Trinidad, and outside the Gap and the festival calendar things close early. The 6 is fair.
bridgetown.nature: Good rather than dramatic. Barbados is coral rather than volcanic, so it is flat and lacks the rainforest peaks of its neighbours, but it has Harrison's Cave, the Animal Flower Cave in the cliffs at the northern tip, and an east coast at Bathsheba where the Atlantic breaks on rock formations. Turtles nest on the west coast beaches.
bridgetown.safety: Reasonable. Barbados is among the safer Caribbean islands and violent crime against visitors is uncommon, though petty theft and opportunistic crime around the beaches and the nightlife strip require ordinary precautions. Gun crime has risen in recent years and is concentrated in specific areas away from where visitors go. Rip currents on the east coast are the more likely hazard.
bridgetown.food: Good. Flying fish and cou-cou is the national dish, the Friday fish fry at Oistins is the best eating on the island and among the cheapest, and pudding and souse is a Saturday tradition worth understanding. Barbados also has a serious fine dining scene along the west coast at prices to match. Rum is a local industry.
bridgetown.community: Modest, which the 4 records. Barbados has more remote workers than any other Eastern Caribbean island because the Welcome Stamp brought them, and there are coworking spaces and meetups as a result. It is still small and turns over constantly, since most people are here on a one-year visa rather than settling. Better than its neighbours, thin in absolute terms.
bridgetown.english: Universal. English is the official language and Bajan, an English-based creole, is what people speak among themselves. There is no barrier of any kind for an English speaker, and the accent is the only adjustment. Barbados was British for over three centuries and the institutions, the school system and the cricket all reflect it.
bridgetown.visa: Excellent. Barbados created the category with the Welcome Stamp in July 2020: twelve months for remote workers earning around $50,000 a year, roughly $2,000 for an individual, with no local tax on the income and an online application processed in days. It is renewable. Short visits are visa-free for most Western nationalities, six months for British and Commonwealth citizens.
bridgetown.culture: Strong for the size. Historic Bridgetown and its Garrison is a UNESCO World Heritage site, the Barbados Museum sits in a former military prison, and Kensington Oval is a genuine cricketing cathedral. Crop Over, the sugar harvest festival that ends in Grand Kadooment, runs for weeks. The island's musical export record is disproportionate for a population of 280,000.
bridgetown.cleanliness: Good. Barbados is well maintained by regional standards, the beaches are cleaned and publicly accessible by law, and waste collection is reliable. Sargassum seaweed on the east and south coasts in some years is the recurring problem and is regional rather than local. Water is safe to drink from the tap, which is unusual in the Caribbean.
bridgetown.airquality: Very good. An Atlantic island with constant trade winds and no heavy industry has little to trap. Annual readings sit well within guidance. The one recurring factor is Saharan dust, which crosses the ocean and reaches the eastern Caribbean in summer, raising particulate levels noticeably for days at a time between roughly June and August.

hamiltonbermuda.climate: Subtropical rather than tropical, and the distinction matters. Summers from May to October are warm and humid in the high twenties with swimmable water; winters sit around eighteen with wind and grey, and the sea is too cold for most from January to April. Hurricane season runs June to November and Bermuda, alone in the Atlantic, is genuinely exposed.
hamiltonbermuda.cost: Among the most expensive places on this site and, by several measures, in the world. Budget around $4,200 a month, with a one-bedroom at roughly $2,200 to $3,200 as the ordinary market. Everything arrives by ship and carries substantial customs duty, so groceries run about double the eastern United States. There is no income tax.
hamiltonbermuda.wifi: Excellent. Bermuda's insurance and reinsurance industry could not function on anything less, so fibre reaches most of the island at high speeds and the professional infrastructure around it is genuinely business grade. Mobile coverage is complete across twenty-one square miles. There is a small coworking market in Hamilton aimed partly at Work From Bermuda certificate holders.
hamiltonbermuda.nightlife: Limited. Front Street in Hamilton has a handful of bars and the island has a small live music scene, but Bermuda is quiet and expensive after dark and much of the social life happens in clubs and private homes. The 4 reflects a small, orderly island rather than a lack of money. Sunday is noticeably still.
hamiltonbermuda.nature: Excellent for the size. Horseshoe Bay and Warwick Long Bay have the pink sand that Bermuda is known for, the reef system is the northernmost in the Atlantic and carries hundreds of wrecks, and Crystal and Fantasy Caves run beneath the island. The Railway Trail follows the old rail bed most of the island's length.
hamiltonbermuda.safety: High. Bermuda has low violent crime and is comfortable at any hour in the areas visitors use, with gang-related incidents concentrated in specific neighbourhoods and rarely touching outsiders. The genuine risks are the roads, which are narrow and busy with scooters, and hurricanes. The building code is strict and the island absorbs storms better than most places do.
hamiltonbermuda.food: Decent but expensive, which is what holds the score at 6. Bermuda fish chowder with sherry pepper sauce and a codfish breakfast on Sunday are the local traditions. Restaurant prices are among the highest anywhere and reflect the import duty on everything on the plate. Self-catering is what most residents actually do.
hamiltonbermuda.community: Weak for visiting remote workers. Bermuda's foreign population is overwhelmingly the insurance and reinsurance industry on work permits, which is a real and international professional network but not one a passing nomad joins. There is minimal coworking culture and no nomad scene. The 3 reflects that gap between a deep industry network and no visitor community.
hamiltonbermuda.english: Universal. English is the only language of public life and Bermuda has been British since 1609, with an accent that sits somewhere between the Caribbean and the American east coast. Portuguese is spoken in a substantial community descended from Azorean migration. No visitor will encounter a language barrier of any kind.
hamiltonbermuda.visa: Excellent on paper. The Work From Bermuda Certificate gives a year to anyone working or studying remotely for an organisation outside Bermuda, costs around $263, and sets no minimum income, making it one of the cheapest and least demanding schemes anywhere. It is renewable. The constraint is not the visa but the rent you must find once you hold it.
hamiltonbermuda.culture: Modest. St George's, the oldest continuously inhabited English town in the New World, is a UNESCO World Heritage site at the eastern end, and the Royal Naval Dockyard at the other end holds the National Museum. Gombey dancers are a genuine local tradition. Beyond that the cultural offer is limited by the size of the population.
hamiltonbermuda.cleanliness: Exceptional. Bermuda is meticulously maintained, litter is essentially absent, and the island's entire drinking water supply is rainwater collected from the stepped white roofs that give the architecture its look. Waste is managed carefully because there is nowhere to put it. The 9 reflects a small wealthy island that takes its appearance seriously.
hamiltonbermuda.airquality: Excellent. A mid-Atlantic island with constant wind, no heavy industry and a population of sixty-four thousand has essentially nothing to trap. Readings sit comfortably within guidance year-round. The only local sources are vehicles and the power station, and the wind disperses both. Air here is about as clean as inhabited air gets.

georgetowncayman.climate: Tropical and warm year-round, around twenty-eight to thirty-one degrees with water temperature that barely moves. December to April is the dry, less humid half and the busiest. May to November is hotter and wetter, and the Atlantic hurricane season runs through it; Hurricane Ivan in 2004 devastated Grand Cayman and still shapes how the island builds.
georgetowncayman.cost: Extremely expensive, which the 2 records honestly. Budget around $3,800 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $2,000 to $2,800 and anything near Seven Mile Beach at the top. Groceries are a standing local complaint. There is no income tax, no capital gains tax and no property tax, which is precisely why the cost structure looks like this.
georgetowncayman.wifi: Excellent. An offshore banking, funds and insurance centre requires it, so fibre covers essentially all of Grand Cayman at high speeds and there are several coworking spaces around George Town and Camana Bay. The grid was rebuilt to a higher standard after Ivan and power is reliable. Connectivity is not a constraint here in any respect.
georgetowncayman.nightlife: Modest. There are bars along Seven Mile Beach and in George Town, and a well-paid expatriate workforce keeps them busy midweek, but the island is not a late-night place and the scene is small. Cruise passengers empty out by evening. The 5 reflects a comfortable rather than exciting social life.
georgetowncayman.nature: Excellent underwater and modest above it. Grand Cayman is flat and low, but the wall diving off the drop-off a few hundred metres offshore is world class, Stingray City puts you in waist-deep water among wild southern stingrays, and the Kittiwake wreck was sunk deliberately for divers. The Mastic Trail crosses the island's remaining old-growth forest.
georgetowncayman.safety: Very high. The Cayman Islands have among the lowest crime rates in the Caribbean, the island is comfortable at any hour, and the wealth and the small population both help. Petty theft exists around the tourist areas. The real hazards are hurricanes and, for divers, the depth: the wall drops fast and it catches people out.
georgetowncayman.food: Good and expensive. Cayman has a restaurant scene well beyond its size, driven by a wealthy resident population, with an annual food festival that draws international chefs. Cayman-style fish, turtle stew and heavy cake are the local dishes. Prices are set for the finance industry, which is what keeps the score at 7 rather than higher.
georgetowncayman.community: Modest. There is a large and genuinely international expatriate workforce in funds, insurance and law, and the Global Citizen programme added a small remote-worker layer to it. Turnover is high and the social scene revolves around industry events and the dive shops. The 4 reflects a real network that is easy to enter only if you work in finance.
georgetowncayman.english: Universal. English is the sole official language and the Cayman accent is closer to the British Caribbean than the American. The workforce is drawn from across the world, so many languages are spoken at home, but nothing public requires anything but English. Signage, administration and business all operate in it exclusively.
georgetowncayman.visa: Good if you qualify and irrelevant if you do not. The Global Citizen Concierge Programme grants two years to remote workers earning around $100,000 a year individually, $150,000 as a couple or $180,000 as a family, with a fee near $1,469. That threshold is deliberate. Short visits are visa-free for most Western nationalities for up to six months.
georgetowncayman.culture: Thin, which the 5 records. The Cayman Islands National Museum in George Town and the restored Pedro St James, where the islands' first elected assembly met, cover the history. Batabano, the spring carnival, is the main event. The islands were sparsely settled until the twentieth century and the culture is young and heavily shaped by the finance industry.
georgetowncayman.cleanliness: Exceptional. Grand Cayman is meticulously maintained, the beaches are cleaned daily, waste management is properly funded and the standard is closer to a wealthy suburb than to the Caribbean. The George Town Landfill, known locally as Mount Trashmore, is the one persistent and much-debated exception. Tap water is safe and desalinated.
georgetowncayman.airquality: Excellent. A flat, low island with constant trade winds, no industry beyond the power station and a small population keeps readings well within guidance. Saharan dust reaches the western Caribbean in summer and raises particulates for periods, which is a regional pattern. Cruise ship emissions in port are a localised and much-discussed exception.

willemstad.climate: Excellent and remarkably stable. Curacao sits below the hurricane belt, averages around thirty-one degrees every month, and gets little rain even in the wetter stretch from October to February. Constant trade winds take the edge off the heat. There is no season to avoid, which is genuinely rare in the Caribbean and is the island's strongest practical card.
willemstad.cost: Moderate. Budget around $1,700 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $600 to $1,000, which makes Curacao considerably cheaper than Barbados or the Cayman Islands. Groceries are imported and priced accordingly, though the Dutch supply chain keeps the range wide and the markup lower than on smaller islands. Local snacks and truk'i pan cost very little.
willemstad.wifi: Good. Fibre from Flow reaches the developed parts of the island at reliable speeds and mobile data is inexpensive. There is a real coworking scene for an island of 150,000, concentrated in Pietermaai and around Punda, much of it grown out of the @HOME remote work programme. Power is stable. Connectivity is not a limiting factor here.
willemstad.nightlife: Decent. Pietermaai is the concentrated strip of bars and restaurants in restored colonial buildings, there is a floating market and a beach club scene along the west coast, and Curacao's carnival season runs for weeks before Lent with the Gran Marcha as its centrepiece. It closes earlier than a European city but there is a genuine scene.
willemstad.nature: Strong, and not in the way people expect. Curacao is arid and covered in cactus and divi-divi rather than rainforest, with Christoffel National Park inland and Shete Boka's blowholes on the wild north coast. The real case is underwater: dozens of shore diving entry points along the leeward coast, and Klein Curacao an hour offshore by boat.
willemstad.safety: Reasonable. Curacao is safe in the areas visitors and residents use, with petty theft and car break-ins the common problems and violent crime concentrated away from them. Ordinary urban caution is enough. Rip currents on the north coast are genuinely dangerous and the blowhole area at Shete Boka should be treated with respect rather than approached casually.
willemstad.food: Good and unusually varied for the size. Curacao's cooking mixes Dutch, Caribbean, Latin American and Indonesian traditions, so keshi yena sits alongside rijsttafel and Venezuelan arepas. Plasa Bieu, the old market hall, serves proper local food at local prices. The Dutch supply chain means the supermarkets carry a range no comparable island manages.
willemstad.community: Modest but real, which is more than most of the region can say. The @HOME programme brought a small, steady flow of remote workers, and Pietermaai has the coworking and cafes to support them. There is also a long-standing Dutch expatriate community. The 5 reflects something you can actually plug into rather than a scene that exists on paper.
willemstad.english: Strong. Papiamentu is the language of daily life and Dutch of administration and education, but English is widely and comfortably spoken and Spanish is common given Venezuela's proximity. Curacaoans switching between four languages in one conversation is entirely normal. An English speaker will have no practical difficulty at any point on the island.
willemstad.visa: Good. The @HOME in Curacao programme grants six months to remote workers employed outside the island, with a simple online application and a modest fee, extendable by a further six. Dutch nationals have residence rights. Others get ninety days visa-free on arrival. Curacao is in the Kingdom of the Netherlands but not the EU, so Schengen counts do not apply.
willemstad.culture: Strong. Willemstad's historic area is a UNESCO World Heritage site, a row of Dutch merchant houses in ice-cream colours along a working shipping channel with the Queen Emma pontoon bridge swinging open across it. The Mikve Israel-Emanuel synagogue is the oldest in continuous use in the Americas, with sand on its floor. Kaya Kaya festivals repaint the old quarters.
willemstad.cleanliness: Good. The restored historic areas and the tourist coast are well maintained and municipal services function to Dutch-influenced standards. The industrial side around the Isla refinery is a different picture, and the refinery's emissions have been a public health controversy for years. Tap water is desalinated and safe. The 7 balances a well-kept centre against that.
willemstad.airquality: Good. Constant trade winds and an arid climate keep general readings low. The significant local exception is the Isla refinery at Schottegat, whose emissions have prompted repeated court cases and health studies, and whose plume affects the neighbourhoods immediately downwind rather than the island as a whole. Saharan dust reaches here in summer as it does across the region.

oranjestad.climate: The most consistent in the Caribbean and genuinely a selling point. Aruba lies below the hurricane belt, gets under 450 millimetres of rain a year, and sits around thirty-one degrees every single month with trade winds that never stop. There is no season to avoid and no bad month, which almost nowhere else in the region can claim.
oranjestad.cost: Expensive. Budget around $2,000 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $800 to $1,300 and anything near Palm Beach or Eagle Beach at the top. Groceries are imported and the markup is real, though the Dutch supply chain keeps the choice wide. Eating at a local snack or one of the fish shacks costs a fraction of the resort strip.
oranjestad.wifi: Good. Aruba's tourism economy underwrites the infrastructure: fibre reaches the developed western side at reliable speeds, mobile data is inexpensive with complete coverage, and power is dependable. Formal coworking exists in a modest way around Oranjestad, though most remote workers here use apartments. The island's connectivity is comfortably ahead of the Caribbean average.
oranjestad.nightlife: Decent. Palm Beach has the concentrated strip of bars, casinos and clubs aimed at the resort crowd, Oranjestad has a more local scene, and the island's carnival season from January to February is the real event, running for weeks and culminating in the Grand Parade. Outside carnival it is polished rather than exciting. The 6 is fair.
oranjestad.nature: Fair, and the 6 is honest. Aruba is a desert island of cactus, divi-divi trees bent permanently by the wind, and white beaches. Arikok National Park covers nearly a fifth of it, with the Natural Pool and wind-carved rock on the wild windward side. There is no rainforest, no river and no mountain, which surprises people expecting the Caribbean of postcards.
oranjestad.safety: High. Aruba has among the lowest crime rates in the Caribbean and is comfortable at any hour, helped by an economy that depends entirely on visitors feeling safe. Petty theft on the beaches is the common issue. The genuine hazards are the sun, which is fierce with the wind masking it, and the north coast surf, which kills swimmers.
oranjestad.food: Good. Aruban cooking mixes Dutch, Caribbean and Latin American influences, with keshi yena, pastechi and fresh fish the staples, and the wind means grilling is the default. The resort strip has an international restaurant scene at international prices. Zeerover, the fish shack at Savaneta where you order by the pound, is the local institution.
oranjestad.community: Modest. Aruba's foreign population is largely Dutch, Venezuelan and Colombian, working in tourism and services rather than remotely, and the One Happy Workation programme added only a small layer on top. There is little coworking culture and no nomad scene. The 4 reflects a friendly island with nothing organised for a visiting professional.
oranjestad.english: Excellent. Papiamento is the language of daily life, Dutch is official, and Spanish is everywhere given Venezuela is thirty kilometres away, but English is spoken fluently across the whole tourism economy and by most Arubans. Four languages in one conversation is routine here. No English speaker will encounter any difficulty at all.
oranjestad.visa: Fair. The One Happy Workation scheme is a ninety-day remote work arrangement, originally for United States nationals and since broadened, which is short by regional standards and closer to a formalised long visit than a residence permit. Dutch nationals have residence rights. Others get ninety days on arrival. Aruba is not in the EU, so Schengen counts do not apply.
oranjestad.culture: Modest. Oranjestad's Dutch colonial architecture along Caya Betico Croes is genuine and attractive, the Archaeological Museum holds Caquetio artefacts from before European arrival, and San Nicolas at the southern end has become a serious street art district. Carnival is the cultural centrepiece. Beyond that the island's identity is heavily shaped by seventy years of tourism.
oranjestad.cleanliness: High. Aruba is well maintained to Dutch-influenced standards, the beaches are cleaned and publicly accessible, and waste collection is reliable. The island has banned single-use plastic bags and certain sunscreens to protect the reef. The former refinery site at San Nicolas is the exception to an otherwise tidy picture. Tap water is desalinated and safe.
oranjestad.airquality: Very good. Relentless trade winds across a small flat island disperse everything, and the closure of the San Nicolas refinery removed the one significant industrial source. Readings sit within guidance year-round. Saharan dust reaches the southern Caribbean in summer and raises particulates for periods, which is regional rather than anything Aruba produces.

nassau.climate: Tropical with a real seasonal swing for the Caribbean. December to April is dry and cooler, around twenty-six degrees with low humidity, and is the busy half. May to November is hot and much wetter, and the Atlantic hurricane season runs through it; the Bahamas sit directly in the track and Hurricane Dorian in 2019 was catastrophic further north.
nassau.cost: Expensive. Budget around $2,600 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $1,200 to $1,800. The grocery bill is the standing complaint: the Bahamas import around ninety per cent of their food and the customs duty is heavy, so a supermarket shop costs roughly double the American equivalent. There is no income tax, which is the offset.
nassau.wifi: Good in the developed areas. Fibre from Cable Bahamas and Aliv reaches most of New Providence at workable speeds and mobile coverage is comprehensive. There is a small coworking presence, some of it created around the BEATS permit. Power outages happen and anyone whose work cannot pause should ask what backup a building has before signing.
nassau.nightlife: Decent. Nassau has bars and clubs along Bay Street and at the resorts, Atlantis on Paradise Island runs a casino and club scene, and Fish Fry at Arawak Cay is where locals actually go. Junkanoo, the street parade with goatskin drums and cowbells at dawn on Boxing Day and New Year's Day, is the real event.
nassau.nature: Good, and mostly elsewhere. New Providence itself is developed, but the Bahamas are seven hundred islands and the Exumas, Eleuthera and Andros hold water that is genuinely among the best on earth. Blue holes, the third-largest barrier reef in the world off Andros, and swimming pigs at Big Major Cay are all short flights away.
nassau.safety: Weak, and the 5 is a real caution rather than a formality. The Bahamas have a high homicide rate and Nassau accounts for most of it, concentrated in specific areas known locally as Over-the-Hill that foreign governments name explicitly in their travel advice. Tourist areas are policed and generally fine. Read the current guidance rather than assuming.
nassau.food: Decent. Conch is the national obsession, cracked, in salad or in fritters, and Fish Fry at Arawak Cay is where to eat it properly and cheaply. Rock lobster and guava duff are the other staples. The resort restaurant scene is expensive and international rather than Bahamian. The 6 records good local food in a limited range.
nassau.community: Modest. Nassau's foreign population is largely offshore finance and tourism management, and the BEATS permit added a small remote-worker layer. There is limited coworking and no nomad scene of any size. The 4 reflects a place where the permit exists but the community around it has not really formed.
nassau.english: Universal. English is the official language and Bahamian Creole is what people speak among themselves. There is no barrier of any kind. The Bahamas were British until 1973 and the legal system, the schooling and the driving on the left all reflect it, even though the cars are mostly imported from the United States with the wheel on the wrong side.
nassau.visa: Good. The Bahamas Extended Access Travel Stay, or BEATS, gives a year to remote workers and students employed or enrolled outside the country, for a fee of around $1,000, handled online and renewable. There is no income tax on money earned under it. Short visits are visa-free for most Western nationalities for ninety days, longer for British citizens.
nassau.culture: Modest. Junkanoo is the genuine article, a costumed parade with brass and goatskin drums that starts at two in the morning and has roots in the era of slavery. The Pompey Museum on Bay Street occupies a former slave market. Beyond Junkanoo, Nassau's cultural offer is thin and heavily shaped by the cruise industry.
nassau.cleanliness: Middling. The tourist corridor along Bay Street and the resort areas are maintained, but waste management across New Providence is inconsistent and the New Providence landfill has caught fire repeatedly, sending smoke across the island. Beaches are generally clean. Tap water is desalinated and safe in Nassau but not on all the Family Islands.
nassau.airquality: Good. An island position with constant trade winds and no heavy industry keeps annual readings within guidance. The exception is specific and recurring: the New Providence landfill has burned several times, most seriously in recent years, producing smoke that has closed schools and prompted health warnings across parts of the island for days at a time.

roseau.climate: Warm and very wet, which is the whole point of Dominica. Mountains over 1,400 metres wring rain out of the trade winds, which is why there are 365 rivers and why the island is green in a way its neighbours are not. February to May is the driest window. Hurricane season runs June to November and Maria in 2017 was devastating.
roseau.cost: Cheap for the Eastern Caribbean. Budget around $1,500 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $500 to $900 and houses outside the capital within reach at figures impossible on Barbados. Dominica grows much of its own food, which is unusual regionally and keeps the market cheap. The East Caribbean dollar is pegged at 2.7 to the United States dollar.
roseau.wifi: Weak, and the 5 is the honest constraint on working here. Fibre has reached parts of Roseau and Portsmouth and is good where it exists, but coverage is patchy outside the towns. Mobile data from Flow and Digicel is the practical fallback. Power cuts are not rare and the grid is still being rebuilt in places after Hurricane Maria.
roseau.nightlife: Minimal. Roseau has a handful of bars and the World Creole Music Festival each October brings the island alive for a weekend, but on an ordinary evening almost nothing is open. The 3 is accurate rather than harsh: Dominica has deliberately not built the resort and nightlife economy its neighbours have.
roseau.nature: Outstanding, and the 10 is earned. Dominica is the Nature Island: rainforest running to the waterline, the second-largest boiling lake in the world at the end of a six-hour walk, Trafalgar Falls, hot springs, and the Waitukubuli National Trail down the length of the island. Sperm whales live offshore year-round, which is close to unique.
roseau.safety: Reasonable. Dominica has low violent crime and is comfortable to move around, with petty theft the main ordinary concern. The genuine hazards are natural and serious: the terrain is steep and the trails demanding, flash floods happen in the rivers after rain, and the island's hurricane exposure has twice in recent memory been catastrophic.
roseau.food: Decent. Dominican cooking runs on what the island grows, which is a great deal: dasheen, breadfruit, plantain, river crayfish and mountain chicken, which is a frog rather than a bird and is now protected. The Roseau market on a Saturday is excellent and cheap. Restaurant range is narrow, which is what holds the score at 6.
roseau.community: Weak. Dominica's foreign population is a scattering of long-term residents, some drawn by the citizenship by investment programme, plus researchers and divers. The Work In Nature visa has attracted a small number of remote workers but no scene has formed around it. The 3 reflects a genuinely quiet island with nothing organised.
roseau.english: Strong. English is the official language and the language of all administration and education. Kwéyòl, an English-influenced French creole, is widely spoken among Dominicans and is a source of local pride. There is no practical barrier for an English speaker, though the creole in rapid conversation is not something a visitor will follow.
roseau.visa: Good. The Work In Nature visa runs eighteen months, the longest single term in the Eastern Caribbean, for remote workers earning around $50,000 a year, with a fee of roughly $800 for an individual and an online application. Short visits are visa-free for most Western nationalities for up to six months, granted at the border.
roseau.culture: Modest but distinctive. Dominica has the last organised Kalinago community in the Caribbean, with a territory on the east coast governed by its own chief, which is genuinely unusual. The World Creole Music Festival each October is the main event. The island's history of resistance and its late colonisation both shaped a culture noticeably different from its neighbours.
roseau.cleanliness: Middling. Roseau and the main towns are reasonably kept and the island's environmental ethic is real, with an ambition to be the world's first climate-resilient nation. Waste management outside the towns is limited and roadside litter is visible in places. Hurricane debris is still being cleared in parts of the island. Tap water is generally safe.
roseau.airquality: Excellent. Rainforest covering most of the island, constant trade winds, high rainfall washing the air and no industry at all give Dominica about the cleanest air in the Caribbean. There is nothing here to trap pollutants. Volcanic sulphur around the Valley of Desolation and the Boiling Lake is a localised natural exception rather than a general one.

stgeorges.climate: Tropical and pleasant, around twenty-nine degrees year-round with the trade winds moderating it. January to May is the dry season. Grenada sits at the southern edge of the hurricane belt and is struck far less often than the islands north of it, though Ivan in 2004 devastated the island and Beryl in 2024 hit Carriacou hard.
stgeorges.cost: Moderate. Budget around $1,700 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $600 to $1,000 and anything near Grand Anse at the top of that. Grenada grows a serious amount of its own produce and the Saturday market is genuinely cheap. St George's University brings a large American student population that pushes the southern rental market up.
stgeorges.wifi: Adequate and improving. Fibre from Flow and Digicel reaches St George's, Grand Anse and the south at workable speeds, and mobile data covers everywhere anyone lives. Formal coworking is limited, but the medical school means cafes and study spaces used to people working are easy to find. Power cuts happen but are not routine.
stgeorges.nightlife: Modest. The bars around Grand Anse and the Lance aux Epines strip serve the student and visitor population, and there is a genuine local scene on the Carenage. Spicemas in August, with its pre-dawn Jouvert covering everyone in oil and paint, is the real event. Outside August and term time it is quiet. The 5 is fair.
stgeorges.nature: Excellent. Grand Etang National Park has a crater lake and rainforest fifteen minutes inland, Seven Sisters and Concord waterfalls are short walks, and the underwater sculpture park at Molinere was the first of its kind in the world. The Bianca C, the largest wreck in the Caribbean, lies off the coast. Grand Anse is a three-kilometre white beach.
stgeorges.safety: High. Grenada is among the safer Caribbean islands, with low violent crime and comfortable movement at most hours, and the presence of a large university population helps. Petty theft around the beaches is the ordinary concern. Steep roads and minibus driving are the more likely hazard, and the interior trails demand proper footwear after rain.
stgeorges.food: Good. Grenada is the spice island in a literal sense, producing a substantial share of the world's nutmeg and mace, and it flavours everything. Oil down, the national dish of breadfruit, callaloo and salted meat cooked in coconut milk, is a communal affair. The Saturday market in St George's is one of the best in the region.
stgeorges.community: Weak for remote workers, though not for foreigners generally. St George's University brings several thousand international medical students, which gives the south of the island a substantial and visible foreign population, but it is a student community rather than a professional one. There is no nomad scene and no remote work visa to build one. The 3 is honest.
stgeorges.english: Universal. English is the official language and the language of all education and administration. Grenadian Creole English is what people speak among themselves and a French-based creole survives in places, reflecting the island's history of changing hands. No English speaker will encounter any practical difficulty here.
stgeorges.visa: Fair. Grenada has no dedicated remote work visa, which is its main gap against its neighbours. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to three months, with extensions available locally and Commonwealth citizens often receiving longer. Grenada operates a citizenship by investment programme with an E-2 treaty route to the United States, which is a separate matter entirely.
stgeorges.culture: Good. St George's harbour, a horseshoe of pastel warehouses under two forts, is among the most beautiful in the Caribbean. Spicemas in August is a genuine carnival with Jab Jab traditions rooted in the island's history. The nutmeg processing station at Gouyave, where the work is still done by hand, is worth an afternoon.
stgeorges.cleanliness: Good. Grenada is reasonably well maintained, the beaches are clean and publicly accessible, and waste collection functions in the developed south. The interior and the smaller villages are less consistently served. Tap water is treated and generally safe. The 7 reflects an ordinary well-run small island rather than anything exceptional in either direction.
stgeorges.airquality: Excellent. Trade winds, rainforest in the interior, no heavy industry and a population of 110,000 keep readings well within guidance. The seasonal exception is Saharan dust, which reaches the Eastern Caribbean each summer and raises particulate levels for days at a time. Vehicle emissions in St George's at rush hour are a localised and minor factor.

castries.climate: Tropical, around twenty-nine degrees year-round with the trade winds. December to May is the dry season and the busy half. June to November is wet and the hurricane season runs through it; Saint Lucia sits within the belt and has taken direct hits. September and October are the wettest and the months when many hotels close for maintenance.
castries.cost: Expensive for the region. Budget around $1,800 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $700 to $1,200 and Rodney Bay and Gros Islet at the top of that. Saint Lucia grows bananas, cocoa and much of its own produce, and the Castries market is where the price difference shows. Imported goods carry the usual island markup.
castries.wifi: Adequate. Fibre reaches Castries, Rodney Bay and the developed west coast at reasonable speeds, and mobile data from Flow and Digicel covers the populated areas. There is a small amount of coworking around Rodney Bay, which is where most long-stay visitors base themselves rather than in Castries. Power cuts happen but are not constant.
castries.nightlife: Modest. The Gros Islet street party on a Friday night is the island's institution, Rodney Bay has the concentrated bar and restaurant strip, and Saint Lucia Jazz in May draws international acts. Castries itself empties after the cruise ships leave. The 5 reflects a real but geographically narrow scene.
castries.nature: Excellent. The Pitons at Soufriere, two volcanic plugs rising straight from the sea, are a UNESCO World Heritage site and unlike anything else in the Caribbean. Sulphur Springs is a drive-in volcanic crater, the rainforest interior has proper hiking, and Anse Chastanet's reef is protected. Whales and dolphins are seen year-round on the west coast.
castries.safety: Mid. Saint Lucia has a higher crime rate than several of its neighbours and both residents and foreign governments identify specific areas of Castries to avoid, particularly after dark. Tourist areas are policed and generally fine with ordinary precautions. Reported incidents against visitors have prompted advisories in recent years, so current guidance is worth reading.
castries.food: Good. Saint Lucian cooking is Creole with a strong French inheritance, and green fig and saltfish is the national dish. The Castries market is excellent for produce and the Friday fish fry at Anse La Raye is the local equivalent of Gros Islet. Cocoa is grown here and the estate tours are genuinely good.
castries.community: Weak. Saint Lucia's foreign population is largely holidaymakers, second-home owners on the west coast and the yachting community around Rodney Bay, which is a real seasonal community but not a professional one. There is no remote work visa and no nomad scene. The 3 reflects a place that has not organised itself around long-stay workers.
castries.english: Universal. English is the official language and the medium of education and administration. Kwéyòl, a French-based creole, is spoken by most Saint Lucians among themselves and reflects the island changing hands between Britain and France fourteen times. No English speaker will have any practical difficulty here.
castries.visa: Fair. Saint Lucia has no maintained remote work visa; the Live It scheme from the pandemic era was not carried forward as a formal category. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to six weeks, with extensions available locally, and British and Commonwealth citizens often receive longer on arrival. Ask for the maximum at the border and extend from there.
castries.culture: Good. Saint Lucia has produced two Nobel laureates, Derek Walcott and Arthur Lewis, from a population under 200,000, which is a claim no other country can make per head. Carnival in July, Jounen Kwéyòl in October and the Saint Lucia Jazz festival in May anchor the calendar. Pigeon Island holds the fort that shaped the island's naval history.
castries.cleanliness: Middling. The resort areas and Rodney Bay are maintained, but waste management across the island is inconsistent and roadside litter is visible outside the tourist corridor. Castries is a working port town and looks like one. Tap water is treated and generally safe. The 6 records an honest gap between the visitor areas and the rest.
castries.airquality: Excellent. Rainforest interior, constant trade winds, no heavy industry and a small population keep readings well within guidance. Saharan dust reaches the Eastern Caribbean each summer and raises particulates for periods, which is regional. The sulphur at Soufriere is a natural, localised and strongly smelling exception that affects that valley alone.

portofspain.climate: Tropical and hot, around thirty-one degrees year-round with high humidity. January to May is the dry season and contains Carnival. June to December brings heavy afternoon rain. The genuinely useful fact is that Trinidad sits south of the hurricane belt and is very rarely struck, which is a real advantage over the rest of the Caribbean.
portofspain.cost: Cheap for the Caribbean. Budget around $1,400 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $500 to $900 and Woodbrook, St Clair and Newtown at the top of that. Food is inexpensive and a doubles from a street cart costs almost nothing. Fuel is subsidised. Obtaining foreign exchange locally can be difficult, which is a real practical constraint.
portofspain.wifi: Good by regional standards, underwritten by an energy sector that requires it. Fibre from Flow and Digicel reaches most of the developed western corridor at solid speeds and mobile coverage is comprehensive. There is a small coworking scene around Port of Spain serving local startups. Power is reliable, which is not true of much of the region.
portofspain.nightlife: Excellent, and the 8 is earned. Trinidad invented soca and steelpan and the country takes going out seriously: Ariapita Avenue is a strip of bars that runs late every weekend, the panyards open for rehearsals in the weeks before Carnival, and the fete season is a months-long calendar of parties. Nothing else in the Caribbean matches it.
portofspain.nature: Good. The Northern Range rises straight behind the city with rainforest and waterfalls, the Caroni Swamp fills with scarlet ibis at dusk in one of the great wildlife spectacles of the region, and Trinidad's bird list is enormous because the island sits on the South American continental shelf. The Asa Wright Nature Centre is world-renowned among birders.
portofspain.safety: Weak, and the 3 is a serious warning rather than a formality. Trinidad and Tobago has one of the higher homicide rates in the Americas, and both residents and foreign governments treat specific parts of Port of Spain, including Laventille and Beetham, as areas to avoid entirely. Take local advice on neighbourhoods and read current travel guidance.
portofspain.food: Excellent. Trinidad has the best food in the Caribbean and it is not close: doubles, roti, bake and shark, pelau and callaloo come from a mix of African, Indian, Chinese, Creole and Syrian traditions on the same street. Street food is cheap and constant. The 8 reflects genuine depth rather than a few good restaurants.
portofspain.community: Weak. Trinidad's foreign population works in energy, finance and the diplomatic sector, and it is a real professional network that a visiting remote worker does not enter easily. There is no nomad scene and no long-stay visa to create one. The 3 records a country with almost no infrastructure for visiting professionals.
portofspain.english: Universal. English is the official language and Trinidadian Creole English is what people speak. Hindi, Bhojpuri and Spanish are all present in communities across the island. There is no barrier for an English speaker, though the local rhythm and vocabulary take a few days to tune into.
portofspain.visa: Fair. Trinidad and Tobago has no remote work visa. Most Western nationalities and Commonwealth citizens enter visa-free for up to ninety days, with extensions applied for at the immigration division in Port of Spain, a process that is bureaucratic rather than difficult. Longer stays need a work permit tied to an employer or residence through marriage or descent.
portofspain.culture: Exceptional, and the 9 is earned. Trinidad invented the steelpan, the only acoustic instrument created in the twentieth century, along with calypso, soca and limbo. Its Carnival is the one every other Caribbean carnival is modelled on, and the panyard season before it is where the music is actually made. Divali and Hosay are major public events.
portofspain.cleanliness: Below average. Port of Spain has visible litter and drainage problems, waste collection is inconsistent outside the central districts, and flooding after heavy rain is a recurring city-wide issue. The Queen's Park Savannah and the botanic gardens are well kept. The 5 records an honest picture of a working city that does not prioritise appearance.
portofspain.airquality: Mediocre. Trinidad has a substantial petrochemical and gas industry concentrated at Point Lisas and along the west coast, and its emissions affect the island's readings in a way no other Caribbean country's do. Traffic in Port of Spain adds to it. Sea breezes disperse well, which is why the 6 is not lower.

georgetownguyana.climate: Hot and humid year-round at around thirty degrees, with the calendar set by rain rather than temperature. There are two wet seasons, a long one from May to August and a shorter one from November to January, and the drier windows are February to April and September to October. Georgetown sits below sea level and floods when the drainage cannot cope.
georgetownguyana.cost: Moderate and rising fast. Budget around $1,300 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $500 to $1,000. Guyana began producing offshore oil in 2019 and has since been among the fastest-growing economies in the world, which has pushed capital rents up sharply as international companies arrive. Market food is cheap and the produce is excellent.
georgetownguyana.wifi: Weak. Fibre reaches parts of Georgetown at workable speeds and mobile data from GTT and Digicel is the fallback, but neither is dependable enough to plan a working day around without a backup. Power cuts are frequent enough that generators are standard in any serious building. Oil money is improving this, slowly and unevenly.
georgetownguyana.nightlife: Limited. Georgetown has bars and a few clubs, and the oil boom has brought new venues aimed at expatriate salaries, but the city empties after dark and most people move by taxi rather than on foot. The 4 reflects a capital where going out is possible but not the point and requires planning.
georgetownguyana.nature: Outstanding, and almost none of it is in Georgetown. Kaieteur Falls is the world's largest single-drop waterfall by volume, nearly five times the height of Niagara, reached by light aircraft. Rainforest covers four-fifths of the country, the Rupununi savannah holds giant anteaters and jaguars, and Shell Beach is a major sea turtle nesting site.
georgetownguyana.safety: Weak, and the 3 is a genuine warning. Guyana has a high rate of violent crime and Georgetown accounts for much of it, with specific areas that foreign governments name in their travel advice. Walking after dark is not advised anywhere in the city. The interior is considerably safer. Read current guidance properly before travelling.
georgetownguyana.food: Good and genuinely distinctive. Guyanese cooking is the meeting point of Indian, African, Amerindian, Chinese and Portuguese traditions: pepperpot, the Amerindian dish cooked with cassareep, is the national dish and is eaten at Christmas. Roti, cook-up rice and metemgee are everyday. Stabroek Market is the place to eat and to see the city.
georgetownguyana.community: Nonexistent for remote workers. Georgetown's foreign population is the oil and gas industry, diplomats and development staff, almost all on postings, and the arrival of that money has been fast enough to change the city's character. There is no nomad scene, no coworking aimed at visitors and nothing organised. The 2 is accurate.
georgetownguyana.english: Strong, and it is Guyana's single biggest practical advantage: this is the only English-speaking country in South America. English is official and used throughout, with Guyanese Creole as the common spoken form. The Caribbean orientation is deeper than the geography suggests, and Guyana belongs to CARICOM rather than to any South American bloc.
georgetownguyana.visa: Reasonable. Guyana gives most Western nationalities and all Commonwealth citizens visa-free entry for up to ninety days on arrival, with extensions available locally. There is no remote work visa and no framework for long-stay visitors. Yellow fever vaccination is required if arriving from an endemic country and is sensible regardless given the interior.
georgetownguyana.culture: Good. Georgetown's wooden colonial architecture is genuinely unusual, with St George's Cathedral among the tallest wooden buildings in the world and the Stabroek Market clock tower over the waterfront. The mix of Indian, African and Amerindian traditions produces Mashramani in February and Phagwah in spring. The country's literature, from Wilson Harris onward, is substantial.
georgetownguyana.cleanliness: Poor. Georgetown's drainage canals, built by the Dutch and essential because the city sits below sea level, are silted and often full of rubbish, and waste collection is inconsistent. Flooding after heavy rain spreads the problem. The oil money has begun to fund infrastructure work but the effect is not yet visible. The 4 is honest.
georgetownguyana.airquality: Mediocre. An ageing vehicle fleet, widespread generator use and open burning are the main sources, and the flat coastal position with limited wind means dispersal is poor on still days. There is limited heavy industry, though the offshore oil sector's onshore support base is growing. Readings sit above guidance for much of the year.

paramaribo.climate: Equatorial, around thirty-one degrees every month with humidity that never drops. The unusual feature is four seasons rather than two: long dry from August to November, short dry from February to April, and two wet periods between them. Suriname sits well south of the hurricane belt and is not exposed to them at all, which is a real advantage.
paramaribo.cost: Cheap. Budget around $1,100 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $350 to $700. The Surinamese dollar has devalued sharply in recent years, so any figure quoted in it dates quickly and locals often price in United States dollars. Market food is very cheap and the range of it is remarkable for a country of 600,000.
paramaribo.wifi: Weak. Fibre from Telesur reaches parts of Paramaribo at workable speeds and mobile data is the fallback, but neither is fast by international standards and prices are high relative to what they deliver. Power cuts happen. There is essentially no coworking aimed at foreigners. Anyone with a call-heavy schedule should test before committing.
paramaribo.nightlife: Modest. Paramaribo has bars along the Waterkant and a scene that reflects the country's mix, with Javanese warungs, Chinese restaurants and Dutch-style cafes all busy in the evening. It is relaxed rather than late. The 5 records a capital where the social life is real but small and unhurried.
paramaribo.nature: Outstanding, and it starts an hour from the city. Rainforest covers over ninety per cent of Suriname, one of the highest proportions on earth, and the Central Suriname Nature Reserve is a UNESCO World Heritage site the size of a small country. The Upper Suriname River, Brownsberg and Galibi's leatherback nesting beaches are all reachable.
paramaribo.safety: Mid. Paramaribo is calmer than Georgetown and violent crime is lower, but street robbery happens and the usual advice about not walking alone at night and avoiding the areas around the market after dark applies. The interior is safe. Ordinary urban caution is generally sufficient, which is not something that can be said of every capital in this region.
paramaribo.food: Excellent, and genuinely one of the reasons to come. Suriname's mix of Javanese, Hindustani, Creole, Chinese, Maroon and Dutch traditions produces roti, pom, moksi meti and nasi in the same street, and the warungs serve Javanese food at prices that are almost nothing. For a country of 600,000 the variety is extraordinary.
paramaribo.community: Nonexistent for remote workers. Suriname's foreign population is Dutch, Brazilian and Chinese business, plus development and mining staff. There is no nomad scene, no coworking aimed at visitors and no long-stay framework. The 2 reflects a country almost entirely off the remote work map, which is either the appeal or the disqualifier.
paramaribo.english: Weak. Dutch is the official language and the language of all administration and education, which makes Suriname the only Dutch-speaking country in South America. Sranan Tongo is the common tongue between communities. English is spoken by younger people and in business but is not something to rely on. Dutch changes the experience entirely.
paramaribo.visa: Reasonable. Suriname operates an e-visa and tourist card system that most Western nationalities can use online before travel, typically granting ninety days. Dutch nationals have easier access given the historic relationship. There is no remote work visa. Yellow fever vaccination is required from endemic countries. The rules have changed more than once, so confirm directly.
paramaribo.culture: Strong. Paramaribo's historic inner city is a UNESCO World Heritage site of white wooden Dutch colonial buildings, and the Neveh Shalom synagogue and the Keizerstraat mosque stand side by side sharing a car park, which is the image the country uses of itself. The Maroon communities of the interior maintain West African traditions carried across in the seventeenth century.
paramaribo.cleanliness: Middling. The restored historic centre is well kept and is genuinely attractive, but waste management across the wider city is inconsistent and the canals carry visible rubbish. Outside Paramaribo the country is largely uninhabited rainforest and the question does not arise. Tap water in the capital is safe. The 5 is an honest reading.
paramaribo.airquality: Good. A small population, enormous forest cover and no heavy industry keep readings low by regional standards. The exceptions are gold mining in the interior, which uses mercury and is an environmental problem of a different kind, and seasonal smoke from agricultural burning across the border in Brazil. Coastal humidity and rain wash the air regularly.

sanpedrobelize.climate: Tropical, around twenty-nine to thirty-one degrees year-round. Late November to April is the dry season with the calmest water, and it is the busy half. June to November is wet and the hurricane season runs through it; the island has been evacuated more than once. Sargassum seaweed lands on this coast between roughly April and August in varying amounts.
sanpedrobelize.cost: Expensive for Central America. Budget around $1,900 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $800 to $1,300. Everything arrives by boat or plane and groceries cost considerably more than on the Belizean mainland, which is a short flight away and where many residents shop deliberately. The Belize dollar is pegged at two to the United States dollar.
sanpedrobelize.wifi: Adequate. Fibre from Belize Telemedia reaches much of the town at workable speeds and mobile data covers the island, but both are expensive relative to what they deliver and outages happen. Power cuts are not rare. There is a small coworking presence and cafes used to remote workers, grown out of the Work Where You Vacation programme.
sanpedrobelize.nightlife: Decent. San Pedro has a concentrated strip of beach bars and restaurants along the front, the Palapa Bar and the Truck Stop are institutions, and the town is busier after dark than most of Belize. It is a tourist scene rather than a local one. The 6 reflects something genuinely lively at a small scale.
sanpedrobelize.nature: Outstanding.
