basseterre.food: Decent. Kittitian cooking runs on goat water stew, saltfish, conch and plenty of local fish, and the Saturday market in Basseterre is the cheapest and best place to buy any of it. Frigate Bay has a run of restaurants aimed at visitors at visitor prices. The 6 records solid, cheap eating without much range at the top end.
basseterre.community: Weak. The federation's foreign population is a scattering of long-term residents, some drawn by the citizenship programme, plus American medical students at Ross University's veterinary school. There is no nomad scene and no coworking. The 3 reflects a place where meeting people is easy socially and where nothing exists for a visiting professional.
basseterre.english: Universal. English is the official language and the medium of everything, with a Kittitian creole spoken among locals. The federation was British until 1983 and the institutions, the schooling and the driving on the left all reflect it. There is no barrier of any kind for an English speaker.
basseterre.visa: Reasonable. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to ninety days, with British and Commonwealth citizens often receiving longer, and extensions are applied for locally. There is no remote work visa, which is the main gap against Antigua or Barbados. The federation runs the world's oldest citizenship by investment programme, launched in 1984, which is a separate matter entirely.
basseterre.culture: Good. Brimstone Hill Fortress, a UNESCO World Heritage site, is the most complete surviving eighteenth-century fortification in the Americas and sits above the sea on a volcanic outcrop. The Saint Kitts Scenic Railway, built to carry sugar cane, is the last operating railway in the West Indies. Sugar Mas at Christmas is the national carnival.
basseterre.cleanliness: Good. Basseterre and the tourist areas are reasonably maintained, waste collection functions, and the beaches are cleaned. Standards drop in the outer villages. Tap water is treated and generally safe. The 7 reflects an ordinary well-run small island rather than anything exceptional in either direction.
basseterre.airquality: Excellent. Trade winds, a small population, no heavy industry and a green interior keep readings well within guidance. Saharan dust reaches the Eastern Caribbean each summer and raises particulates for periods, which is regional rather than local. The sugar industry's cane burning ended with the industry in 2005.

kingstown.climate: Tropical, around twenty-nine degrees year-round. January to May is the dry season and the best sailing window in the Grenadines. June to November is wetter and the hurricane season runs through it. The genuinely important variable here is not weather but geology: La Soufriere at the northern end of the island erupted explosively in April 2021 and remains active and monitored.
kingstown.cost: Cheap for the Eastern Caribbean. Budget around $1,400 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $450 to $800. Saint Vincent grows a great deal of its own produce and the Kingstown market is genuinely inexpensive. The Grenadines are a different economy entirely, with Mustique and Canouan priced for people arriving by private aircraft. The East Caribbean dollar is pegged at 2.7 to the dollar.
kingstown.wifi: Weak to adequate. Fibre from Flow and Digicel reaches Kingstown and the developed south at workable speeds, and mobile data covers the main island and the larger Grenadines. There is essentially no coworking. Power cuts happen and the 2021 eruption disrupted supply across the north for months. Connectivity gets noticeably worse the further down the island chain you go.
kingstown.nightlife: Limited. Kingstown has a few bars and the waterfront comes alive when the ferries are running, and Vincy Mas at the end of June is the year's main event. Bequia has its own small scene aimed at the sailing crowd. The 4 reflects a working capital where the evening is quiet rather than absent.
kingstown.nature: Outstanding. La Soufriere is walkable to the crater rim on a hard day, the Vermont nature trail holds the endemic Saint Vincent parrot, and the Falls of Baleine are reachable only by boat. Offshore, the Tobago Cays are a horseshoe reef enclosing four uninhabited islands and are among the finest anchorages anywhere. Black volcanic sand on much of the main island.
kingstown.safety: Mid. Saint Vincent is generally calm and violent crime against visitors is uncommon, though the country's homicide rate has risen in recent years and Kingstown after dark warrants ordinary caution. The genuine hazards are natural: the volcano, the strong currents on the windward coast, and the ferries in rough weather. Read current travel advice rather than assuming.
kingstown.food: Decent. Vincentian cooking runs on breadfruit, which Captain Bligh brought here in 1793 and which is now the national dish as roasted breadfruit and jackfish, along with plenty of seafood. The Kingstown market is excellent and very cheap. Restaurant range is narrow outside Bequia and the resorts. The 6 records honest adequacy.
kingstown.community: Weak. The foreign population is the sailing community moving through the Grenadines, a small number of long-term residents, and the second-home owners of Mustique, who do not mix. There is no nomad scene and no coworking. The 3 reflects a country with no infrastructure for visiting professionals of any kind.
kingstown.english: Universal. English is the official language and the medium of everything, with Vincentian Creole spoken among locals. The country was British until 1979 and the institutions reflect it. There is no practical barrier for an English speaker anywhere in the country, including the smallest of the Grenadines.
kingstown.visa: Reasonable. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to a month, extendable at the immigration department in Kingstown, and Commonwealth citizens often receive longer on arrival. There is no remote work visa. Unusually for the region, the country runs no citizenship by investment programme. Anyone arriving by yacht clears in at Kingstown, Bequia, Union Island or Chateaubelair.
kingstown.culture: Moderate. The Botanical Gardens in Kingstown, founded in 1765, are the oldest in the western hemisphere and hold a descendant of Bligh's original breadfruit tree. Fort Charlotte looks down over the harbour. Vincy Mas at the end of June is the carnival. Beyond that the country's cultural weight is in its boat-building tradition, particularly on Bequia.
kingstown.cleanliness: Middling. Kingstown's centre and the market area are busy and not especially tidy, waste collection outside the main towns is inconsistent, and the volcanic ash from 2021 took a long time to clear. The Grenadines are considerably cleaner. Tap water is treated and generally safe. The 6 is an honest reading.
kingstown.airquality: Excellent normally, with trade winds, forest cover and no industry keeping readings low. The exception was severe and recent: the April 2021 eruption of La Soufriere blanketed the northern two-thirds of the island in ash for weeks, closing the airport and contaminating water supplies. That is a volcanic risk rather than a chronic condition.

englishharbour.climate: Tropical and drier than most of the Eastern Caribbean, since Antigua is low and lacks the mountains that pull rain out of the trade winds. Around twenty-eight degrees year-round with steady wind. December to April is the dry season and the sailing season. June to November is the hurricane season; Antigua was spared in 2017 while Barbuda was not.
englishharbour.cost: Expensive. Budget around $2,000 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $800 to $1,300 and anything on the water at the top. Antigua imports nearly all of its food and the supermarket bill is the line most people underestimate. Eating in Falmouth or Liberta costs a fraction of the dockyard restaurants. The East Caribbean dollar is pegged at 2.7 to the dollar.
englishharbour.wifi: Adequate, and better around the harbour than the island average because the yachting industry requires it. Fibre reaches the dockyard area and Falmouth at workable speeds and mobile data covers the island. There is a small amount of coworking in St John's and near the harbour, some of it created for holders of the Nomad Digital Residence visa.
englishharbour.nightlife: Modest but real. The dockyard and Falmouth have a genuine bar scene through the sailing season, driven by yacht crews rather than tourists, and the Sunday sunset party at Shirley Heights above the harbour has run for decades. It empties considerably from June. The 5 reflects a scene that is seasonal rather than constant.
englishharbour.nature: Strong. Antigua claims a beach for every day of the year and while nobody has counted, the coastline is genuinely exceptional. Great Bird Island and the north-east marine reserve are reachable by boat, the Wallings rainforest is a small remnant of what covered the island, and Barbuda's frigate bird colony is among the largest in the world.
englishharbour.safety: High. Antigua is among the safer Caribbean islands and English Harbour in particular, with its yachting population and small permanent community, is comfortable at most hours. Petty theft from boats and unlocked accommodation is the common problem. The genuine hazards are marine: currents on the Atlantic coast and the boat traffic in the harbours.
englishharbour.food: Good. Antiguan cooking is built on fungee and pepperpot, saltfish and plenty of seafood, and the Sunday breakfast at a local place is the meal worth finding. The yachting economy has also produced a restaurant scene around the harbour well beyond what an island of ninety thousand would otherwise support. Prices reflect that.
englishharbour.community: Modest, and unusually so for a small island. The sailing community at English Harbour is genuinely international, largely transient and easy to fall into, and the Nomad Digital Residence visa has added a small remote-worker layer on top. The 5 reflects something a newcomer can actually join, which most Caribbean islands cannot offer.
englishharbour.english: Universal. English is the official language and the medium of everything, with Antiguan Creole spoken among locals. The island was British until 1981. The yachting population brings a great many other languages into the harbour, but nothing public requires anything but English.
englishharbour.visa: Good. The Nomad Digital Residence grants two years to remote workers earning around $50,000 a year, with a fee of roughly $1,500 for an individual and an online application, which is among the longest terms offered anywhere. Short visits are visa-free for most Western nationalities for up to three months. The country also runs a citizenship by investment programme.
englishharbour.culture: Strong. Nelson's Dockyard is the only continuously working Georgian naval dockyard in the world, a UNESCO World Heritage site whose buildings are still in commercial use as hotels and marina facilities rather than as exhibits. Shirley Heights and the fortifications above it were built to guard it. Antigua Sailing Week each April is the region's largest regatta.
englishharbour.cleanliness: Good. The dockyard area is maintained to a high standard as a World Heritage site, the beaches are clean and publicly accessible by law, and waste collection functions in the developed parts of the island. Standards drop in the inland villages. Tap water is desalinated and safe. The 7 is fair.
englishharbour.airquality: Excellent. A low island with constant trade winds, no heavy industry and a small population keeps readings well within guidance. Saharan dust reaches the Eastern Caribbean each summer and raises particulates for periods, which is a regional pattern rather than anything Antigua produces. The air around the harbour is as clean as anywhere on this site.

roadtown.climate: Tropical, around twenty-eight degrees year-round with steady trade winds that are the reason the sailing here works. December to April is the dry season and the charter season. May to November is hotter and wetter and the hurricane season runs through it; Hurricane Irma passed directly over the territory in 2017 as a category five and the exposure is not theoretical.
roadtown.cost: Expensive, which the 3 records. Budget around $2,600 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $1,200 to $1,800. Everything arrives by ship and the grocery bill is high even by Caribbean standards. Rents rose sharply after Irma destroyed much of the housing stock and have not fully settled. The territory uses the United States dollar.
roadtown.wifi: Good. Tens of thousands of companies are registered here and the connectivity reflects that: fibre reaches Road Town and the developed parts of Tortola at solid speeds. Mobile coverage is good on Tortola and thinner on the outer islands. Power was rebuilt after Irma and is more reliable than before. There is a small amount of coworking.
roadtown.nightlife: Limited on Tortola and legendary elsewhere. Road Town itself is quiet after dark, but the beach bars of Jost Van Dyke, particularly Foxy's and the Soggy Dollar, are institutions that sailors cross the archipelago for. The 4 reflects the capital rather than the territory, where the social life happens at anchor.
roadtown.nature: Outstanding. Sixty islands within sight of each other, the granite boulders of the Baths on Virgin Gorda, the wreck of the RMS Rhone, Anegada's reef and flamingos, and anchorages in every direction. The trade winds and short line-of-sight passages are what make this the charter capital of the world rather than merely a pretty archipelago.
roadtown.safety: High. The British Virgin Islands have low violent crime and Road Town is comfortable at most hours, with petty theft from boats the common problem. The genuine hazards are marine: the passages between islands carry real current, and the anchorages are exposed in a northerly swell. Hurricane exposure is the other serious consideration.
roadtown.food: Decent. The territory eats well around the marinas, with a restaurant scene serving the charter fleet, and the local cooking runs on fish, conch and roti. Prices reflect the import cost and the captive market. Anegada lobster is the one dish worth planning a passage around. The 6 records adequacy at a high price.
roadtown.community: Modest. The territory's foreign population is offshore finance professionals and the marine industry, both of which are real international networks, though neither is one a passing remote worker joins easily. There is no nomad scene. The 4 reflects genuine professional depth in two narrow sectors and nothing organised for anyone else.
roadtown.english: Universal. English is the official language and the medium of everything. The territory has been British since 1672 and the institutions reflect it, though the currency is the United States dollar and the cars are American with the wheel on the left, driven on the left. No visitor will encounter a language barrier.
roadtown.visa: Reasonable. Most Western nationalities enter for up to thirty days on arrival, extendable at the immigration department, and British citizens receive longer. There is no standing remote work visa, though a one-year programme ran after the pandemic and was not maintained. Working for a local employer requires a work permit, which is a considerably harder process.
roadtown.culture: Thin. The territory's identity is maritime and commercial rather than cultural, with the Callwood Rum Distillery at Cane Garden Bay and the ruins of the Copper Mine on Virgin Gorda the main historic sites. The August Emancipation Festival is the largest annual event. Most of what draws people here is geological and nautical rather than built.
roadtown.cleanliness: High. Road Town and the marinas are well maintained, the beaches are clean, and waste management functions, funded by the financial sector's contribution to public revenue. Rebuilding after Irma also modernised a good deal of infrastructure. Tap water is desalinated and safe. The 8 reflects a well-funded small territory.
roadtown.airquality: Excellent. Small islands with constant trade winds, no industry and a population of thirty thousand leave nothing to trap, and readings sit well within guidance. Saharan dust reaches the region each summer and raises particulates for periods. Diesel generators on boats in the anchorages are a localised and minor exception.

charlotteamalie.climate: Tropical, around twenty-eight degrees year-round with trade winds. December to April is the dry season and the busy half. May to November is hotter and wetter and the Atlantic hurricane season runs through it; St Thomas was struck by both Irma and Maria within two weeks in September 2017 and the recovery took years, which shapes what things cost here.
charlotteamalie.cost: Expensive, which the 3 records. Budget around $2,700 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $1,300 to $1,900. Groceries cost substantially more than the American mainland and electricity is among the most expensive under the United States flag, which residents discuss constantly. There is no conversion to do, since the territory uses the dollar and sits inside the American customs zone.
charlotteamalie.wifi: Good. Submarine cable serves the territory, fibre reaches most of St Thomas at solid speeds, and American carriers operate here with domestic roaming, so a United States mobile plan works without international charges. That is a genuine advantage over every other Caribbean island. There is a small coworking presence. Power outages are more frequent than on the mainland.
charlotteamalie.nightlife: Modest. Charlotte Amalie has bars along the waterfront and at Frenchtown, and Red Hook on the eastern end has the liveliest scene, driven by the ferry crowd and the charter fleet. The town empties when the cruise ships leave. The 5 reflects a real but geographically scattered scene rather than a concentrated one.
charlotteamalie.nature: Excellent, and mostly next door. St Thomas itself is developed, but St John, twenty minutes by ferry, is roughly two-thirds Virgin Islands National Park, with Trunk Bay and an underwater snorkelling trail. Buck Island off St Croix is a national monument. The reef, the wrecks and the surrounding waters are the case for being here.
charlotteamalie.safety: Weak, and the 5 is a real caution. The United States Virgin Islands have a homicide rate among the highest under the American flag, concentrated in specific communities, and both residents and the State Department name particular areas of Charlotte Amalie to avoid. Tourist areas are policed and generally fine with ordinary awareness. Read current guidance properly.
charlotteamalie.food: Decent. Virgin Islands cooking mixes Caribbean, Danish and American influences, with pate, kallaloo and fish the staples, and Frenchtown has a genuine local restaurant scene. Prices are high and much of the visible dining is aimed at cruise passengers. The 6 records solid local food behind a great deal of tourist retail.
charlotteamalie.community: Modest. The territory's foreign population is largely mainland Americans who have relocated, which is a real and substantial community rather than a transient one, plus the marine industry at Red Hook. There is no nomad scene as such. The 4 reflects somewhere an American can settle into and where nothing is organised for visiting professionals.
charlotteamalie.english: Universal. English is the official language and the medium of everything, with Virgin Islands Creole spoken among locals. Spanish is widely spoken given the proximity to Puerto Rico. The territory was Danish until 1917, which survives in the architecture and street names rather than the language.
charlotteamalie.visa: The question does not arise for Americans, which is the whole point: this is United States territory, no passport is needed from the mainland, and there is no limit on how long you may stay or work. That makes it the simplest Caribbean option available to a United States citizen. Everyone else faces the ordinary American visa rules with none of the compensating benefits.
charlotteamalie.culture: Good. Charlotte Amalie has a genuine Danish colonial core, with Fort Christian dating from 1672 as the oldest standing structure in the territory, the ninety-nine steps cut into the hillside, and the synagogue at St Thomas, the second oldest in the western hemisphere. Carnival through April is the largest annual event.
charlotteamalie.cleanliness: Middling. The waterfront and the shopping district are maintained for the cruise trade, but waste management across the island is inconsistent and the territory has struggled with landfill capacity for years. Beaches are generally clean. Tap water is mostly desalinated and safe. The 6 records an honest gap between the tourist corridor and the rest.
charlotteamalie.airquality: Good. Trade winds and an island position keep readings within guidance. The refinery on St Croix, one of the largest in the western hemisphere, has a long history of emissions problems including a 2021 incident that rained oil on nearby homes, but that is a different island. Cruise ship emissions in port are a localised factor here.

providenciales.climate: Tropical and dry, around twenty-eight degrees year-round with steady trade winds and low rainfall. December to April is the driest and busiest window. May to November is hotter and wetter and the Atlantic hurricane season runs through it; Irma and Maria both affected the territory in 2017. Water temperature stays swimmable all year, which is the argument for the low season.
providenciales.cost: Extremely expensive, which the 2 records honestly. Budget around $3,200 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $1,600 to $2,400 and anything near Grace Bay at the top. There is no local agriculture to speak of, so everything is imported and a supermarket shop costs well over double the American equivalent. There is no income tax and the territory uses the dollar.
providenciales.wifi: Good. Fibre reaches the developed parts of Providenciales at solid speeds and mobile coverage is comprehensive. Prices are high. There is a small amount of coworking. Power is reasonably reliable and expensive. The islands run on Eastern time with daylight saving, keeping them aligned with New York year-round, which makes this a straightforward base for American hours.
providenciales.nightlife: Limited. Grace Bay has hotel bars and a handful of restaurants that stay open, and Blue Hills has a more local scene, but Providenciales closes early and the island is not a going-out destination. The 4 reflects a resort island where the day is the point and the evening is quiet.
providenciales.nature: Excellent underwater and modest above it. The barrier reef here is the third largest on earth, the wall diving off West Caicos and French Cay is exceptional, and Chalk Sound's improbable turquoise lagoon is a short drive. The islands are flat, dry and scrubby on land, with no rivers, hills or forest of any kind.
providenciales.safety: Mid. Turks and Caicos is generally calm and violent crime against visitors is uncommon, though the territory's homicide rate rose sharply in recent years and prompted travel advisories, with the problem concentrated in specific communities. Petty theft and vehicle break-ins are the common issues. Read current guidance rather than assuming a luxury destination means low crime.
providenciales.food: Decent and expensive. Conch is the national dish, served cracked, in salad and in fritters, and the conch shacks at Blue Hills are the honest version of it. Grace Bay has an international restaurant scene at international prices. Almost every ingredient is imported. The 6 records good local seafood behind a great deal of resort dining.
providenciales.community: Modest. The foreign population is resort staff, construction workers from Haiti and the Dominican Republic, and second-home owners from North America, none of which forms a community a remote worker joins. There is no nomad scheme to build one around. The 4 reflects a genuine foreign presence organised entirely around the resort economy.
providenciales.english: Universal. English is the official language and the medium of everything, with Turks and Caicos Creole spoken among locals and Haitian Creole widely heard given the size of the Haitian community. The territory is British and the institutions reflect it, though the dollar is the currency and driving is on the left.
providenciales.visa: Reasonable. Most Western nationalities and British citizens enter visa-free for up to ninety days on arrival, with extensions available from the immigration department for a fee. There is no remote work visa, which is the main gap against the Bahamas or Barbados. A work permit for a local employer is expensive and tied to a sponsor.
providenciales.culture: Thin, which the 4 records. The islands were sparsely settled and their history is salt raking rather than sugar, with the salinas on Salt Cay and Grand Turk the physical record of it. Grand Turk, the actual capital, has the National Museum and a genuine old town that almost no visitor to Providenciales sees.
providenciales.cleanliness: High. Providenciales is well maintained, Grace Bay is cleaned daily, and waste collection functions, funded by a tourism economy that depends on appearances. Landfill capacity on a small island is the persistent underlying problem. Tap water is desalinated and safe. The 8 reflects a well-funded resort island rather than anything exceptional.
providenciales.airquality: Excellent. A flat, dry, low island with constant trade winds, no industry and a small population leaves nothing to trap, and readings sit well within guidance. Saharan dust reaches the region in summer and raises particulates for periods. This is among the cleanest air on this site and it is one of the genuinely easy things about being here.

philipsburg.climate: Tropical, around twenty-eight degrees year-round with trade winds. December to April is the dry season and the busiest half. May to November is hotter and wetter and the hurricane season runs through it. Sint Maarten's exposure is severe: Irma passed directly over the island in 2017 as a category five and destroyed most of the buildings and the airport terminal.
philipsburg.cost: Expensive. Budget around $2,200 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $900 to $1,500. Groceries are imported and heavily marked up, though the French side has cheaper supermarkets and shopping across the border deliberately is a genuine and widely used trick. The guilder is pegged to the dollar and dollars circulate everywhere on both sides of the island.
philipsburg.wifi: Adequate. Fibre reaches the developed parts of the Dutch side at workable speeds and mobile data covers the island, though a French SIM and a Dutch SIM behave differently on the two halves and roaming charges can appear without warning. There is a small amount of coworking. Power cuts happen. Connectivity is fine for ordinary work and not exceptional.
philipsburg.nightlife: Good. Sint Maarten has more going on after dark than almost any island of its size, with casinos and bars in Philipsburg and Simpson Bay, and Grand Case on the French side offering the best restaurant strip in the Eastern Caribbean. The 6 reflects a genuinely busy island rather than a quiet one.
philipsburg.nature: Fair, and the 6 is honest. Sint Maarten is small, hilly and heavily developed, with good beaches on both sides and Pinel Island and Tintamarre reachable by boat from the French coast. The Loterie Farm on Pic Paradis is the one substantial patch of remaining forest. Anguilla and St Barts, both twenty minutes by ferry, offer more.
philipsburg.safety: Mid. Sint Maarten has moderate crime, with vehicle break-ins, theft from accommodation and occasional armed robbery the reported problems, concentrated in specific areas that both sides' police name. Tourist areas are generally fine with ordinary precautions. The rebuilding since Irma has been uneven and some districts remain in poor condition.
philipsburg.food: Excellent, and the 8 is earned. Grand Case on the French side calls itself the gastronomic capital of the Caribbean and the claim is defensible, with a strip of restaurants and lolo grills that no other island matches. The Dutch side has good Caribbean and Indonesian food. The two culinary traditions on one small island are the point.
philipsburg.community: Modest. The island's foreign population is Dutch, French, and a substantial workforce from across the Caribbean and Latin America, along with the yachting community around Simpson Bay Lagoon. There is no nomad scene. The 4 reflects a genuinely international island with nothing organised for visiting professionals.
philipsburg.english: Strong. Dutch is official on the southern half and French on the northern, but English is the working language of almost everything commercial on both sides and is what most residents speak among themselves. Spanish and Papiamento are also common. An English speaker will have no difficulty anywhere on the island.
philipsburg.visa: Reasonable and split in two. Sint Maarten, the Dutch side, grants most Western nationalities up to ninety days on arrival. Saint-Martin, the French side, is a French collectivity outside Schengen where European Union citizens have freedom of movement. There is no remote work visa on either side. Which set of rules applies depends on where you sleep, since the border is unmarked.
philipsburg.culture: Modest. The island's interest is the division itself, agreed in 1648 and marked now only by a monument, and the way two European administrations produced two visibly different places on thirty-seven square miles. Carnival runs on both sides at different times. Beyond that the cultural offer is limited by the dominance of cruise tourism.
philipsburg.cleanliness: Middling. Front Street and the resort areas are maintained, but waste management on the island is a long-standing problem, the Philipsburg landfill has burned repeatedly, and rebuilding since Irma has left derelict structures in several districts. Tap water is desalinated and safe. The 6 is an honest reading.
philipsburg.airquality: Good. Trade winds and a small island keep readings within guidance most of the time. The recurring exception is specific: the Philipsburg landfill has caught fire more than once, sending smoke across the Dutch side for days and prompting school closures. Cruise ship emissions in port are a localised factor.

kralendijk.climate: Excellent and remarkably consistent. Bonaire sits below the hurricane belt, is dry and windy, and stays around thirty degrees every month with very little rain. There is no season to avoid, which almost nowhere in the Caribbean can claim, and it is why the island's visitor numbers are far steadier through the year than its neighbours'.
kralendijk.cost: Expensive. Budget around $1,900 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $800 to $1,300. Everything is imported and groceries carry a markup, though the Dutch supply chain keeps the choice wide. Bonaire uses the United States dollar rather than a guilder, which is unusual in the Dutch Caribbean. Diving is the line that dominates any real budget here.
kralendijk.wifi: Good for the size. Fibre reaches Kralendijk and the developed west coast at workable speeds and mobile data covers the island. Prices are high. Power is reliable and substantially wind-generated, since the island runs a large wind farm. There is a small amount of coworking aimed at the long-stay diving population. Connectivity is not a constraint here.
kralendijk.nightlife: Minimal. Kralendijk has a handful of bars along the waterfront and the dive shops generate a social evening of their own, but the island is quiet and early. The 3 reflects a place organised around getting up to dive rather than staying up. Anyone wanting a night out is on the wrong island.
kralendijk.nature: Outstanding. Bonaire declared its entire surrounding sea a national park in 1979, one of the first marine reserves anywhere, and the reef is healthy and reachable from the shore at some ninety marked entry points. On land, Washington Slagbaai National Park covers the north, and the southern salt pans hold a resident flamingo colony.
kralendijk.safety: High. Bonaire has low crime and is comfortable at any hour, helped by a small population and a visitor economy of divers rather than partygoers. Theft from unlocked vehicles at dive sites is the one persistent problem and is why residents leave their trucks unlocked with nothing in them. The real hazards are diving-related rather than criminal.
kralendijk.food: Decent. Kralendijk has a restaurant scene disproportionate to its size, serving the diving population, mixing Dutch, Caribbean and Latin American influences. Local goat stew and fresh fish are the traditional dishes. Almost everything is imported and prices reflect it. The 6 records solid, varied eating at a high cost rather than any culinary distinction.
kralendijk.community: Modest and specific. Bonaire has a genuine long-stay community of divers, dive professionals and Dutch residents, and it is unusually easy to join because everyone is doing the same thing and using the same handful of shops and bars. The 5 reflects a real community that happens to be a diving one rather than a nomad one.
kralendijk.english: Strong. Papiamentu is the language of daily life and Dutch is official, but English is widely spoken across the diving economy and Spanish is common given Venezuela is eighty kilometres away. Four languages in one conversation is normal here. An English speaker will have no practical difficulty anywhere on the island.
kralendijk.visa: Good. Bonaire is a special municipality of the Netherlands, outside the European Union and outside Schengen. Dutch and European Union citizens can live and work here with minimal formality. Most other Western nationalities get ninety days on arrival. There is no remote work visa, but ninety days plus an easy exit to Curacao makes a longer stay practical.
kralendijk.culture: Thin. Bonaire's history is salt, and the restored slave huts on the southern coast, tiny stone shelters where enslaved workers in the salt pans slept, are the most affecting thing on the island. Rincon, the oldest settlement, holds the Dia di Rincon festival each April. Beyond that the island's identity is entirely marine.
kralendijk.cleanliness: High. Kralendijk and the dive sites are well maintained, the marine park is actively managed and monitored, and the island's whole economy depends on the water staying clear. Waste management on a small island is the underlying constraint. Tap water is desalinated and among the best in the Caribbean. The 8 is fair.
kralendijk.airquality: Excellent. Constant trade winds, an arid climate, no industry beyond the salt works and a population of twenty thousand keep readings well within guidance. The wind farm has displaced a substantial share of diesel generation. Saharan dust reaches the southern Caribbean in summer and is the only recurring factor that raises particulates.

pointeapitre.climate: Tropical, around twenty-eight degrees year-round. December to April is the dry season, known locally as careme, and the busiest half. June to November is the wet season, called hivernage, and the hurricane season runs through it; Guadeloupe sits within the belt. Basse-Terre's rainforest side is dramatically wetter than Grande-Terre's limestone plain, which surprises people who expect one climate.
pointeapitre.cost: Expensive. Budget around $1,900 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $700 to $1,200. Groceries cost noticeably more than mainland France, which has driven serious and sustained protest movements here. The local markets and the lolos, the small Creole grills, are considerably cheaper. The euro is the currency and French banking applies, which removes a set of problems other islands create.
pointeapitre.wifi: Good. Guadeloupe has European infrastructure: fibre reaches the developed parts of the archipelago at good speeds, mobile coverage is comprehensive, and French mobile plans work here without roaming charges, which is a substantial advantage for anyone based in Europe. Power is reliable. There is a small coworking scene around Pointe-a-Pitre and Le Gosier.
pointeapitre.nightlife: Modest. Le Gosier and the Bas-du-Fort marina have the concentration of bars and restaurants, and Guadeloupe's carnival, running from January to Ash Wednesday, is a serious weeks-long affair with its own musical tradition. Pointe-a-Pitre itself is quiet after dark. The 5 reflects a real scene that is spread out rather than concentrated.
pointeapitre.nature: Outstanding. La Soufriere, an active volcano at nearly 1,500 metres, sits in a national park covering most of Basse-Terre, with the Carbet waterfalls and rainforest trails below it. The Cousteau reserve at Pigeon Island is among the best diving in the Eastern Caribbean. Grande-Terre has the beaches and the Pointe des Chateaux headland.
pointeapitre.safety: Mid. Guadeloupe has a higher crime rate than mainland France, with theft and vehicle break-ins the common problems and violent crime concentrated in specific areas of Pointe-a-Pitre and Les Abymes. Tourist areas are generally fine with ordinary precautions. Rip currents on the Atlantic coast are the more likely hazard for visitors.
pointeapitre.food: Excellent. Guadeloupean cooking mixes French technique with Creole ingredients: colombo curry, boudin creole, accras and court-bouillon, with the lolos serving grilled fish at prices far below the restaurants. The rum here is agricole, distilled from cane juice rather than molasses, and the distilleries are working businesses. The 8 is genuinely earned.
pointeapitre.community: Weak. The foreign population is mainland French on posting, second-home owners and the sailing community around Bas-du-Fort. There is no nomad scene and very little English-language social infrastructure. The 3 reflects a French department where an outsider without French will find almost nothing to plug into.
pointeapitre.english: Weak. French is the language of everything administrative and commercial, with Guadeloupean Creole spoken among locals, and English is limited to parts of the tourism industry. This is the main practical filter: Guadeloupe is straightforward for a French speaker and considerably harder for anyone else, despite being in the Caribbean.
pointeapitre.visa: Reasonable, and excellent if you are European. Guadeloupe is an overseas department of France and part of the European Union while lying outside the Schengen area. European Union citizens have full freedom of movement and can live and work here without any permit at all. Most other Western nationalities receive ninety days visa-free; longer stays need a French long-stay visa.
pointeapitre.culture: Good. Guadeloupe's Creole culture is distinct and confident, with gwoka drumming recognised by UNESCO as intangible heritage, a carnival that runs for two months, and the Memorial ACTe in Pointe-a-Pitre, a substantial museum of slavery and the slave trade opened in 2015 on the site of a former sugar refinery.
pointeapitre.cleanliness: Middling. The resort areas and the newer developments are maintained to European standards, but Pointe-a-Pitre itself has visible decay in parts, waste collection has been disrupted by industrial disputes more than once, and sargassum on the Atlantic coast has been a serious recurring problem. Tap water is treated. The 6 is honest.
pointeapitre.airquality: Good. Trade winds, forest cover on Basse-Terre and limited industry keep readings within guidance. The recurring factors are Saharan dust in summer and, more seriously, the sargassum decomposing on the Atlantic coast, which releases hydrogen sulphide and has prompted health warnings and school closures in affected communes in bad years.

fortdefrance.climate: Tropical, around twenty-eight degrees year-round. December to April is the dry season and the busiest half. June to November is the wet season and the hurricane season runs through it. Mount Pelee's northern slopes are among the wettest places in the Caribbean while the southern beaches are notably drier, which is a real difference across a small island.
fortdefrance.cost: Expensive. Budget around $1,900 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $700 to $1,200 and Schoelcher and the Pointe du Bout side at the top. Imported food is costly and its price has driven repeated protest movements across the French Caribbean. The market and the local snack bars are far cheaper. The euro is the currency.
fortdefrance.wifi: Good. Martinique has European infrastructure: fibre reaches most of the developed west coast at good speeds, mobile coverage is comprehensive and French plans roam here without charge. Power is reliable. There is a small coworking scene in Fort-de-France and around Le Lamentin. Connectivity here is comfortably ahead of the independent islands nearby.
fortdefrance.nightlife: Modest. Fort-de-France has bars around the Savane and the Pointe du Bout side has the resort scene, and Martinique's carnival, ending with the burning of Vaval on Ash Wednesday, is the year's largest event. The capital is quiet on ordinary evenings. The 5 records a real scene that requires knowing where to go.
fortdefrance.nature: Outstanding. Mount Pelee, whose 1902 eruption destroyed Saint-Pierre and killed thirty thousand people in minutes, is walkable and the ruins below it can be visited. The northern rainforest, the Gorges de la Falaise and the Route de la Trace are excellent, and the southern beaches at Les Salines are the best on the island.
fortdefrance.safety: Mid. Martinique has a higher crime rate than mainland France, with theft and vehicle break-ins common and violent crime concentrated in specific areas of Fort-de-France. Tourist areas are generally fine with ordinary precautions. The island has also seen periods of serious social unrest over the cost of living, which can close roads and ports.
fortdefrance.food: Excellent. Martinican cooking is Creole with a strong French inheritance, and the island produces the only appellation-controlled rum in the world, distilled from cane juice at estates that are working agricultural businesses. Accras, colombo and boudin are everyday. The market in Fort-de-France is excellent. The 8 reflects genuine depth at every price point.
fortdefrance.community: Weak. The foreign population is mainland French on posting and second-home owners, plus a sailing community around Le Marin, which holds one of the largest charter fleets in the Caribbean. There is no nomad scene. The 3 reflects a French department with nothing organised for a visiting remote worker.
fortdefrance.english: Weak. French is the language of everything, with Martinican Creole spoken among locals, and English is limited outside the tourism industry. This is the practical filter: without French, Martinique is considerably harder than its infrastructure would suggest, and daily administration will be genuinely difficult.
fortdefrance.visa: Reasonable, and excellent for Europeans. Martinique is an overseas department of France and part of the European Union while lying outside Schengen. European Union citizens can live and work here with no permit and no time limit. Most other Western nationalities receive ninety days visa-free. Non-EU citizens wanting longer need a French long-stay visa applied for before travel.
fortdefrance.culture: Strong. Martinique produced Aime Cesaire, who coined negritude and served as mayor of Fort-de-France for over half a century, and Frantz Fanon, whose work shaped anticolonial thought worldwide. The Schoelcher Library, built for the 1889 Paris Exposition and shipped here piece by piece, is remarkable. The rum estates are a living industrial heritage.
fortdefrance.cleanliness: Good. Municipal services function to French standards in most of the island and the beaches are maintained. Fort-de-France itself has visible decay in parts and waste collection has been disrupted by strikes. Sargassum on the Atlantic coast is a serious recurring problem. Tap water is treated and safe. The 7 is fair.
fortdefrance.airquality: Good. Trade winds, rainforest in the north and limited industry keep readings within guidance. The recurring problems are Saharan dust in summer and sargassum decomposition on the Atlantic coast, which releases hydrogen sulphide and has prompted health warnings in affected communes. Chlordecone contamination of soil and water from banana farming is a separate and serious legacy issue.

cayenne.climate: Equatorial and hard work, which the 5 records. Hot and humid all year at around thirty-one degrees with rain that governs the calendar. The long dry season from July to November is the practical window, with a short drier spell in March. The heavy rains from December to June make interior travel difficult and the coast permanently damp.
cayenne.cost: Expensive, and the 4 reflects a French department where almost everything arrives from Europe. Budget around $2,000 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $700 to $1,200. Groceries cost substantially more than mainland France and the cost of living has driven serious social movements. The Hmong market at Cacao and the Saturday market in Cayenne are the exceptions.
cayenne.wifi: Good by South American standards and modest by European ones. Fibre reaches Cayenne and Kourou at workable speeds, mobile coverage is good along the coastal strip and effectively absent inland, and French plans roam here without charge. Power is reliable in the towns. There is a small amount of coworking, much of it connected to the space industry at Kourou.
cayenne.nightlife: Limited. Cayenne has bars around the Place des Palmistes and a small scene serving the space centre and administrative population, and the carnival from January to Ash Wednesday is a genuinely serious affair with its own touloulou tradition. Ordinary evenings are quiet. The 4 reflects a small administrative capital rather than a dull one.
cayenne.nature: Outstanding, and the 10 needs no argument. Rainforest covers around ninety-eight per cent of French Guiana, the highest proportion of any territory on earth, and the Guiana Amazonian Park is one of the largest protected areas anywhere. Leatherback turtles nest on the beaches between March and July in globally significant numbers. The Iles du Salut sit offshore.
cayenne.safety: Weak. Cayenne has a high crime rate by European standards, with armed robbery and theft the reported problems, and both residents and the French authorities identify specific districts to avoid, particularly after dark. Illegal gold mining in the interior brings its own serious problems. Read current guidance rather than assuming European Union territory means European crime rates.
cayenne.food: Good. Guianese cooking mixes Creole, Brazilian, Hmong, Chinese and French traditions, with bouillon d'awara at Easter as the dish that defines the place. The Hmong market at Cacao, run by a community that settled here from Laos in the 1970s, is remarkable. The 7 reflects genuine variety in a small population.
cayenne.community: Nonexistent for remote workers. The foreign population is the space centre at Kourou, the French Foreign Legion, gendarmerie and administrative staff, all on posting. There is no nomad scene and no coworking aimed at visitors. The 2 records a territory almost entirely off the remote work map, which is either the appeal or the disqualifier.
cayenne.english: Weak. French is the language of everything administrative and commercial, with Guianese Creole widely spoken and Portuguese, Hmong, Chinese and several Amerindian languages present in their communities. English is rare. Operating here without French is genuinely difficult in a way that shapes the whole experience.
cayenne.visa: Reasonable, and excellent for Europeans. French Guiana is an overseas department of France and part of the European Union while lying outside Schengen. European Union citizens have full freedom of movement and can live and work here without a permit. Yellow fever vaccination is mandatory for entry, which is unusual for EU territory and is enforced properly.
cayenne.culture: Good. The penal colony at the Iles du Salut and Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni, where France transported prisoners until 1953, is the territory's most substantial heritage and is genuinely affecting. The Maroon communities on the Maroni river maintain West African traditions. The carnival, with its masked touloulou balls, runs for two months and is unlike any other.
cayenne.cleanliness: Middling. Cayenne's centre is reasonably maintained but the wider city has visible waste problems and the drainage struggles in heavy rain. Illegal gold mining contaminates rivers in the interior with mercury, which is an environmental problem of a different order. Tap water in the towns is safe. The 5 is an honest reading.
cayenne.airquality: Good. Enormous forest cover, a small population and constant rainfall washing the air keep readings low. The exceptions are seasonal smoke from agricultural burning in neighbouring Brazil, which reaches the territory in bad fire years, and the rocket launches at Kourou, which are spectacular and infrequent rather than a pollution source of any consequence.

thevalley.climate: Excellent and consistent, around twenty-eight degrees year-round with steady trade winds and low rainfall, since Anguilla is flat coral rather than a mountainous island that pulls rain from the clouds. December to April is the dry season and the busiest. The hurricane season runs June to November and Anguilla is exposed, as Irma demonstrated in 2017.
thevalley.cost: Expensive, which the 3 records. Budget around $2,600 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $1,100 to $1,700. Groceries are heavily marked up and many residents shop in Sint Maarten, twenty minutes away by ferry, where prices are lower. The East Caribbean dollar is pegged at 2.7 to the dollar and both circulate freely.
thevalley.wifi: Good. Fibre reaches most of the island at workable speeds and mobile data is comprehensive, both invested in specifically to support the remote work programme the government launched in 2020. There is a small amount of coworking. Power is reasonably reliable and expensive. Connectivity here is genuinely better than on several larger and better-known Caribbean islands.
thevalley.nightlife: Limited but distinctive. Anguilla has a small number of beach bars, several of them long-established institutions with live music, and the island has produced a disproportionate amount of Caribbean string band and reggae music. It is early and quiet by any measure. The 4 reflects a deliberately calm island rather than an empty one.
thevalley.nature: Good rather than dramatic. Anguilla is flat, sixteen kilometres long and has thirty-three beaches, and the absence of rivers is exactly why the water at Shoal Bay and Rendezvous Bay is as clear as it is. There is no rainforest, no hill and no waterfall. The offshore cays and the reef are the natural interest here.
thevalley.safety: Very high. Anguilla has one of the lowest crime rates in the Caribbean and is comfortable at any hour, helped by a population of fifteen thousand where anonymity is difficult. Petty theft is uncommon. The genuine hazards are the sea, with strong currents on some of the north-facing beaches, and the hurricane exposure.
thevalley.food: Excellent for the size. Anguilla has a restaurant scene well beyond what fifteen thousand people would otherwise support, built partly on the same French Caribbean supply chain that feeds Saint-Martin next door, with crayfish and grilled fish the local staples. Prices are high. The 8 reflects genuine quality rather than merely adequacy.
thevalley.community: Weak. The foreign population is second-home owners, resort staff and a small number of remote workers on the twelve-month visa, and the island is too small and too quiet to have formed a scene around them. There is limited coworking. The 3 reflects a generous visa arrangement that has not yet produced a community.
thevalley.english: Universal. English is the official language and the medium of everything, with an Anguillian creole spoken among locals. The island is a British Overseas Territory and the institutions reflect it. There is no barrier of any kind for an English speaker.
thevalley.visa: Good. Anguilla's remote work programme grants stays of up to twelve months to people working for employers outside the island, with a fee of around $2,000 for an individual, proof of health insurance and a clean record. It was among the earliest such schemes anywhere and remains straightforward. Short visits are visa-free for most Western nationalities for three months.
thevalley.culture: Modest. Anguilla's identity is boat racing, which is the national sport and involves wooden sloops built on the island and raced by whole communities through the summer. The Heritage Collection Museum records the island's history including the 1967 revolution against association with Saint Kitts. Beyond that the cultural offer is limited by the size of the place.
thevalley.cleanliness: High. The island is well maintained, the beaches are clean and publicly accessible, and waste collection functions. Landfill capacity on a small island is the underlying constraint. Rebuilding after Irma has been substantially completed. Tap water is desalinated and safe. The 8 reflects a small territory that keeps itself in order.
thevalley.airquality: Excellent. A flat, low island with constant trade winds, no industry and fifteen thousand people leaves nothing to trap, and readings sit well within guidance. Saharan dust reaches the Eastern Caribbean each summer and is the only recurring factor. This is among the cleanest air anywhere on this site.

andorralavella.climate: Continental mountain, which the 5 records as variability rather than harshness. Andorra la Vella sits above a thousand metres, so winters are properly cold with snow in the town itself, and summers are warm and dry in the low twenties. December to April is the ski season and June to September the walking season. May and November are the shoulder months when much closes.
andorralavella.cost: Moderate for western Europe. Budget around $1,900 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $700 to $1,200, and the rental market is genuinely tight because much of the housing stock is holiday property. The tax position is the real story: a maximum of ten per cent income tax and four and a half per cent value added tax, the lowest in Europe.
andorralavella.wifi: Excellent. Andorra Telecom has rolled fibre to essentially every household in the country, which makes it one of the best-connected places in Europe per head, and speeds are high. Mobile coverage is complete in the valleys and patchy on the high passes. Power is entirely reliable. There is a small coworking scene aimed at the digital businesses the government has courted.
andorralavella.nightlife: Limited. Andorra la Vella has bars along the main street and the ski season brings an apres crowd to Pas de la Casa and Soldeu, but the capital is quiet on an ordinary evening and much of it is shopping rather than going out. The 4 reflects a small mountain town rather than a nightlife destination.
andorralavella.nature: Outstanding. Andorra is entirely Pyrenean, with peaks over 2,900 metres, the Madriu-Perafita-Claror valley protected as a UNESCO World Heritage site for its glacial landscape and centuries of pastoral use, and Grandvalira and Ordino-Arcalis forming the largest ski area in the Pyrenees. Walking trails run from the edge of the capital into high country.
andorralavella.safety: Very high. Andorra has among the lowest crime rates in Europe and is comfortable at any hour, with a police force of a few hundred for eighty thousand people. The genuine hazards are mountain ones: weather on the high passes, avalanche risk in winter and the road conditions when it snows. The country also records the highest life expectancy in the world.
andorralavella.food: Good. Andorran cooking is Catalan mountain food, with trinxat, escudella and grilled meats, and the restaurants along the border valleys serve French and Spanish traditions alongside it. Prices are lower than France or Spain on alcohol and tobacco because of the tax regime, which is what the duty-free shopping is about. The 7 is fair.
andorralavella.community: Weak. Andorra's foreign population is large in proportion, with Spanish, Portuguese and French residents making up well over half the country, but it is a working population rather than a nomad one. There is a small and growing digital business community. The 3 reflects a country where an outsider without Catalan or Spanish will find little to join.
andorralavella.english: Weak. Catalan is the only official language, with Spanish and French both widely spoken and Portuguese common given the size of that community. English is limited outside the ski resorts and the newer digital businesses. Anyone staying here for a season will need Spanish at minimum for daily life.
andorralavella.visa: Poor for a visitor and demanding for a resident. Andorra is not in the European Union or Schengen, though it has no border controls with France or Spain and uses the euro, so reaching it means entering Schengen and that day count applies. Residence requires either running a company here or a substantial investment in Andorran assets plus an interest-free state deposit.
andorralavella.culture: Modest. Andorra is a co-principality whose heads of state are the President of France and the Bishop of Urgell, which is a constitutional arrangement unique in the world. The Romanesque churches scattered through the parishes, particularly Santa Coloma and Sant Joan de Caselles, are the built heritage. Beyond that the capital is largely retail.
andorralavella.cleanliness: Exceptional. Andorra is meticulously maintained, litter is essentially absent, the mountain paths are well kept and the country invests heavily in appearance because tourism is the whole economy. Waste is exported for processing. Tap water comes from the mountains and is excellent. The 9 reflects a small wealthy country that takes this seriously.
andorralavella.airquality: Excellent. Altitude, mountain wind, no industry and a small population keep readings very low, and the air in the high valleys is as clean as anywhere in Europe. The one local factor is traffic through the narrow capital, which is heavy because of the shopping and produces a measurable but modest effect on the valley floor.

monaco.climate: Excellent Mediterranean, around sixteen degrees in winter and the high twenties in summer, with over three hundred days of sunshine a year and the Alps close enough to block the northern weather. The sea is swimmable from June to October. There is no bad season here, which is a large part of why the principality became what it is.
monaco.cost: The most expensive place on this site, and the 1 is literal rather than rhetorical. Budget around $5,200 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $3,500 to $5,000 as the ordinary market. Monaco has the highest property prices per square metre in the world. There is no income tax for residents other than French nationals, which is the point.
monaco.wifi: Excellent. Fibre throughout, comprehensive 5G, and a state that has invested in being an early adopter of network technology on principle. Power is entirely reliable. There is coworking aimed largely at the financial and yachting sectors. Connectivity is as good as anywhere in Europe and better than most, in two square kilometres where everything is close to everything.
monaco.nightlife: Good but narrow. The casinos, the clubs at the Sporting and the bars around Port Hercule are genuinely busy, particularly during the Grand Prix and the Yacht Show, and the scene is heavily weighted towards money. Nice, twenty minutes by train, offers considerably more range. The 6 reflects quality rather than variety.
monaco.nature: Weak, and the 5 is honest. Monaco is two square kilometres of almost entirely built environment, with the Exotic Garden on the cliff and the Japanese Garden as the green space. What saves it is proximity: the Mercantour National Park and the Alps are an hour inland, and the coastal path east and west of the principality is excellent.
monaco.safety: The highest on this site. Monaco has one police officer for roughly every seventy residents and a dense network of surveillance cameras, and the result is a crime rate close to zero for anything violent. Walking anywhere at any hour is entirely unremarkable. The genuine hazards are traffic and the steep gradients rather than anything criminal.
monaco.food: Very good. Monaco has several Michelin-starred restaurants including the Louis XV, and the local Monegasque cooking, with barbagiuan and socca, survives in a few places alongside the international dining. The market at La Condamine is where residents actually shop and is far cheaper than the restaurants around it. The 8 reflects quality at a price.
monaco.community: Weak for remote workers. Monaco's population is around three-quarters foreign, which is a genuinely international community, but it is one of residents and industry rather than of visiting professionals, and the barrier to joining it is capital rather than sociability. There is coworking. The 3 reflects a place where community exists and is expensive to enter.
monaco.english: Moderate. French is the official language and the language of administration, with Italian widely spoken and English common in the financial and yachting sectors and in the international schools. Monegasque survives ceremonially. English will carry a visitor through most situations and will not handle anything administrative.
monaco.visa: Poor as a route. Monaco is in the Schengen area in practice, with border controls handled by France, so Schengen rules and day counts apply exactly as in France. There is no remote work visa. Residence requires proving accommodation in the world's most expensive property market plus a substantial bank deposit, generally several hundred thousand euros.
monaco.culture: Good. The Oceanographic Museum, which Jacques Cousteau directed for over thirty years, is a serious institution built into the cliff face. The Prince's Palace, the Monte Carlo Opera and the Grimaldi dynasty's seven hundred years in charge are the rest of it. The Grand Prix, run on public streets since 1929, is arguably the cultural event.
monaco.cleanliness: Exceptional, and the 10 is deserved. Monaco is maintained to a standard that has no real comparison: streets washed, no litter, public lifts and escalators immaculate, and a waste system that runs largely underground. The state has the money and a small area to spend it on. Tap water is excellent.
monaco.airquality: Mediocre for a place this wealthy, which the 7 reflects. The principality sits in a bowl between the Alps and the sea with heavy traffic on the three corniche roads above it and constant cruise and yacht activity in the port, and the topography traps what that produces. Readings are worse than the surrounding French coast.

torshavn.climate: Subpolar oceanic and genuinely difficult, which the 2 records. Temperatures barely move through the year, sitting between three and thirteen degrees, but the wind, fog and rain are relentless: the islands get some three hundred days with precipitation. Locals say you can have all four seasons in an afternoon and they are not exaggerating. Winter is dark rather than cold.
torshavn.cost: Expensive. Budget around $2,400 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $900 to $1,400 and a housing shortage that makes finding one harder than affording it. Groceries are Nordic-priced and eating out is expensive. Heating runs all year rather than seasonally. The Danish krone is the currency, issued locally as Faroese notes.
torshavn.wifi: Excellent, and one of the genuine surprises about the islands. Submarine cables to Denmark and Iceland, fibre to essentially every household, and mobile coverage that works inside the sub-sea tunnels linking the main islands. Speeds are high and reliable. Power is reliable and increasingly wind and hydro. There is a small coworking presence in Torshavn.
torshavn.nightlife: Limited. Torshavn has a handful of bars and a music scene that is disproportionately good for a town of twenty thousand, with the G! Festival in July and a strong Faroese songwriting tradition. Ordinary evenings are quiet and alcohol was only fully legalised in the islands in 1992. The 3 reflects a small and improving scene.
torshavn.nature: Outstanding, and the 10 is straightforward. Eighteen basalt islands rising vertically out of the North Atlantic, with sea cliffs over seven hundred metres, the waterfall at Gasadalur falling off a cliff into the ocean, puffin colonies at Mykines, and a lake that appears to hang above the sea at Sorvagsvatn. There are almost no trees anywhere.
torshavn.safety: The highest anywhere. The Faroe Islands have essentially no violent crime, the prison holds a handful of people, and doors are routinely left unlocked. Walking anywhere at any hour is unremarkable. The genuine hazards are entirely environmental: cliff edges in fog, weather that changes in minutes, and roads and tunnels that close in a serious storm.
torshavn.food: Good and improving sharply. The traditional diet is fermented lamb and air-dried fish, which is an acquired taste, but Torshavn now has a genuine restaurant scene including KOKS, which held two Michelin stars and put Faroese cooking on the map. Fish and lamb are the only things not imported. The 7 reflects real ambition at small scale.
torshavn.community: Weak. The islands' foreign population is largely Danish, plus workers in fishing and aquaculture and a small number of researchers. There is no nomad scene and no coworking culture beyond one small space. The 3 reflects a place where people are friendly and where nothing exists for a visiting professional to join.
torshavn.english: Strong. Faroese is the language of daily life and Danish is taught throughout, but English is widely and comfortably spoken, particularly by anyone under fifty, and signage and services accommodate visitors. An English speaker will have no practical difficulty anywhere in the islands.
torshavn.visa: Reasonable, with one detail that matters enormously. The Faroe Islands are an autonomous Danish territory but are not in the European Union and not in Schengen: a Schengen visa does not admit you here and time spent here does not count against a Schengen allowance. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for ninety days. There is no remote work visa.
torshavn.culture: Good. Tinganes, the turf-roofed peninsula in Torshavn, has been the seat of government since the Viking age and is among the oldest parliamentary sites in the world. The chain dance and the ballad tradition are living practice. The grindadrap, the pilot whale drive, is a genuine and controversial part of Faroese life that visitors should read about rather than discover.
torshavn.cleanliness: Exceptional. The islands are meticulously kept, litter is absent, and the combination of wind, rain and a small careful population means nothing accumulates. Waste is managed carefully because there is nowhere to put it. Tap water is excellent and comes straight from the hills. The 10 is deserved.
torshavn.airquality: Exceptional. A North Atlantic archipelago with constant wind, no heavy industry and fifty-four thousand people has nothing to trap, and the air here is about as clean as inhabited air gets anywhere on earth. The salmon farming industry and the fishing fleet are the only local sources, and neither registers against that wind.

nuuk.climate: Arctic, and the 1 is honest rather than harsh. Winter sits around minus eight in Nuuk, moderated by the sea and far milder than inland Greenland, with darkness for much of the day. Summer reaches around ten degrees with very long days. Ice conditions rather than temperature govern what is possible in any given month.
nuuk.cost: Expensive. Budget around $2,600 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $1,100 to $1,700, and housing is genuinely scarce with waiting lists that are a standing feature of Greenlandic life. Groceries are Nordic-priced with an Arctic freight premium on top, and fresh produce is limited and costly. Heating runs all year. The Danish krone is the currency.
nuuk.wifi: Adequate. Submarine cable to Iceland and Canada has improved things substantially and fibre reaches Nuuk at workable speeds, though prices are high and capacity outside the main towns is limited. Mobile coverage exists in the settlements and nowhere between them. Power is reliable and largely hydroelectric. There is a small amount of coworking.
nuuk.nightlife: Limited but real. Nuuk has a handful of bars and a music scene that is surprisingly active for nineteen thousand people, with Greenlandic hip-hop and rock both established. Alcohol is expensive and its social effects are a serious public issue in Greenland. The 3 reflects a small capital rather than a dead one.
nuuk.nature: Outstanding, and the 10 requires no argument. Nuuk sits at the mouth of one of the largest fjord systems on earth, with icebergs drifting past the town, humpback whales in the fjord in summer, and the ice sheet inland. The northern lights are visible on clear nights from September to April. There are no trees.
nuuk.safety: High for crime and demanding for everything else. Greenland has low violent crime and Nuuk is comfortable to move around, though the country has serious social problems around alcohol and suicide that are openly discussed. The genuine hazards are environmental: weather that cancels all transport, sea ice, and the complete absence of infrastructure outside the settlements.
nuuk.food: Modest. Greenlandic food is seal, whale, musk ox, reindeer and fish, which is genuinely good and unfamiliar, and Nuuk has a small number of serious restaurants working with it. Everything else is imported at Arctic prices and fresh vegetables are limited and expensive. The 5 records real interest constrained by supply.
nuuk.community: Weak. Nuuk's foreign population is Danish administrators, teachers, health workers and researchers, almost all on contract. There is no nomad scene, no coworking culture aimed at visitors and no framework for one. The 2 reflects a capital that has never had reason to think about remote workers.
nuuk.english: Moderate to good. Greenlandic is the official language and Danish is universally taught, but English is widely spoken among younger people and in business and tourism, which makes Nuuk considerably easier than its remoteness suggests. Anything administrative will be in Danish or Greenlandic. This consistently surprises visitors who expected a language wall.
nuuk.visa: Reasonable, with the same important detail as the Faroes. Greenland is an autonomous Danish territory but left the European Community in 1985 and is not in Schengen: a Schengen visa does not admit you and time here does not count against a Schengen allowance. Most Western nationalities enter visa-free for ninety days. There is no remote work visa.
nuuk.culture: Strong. Greenlandic Inuit culture is living rather than preserved, with kayaking, drum dancing and mask traditions all practised, and the National Museum in Nuuk holds the Qilakitsoq mummies, five hundred years old and remarkably preserved. The country has been steadily taking powers back from Denmark since 1979, and that political process is the live cultural question.
nuuk.cleanliness: High. Nuuk is well kept and the cold does a great deal of the work, though waste management in a country with no roads between towns is genuinely difficult and every settlement handles its own. Tap water comes from meltwater and is excellent. The 8 reflects a clean place with structural disposal constraints.
nuuk.airquality: Exceptional. An Arctic coastal town of nineteen thousand with hydroelectric power, constant wind and no industry has essentially nothing to put into the air. Readings are among the lowest measured anywhere. The one local source is diesel generation in the smaller settlements, which does not affect the capital.

douglasiom.climate: Oceanic and grey, which the 4 records. Summers reach the high teens and winters sit around seven degrees, so nothing is extreme, but the island is wet and windy and the Irish Sea keeps it that way. May to September is the comfortable half. Winter storms cancel ferries and occasionally flights, which is a practical planning consideration.
douglasiom.cost: Moderate to expensive. Budget around $2,300 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $900 to $1,400 in a tight housing market. Groceries are close to United Kingdom prices since the supply chain is the same, though the Irish Sea freight shows in some categories. The island has its own income tax with a cap on total liability, which attracts some high earners.
douglasiom.wifi: Good. The Isle of Man's economy depends on connectivity: substantial e-gaming, financial services and insurance sectors mean fibre reaches most of Douglas and the main towns at solid speeds, and mobile coverage is comprehensive. Power is reliable. There is a small coworking market. The island runs its own top-level internet domain and its own telecoms regulation.
douglasiom.nightlife: Limited. Douglas has pubs along the promenade and a small number of clubs, and the island has a genuine live music tradition, but it is a town of twenty-eight thousand and closes early. TT fortnight in late May and early June is an entirely different matter and transforms the place. The 4 is fair.
douglasiom.nature: Strong. The Raad ny Foillan coastal path runs the whole hundred miles around the island, Snaefell at 620 metres gives a view of six kingdoms on a clear day, and the Calf of Man at the southern tip is a bird observatory. The entire island is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, the only whole nation with that designation.
douglasiom.safety: Very high. The Isle of Man has low crime and is comfortable at any hour, with a population small enough that anonymity is difficult. The genuine hazard is the road: the island has unrestricted speed limits on much of its rural network, which is unusual in the British Isles and contributes to a road casualty rate above the mainland's.
douglasiom.food: Decent. Manx queenies, the small scallops, and Manx kippers from Peel are the local specialities, and the island produces good beef and lamb from its own farms. Douglas has a reasonable restaurant scene for its size. Prices are close to United Kingdom levels. The 6 records solid local produce without much culinary ambition.
douglasiom.community: Weak. The island's foreign population is largely British and Irish arrivals working in e-gaming, insurance and fund administration, which is a real professional network but not one organised for visitors. There is a small coworking market. The 3 reflects a working island with nothing aimed at remote workers passing through.
douglasiom.english: Universal. English is the language of everything, with Manx Gaelic revived, taught in schools and appearing on signage and in official use, though it has few daily speakers. The island has been self-governing for centuries and the institutions are Manx rather than British, but the language is not a barrier in any respect.
douglasiom.visa: Fair. The Isle of Man is a Crown Dependency, not part of the United Kingdom and never part of the European Union, though it sits inside the Common Travel Area. British and Irish citizens can live and work here freely with no border control on arrival. Everyone else needs the island's own immigration permission, administered separately from Britain's, including a work permit system.
douglasiom.culture: Good. Tynwald, the island's parliament, has met since around 979 and is the oldest continuous parliamentary body in the world, with an annual open-air sitting at St John's each July. The Manx Museum records a Norse and Celtic history that is genuinely distinct from Britain's. The TT races have run since 1907 and are the island's global identity.
douglasiom.cleanliness: High. The island is well maintained, waste collection functions, the coastal path and the countryside are looked after, and the Biosphere designation has sharpened how the landscape is managed. Douglas promenade was comprehensively rebuilt recently. Tap water is excellent. The 8 reflects an ordinary well-run British Isles jurisdiction.
douglasiom.airquality: Excellent. A small island in the Irish Sea with constant wind, no heavy industry and eighty-four thousand people has little to trap, and readings sit well within guidance. Domestic heating raises particulates on still winter days in Douglas. The TT fortnight is a localised and temporary exception that nobody measures seriously.

sanmarino.climate: Mediterranean modified by altitude. Monte Titano rises to 750 metres, so the ridge is cooler than the Adriatic plain below and frequently in cloud when the coast is clear. Summers are warm in the high twenties and winters cold with occasional snow on the mountain. May, June, September and October are the best months by a distance.
sanmarino.cost: Moderate. Budget around $1,900 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $600 to $1,000, and much of the affordable housing is in the lower towns of Borgo Maggiore and Dogana rather than on the mountain. Groceries are Italian-priced, which is to say reasonable. The republic sets its own indirect taxes, which makes some goods slightly cheaper than in Italy.
sanmarino.wifi: Good. Fibre reaches the populated areas at solid speeds and mobile coverage is comprehensive, with the surrounding Italian networks also reaching most of the republic. Power is reliable. There is very little coworking, since San Marino has almost no visiting professional population. Connectivity is not a constraint anywhere in the country.
sanmarino.nightlife: Minimal. The historic city on the mountain empties completely when the day-trippers leave, and the lower towns have a handful of bars. Rimini, fifty minutes away, has one of the largest nightlife scenes in Italy and is where anyone goes for an evening. The 3 reflects a small republic where the evening happens elsewhere.
sanmarino.nature: Fair. Monte Titano itself is a limestone crag with paths along the ridge and views to the Adriatic on a clear day, and the surrounding countryside is rolling Romagna farmland. There is no wilderness and no substantial protected area. The Apennines proper and the Adriatic beaches are both within an hour, which is what most residents use.
sanmarino.safety: The highest tier anywhere. San Marino has essentially no violent crime, a police force of a few hundred for thirty-four thousand people, and one of the lowest crime rates in Europe. Walking anywhere at any hour is unremarkable. The genuine hazards are the steep cobbled streets in wet weather and the mountain road in ice.
sanmarino.food: Excellent. San Marino eats Romagna food, which is among the best regional cooking in Italy: piadina, tagliatelle al ragu, passatelli and the local torta tre monti. The republic also produces its own wine and has a serious food culture despite the tourist retail on the mountain. Prices are Italian rather than resort. The 8 is earned.
sanmarino.community: Nonexistent for remote workers.
