San Marino's foreign population is largely Italian, and the republic has no visiting professional presence, no coworking and no residence route that would create one. The 2 reflects a country that is easy to visit and effectively closed to anyone hoping to settle without capital or a job here.
sanmarino.english: Weak. Italian is the only language of daily life and administration. English is spoken in the tourism economy on the mountain and is limited elsewhere. Anyone staying here for a season will need Italian for anything beyond a shop counter, which is the main practical filter given how close the republic is to a major Italian tourist coast.
sanmarino.visa: Poor as a distinct route. San Marino is not in the European Union and not formally in Schengen, but has open borders with Italy on every side and no controls, so reaching it means entering Schengen through Italy and that day count applies. Residence is tightly controlled and generally requires substantial investment or genuine employment with a Sammarinese company.
sanmarino.culture: Strong. San Marino claims to be the oldest surviving sovereign state and the oldest constitutional republic in the world, founded by a stonemason in 301, with a constitution dating from 1600 and two heads of state elected every six months. The three towers on the ridge are the national emblem and are visible for fifty kilometres.
sanmarino.cleanliness: Exceptional. The republic is meticulously maintained, the historic city is kept in order as the national asset it is, and waste collection functions to a high standard. Litter is essentially absent. Tap water is good. The 9 reflects a small wealthy country whose whole economy depends on how it looks.
sanmarino.airquality: Good. The ridge position, low industry and modest population keep readings reasonable. The qualification is regional rather than local: San Marino sits at the edge of the Po valley, one of the most polluted air basins in Europe, and winter inversions there push particulates across the whole area. The mountain sits above the worst of it.

libreville.climate: Equatorial and demanding, which the 5 records. Hot and humid all year at around thirty degrees with two dry seasons, a long one from June to September and a short one in December and January, and heavy rain the rest of the time. The long dry season is also the best window for the coastal national parks.
libreville.cost: Expensive, and the 3 is honest. Budget around $1,800 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $700 to $1,200 and Quartier Louis and the embassy areas at the top. An oil economy with a small population and heavy import dependence makes Libreville one of the costlier African capitals for expatriates. The CFA franc is pegged to the euro.
libreville.wifi: Weak. Fibre reaches parts of the city and mobile data from Airtel and Moov is the usual answer, with prices high relative to speed. Power cuts happen and any serious office runs a generator. There is very little coworking. Connectivity here is a genuine planning constraint rather than a minor inconvenience for anyone with a call-heavy schedule.
libreville.nightlife: Moderate. Libreville has a real bar and live music culture, and Gabonese music has a substantial regional following, with the venues along the Boulevard Triomphal and in Louis busy at weekends. Prices are high. Safety shapes how people move rather than whether they go out. The 5 reflects something genuine at a cost.
libreville.nature: Outstanding, and it is the whole case for Gabon. The country protects around eleven per cent of its territory in thirteen national parks created in a single decision in 2002, and Loango is famous for forest elephants and buffalo walking out onto Atlantic beaches, which happens nowhere else. Nearly ninety per cent of the country is forest.
libreville.safety: Weak. Libreville has significant street crime, with robbery and theft the common problems, and walking after dark is generally avoided. Gabon has also had recent political instability including a coup in 2023. Ordinary caution is not sufficient here; local advice on specific areas is. Read current government guidance before planning a stay.
libreville.food: Decent. Gabonese cooking runs on cassava, plantain and smoked fish with nyembwe, a palm nut sauce, as the national dish, and the French colonial legacy left proper bread and a genuine restaurant tradition in the expensive parts of town. Street food is cheap and good. The 6 records solid eating at a wide price spread.
libreville.community: Nonexistent for remote workers. Libreville's foreign population is oil, timber, conservation and diplomatic staff, almost all on posting, plus a substantial French community of long standing. There is no nomad scene and no coworking aimed at visitors. The 2 reflects a working capital with nothing organised for anyone passing through.
libreville.english: Weak. French is the language of everything administrative and commercial, and English is genuinely rare outside international organisations and the oil sector. Fang and several other Bantu languages are spoken at home. Operating here without French is difficult in a way that shapes the whole experience of the country.
libreville.visa: Fair. Gabon operates an e-visa that most nationalities can apply for online before travel, with approval usually returned within days and the visa issued on arrival, typically for up to ninety days. A yellow fever certificate is required. There is no remote work visa. Procedures have changed more than once recently, so confirm the current position directly.
libreville.culture: Good. Gabon's mask traditions, particularly the white Punu masks and the Fang reliquary figures, shaped European modernism when Picasso and others encountered them, and the Bwiti religious practice is living rather than historical. Libreville itself was founded in 1849 as a settlement for freed slaves, which is the origin of its name.
libreville.cleanliness: Middling to poor. The embassy quarters and the seafront are maintained, but waste collection across the city is inconsistent, drainage floods in the heavy rains, and the informal settlements are underserved. Tap water should not be drunk. The 5 records an honest gap between the well-resourced districts and the rest.
libreville.airquality: Mediocre. An ageing vehicle fleet, widespread generator use and waste burning are the main sources, and the humid stagnant coastal air disperses poorly on still days. There is limited heavy industry beyond the port and the oil terminals. The heavy rainfall washes the air regularly, which is the one factor working the other way.

freetown.climate: Tropical monsoon, and the 5 reflects the rain rather than the heat. Around thirty degrees all year with high humidity. November to April is the dry season and the practical window. The rains from May to October are among the heaviest in West Africa, with Freetown receiving well over three metres a year and the mountain slopes above the city prone to landslides.
freetown.cost: Very cheap, and the 8 is genuine. Budget around $800 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $250 to $500 and Aberdeen and the peninsula beaches at the top. Market food costs very little and Sierra Leonean cooking is good. Imported goods are expensive. The leone was redenominated in 2022, dropping three zeros, so older prices need checking.
freetown.wifi: Weak. Fibre has reached parts of the city and works where it exists, mobile data from Orange and Africell is the common fallback, and neither is fast. Power cuts are frequent and generators are standard in anything serious. There is a small startup and coworking presence, more developed than the country's profile would suggest.
freetown.nightlife: Moderate. Freetown has a genuine bar and music scene, particularly along the Aberdeen strip and at the beach bars on the peninsula, and Sierra Leonean music from palm-wine guitar to contemporary Afrobeats has a real following. It runs late. Safety shapes movement rather than participation. The 5 reflects something real.
freetown.nature: Strong. The Freetown peninsula has a run of beaches, at Lumley, Tokeh and River Number Two, that are among the best in West Africa and almost entirely undeveloped. Tacugama Chimpanzee Sanctuary sits in rainforest twenty minutes from the city, and Tiwai Island's primate reserve is a longer trip inland. The mountains rise straight behind the city.
freetown.safety: Weak. Freetown has significant street crime, with theft and robbery the common problems, and walking after dark is generally avoided. Sierra Leone is politically calmer than its history suggests but had unrest in 2023. The more likely hazards are practical: road conditions, the Lungi airport crossing, and the landslide risk in the rains after the 2017 Regent disaster.
freetown.food: Decent. Sierra Leonean cooking runs on cassava leaf, groundnut stew and jollof rice, with fish from the Atlantic and plenty of pepper, and the street food is very cheap. The Krio tradition has its own dishes. Restaurant range in Freetown is limited and mostly Lebanese and Indian. The 6 records honest adequacy.
freetown.community: Nonexistent for remote workers. Freetown's foreign population is development, public health and mission staff, which is substantial given the country's history, plus a long-established Lebanese business community. There is a small local startup scene. The 2 reflects a city where nothing exists for a visiting remote worker to join.
freetown.english: Strong. English is the official language and the medium of education, government and business, and Krio, an English-based creole, is spoken by almost the whole country as a lingua franca. That combination makes Sierra Leone considerably easier for an English speaker than any of its francophone neighbours, and it is the country's clearest practical advantage.
freetown.visa: Fair. Sierra Leone requires a visa of most nationalities, available through an e-visa before travel or on arrival at Lungi, typically for thirty days with longer options. A yellow fever certificate is required. There is no remote work visa. Extensions are applied for in Freetown. Entry procedures have changed several times recently, so confirm the current requirement.
freetown.culture: Strong. Freetown was founded in 1792 by freed slaves from Nova Scotia and Britain, and that history runs through the Krio language, the board houses of the old city and the Cotton Tree that stood at the centre until it fell in 2023. Bunce Island, a slave trading fort upriver, is one of the most significant sites of its kind anywhere.
freetown.cleanliness: Poor. Waste collection is inconsistent outside the central and wealthier districts, drainage floods badly in the rains, and plastic accumulates in the informal settlements and along the waterways. Deforestation of the peninsula hills compounds the landslide and runoff problem. Tap water should not be drunk. The 4 is an honest reading.
freetown.airquality: Mediocre. An ageing vehicle fleet, generator use, charcoal cooking and waste burning are the main sources and readings sit above guidance for much of the year. The harmattan in December and January brings Saharan dust that raises particulates substantially. The very heavy rainfall does wash the air thoroughly for half the year.

serrekunda.climate: Tropical savanna, around thirty-two degrees through the dry season with low humidity and the Atlantic breeze. November to May is the dry season and the practical window, with the harmattan bringing dust in December and January. June to October is hot, humid and wet, and much of the tourist infrastructure closes entirely.
serrekunda.cost: Very cheap. Budget around $700 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $200 to $400 and the coastal strip at Kololi and Bijilo at the top. Market food is very cheap and the fish landing at Tanji is among the best value anywhere. Imported goods carry a markup. The dalasi has weakened steadily, which helps a visitor and hurts residents.
serrekunda.wifi: Weak. Fibre has reached parts of the coastal strip and mobile data from Africell, QCell and Gamcel is the usual answer, with prices high relative to speed and evening congestion common. Power cuts are frequent and any serious business runs a generator. There is a small coworking presence around the tourist coast.
serrekunda.nightlife: Moderate. The Senegambia strip at Kololi has a concentration of bars and clubs aimed at the charter tourism market, and there is a genuine local scene with Gambian and Senegalese music. It runs late in season and is quiet outside it. The 5 reflects a real scene that is heavily shaped by the visitor economy.
serrekunda.nature: Good. The Gambia is a strip of land along one river and the birdlife is exceptional, with well over five hundred species recorded in a country smaller than Yorkshire, which is why so many visitors carry binoculars. Abuko Nature Reserve is close to Serrekunda, Kiang West and the River Gambia National Park with its chimpanzees are upriver.
serrekunda.safety: Mid. The Gambia is generally calm and violent crime against visitors is uncommon, though petty theft happens and the tourist strip has a well-documented problem with persistent hustling, known locally as bumsters. The country also has a documented sex tourism problem that visitors should be aware of. Road safety is the more likely practical hazard.
serrekunda.food: Decent. Gambian cooking is shared with Senegal: benachin, the local jollof, domoda groundnut stew and yassa, along with excellent grilled fish from Tanji and Gunjur. The markets are very cheap. Restaurant range on the tourist strip is aimed at European visitors rather than local tastes. The 6 records good food narrowly served.
serrekunda.community: Weak. The Gambia's foreign population is European charter tourists, a substantial number of British and Scandinavian long-stay winter residents, and development staff. There is a small coworking presence. The 3 reflects a genuine foreign presence that is seasonal and retired rather than professional, with nothing organised for remote workers.
serrekunda.english: Strong. English is the official language and the medium of education, government and business, which is unusual in a region that is otherwise francophone, and it removes the language barrier entirely. Mandinka, Wolof and Fula are the languages of daily life. This is the Gambia's clearest practical advantage over its neighbours.
serrekunda.visa: Reasonable. The Gambia grants visa-free entry to citizens of most Commonwealth countries and a number of European states for up to ninety days, with everyone else obtaining a visa on arrival or in advance. The rules vary more by nationality than in most countries. There is no remote work visa. A yellow fever certificate is required from endemic countries.
serrekunda.culture: Good. Juffureh and Kunta Kinteh Island on the river, central to the story Alex Haley told in Roots, are among the most visited historical sites in West Africa, and the Wassu stone circles upriver are a UNESCO World Heritage site of megaliths built over a thousand years. Gambian kora music is a living griot tradition.
serrekunda.cleanliness: Poor. Waste collection is inconsistent outside the tourist strip, plastic accumulates along the roads and the coast, and there is essentially no recycling. The Bakoteh dump has been a public health issue for years. The beaches in the tourist areas are cleaned. Tap water should not be drunk. The 4 is honest.
serrekunda.airquality: Mediocre. Charcoal cooking, an ageing vehicle fleet, waste burning and dust from unpaved roads are the main sources, and readings sit above guidance for much of the year. The harmattan from December to February brings Saharan dust that raises particulates substantially for weeks. The Atlantic breeze provides real dispersal along the coast.

djibouti.climate: Desert and severe, which the 2 records honestly. November to February is the only comfortable window, around twenty-eight degrees. From June to August temperatures regularly exceed forty-five with the khamsin wind off the desert making it worse, and Djibouti is among the hottest inhabited places on earth. Rainfall is negligible year-round.
djibouti.cost: Expensive, and the 3 is honest. Budget around $1,600 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $600 to $1,000 and the European Quarter at the top. The country imports almost everything and hosts several foreign military bases whose personnel set the rental market well above what the local economy would support. The franc is pegged to the dollar.
djibouti.wifi: Weak in practice despite an unusual asset. Djibouti sits at the landing point of several submarine cables carrying traffic between Europe and Asia, but the domestic market is a state monopoly and retail prices are high relative to speed. Fibre reaches the city at workable speeds and mobile data covers the populated areas. There is very little coworking.
djibouti.nightlife: Limited. Djibouti City has bars and restaurants serving the military and expatriate population, and there is a khat culture that shapes the afternoon and evening across the country in a way visitors notice immediately. Prices are high. The 3 reflects a small capital where the social rhythm is not built around going out.
djibouti.nature: Outstanding, and it is the reason to come. Lac Assal is the lowest point in Africa at 155 metres below sea level and one of the saltiest bodies of water on earth, Lac Abbe's limestone chimneys are among the strangest landscapes anywhere, and the Gulf of Tadjoura gathers whale sharks every winter in internationally significant numbers.
djibouti.safety: Mid. Djibouti City is generally calm and the substantial foreign military presence contributes to a heavy security posture, with petty theft the common problem. The genuine hazards are environmental and regional: the heat is dangerous, and the borders with Eritrea and Somalia require checking current advice. Photography near military and port installations is restricted.
djibouti.food: Decent. Djiboutian food sits between Somali, Afar, Yemeni and French traditions, with skoudehkaris, fah-fah and excellent grilled fish, and the French colonial legacy left proper bread and a genuine restaurant scene in the European Quarter at high prices. The 6 records real variety in a small and expensive market.
djibouti.community: Nonexistent for remote workers. Djibouti's foreign population is French, American, Chinese, Japanese and Italian military, plus shipping and logistics staff, all on posting. There is no nomad scene, no coworking and no framework for one. The 2 reflects a country whose foreign presence is entirely institutional.
djibouti.english: Weak. French and Arabic are the official languages, Somali and Afar are the languages of daily life, and English is limited to the military and shipping sectors. French is close to necessary for anything administrative or commercial. This is the main practical filter for anyone considering a stay here.
djibouti.visa: Reasonable. Djibouti operates an e-visa that most nationalities can apply for online before travel, typically for up to ninety days, with approval returned in a few days. Visa on arrival has been available at times and the policy has shifted, so the e-visa is the reliable route. There is no remote work visa. A yellow fever certificate is required from endemic countries.
djibouti.culture: Moderate. Djibouti's identity is the meeting of Somali and Afar cultures at a strategic chokepoint, and the country has been shaped by its port and by a century of French administration. The Ethio-Djibouti railway, rebuilt in 2017, is the modern version of a line first laid in 1897. The old quarter's Arab and Indian architecture survives in parts.
djibouti.cleanliness: Poor. Waste collection is inconsistent outside the European Quarter, plastic accumulates in the dry watercourses and blows across the desert, and the port areas are heavily industrial. The heat and the absence of rain mean nothing is washed away. Tap water should not be drunk. The 4 is an honest reading.
djibouti.airquality: Weak. Dust is the dominant factor: Djibouti sits in a desert with almost no vegetation and the wind carries particulates constantly, which pushes readings above guidance for much of the year regardless of human activity. Vehicle emissions, generator use and the port's shipping traffic add to it. This is geographic rather than industrial.

saotome.climate: Equatorial, hot and humid all year at around twenty-eight degrees. June to September is the gravana, the main dry season and the practical window, with a shorter dry spell in January and February. The southern half of Sao Tome is among the wettest places in Africa. The islands sit outside any cyclone belt, which is a real advantage.
saotome.cost: Moderate. Budget around $1,100 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $350 to $650. Almost everything is imported and the islands sit a long way off the West African coast, which shows on the shelves. Market food is cheap and the fish is exceptional. The dobra is pegged to the euro through an arrangement with Portugal, removing currency volatility.
saotome.wifi: Weak, and the main practical constraint. The islands are served by a single submarine cable and domestic prices are high relative to speed, with mobile data from CST and Unitel the usual fallback. Power cuts are frequent and generators are standard in anything serious. There is no coworking anywhere in the country.
saotome.nightlife: Minimal. Sao Tome city has a handful of bars and the occasional live music night, and the islands have their own musical traditions in ussua and puita. It is quiet and early by any measure. The 3 reflects a country of two hundred thousand people that receives very few visitors of any kind.
saotome.nature: Outstanding, and the 10 is deserved. Obo National Park covers roughly a third of the country in primary rainforest, Pico Cao Grande is a volcanic plug rising three hundred metres out of the jungle like a needle, and the islands hold around thirty endemic bird species in an area smaller than most national parks. Principe is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve.
saotome.safety: High. Sao Tome and Principe is among the safest countries in Africa, with very low violent crime and a population small enough that anonymity is difficult. Petty theft is uncommon. The genuine hazards are practical: limited medical facilities, poor roads in the south, and sea conditions on the crossing to Principe.
saotome.food: Decent. Sao Tomean cooking is Portuguese-influenced with excellent fish, breadfruit and banana, and calulu as the national dish. The cocoa is world class and several of the old plantation estates now run their own small chocolate operations. Restaurant range is very limited. The 6 records excellent ingredients with almost no infrastructure around them.
saotome.community: Nonexistent for remote workers. The foreign population is Portuguese business and development staff, a handful of hotel operators and the occasional researcher. There is no nomad scene, no coworking and no long-stay framework aimed at visitors. The 2 reflects a country almost entirely off every map that matters here.
saotome.english: Weak. Portuguese is the official language and the language of everything, with Forro and the other creoles spoken at home. English is genuinely rare outside a few hotels. Portuguese is close to necessary here, which is the main practical filter, and Spanish will not substitute for it as reliably as people expect.
saotome.visa: Good. Sao Tome and Principe abolished visa requirements for citizens of the European Union, the United States and several other countries in 2017, granting up to fifteen days visa-free, with a straightforward e-visa for longer stays. That is unusually open for a country this obscure. A yellow fever certificate is required from endemic countries.
saotome.culture: Good. The roca plantation houses, built for the cocoa boom when these islands were the largest producer in the world, stand half-ruined in the forest with communities still living in their outbuildings, and they are the country's most striking heritage. The tchiloli, a Portuguese-derived masked drama performed for centuries, is a living tradition found nowhere else.
saotome.cleanliness: Middling. The city centre is reasonably kept and the islands are too sparsely populated for waste to accumulate in the way it does on the mainland, but collection is limited and there is no recycling. Plastic is visible along the roads. Tap water should not be drunk. The 5 is honest.
saotome.airquality: Excellent. Two small volcanic islands on the equator with enormous forest cover, constant sea breeze, heavy rainfall and two hundred thousand people have essentially nothing to trap. Readings are among the lowest anywhere. Cooking fires and the occasional agricultural burn are the only local sources and neither persists.

maseru.climate: Subtropical highland, governed entirely by altitude. Lesotho is the only country in the world entirely above a thousand metres and Maseru itself sits at 1,600, so summers from December to February are warm with afternoon storms and winters from June to August are cold with frost in the city and real snow in the mountains.
maseru.cost: Cheap. Budget around $800 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $250 to $450. Food is inexpensive and much of it crosses the border from South Africa, where a great many residents shop deliberately since Bloemfontein is around two hours away. The loti is pegged one to one with the rand and rand circulate freely alongside it.
maseru.wifi: Weak to adequate. Fibre has reached parts of Maseru and mobile data from Vodacom Lesotho and Econet is the common fallback, with prices high relative to income. Power comes largely from the Muela hydropower station and is more reliable than in several neighbouring countries, though cuts happen. There is very little coworking.
maseru.nightlife: Limited. Maseru has a handful of bars and hotel venues and the border town character means a fair amount of weekend traffic from South Africa, but the capital is quiet on ordinary evenings. Famo music, the accordion-driven Basotho tradition, is the local sound. The 3 reflects a small capital rather than a dull country.
maseru.nature: Outstanding. Lesotho is the Mountain Kingdom in a literal sense: the Maloti range runs through it, Sehlabathebe National Park is a UNESCO World Heritage site, Maletsunyane Falls drops two hundred metres in a single sheet, and the Sani Pass is one of the great mountain roads in Africa. Basotho pony trekking is the traditional way to see it.
maseru.safety: Weak to mid. Maseru has moderate crime with theft and robbery the common problems, and Lesotho's homicide rate is high by international standards. Walking after dark is generally avoided. Ordinary urban caution and local advice on neighbourhoods are both needed. Mountain travel carries its own real risks from weather and road conditions.
maseru.food: Modest. Basotho cooking centres on papa, a maize porridge, with moroho greens and meat, and the markets are cheap. Maseru's restaurant scene is small and largely South African chains. The 5 records honest limitation rather than anything poor: this is a country where the food is home cooking rather than a restaurant culture.
maseru.community: Nonexistent for remote workers. Maseru's foreign population is development staff, textile industry management and South Africans crossing for business. There is no nomad scene, no coworking and nothing organised for visitors. The 2 reflects a capital that functions as a border town and administrative centre rather than a destination.
maseru.english: Strong. English is an official language alongside Sesotho and is the medium of education, government and business, so every official interaction happens in it. Sesotho is the language of daily life and is spoken by essentially the whole population, which makes Lesotho unusually linguistically unified. There is no barrier for an English speaker.
maseru.visa: Reasonable. Lesotho grants visa-free entry to citizens of most Commonwealth countries, the European Union and the United States for between fourteen and ninety days depending on nationality, with an e-visa available for everyone else. There is no remote work visa. Because the country is entirely surrounded by South Africa, any overland arrival requires South African entry first.
maseru.culture: Good. The Basotho blanket, worn as everyday dress rather than costume, and the conical mokorotlo hat on the national flag are genuine living traditions. Thaba Bosiu, the mountain stronghold where Moshoeshoe I founded the nation in the 1820s, is the national site. Lesotho's sandstone also holds some of the best-preserved dinosaur trackways anywhere.
maseru.cleanliness: Middling. Central Maseru and the better residential areas are reasonably kept, but waste collection is inconsistent, litter is visible on the outskirts and there is little recycling. The mountain areas are largely unspoiled by virtue of being empty. Tap water in Maseru is treated but most residents filter it. The 5 is fair.
maseru.airquality: Mediocre. Winter is the problem: coal and wood heating across the highlands, an ageing vehicle fleet and the city's position in a valley combine to raise particulates from May to August. Dust from unpaved roads adds to it in the dry season. Summer air at this altitude is clean, which the annual average hides.

mbabane.climate: Subtropical highland, and the altitude does the work. Mbabane sits at around 1,150 metres, so summers from October to March are warm rather than hot with afternoon storms, and winters from April to September are dry with cold nights and mist rolling through the hills. The lowveld an hour east is considerably hotter in every season.
mbabane.cost: Cheap. Budget around $900 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $300 to $550. Food is cheap and largely South African, and many residents shop across the border or in Manzini, the larger commercial city half an hour away. The lilangeni is pegged one to one with the South African rand and rand circulate freely.
mbabane.wifi: Weak to adequate. Fibre has reached parts of Mbabane and Manzini and mobile data from Eswatini Mobile and MTN is the common fallback. Power comes largely from South Africa and is affected when that grid is under strain, which it frequently is. There is very little coworking. Connectivity is workable rather than good.
mbabane.nightlife: Limited. Mbabane has a handful of bars and the Ezulwini valley below has hotel venues and a casino, but the capital is small and quiet after dark. The country's social life runs on family, church and the ceremonial calendar rather than on venues. The 3 reflects a small highland capital honestly.
mbabane.nature: Strong. Eswatini packs a great deal into a small area: Mlilwane Wildlife Sanctuary sits in the Ezulwini valley twenty minutes from the capital, Hlane and Mkhaya hold rhino, elephant and big cats an hour east, and Malolotja in the northwest is serious mountain walking country with some of the oldest rock formations on earth.
mbabane.safety: Mid. Eswatini is calmer than South Africa and violent crime against visitors is uncommon, though theft and burglary happen and ordinary urban caution applies. The country has the highest HIV prevalence in the world, which is a public health rather than a visitor safety matter. Pro-democracy protests in 2021 were met with force and the political situation remains tense.
mbabane.food: Modest. Swazi cooking centres on maize meal with stews and greens, and the markets are cheap and good. Mbabane and the Ezulwini valley have a small restaurant scene largely serving visitors and the South African market. The 5 records honest limitation, though the beef and the local produce are both good.
mbabane.community: Nonexistent for remote workers. The foreign population is development staff, South African business and a small number of long-term residents in the Ezulwini valley. There is no nomad scene and no coworking. The 2 reflects a country that receives visitors on their way somewhere else rather than as a destination.
mbabane.english: Strong. English is an official language alongside siSwati and is the medium of education, government and business, so every official interaction happens in it. siSwati is the language of daily life and is spoken by essentially the whole population. There is no practical barrier for an English speaker anywhere in the country.
mbabane.visa: Reasonable. Eswatini grants visa-free entry to citizens of most Commonwealth countries, the European Union and the United States for between thirty and ninety days depending on nationality, with an e-visa available for everyone else. There is no remote work visa. Extensions are applied for at the immigration department. Each border with South Africa has its own hours.
mbabane.culture: Good. Eswatini is one of the last absolute monarchies in the world and its ceremonial calendar is living practice rather than performance: the Umhlanga reed dance in late August brings tens of thousands of young women to the royal residence, and the Incwala kingship ceremony around December is closed to outsiders in its most important parts.
mbabane.cleanliness: Middling to good. Mbabane and the Ezulwini valley are reasonably kept and the country is tidier than most of its neighbours, with waste collection functioning in the main towns. The rural areas are underserved and litter is visible along the main roads. Tap water in Mbabane is treated. The 6 is fair.
mbabane.airquality: Good. Altitude, a small population and limited industry keep readings reasonable for most of the year. The exceptions are seasonal: sugarcane burning in the lowveld between April and November produces visible smoke across the eastern half of the country, and winter wood and coal heating raises particulates in the highlands on still mornings.

saintdenis.climate: Tropical, moderated by altitude and by the trade winds. The coast sits around twenty-five degrees and the interior is considerably cooler, with frost on the Piton des Neiges at over three thousand metres. May to November is the dry, cooler season and the practical window. December to April is the wet season and Reunion is in the Indian Ocean cyclone belt.
saintdenis.cost: Expensive. Budget around $1,800 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $700 to $1,100. Groceries cost noticeably more than mainland France and the price of living here has driven sustained protest movements, including gilets jaunes actions that were more prolonged on Reunion than almost anywhere. The euro is the currency and French banking applies.
saintdenis.wifi: Good. Reunion has European infrastructure: fibre reaches most of the coastal ring at good speeds, mobile coverage is comprehensive and French plans roam here without charge, which matters for anyone based in Europe. Power is reliable. There is a small coworking scene in Saint-Denis and Saint-Pierre. Connectivity is not a constraint anywhere on the island.
saintdenis.nightlife: Modest. Saint-Denis has bars around the centre and Saint-Pierre in the south has the livelier scene, with maloya and sega music both played live. Maloya, the music of the enslaved, was recognised by UNESCO in 2009 and is genuinely current rather than heritage. The 5 reflects a real scene spread across the island.
saintdenis.nature: Outstanding, and the 10 is straightforward. Piton de la Fournaise is one of the most active volcanoes on earth and erupts most years, with the eruptions announced and viewable. The three cirques, collapsed calderas with villages reachable only on foot, hold over a thousand kilometres of marked trail. Forty per cent of the island is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
saintdenis.safety: Reasonable. Reunion has a higher crime rate than mainland France but is calm by regional standards, with theft and vehicle break-ins the common problems. Policing and emergency services are French and function accordingly. The genuine hazards are the sea, where shark attacks led to a swimming ban on much of the west coast that has stood for over a decade, and the mountain weather.
saintdenis.food: Excellent. Reunionese cooking is a genuine Creole fusion of French, African, Indian, Chinese and Malagasy traditions, with rougail saucisse, cari and the local rhum arrange, and the markets are excellent. The island grows its own vanilla, sugar and tropical fruit. The 8 reflects real depth and genuine distinctiveness rather than French cooking transplanted.
saintdenis.community: Weak. The foreign population is mainland French on posting, plus a small tourism sector. There is no nomad scene and very little English-language social infrastructure. The 3 reflects a French department where an outsider without French will find almost nothing to plug into, despite the excellent infrastructure.
saintdenis.english: Weak. French is the language of everything administrative and commercial, with Reunion Creole spoken among locals, and English is limited outside a few tourism businesses. This is the practical filter: Reunion is straightforward for a French speaker and considerably harder for anyone else, despite being easier than most of the Indian Ocean in every other respect.
saintdenis.visa: Reasonable, and excellent for Europeans. Reunion is an overseas department of France and part of the European Union while lying outside Schengen: a Schengen visa does not admit you and time here does not count against a Schengen allowance. European Union citizens have full freedom of movement and can live and work here with no permit at all.
saintdenis.culture: Good. Reunion's Creole culture blends French, Malagasy, Indian, Chinese and East African elements more visibly than most French departments, with Hindu temples, Chinese pagodas and Catholic churches within streets of each other. Maloya, the music of the plantation, was banned until the 1980s and is now UNESCO-recognised. The Grand Raid ultramarathon each October is the island's sporting obsession.
saintdenis.cleanliness: Good. Municipal services function to French standards, the towns are well kept and the national park is properly managed. Saint-Denis has visible decay in parts and waste collection has been disrupted by industrial action. Tap water is treated and safe. The 7 reflects European standards applied to island logistics.
saintdenis.airquality: Good. Trade winds, forest cover and limited industry keep readings within guidance. The recurring exceptions are volcanic: eruptions of Piton de la Fournaise release sulphur dioxide and ash, and sugarcane burning at harvest produces smoke across the coastal plain. Neither persists in the way an industrial source would.

macau.climate: Humid subtropical. October to December is the best window, with warm dry days in the low twenties and clear air. March to May is humid and often foggy. Summer from June to September is hot, humid and the typhoon season, and Macau is exposed; Typhoon Hato in 2017 flooded the city and killed ten people. Winter is mild at around fifteen.
macau.cost: Expensive. Budget around $2,400 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $1,100 to $1,700 in one of the most densely populated places on earth. Food is the compensation: Macau eats extraordinarily well at every price point and a bowl of noodles costs very little. The pataca is pegged to the Hong Kong dollar and both circulate freely.
macau.wifi: Excellent. Fibre throughout, comprehensive 5G and entirely reliable power, all underwritten by an economy that turns over more gaming revenue than anywhere else in the world. There is a small coworking market. Connectivity is as good as anywhere in Asia and better than most, in a territory small enough that nothing is far from anything.
macau.nightlife: Good. The casinos run around the clock and the bars around Taipa Village and the Cotai strip are busy, though Macau's nightlife is heavily shaped by the gaming economy rather than by an independent scene. Hong Kong is an hour away by ferry for anything different. The 6 reflects genuine activity of a particular kind.
macau.nature: Weak, and the 4 is honest. Macau is thirty square kilometres and mostly built, much of it on reclaimed land that did not exist thirty years ago. Coloane, the southern island, keeps a hiking trail, a village and a stretch of black sand beach, and Guia Hill in the centre has a small park. That is essentially all of it.
macau.safety: Very high. Macau has among the lowest violent crime rates in Asia, the casinos are among the most heavily surveilled spaces anywhere, and walking at any hour is unremarkable. Petty theft in crowded areas is the ordinary concern. The genuine hazards are typhoons, which flood the low-lying inner harbour, and the traffic in very narrow streets.
macau.food: Exceptional, and the 9 is earned. Macanese cuisine is recognised as the world's first fusion food, developed over four centuries from Portuguese, Chinese, Malay, Indian and African ingredients, and dishes like minchi, African chicken and the Portuguese egg tart exist nowhere else in this form. Cantonese cooking sits alongside it at every price point.
macau.community: Weak. Macau's foreign population is gaming industry management, Filipino and Vietnamese workers, and a small Portuguese community, none of which forms a scene a remote worker joins. There is limited coworking. The 3 reflects a territory that receives forty million visitors a year and almost no long-stay independent ones.
macau.english: Moderate. Cantonese is the language of daily life, Portuguese remains co-official and appears on every street sign though few people speak it, and Mandarin is increasingly common. English works in the casinos, the hotels and business, and thins quickly outside them. Enough English exists to function comfortably as a visitor.
macau.visa: Good. Macau is a Special Administrative Region of China with its own immigration system entirely separate from the mainland's, and it is generous: most Western nationalities receive between thirty and ninety days visa-free on arrival, with British citizens getting six months. A Chinese visa neither admits you nor is needed. There is no remote work visa.
macau.culture: Exceptional. Four centuries of Portuguese administration on the edge of China produced a UNESCO World Heritage historic centre where baroque churches, Chinese temples and colonial squares sit on the same streets, with the ruins of St Paul's as the emblem. The A-Ma Temple predates the Portuguese arrival. Colonial architecture survives here more completely than anywhere else in East Asia.
macau.cleanliness: High. Macau is well maintained, waste collection is comprehensive, and the gaming revenue funds public services generously for a population of seven hundred thousand. The older inner harbour districts are shabbier than the Cotai strip. Tap water is safe. The 8 reflects a wealthy territory that keeps itself in order.
macau.airquality: Weak. Macau sits in the Pearl River Delta, one of the most industrialised regions on earth, and the regional background is the dominant factor rather than anything the territory produces. Vehicle density in very narrow streets and construction dust add to it. Readings regularly exceed guidance, particularly in winter when the northeast monsoon carries mainland emissions south.

koror.climate: Tropical rainforest, warm and humid all year at around thirty degrees with no real seasonal variation in temperature. November to April is the drier half with the calmest seas and best diving visibility. May to October is wetter. Palau sits at the edge of the western Pacific typhoon belt and is struck far less often than the Philippines or Guam.
koror.cost: Expensive. Budget around $2,100 a month, with a one-bedroom running roughly $800 to $1,300. Groceries carry the full Pacific freight markup and fresh produce is limited. Palau uses the United States dollar, which removes any conversion. Diving and the country's environmental fees together dominate a real budget here rather than accommodation alone.
koror.wifi: Weak to adequate. Connectivity improved with the Belau submarine cable and a second connection added since, and fibre reaches Koror at workable speeds, though prices are high and outages happen. Mobile data covers the populated islands. Power is reliable in Koror and expensive. There is essentially no coworking anywhere in the country.
koror.nightlife: Limited. Koror has a handful of bars serving the diving population and the expatriate community, and the social life revolves around the dive shops and their evening debriefs. It is early and small. The 3 reflects a country of eighteen thousand people organised entirely around getting into the water in the morning.
koror.nature: Outstanding, and the 10 requires no argument. Palau made its entire exclusive economic zone a marine sanctuary in 2015, closing eighty per cent to commercial fishing. The Rock Islands are a UNESCO World Heritage site, Jellyfish Lake holds millions of stingless jellyfish, and Blue Corner and German Channel are regularly called the best dive sites in the world.
koror.safety: Very high. Palau has very low crime and Koror is comfortable at any hour, with a population small enough that anonymity is difficult. Petty theft is uncommon. The genuine hazards are all marine: Blue Corner is a current dive requiring a reef hook, the channels run strongly, and medical evacuation from here is a long and expensive proposition.
koror.food: Decent. Palauan food is fish, taro, cassava and fruit bat soup, and Koror has a restaurant scene reflecting the Japanese, Filipino and American influences on the country, which is broader than the population would suggest. Almost everything else is imported at Pacific prices. The 6 records real variety constrained by supply.
koror.community: Weak. Palau's foreign population is dive professionals, Filipino and Bangladeshi workers, and American administrators under the Compact of Free Association. The diving community is real and easy to join for anyone diving. There is no nomad scene. The 3 reflects a genuine community of a specific kind rather than a general one.
koror.english: Strong. Palauan and English are both official and English is used throughout government, business and education, a legacy of American administration after 1945. Japanese is still spoken by older Palauans. An English speaker will have no practical difficulty anywhere, which makes Palau one of the easiest Pacific nations to operate in.
koror.visa: Good. Palau grants visa-free entry to citizens of most countries for thirty days, extendable in-country, and to United States citizens indefinitely under the Compact of Free Association. Every visitor signs the Palau Pledge, stamped into the passport, a commitment to the environment addressed to the children of Palau and the only such requirement anywhere. Rock Islands permits are separate.
koror.culture: Moderate. Palauan culture is matrilineal, with land and title passing through the female line, and the bai meeting houses with their painted storyboard gables are the traditional architecture. The Second World War is the other layer: the Peleliu battlefield south of Koror is largely as it was left in 1944, with wrecks, caves and equipment in place.
koror.cleanliness: Good. Koror is reasonably kept and the marine park is actively managed and protected, which is the country's central policy commitment. Waste management on small islands is a genuine constraint and the landfill is a known issue. Sunscreen containing certain chemicals is banned to protect the reef. Tap water should be filtered. The 7 is fair.
koror.airquality: Excellent. Small islands in the western Pacific with constant trade winds, no industry and eighteen thousand people leave nothing to trap, and readings sit well within guidance. Diesel generation is the only local source of any consequence. The air here is as clean as almost anywhere on this site.
